en: The section on pediatrics (kaumārabhṛtya), the foundational treatise (sūtrasthāna),
what should be administered as a linctus, and the characteristics of one who has taken a linctus.
What are the defects of excessive licking, and what are the defects of not licking at all?

What is the appearance of that which has been licked only slightly? What are the defects of jaggery (guḍa) in this context, and what diseases arise from licking it? What is the treatment for those [diseases]?
"O Blessed One, you ought to explain all of this to me in accordance with reality:
for it is observed that the pleasure and pain of fools depend upon licking [the honey].
Thus was the illustrious Kaśyapa, honored by the world, questioned.
Out of a desire for the welfare of all beings, he explained the entire question:
whatever food and drink a pregnant woman generally consumes,
such a rasa (nutritive essence) is produced, and it proceeds through her in three ways.
One part [of the food] is for the nourishment of the mother, the second for the nourishment of the fetus,
and the third for the nourishment of the woman's breasts; thus the fetus thrives through such natural dispositions, and from that moment of conception onward, the embodied being [is sustained].
The three pillars are wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha), and these are the constitutions (prakṛti).
Some embodied beings are of a windy constitution, some of a bilious constitution, and some of a phlegmatic constitution;
others have a dual constitution, while still others have all three as their pillars.

O Vṛddhajīvaka, those who are free from disease are called *samasthūṇas*, while those suffering from wind disorders (*vātika*) and the like are always afflicted; these are declared to be the constitutions (*prakṛtis*) of embodied beings.
Relying upon these, the knower of reality should prepare medicinal remedies.
He who knows these things in their true essence is not deluded regarding medicine.
For a living being immediately after birth, a wise physician should prescribe as medicine merely the fruit of *vilanga* mixed with honey and clarified butter.
For a growing infant, one should increase the dose month by month; however,
once it reaches the size of an *āmalaka* fruit, the wise physician should not increase it further,
especially in cases where the mother has no milk or has very little milk.
Those whose wet-nurse has spoiled milk, or who is such that she has recently given birth,

or those sons of a woman who has had a difficult delivery and is afflicted by severe disease; as well as those who are dominated by wind (vātika), those by bile (paittika), and those who are devoid of phlegm (kapha).
Those who are not satisfied by breast milk and weep after drinking it repeatedly; those who remain sleepless at night; those children who eat excessively;
those who have little urine and feces; and those children whose digestive fire is blazing.

Kaśyapa says that one should administer a linctus to children who are free from disease, whose limbs are soft, who have been emaciated, who do not pass feces, or who have not passed it for more than three days. Such children are those to whom it should be given.
Furthermore, a person with weak digestive fire, abdominal distension, excessive sleepiness, and frequent evacuation of feces and urine; one who is small-statured yet has firm limbs;
one born of a virtuous mother; one suffering from indigestion; and one who consumes heavy breast milk—[these are those for whom this is prescribed].
The Suta [rasa] is indicated for those suffering from diseases above the clavicle,
as well as for fever, diarrhea, jaundice, edema, anemia, heart disease, dyspnea, cough, and disorders of the anus, bladder, and abdomen caused by undigested matter (āma).
One should administer it as a linctus in cases of intestinal obstruction, glandular swellings, erysipelas, vomiting, anorexia, and all types of spirit possession; however,
it should not be given daily in cases of alasaka (intestinal stasis) nor when food has already been consumed.
A pregnant woman should avoid foul weather, adverse winds, unwholesome things, and foods and drinks consumed in excessive quantities;
those things which were wholesome for her should be administered to the infant. Therefore, one should employ those very things.
One should not transgress the requirements of place, time, fire, or dosage; furthermore, the procedure for substances intended for licking will now be taught:
having ground [the substance] on a washed stone slab with light water while facing the east.
Having stirred it with honey and ghee, one should have the child lick the gold;
for this consumption of gold increases intelligence, digestive fire, and strength,
and it is life-prolonging, auspicious, meritorious, aphrodisiac, complexion-enhancing, and a destroyer of seizing spirits.
After one month, one becomes highly intelligent and is not overcome by diseases;
after six months, through the consumption of gold, one becomes a retainer of what has been heard (a scholar).
[The herbs used are] Brāhmī, Maṇḍūkaparṇī, Triphalā, Citraka, and Vacā.

One should practice the daily consumption of *śatapuṣpā*, *śatāvarī*, *dantī*, *nāgabalā*, and *trivṛt*— each with honey and ghee— to generate intelligence; likewise, one should use *kalyāṇaka*, *pañcagavya*, and *brāhmī-ghṛta*, which promote mental clarity.

One should consume samaṅgā, triphalā, brāhmī, the two types of bala, and likewise citraka, along with honey and ghee, for the increase of intelligence, longevity, and strength. [Also beneficial are] kuṣṭha, vaṭāṅkura, gaurī, pippalī, triphalā, and vacā.
Ghee cooked with rock salt is an excellent promoter of intelligence.
Ghee prepared with brāhmī, siddhārthaka, kuṣṭha, rock salt, sārivā, vacā, and pippalī is known by the name Abhaya-ghṛta.
Neither Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas, nor Yakṣas, nor Mātṛs shall afflict that boy who consumes this ghee containing khadira,
pṛśniparṇī, syonāka, and rock salt for the sake of strength.
Kevuka is a decoction (kaṣāya) prepared from one-quarter of an āḍhaka of water;
one should cook half a prastha of this with an equal amount of milk and ghee.
This ghee, when combined with honey, is always to be used as a linctus named Saṃvardhana.
One free from disease recovers quickly, moves swiftly, and proceeds rapidly;
even the lame, the mute, the deaf, and the dull-witted are soon joined with their respective functions.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with one āḍhaka of brāhmī juice.

One should pour in one *āḍhaka* each of cow's milk, goat's milk, and ghee, along with one *āḍhaka* each of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *aṃśumatī*, grapes, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *hareṇu*, long pepper (*pippalī*),
long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), *cavya*, *citraka*, and ginger (*nāgara*).
Cinnamon bark, *patra*, *bālaka*, *uśīra*, sandalwood, blue lotus, *padmaka*,
*śatāvarī*, *nāgabalā*, *dantī*, *pāṭhā*, *priyaṅgu*, *devadāru*, the two types of *haridrā*, and the group of drugs known as the *jīvanīya*.
Viḍaṅga, guggulu, and jāti;
Chapter Nineteen: Śakunī, kaṭu, and tikta.
Skanda and Ṣaṣṭhī should be known as the two grahas [afflicting children] in cases of *sānnipātika* (combined) morbidity;
Pūtanā occurs in the sweet (*svādu*) and pungent (*kaṭuka*) types, while the remaining ones arise from the combination of the humors (*saṃsṛṣṭadoṣaja*).
In the sweet type there is excessive feces and urine; in the astringent (*kaṣāya*) type, there is retention of urine and feces.
If the color of the oil is like that of ghee, it brings strength; if like ghee, it brings great wealth;
if smoke-colored, one becomes famous; but if it is pure, one is endowed with all virtues. Therefore, a nurse who is constantly devoted to purification is highly praised.
Milk is purified by the drinking of decoctions, emetics, purgatives, wholesome diets, and by unctuous substances prepared with aphrodisiacs;
likewise by triphalā, trikaṭu, pāṭhā, madhurasā, and vacā.
The powder of *kola*, the bark of the *jambu* tree, and *devadāru*, ground together and mixed with a handful (*prasṛta*) of mustard seeds and combined with honey, should be drunk;
this is said to be the best purifier for vitiated breast milk.
One should provide a wholesome soup made from ginger and *paṭola*, seasoned with powdered *pippalī*; furthermore, food and drink that are light should be administered,
along with *dhātakī* flowers, cardamom, *samaṅgī*, and black pepper.
Jambu bark with madhuka is an excellent purifier of milk;
a tube prepared with jaggery, asafoetida, and nutmeg is highly refined;
and milk, meat broth, and wine are the best for increasing the quantity of milk.
Or milk prepared with aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa) increases the quantity of milk; likewise, the consumption of ghee and oil, enemas that increase milk, as well as pāṭhā,
ginger, devadāru, mūrvā, mustaka, and vatsaka [are beneficial].
Sārivā, ariṣṭa, kaṭukā, kairāta, triphalā, vacā, guḍūcī, madhuka, drākṣā, daśamūla with digestive stimulants (dīpana),
and the rakṣoghna and paṭola groups constitute the group that purifies the breast milk.
A decoction of these [drugs] is prepared according to their availability; when consumed with honey,
it quickly purifies the breast milk even if it has been corrupted for a long time,
and when combined with ghee, it is effective in the remaining two cases where kapha is involved.
"No," say some; for milk originates from phlegm (kapha) due to its location in the seat of phlegm.
[The following are beneficial]: masūra lentils, ṣaṣṭika rice, mung beans, horse gram, śāli rice, ghee, cow's milk, goat's milk, and rock salt taken at the proper time.
The regimen for diet during the period of breast-milk purification has been described; one should avoid heavy foods, fats, meats, and sleeping during the day.
For a woman whose milk dries up either due to purification or by its own nature, [the following should be observed].
A wise person should strive for the production of milk in her by means of sweet foods and drinks, liquids,
and salts, as well as wines excluding *sīdhu*, and vegetables other than white mustard.
After the meat of boar and buffalo, the essence of meats is beneficial;
one should consume garlic and onions, enjoy pleasant sleep,
and avoid anger, travel, fear, grief, and physical exertion.
That which is called *vatsa* increases the milk; likewise,
the bark of trees such as the *vaṭa* and the *kṣīrikā* is boiled to produce a decoction (*kaṣāya*), and with that, [the milk] is boiled again.
One should have her eat boiled *śāli* rice mixed with jaggery, salt, and ghee;
this is the supreme means for generating milk even in women whose breasts are dry.
[Likewise, one may use] *śāli*, *ṣaṣṭika*, *darbha*, *kuśa*, *gundra*, and *utkaṭa*.

The roots of sārivā, vīraṇa, ikṣu, kuśa, and kāśa should be drunk according to the previously described method; this is an excellent means for increasing milk. It is beneficial when the milk is naturally deficient, dried up, or vitiated, provided it has been properly examined.
The child grows happily with unimpeded strength, limbs, vitality, and freedom from disease;
this lack of affliction for both the infant and the nurse is the characteristic of pure milk.
Great diseases arise from the consumption of impure milk.
The pacification of those very [defects] occurs through the consumption of pure milk.
One should understand that grass, insects, husks, awns, flies, the eight types of bodily impurities, hair, wool, bones, and so forth, are metaphorically designated as "diamonds" (vajra).
When the *dhātrī* (uterus) consumes the *vajra* (semen) along with food and drink,
it does not undergo digestion because it is not [composed of] food; yet,
being undigested and moistened, it is stirred up by the wind (*vāyu*).
Combined with the rasa, it enters the milk-carrying vessels; for the channels of women are especially open. Having reached the breasts, it quickly undergoes transformation in the woman.
Hereafter, I shall describe the symptoms of yellow Vajrā: indigestion, restlessness, malaise, causeless distress, loss of appetite,
splitting pain in the joints, body ache, headache, and suppression of sneezing.
There is moistening by *kapha*, fever, thirst, diarrhea, retention of urine, stiffness,
and discharge from the breasts, which are covered with a network of veins;
the breast cannot be touched due to swelling, piercing pain, aching, and burning sensations.
Wise physicians call this "stanakīlaka" (the breast-nail),
for it remains in the limbs like a nail, hard and causing pain;
due to its nature as pitta, it quickly undergoes suppuration and bursting.
Due to *kapha*, it causes suffering for a long time; due to *vāta*, it subsides quickly.
However, if it does not enter the wrong channels (*vimārga*) via the branches or the head, and is not drawn out by the child, it quickly flows out from the breast.
If, due to excessive pressure during milking, the breast suddenly discharges milk mixed with blood like a diamond (vajra),
or if this is directly observed,
the drinking of clarified butter is recommended first for a case of stana-kilaka (breast-nail).

The channels become softened, oleation and other treatments take effect, and even a diamond can be worn down; through proper massage, nourishment, and gargling with the throat, as well as cold affusions, plasters, purgation, and a wholesome diet, [the condition is cured].
One should perform the draining of an undigested [abscess] in consideration of the humors and the body; one should effect its incision like a carbuncle (*vidradhi*),
and that [treatment] is for the sake of another, like a benefactor who enjoys [the fruit] while being cherished and satisfied by others.
A nurse who delights in another's house is released from the pain of her nipples;
seeing breasts that are beautiful, full, well-formed, firm, symmetrical, easy to suckle, and well-rounded, even those with malicious intent look on with envy.
"From that, one incurs diseases; therefore, the application of the medical treatise must be undertaken," so said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
"Having avoided raw meat, however, [the corpse] should be carried at night to a crossroads."
Having heard these truthful words, the wives of the sages were filled with joy and praised the high-souled Kaśyapa, who is honored by the world.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Origin of the Milk Ocean."
The Twentieth Chapter.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the eruption of teeth.
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.

Furthermore, Blessed One, for embodied beings who have been born and are growing, in how many months do the teeth erupt? And once erupted, after what length of time do they become fully formed? And when do those that are formed break through [the gums]? What are their premonitory signs, and what are their complications? What is the treatment for them? What is auspicious and what is inauspicious regarding the eruption of teeth? Why does an increasing part of one's own body lead to a threat to life? How many teeth are there, and how many are these "twice-born" (teeth), and by what measure?

"At what time do they fall, or having fallen, when are they born again? And what is the perfection of the teeth's growth? Then the Blessed Kaśyapa said: "In this world, humans indeed have thirty-two teeth. Among them, eight are born at once and remain as the permanent teeth; the remaining are the secondary teeth (*dvija*). In exactly as many months as the teeth are first shed, in that many days they begin to erupt. And in exactly as many years as they were shed after birth, in those same years they erupt again."

In that [jaw], in the middle, there are two upper teeth known as *rājadanta* (king-teeth); they are pure, therefore a *śrāddha* ceremony is not fit to be performed with fragments from them, for he would thereby be deprived of his ancestors (*apapitṛ*). On both sides of those two are the two *vastu* teeth; the remaining teeth, including the fangs, are called *svarūḍha* and *hānavya*, and likewise those below.

In that regard, they say that for girls, the eruption of teeth is faster and causes less affliction because the teeth have hollow roots and a soft nature; however, for boys, it occurs over a longer period and involves more frequent affliction because the teeth have solid roots and a firm nature. They further explain that the impregnation, formation, emergence, growth, falling out, re-emergence, cessation, stability, decay, shifting, falling, firmness, and weakness of the teeth result from the specific species, the initial impregnation, the inherent nature, the imitation of the mother and father, and the particularity of one's own karma.
The great seers and others likewise [observe] the emergence of the qualities and defects of the growth and decline of the body.

However, for human beings, teeth begin to erupt during the fourth month and subsequent months. In that regard, the birth of teeth with [abnormalities], such as the premature eruption of upper teeth, the late eruption of upper teeth, the sparse eruption of teeth, the deficiency of teeth, the excess of teeth, the jaggedness of teeth, the discoloration of teeth, and the cracking of teeth, is inauspicious.

In that case, for the sake of pacification, one should perform an offering (*iṣṭi*) to Vāyu; for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, some say a *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Prajāpati should be offered. Likewise, in other instances where there is an excess or deficiency of one's own limbs, that terrible [omen] is thus pacified. They describe the emergence of teeth as being of four kinds: *sāmudga*, *saṃvṛta*, *vivṛta*, and *dantasaṃpad*. Among these, *sāmudga* is ruinous due to constant falling out; *saṃvṛta* is inauspicious and most filthy; *vivṛta* is devoid of constancy and struck by loss, causing the teeth to quickly become discolored due to their lack of covering, and bringing about imminent affliction.

In the fourth month, however, the teeth are formed but remain weak, quickly decaying, and prone to many diseases; in the fifth, they become mobile, sensitive, and subject to many ailments; in the sixth, they become irregular, retain impurities, are discolored, and have worm-like cavities; in the seventh, they become double-layered, eruptive, striated, fractured, rough, uneven, and protruding; likewise, in the eighth month, they become endowed with all excellent qualities.

Fullness, evenness, density, whiteness, glossiness, smoothness, clarity, healthiness, a slight upward prominence, and the evenness, redness, glossiness, and broad, firm-rooted nature of the dental junctions—this is called the perfection of the teeth. The sages declare that having deficient, excessive, white, or black teeth, and uneven dental junctions, is unfavorable. By its very nature, the blood that was infused into the embryo within the dental sockets develops gradually in the one born and growing child—Chapter Twenty-one.

One should cook half a *prastha* of ghee with the roots of *rohiṇī* and *svayaṅguptā*, the two types of *haridrā*, and the fruit-juice of *bṛhatī*. While it is being cooked, one should add *apāmārga*. With this prepared medicine, one should rub and massage the ear-lobe (*karṇapālī*) day after day; it will quickly grow, becoming thick and even. Having burnt beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*), resin (*sarjarasa*), barley, *vatsaka*, and castor seeds by the internal-smoke method (*antardhūma*), one should rub the ear-lobe with that ash and massage it; it will quickly grow, becoming thick and even. Regarding this, there are these verses: [The verses follow.]
One who desires happiness in this world and the next should not pierce the ears of consecrated princes, other high-souled men, or anyone else;
for in this matter, a transgression arises from cutting them improperly or piercing them poorly.
In that situation, what will an ignorant surgeon do, being dull-witted and unlearned in the scriptures?
When should one pierce, how should one pierce, where should one pierce, and how should the piercing be performed?
What is beneficial, what is harmful, and what is fatal? In such a case, what will an unwise person achieve?
Therefore, a physician who is highly skilled and discerning should pierce the ear of a child who is joyful and not distracted, for the sake of accomplishing his dharma, pleasure, and wealth;
thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, on the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākaraṇīya).
Chapter Twenty-two: Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on oleation therapy (sneha). 1.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa:

"Affection is said to have two origins and four varieties, arising from both the mobile and the immobile; they say it consists of what is known as clarified butter, marrow, and fat, originating from birds, wild animals, and aquatic creatures."
Oils are derived from *udbhida* sources: sesame, mango, mustard, *bibhītaka*, and *bilva*;
from castor, *atasī*, *śigru*, *madhūka*, radish, and *karañja*.
Among ghee, oil, muscle fat, and marrow, each preceding one is superior to the others.
Among all types of clarified butter, that derived from cow's milk is the foremost because of its processing and its suitability for all constitutions.
When drunk, it subdues pitta and vāyu and does not increase kapha;
it generates strength, digestive fire, and intellect, and it purifies both the semen and the female reproductive tract.

Oil is hot; it destroys phlegm and wind, improves the voice and complexion, stabilizes the body, heals fractures and dislocations, and purifies tissues and wounds. Bone marrow is especially wind-destroying and is considered an aphrodisiac.
For those who are strong and accustomed to such [substances], the wise man should employ sesame oil and ghee in the daily and occasional regimen for stabilizing progeny, strength, and longevity;
there is no other laxative or rejuvenative (rasāyana) superior to that derived from castor and śaṅkhinī.
One should drink oil during the spring and the rainy season, and ghee in the autumn;
or rather, ghee may be drunk by everyone at all times.
Hot water is the desired after-drink for ghee, while broth is preferred for oil.
Kaśyapa states that for all [fermented liquors], the scum of the marrow and the base is best;
hot water is praised as a digestive stimulant that destroys pain, phlegm, wind, thirst, hiccups, anorexia, constipation, and abdominal tumors, and it softens the tissues of wounds.
Water boiled with drugs that destroy those [vitiated] humors, reduced to one-fourth its original volume, is the primary liquid to be drunk;
likewise, oil should be taken as a gargle (kavalagraha), for it dissolves [the morbid matter]. When milk, curd, or honey is prescribed, hot water should not be used; rather, warm water is wholesome.
In cases of bile disorders, hemorrhaging, miscarriage, and burning sensations in the womb (14),

[these should be administered] with boiled rice and thick gruel, meat broth, milk, curd, barley gruel, *kāmbalika*, soups, and broths, as well as through various preparations of drinks, foods, and edibles (15).

The administration of oleation (sneha) is desired through upward and downward purificatory procedures, as well as through enemas, massages, and the application of oil to the eyes, face, and ears; it should also be practiced with retention techniques by those who know what is wholesome.
Those of a pitta and vata constitution should drink oleation at night and during warm weather.
One with a predominance of phlegm (śleṣman), drinking [the water] when it is hot during the day, under a cloudless sun, and while feeling light, suffers from thirst,
fainting, insanity, and so forth; the other [type of person], drinking by the opposite method, suffers from constipation, loss of appetite, joint pain, and swelling.
Regarding the drinking of unctuous substances, there are three types of dosage:
small, medium, and thirdly, large;
the small dose is taken within half a day, and the medium dose within a full day.

Due to the passage of day and night, they age; they are primarily those with blazing digestive fires, the strong, those constantly using unctuous substances, the insane, and those obstructed by their sense of fortitude, feces, and urine.
Those afflicted by gulma, those bitten by snakes, those who are parched,
and those suffering from visarpa should drink this excellent [preparation] for [the cure of] prameha, kuṣṭha, vāta-rakta, and loss of appetite. 20.
They declare that [the *madhyama* breath] is for eczema, boils, specific types of poison,
itching, mild fever, and likewise for those who are moderate in strength and moderate in their eating. (21)
In children, the elderly, those accustomed to comfort, and in cases of chronic diarrhea, fever, or cough—
for these, an empty digestive tract (koṣṭha) does not lead to well-being.
In cases of weak digestion and emaciation, the *kanīyasī* [formulation] should be used;
it draws out the humors (*doṣa*), follows their course,
requires careful administration, and increases strength.
The long [fingers] destroy strength; the medium ones do not destroy strength but cause mutual affection and comfort;
the short ones are comfortable for avoidance and free from deformity. 23.
It is aphrodisiac, strengthening, and sustaining;
a wise physician should administer it after considering the region, age, season, strength, digestive fire, suitability, and the specific signs and dosage. 24
A child whose constitution is dominated by pitta and vāta, or who suffers from diseases of vāta and pitta, becomes emaciated; yet such a child gains complexion, strength, longevity, and blood.
One desiring fatness and sensory faculties [should avoid] poison, weapons, and burns.
Those afflicted by increased fat, phlegm, muscle tissue, and wind, or those whose bodies are tormented by sinus diseases, worms, and disorders of the vital air, should drink ghee at the proper time.
Those who are cruel, possess small internal cavities, and desire diminished vigor should drink oil, but not in cases of severe kuṣṭha, nor when the fat, phlegm, blood, and semen are dried up.
26. saṃśuṣkamedaḥkapharaktaśukrāḥ.
Those who are constantly exposed to wind, heat, travel, and fatigue, those who are parched, those whose bodies are afflicted by wind,
and those desiring fortitude and the nourishment of the bodily tissues should drink muscle fat (vasā). 27.

The physician should administer marrow to those who have a blazing digestive fire, who are voracious eaters, who are constantly requiring oleation, who are capable of enduring affliction, and who suffer from a harsh bowel and disorders of wind (vāta).
One for whom oil becomes wholesome due to habituation,
or those who are constantly engaged in physical exercise, alcohol, anxiety, and sexual intercourse, as well as those with bodies emaciated by fatigue and travel—
such individuals should be oleated by those who know how to assess strength, time, age, digestive fire, and suitability.
One should not apply oil treatments to a pregnant woman, nor to one who has recently given birth, nor to a nursing infant, nor to those who are emaciated,
excessively old, or whose internal digestive fire is impaired by phlegm and bile.

In cases of fainting, aversion to food, exhaustion, excessive thirst, urinary disorders, and when the procedure involves nasal administration, as well as in vomiting, fever, constipation, and phlegm disorders; 30.

One should not administer unctuous substances (sneha) to those suffering from excessive corpulence, coldness, diseases of the throat, or disorders caused by the over-consumption of unctuous substances; for in these cases, their diseases increase greatly after drinking unctuous liquids.
Or, those who have been excessively increased by the drinking of unctuous substances may go toward incurability.
The lack of normal flow in the *vāyu*, dryness, roughness, instability, loss of digestive fire, and hard,
parched stools are the characteristics of one whose body has not been properly lubricated.

They say the signs of one who has been properly oleated are: fortitude, softness of stool, and the increase of intellect, nourishment, digestive fire, and vitality; as well as the timely functioning of the body (34).
Heaviness, stupor, nausea, and flatulence indicate that the stool is undigested.
Loss of appetite, pallor, and lassitude are said to be the signs of excessive unctuousness (atisneha).

One who desires to drink medicated fats should eat food that is liquid, mild, light, warm, seasonal, wholesome, and suited to one's strength, digestive fire, and constitution; thereafter, one should lie down in a secluded place.
One who uses warm water, has conquered his senses, stays in a windless place while lying down, avoids physical exertion, natural urges, and anger, and abstains from sleep after the oily enema,
becomes softened in his bowels within three nights; [and] with seven nights, he is fully lubricated.
O Jīvaka, one with a hard bowel (krūra-koṣṭha) who has undergone the administration of unctuous drinks and purgatives [is the one who will purge];

whereas one with a soft bowel (mṛdu-koṣṭha), having eaten grapes, *pīlu*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), cow's milk, warm water, and fresh wine, and then consuming milk-rice (*pāyasa*), will purge, and no other will.

In those with a soft bowel, the *grahaṇī* is predominantly characterized by pitta and only slightly by other doshas; therefore, those with soft bowels are generally easy to purge, for pitta tends to move downward. [One may recognize this condition] by thirst, fainting, dryness of the mouth, aversion to sound, body ache, and yawning.
One who knows [the signs of] oleation says that [the medicine] is being digested when there is lassitude, weakness of speech, and weakness of the body.
(41) One who doubts whether it has been digested or not should drink only warm water; for that produces purity of eructation and a desire for food. (42)

In oil, there is excessive burning; in ghee, fainting; in muscle fat, nausea; and in marrow, heaviness of these [organs]. Furthermore, when the unctuous substance is undigested, there is thirst, colic, and cutting pain in the rectum for the patient. (43)
When the time for digestion has passed, its vomiting is beneficial.

(44) When the oil is digested, there is purity of eructation, freedom from longing, stability, lightness, absence of despondency, perfection of strength and the faculty of speech, as well as vigor and happiness. (45)

After consuming [the oil], there is an increase in the strength of the ears, eyes, and voice, as well as memory, hair, and vitality; it provides fortitude, nourishment, and the pacification of those diseases [caused by] the oil when drunk.
It destroys disorders of pitta and vāta, strengthens the bladder, thighs, and waist, and is aphrodisiac.
One should know that the *snehāvapīḍa* (oil-press) increases vigor and destroys fatigue.
From the application of oil during a meal, there arises an increase in complexion, voice, intellect, vitality, semen, longevity, fortitude, strength, and digestive fire,
as well as the easy passage of feces, urine, and flatus.
Fever, anemia, skin diseases, edema, thirst, fainting, vomiting, anorexia, excessive moisture, malabsorption syndrome,
impairment of the sense organs, numbness, flatulence, colic, and other such diseases arising from the improper administration of oleation are cured by the application of sudation. 49.
The formulations for emesis and purgation consist of dry foods, fasting, physical exercise, urine, and so forth.
(50) When oleation is administered without regard for dosage and time, or when it lacks the qualities of suitability and proper conduct, it leads to complications;
in such a case, purification therapy is the appropriate remedy. (51)

Those who have an aversion to fats, those who are emaciated, those with a soft bowel, and those who consume fats and wine habitually; as well as those exhausted by travel, staying awake at night, or sexual intercourse—these should not drink clear fat.
For them, the administration of fat should be determined by various foods according to their suitability (*sātmya*). 52.
Having prescribed [the treatment] for one month and so forth, and due to the intensity of the fire of time and age (53),

one should not apply oleation with heavy drinks, food, or meat, nor with jaggery, curd, sesame, vegetables, milk, or decoctions, in cases of prameha, nor for those afflicted by skin diseases, phlegm disorders, or wasting diseases (54).

Those who require oleation (snehya) should be treated with three types of substances— specifically those that pacify their respective defects— prepared with appropriate fats according to the particular disorder, such as triphalā, vyōṣa, salts, and so forth.
Once the body has been oleated, one should first apply sudation (sveda) immediately thereafter.
Immediately after [the patient has been made] properly oleated, sudated, and cleansed, purification therapy (viśodhana) should be performed.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter on Oleation (sneha).
Chapter Twenty-three.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on sudation (sveda).
Thus said the venerable Kaśyapa.
"O Blessed One, how should one apply sudation to a person who has been properly oleated?"
"What substances and what sudation-inducing agents are used for children? What are the signs of insufficient, excessive, and proper sudation in children?

Who should be subjected to sudation and who should not? Thus questioned, Kaśyapa replied: 3–4. "What substances and what sudation-inducing agents are used for children? What are the signs of insufficient, excessive, and proper sudation in children? Who should be subjected to sudation and who should not? Having been asked this, Kaśyapa spoke.
Listen, O Vṛddhajīvaka, to the entire procedure for sudation according to its true principles: how it should be applied to a child and how its application is beneficial.
[It is indicated] by stiffness, pain, rigidity, constipation, distension, and obstruction of speech.
Having observed nausea, loss of appetite, lassitude, intolerance to cold, and trembling— whether arising from vāta and kapha combined or separately— sweating is prescribed.
It is considered unctuous for vāta, dry for kapha, and moderate for both.

Sudation is beneficial in specific stages for those who are emaciated or of middle build, as well as for those with cold-related diseases and especially for children. However, one should not apply sudation to the testicles, the heart, or the eyes, or do so gently.
The joints of the penis and the groins [should be smeared] with the middle [quantity], and the remainder as desired.
Having covered the eyes with the petals of the kumuda, utpala, or padma lotuses,
or else with a smooth cloth, one should apply sweat to the child.
In the treatment of perspiration, one should repeatedly touch the child's heart with pearl necklaces, moonstones, cool water, or lotus stalks; furthermore,
for one who is sweating, it is pleasant to hold camphor powder in the mouth.
A wise person should administer sugar-candy mixed with sour fruits, or grapes with sugar,
for the alleviation of coldness, heaviness, constipation, colic, and similar conditions;
and one should likewise apply sudation when the opposite of those conditions is present.

Despair, fainting, thirst, burning sensations, provocation of pitta, exhaustion, vertigo, loss of voice and bodily strength, and agitation— these are the symptoms of one who has been excessively sweated.
One should apply its treatment in the same manner as that for those suffering from excessive perspiration (vaisarpin).
One should designate that [condition] as difficult to cure when it is accompanied by the sensations of passion, a wound, or poison;

likewise, when there is a lack of functional mobility in the *vāta*, heaviness, stiffness of the limbs, a lack of perspiration despite mild heating, absence of exhaustion, and a derangement of thirst and other such symptoms. (15–16)

In that regard, the physician, further deliberating upon the strength, time, age, and the [nature of the] doshas, as well as the diet, activities, food, and lifestyle, should administer sudation (sveda).
One who delights in sudation experiences comfort and softness of both the disease and the body.
Discharge at the proper time, along with hunger and thirst, are the characteristics of one who has been properly sweated.

Those of a pitta constitution, those suffering from pitta diseases, pregnant women, those with diabetes, those afflicted by hunger, thirst, emaciation, or anger, as well as those with jaundice, abdominal enlargement, or wounds—[should avoid this]. 18–19.

Those afflicted by emaciation, alcohol, or poison; those suffering from excessive digestive fire, cataracts, or discharge from the eyes; those with limbs that are fallen, fractured, or ulcerated; and those with hoarseness of voice, catarrh, throat obstruction, or headache—these should never be subjected to sudation under any circumstances. (20)
In cases of pain in the neck, ears, and head; in heaviness, dyspnea, and cough;
in stiffness of the abdomen, flanks, waist, and back; in urinary disorders, consumption, obstruction of semen, hemiplegia, abdominal distension, and constipation. (21–22)
In cases of emaciation, yawning, lockjaw, stiffness of the neck and head, severe aching of the limbs, trembling, and "itching of the wind" (vātakaṇṭaka),
as well as cold swelling, colic, and gravel-like pain, [these remedies are used] for the wind affecting the hands, feet, and limbs.
Fomentation (sveda) is most beneficial for humans in cases such as cramps, convulsions,
and colic; a physician should administer the eight types of fomentation to children from birth onwards at the appropriate time, in consideration of the disease and the state of the body.
Hand-sudation, poultice, tube-sudation, bed-sudation, mixed-sudation, fomentation, immersion, and eighthly, affusion— these are the eight [types].
One should employ hand-sudation for four months after birth.
Being vigilant and remaining in a windless place, one should gradually increase their perspiration by means of the heat of smokeless fire.
As the softness of the fool recedes in due order and hardness sets in, one should cause that perspiration to increase.
There are also other fools who are delicate and always accustomed to comfort, well-nourished by consuming ghee and milk, and belonging to wealthy, high-souled masters (29).
There are those who are middling among the middling, and those who are poor and suffering.
A wise physician should recognize those [diseases] according to the suitability of the place of conception; for all diseases afflict all men without distinction,
yet a great difference is observed regarding the southern region, diet, and medicine.
Sudation that is excessive or deficient— due to the considerations of place, time, age, dosage, and the relative severity or mildness of all diseases—

may destroy the patient, just as poison destroys a child. Therefore, having carefully observed the place and other factors, as well as the hardness or tenderness [of the body], [one should administer it].
One should apply sudation to an infant for the sake of attaining fame, merit, and success.
When the throat, ears, head, nape of the neck, temples, eyes, chin, and chest are swollen due to excessive secretions (abhiṣyanda), poultice-sudation (pradeha-sveda) is prescribed. 33–34.
A poultice made from the paste of the bark and leaves of *eraṇḍa*, *vṛṣa*, and *śigru*, prepared with cow’s urine, *bukka* salt, and rock salt, should be applied while still warm;
once it has cooled, one should wipe it away and apply another layer.
Having recognized [the condition] many times, one should stop the sweating once perspiration has occurred (verse 36).

An external application (pradeha) made with substances that subdue Vāta and Kapha, such as Śigru, is beneficial; likewise, other applications using dried cow dung (karīṣa) derived from cows, donkeys, horses, sheep, or goats are also recommended. (Verse 37)
One should apply tubular fomentation (nāḍīsveda) using bamboo, muñja grass, reeds, and so forth, as appropriate and according to comfort, in a windless place and covered with cloth;
having spread out warm parched grains, milk-rice, or kṛsarā and similar foods.
One should lay the child comfortably on a bed covered with a cloth after it has been anointed with oil.
They call this "bed-sudation" (*prastara-sveda*), which consists of leaves of *pañcāṅgula*, *uruvūka*, or *arka*—anointed with oil and heated—applied while being turned over repeatedly. (39–40)
With milk-rice, kṛśara, meats, boiled rice, and trikaṭhora, all warm, seasoned with salt and oil, served comfortably on cloth-covered seats;
and with cakes prepared from a mixture of fermenting agent, linseed, curd, and milk.
They desire localized sweating; this is called mixed fomentation (saṅkarasveda).
A poultice (upanāha) made of yeast, linseed, curd, milk, salt, sour substances, unctuous materials, and drugs such as kuṣṭha is highly recommended. 42–43.
Chapter Twenty-four: The treatment [of poisoning] produced by the ass, jackal, cat, leopard, lion, and hyena has been declared.
Therefore, from among the five classes of people, he desired someone who was perfectly pure,
sought after, agile, with all limbs clear and bright, with serene senses, desirous,
with all his limbs sprinkled with pleasant water, anointed, and adorned.
Having performed worship and salutation, he went to a pleasant seat and chamber;
there was a gruel made from old red śāli rice,
prepared with ghee, strained three times, warm, and seasoned with digestive stimulants.
One should eat food that is moderately salty and non-unctuous, and one should consume it in moderation;
during meals that are pleasant to friends, at mid-afternoon, and when the head,
forehead, heart, neck, testicles, eyes, and temples have been well-washed.
If perspiration occurs after drinking the *maṇḍa*, one should declare that [the patient] is properly purified;
by means of daily eructations and wind-discharges that are pure,
and by the absence of complications and the presence of nourishment, one should designate him as being thoroughly cleansed.
When he has slept comfortably and his food has been digested, one should feed him on the second day;
on the third day, one should give him gruel (yavāgū), then a thin porridge (vilepikā) prepared with digestive stimulants and water— dry, warm, and seasoned with rock salt.
In the fourth [day], there should be a gruel of mung beans and well-prepared rice of old red śāli; or for one who is emaciated,
there should be a gruel of dehusked mung beans prepared according to the aforementioned method.
On the fifth day, a thin gruel of mung beans, slightly sour with fruit-acid, should be prepared;
on the sixth and seventh days, a small amount of fat is prescribed,
along with a thin broth of wild animals, prepared without the meat.
On the eighth or ninth day, one should give rice prepared with a small amount of fat;
on the tenth or eleventh day, rice with meat broth (rasakaudana) seasoned with salt and fat, prepared with sour fruits, and served warm, is recommended.
For those [emesis-inducing substances] characterized by Vāta and Kapha, warm water should be used as a post-drink;
thereafter, their association with food is recommended,
as their combination with *maṇḍa* (scum of boiled rice) and other such items is beneficial for the treatment of all diseases.
By transgressing against him out of delusion, one incurs terrible diseases: fever, consumption, jaundice, anemia, ear-diseases, leprosy,
throat ailments, hiccups, diarrhea, swelling, cough, and other such maladies born of infidelity.

For one who has been purified [by purgation] but suffers from colic and diarrhea due to the consumption of cold drinks and food, there may arise swelling, abdominal enlargement, and fever; however, from the use of sour substances, excessive unctuousness, and sleeping during the day,
there comes a desire for food, hunger, clarity of the senses, lightness, stability, and well-being.
Adherence to the regimen for those in good health and the proper digestion of food are the characteristics of well-being.
Despondency, heaviness, drowsiness, salivation, lack of interest, vertigo,
and the impairment of one's healthy lifestyle are the characteristics of indigestion.

Undigested food (āmājīrṇa), indigestion due to burning (vidagdhājīrṇa), that accompanied by phlegm (saśleṣmajīrṇa), and likewise the state where only the essence remains (rasaśeṣājīrṇa)—these are the four types of indigestion; I shall now describe their symptoms.
In the case of āma, there is belching with a smell like smoke and a burning sensation in the chest.
When associated with phlegm (kapha), there is heaviness; when the residue of the taste remains, there is a sense of fluidity in the heart.

Drowsiness, pain, restlessness, exhaustion, thirst, burning sensations, anorexia, vertigo, body ache, fever, and flatulence—all these ailments manifest, though in slight measure, in all [three] types.
When all the most excellent treatments have failed, it is gradually managed as a palliative;
now listen as I describe the treatment for those cases that are curable:
extraction is beneficial for undigested (āma) matter, while one should sleep covered up when it is partially digested (vidagdha).

If there is an excess of phlegm, one should apply sudation; if there is an excess of plasma (rasa), one should employ drying measures. Whatever wholesome diet has been prescribed is recommended for these conditions as well;
however, for long-term medicinal treatment, a lentil gruel with pomegranate is always advised.

A meat broth containing oil, salt, and the three pungents (vyoṣa) should be drunk, or a soup of young radish is beneficial; likewise, boiled śāli rice is suitable. This is the treatment for five people of a king or one equal to a king.
Whether for the wealthy or the poor, one should prepare [medicines] according to their means;
having performed a proper purification that destroys morbid humors, pacifies defects, and brings strength, complexion, and happiness, one attains a long life.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, which is to be prepared;
[now begins] the twenty-fifth chapter.
"Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on sensations (vedanādhyāya).
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Vṛddhajīvaka [approached] Kaśyapa while he was being attended by the sages.
Urged by Dāruvāha, he inquired about the nature of sensation:
"How might a physician come to know, through the signs and their meanings, the various bodily sensations that arise from the cries of children? (3–4)
Thus questioned, the illustrious Kaśyapa, the protector of the world’s elders,
explained to him the sensations arising from the body of a child:
"He shakes his head violently and closes his eyes."
One who groans, suffers from restlessness and insomnia, and has pain in the head;
who touches the ears with both hands and frequently whirls the head around— one should recognize such a person as suffering from earache due to restlessness, anorexia, and lack of sleep.
Excessive salivation, aversion to the breast, distress from restlessness, vomiting of the milk one has drunk, labored breathing through the nose, and oral diseases occur in mouth ailments; likewise,
when there is suppression and the consumption of phlegm, one vomits the breast milk that was drunk.
One should recognize *adhijihvikā* by slight fever, loss of appetite, exhaustion,
affliction with throat pain, salivation, distaste, lassitude, swelling in the cheeks,
and a painful opening of the mouth. (9–10)
In *galagraha*, there is fever, anorexia, salivation, and spitting;
there is itching and swelling in the throat, as well as fever, anorexia, and headache.
One repeatedly bends the limbs, yawns, and coughs frequently.
The child suddenly clings to the nurse, yet does not take much pleasure in the breast;
there is excessive heat and discoloration of the urine, excessive heat on the forehead,
loss of appetite, and coldness of the feet— these are the premonitory symptoms of fever.
Discoloration of the body, restlessness, facial exhaustion, insomnia, and the cessation of flatus— these are the premonitory symptoms of diarrhea.
The child rejects the breast, cries, and lies on his back with his limbs drawn up.

Stiffness of the abdomen, coldness, and perspiration on the face occur in one suffering from colic (śūla). For one who frequently belches without cause while overcome by drowsiness and yawning, a covering (chadiḥ) arises.
He groans with his chest and a very hot breath arises within him;
suddenly, wind-like eructations occur, and in this emaciated state, hiccups set in.
He drinks excessively at the breast yet remains unquenched by thirst and weeps.
With dry lips and palate, seeking water, weak and afflicted by thirst; with wide and fixed eyes, suffering from joint-pains, aversion to food, and exhaustion;
with suppressed urine, flatus, and feces—the infant suffers from the pain of abdominal distension (ānāha). 18–19.
Sudden, uncontrollable laughter indicates epilepsy (apasmāra);
one should recognize insanity (unmāda) by means of incoherent speech, excessive restlessness, and mental derangement. 20.
Horripilation, trembling of the limbs, and pain at the time of urination [are also signs].
In *mūtrakṛcchra* (dysuria), the two lips of the urethra touch the bladder when touched by the hand.
In *prameha* (urinary disorders), there is heaviness, obstruction, and sudden stiffness, followed by the discharge of urine; the urine is white, thick, and attractive to flies.

In the case of a person who is emaciated, one should observe the binding of the feces or their passage with blood, as well as pressure on the anus, itching, and pricking pain in the hemorrhoids (23). Furthermore, there is the presence of gravel-like particles in the urine, excessive urination, and pain at the time of voiding.
One who weeps incessantly and has an emaciated body should be told to have the disease of urinary calculi (aśmarī).
The appearance of red circular patches, thirst, burning sensation, fever, restlessness,
a desire to lie on sweet and cold things, and the initial pain of spreading erysipelas (visarpa) are its premonitory symptoms.
In *visūcikā*, the limbs burn, throb, and break; the child groans excessively, and pain increases in the heart.
He cannot hold up his head, suffers from splitting headaches, and yawns repeatedly. (26)

If the infant does not suckle excessively and even vomits what has been swallowed, one should recognize this as *alasaka* (intestinal obstruction) in the child due to depression, flatulence, and loss of appetite.
When the symptoms and remedies for *visūcikā* (cholera-like gastroenteritis) and *alasaka* are difficult to distinguish, [the following applies]. 27–28.
In eye disease, there is agitation of vision, pricking pain, swelling, colic, and redness;
when asleep, the eyes feel as if they are being smeared. The patient rubs his limbs against the bed, weeps, and desires massage. (29)
One should know that the dry stage (śuṣkakaṇḍū) is afflicted by itching; thereafter, the moist stage (ārdra) sets in.
When massaged, it feels pleasant, yet as it is repeatedly massaged, it becomes swollen; once swollen, it exudes a discharge.
In the moist stage, it is accompanied by aching pain and a burning sensation, like a field being plowed.
Stiffness, loss of appetite, sleepiness, paleness of the body, and restlessness;
she constantly hates her husband, her food, her bed, and even her nurse (32).
Though unanointed, she appears as if anointed, and though anointed, she has the appearance of one who is not.
A physician should recognize these as the signs of impending *āma* (undigested morbid matter):
swelling all around the navel, whiteness of the eyes, nails, and face, loss of digestive fire (*agnisāda*), and swelling of the eye-sockets in cases of *pāṇḍuroga*. 33–34.
One afflicted by jaundice has yellow eyes, nails, face, feces, and urine;
he is devoid of energy in both [body and mind], his digestive fire is extinguished, and he craves blood.
He suffers from fainting, insomnia, vomiting, aversion to the *dhātrī* fruit, restlessness, and dizziness. (35)
One should recognize "excessive intoxication" (madātyaya) in a child by fear, agitation, and thirst.
He breathes repeatedly through his mouth after drinking again and again from the breast; moreover, his nostrils and forehead become parched. (36–37)

In chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), the channels are frequently affected; one sneezes and coughs, and likewise, in chest affliction (uroghāta), there is excessive groaning from the chest. When a child, though devoted to healthy habits, does not sleep at night, [it indicates a disorder].
And when one's limbs are covered with red spots, one should know that person to be afflicted by *jantuka* and similar parasites.
When the nurse Lalitā is happy and enjoying all pleasures, yet repeatedly sees a bad dream, milk flows forth from her breast of her own accord. 39–40.
A fool forgets her, and she may even fall from his lap;

he enters into association with the wicked, as well as sharing meals with them—those who have lost their children, those who are promiscuous, and those who cannot endure the prosperity of others. (41)
He beholds and even practices terrible, inauspicious deeds;
he pursues contrary courses and summons death for the child.
While the infant sleeps, birds of dreadful omen settle upon him.
A cat leaps over it, smells the smoke of another,
observes the offering made for crossing over, and even leaps over [the fire];
there is a foul odor from the body and mouth, and filth appears at the tip of the nose.
The mother and son resort to garlands that are unpleasant and blood-red;
they climb upon or frequent ashes, charcoal, husks, and the like; he weeps and trembles without cause, and there is a reversal of his shadow and character. 45–46.

One who eats little will have excessive excrement and urine, while in the opposite case, one will have no excrement or urine; these are the signs of impending [diseases] and the afflictions caused by the planets.
One who cannot hold up his head and whose limbs tremble is weak.
Overwhelmed by labored breathing and abdominal distension, he appears as if he were inside [a vessel];
though entertained in many ways, he finds no pleasure in diversion; afflicted by thirst, exhaustion, and sleeplessness, he coos like a pigeon. (48–49)

Upon seeing the symptoms of one afflicted by fever, vomiting, and diarrhea, the physician should know that the entire condition is difficult and will not be cured. Thus have these various pains arising in the bodies of children been described.

Having observed the respective treatments for those diseases arising mostly from the [three] humors, as set forth by the great seer Kaśyapa in due order and without contradiction, one should proceed with the therapeutic measures according to the specific disorder in the section on therapeutics (Cikitsitasthāna).
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa. Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter on Knowledge.
Chapter Twenty-six.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the perfection of medical treatment (Cikitsā-saṃpad).

Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa. We shall explain the means by which the perfection of medical treatment is achieved. Indeed, there are four pillars upon which medical treatment rests. When these are endowed with their respective qualities, a curable disease does not persist beyond control. They are as follows: the physician, the medicine, the patient, and the attendant.

In this regard, the physician is one who possesses an excellent lineage (*sutīrtha*), has attained knowledge through the traditional scriptures (*ārṣajñāna*) by means of right method, is possessed of discernment (*vijñānavat*), has observed medical practice many times, is proficient in proven formulations (*siddhayoga*), is skillful, upright, pure, and modest in appearance; he is a kinsman to all beings, successful, a perceiver of the goals of *dharma* and *artha*, devoted to truth, compassion, charity, and honesty; he is a worshiper and a visitor of gods, the twice-born, teachers, and perfected ones (*siddhas*); he is skilled in progressive understanding, serves his gurus and elders, is intent on right method, and is free from fear, greed, delusion, anger, falsehood, malice, intoxication, and lewdness; and he is pleasant-faced and free from vices. (4)

In that regard, the excellence of the medicine (*bhaiṣajya-saṃpad*) consists of: being grown in good soil, harvested at the proper time, produced at the proper time, unaltered by fire, water, insects, excrement, urine, aging, and so forth, suitable for the specific disease, and prepared in due order according to the prescribed rules.

In that regard, the excellence of the patient (*ātura-saṃpad*) consists of: having a curable disease; firmness of mind, strength, intellect, body, sense organs, fortitude, and vitality; a correct description of the etiology (*nidāna*), premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*), the disease itself (*ātaṅka*), complications (*upadrava*), distress (*yātra*), therapeutic suitability (*upaśaya*), and unsuitability (*anupaśaya*); and faith in the nurse, the gods, the twice-born, teachers, physicians, medicines, and friends.
Joy, faith, preeminence in discipline, acting according to what has been instructed, and self-control.

(6) Therein, the excellence of the attendants consists of: the ripening of the passions, health, strength, devotion to the master, knowledge of service, dexterity, purity, swiftness in action, skill in all tasks, lack of cruelty, not having small children, freedom from duplicity, self-restraint, having conquered anger and the like, and forbearance. (7)

Regarding this, there are these verses: They consider the fourth quarter of this [teaching] to be the most excellent, for it is by means of its meaning that the three virtuous quarters here are desired. (8)
"No," said Prajāpati; "the root of medical treatment is the physician.
For the three goals of life depend upon the physician, and success rests with the physician.
He joins [the patient], he applies [therapies], and he instructs, by means of the eye of knowledge."
Therefore, a physician who is endowed with both knowledge and discernment is the most excellent.
O Jīvaka, when there is a perfection of these four factors, then the physician becomes a vessel for dharma, wealth, and fame.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Perfection of Medical Treatment.
Chapter Twenty-Seven.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on diseases;
thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.

Bhārgava Pramati maintains that there is one disease, based on the commonality of causing pain; Vāryovida holds that there are two diseases, the innate (*nija*) and the exogenous (*āgantu*); Kāṅkāyana says there are three diseases: curable, palliable, and incurable; Kṛṣṇa Bhāradvāja asserts there are four diseases: exogenous, and those arising from *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*; Dāruvāha, the royal sage, claims there are five diseases: exogenous, and those arising from *vāta*, *pitta*, *kapha*, and the three *doṣas* combined; the six sages maintain there are six diseases because food and drink consist of six tastes; Hiraṇyākṣa says there are seven diseases: those arising from each of the *doṣas* individually, from pairs of them, and from all three together; [others] say there are eight diseases: [those arising from] *vāta* and the others individually, in pairs, and in groups of three.

"Exogenous causes" refers to [factors] such as those of Vaideha and Nimi; "innumerable" refers to the distinctions among defects that are equal, inferior, or superior—so says Vriddhajīvaka. Having observed this instability, the Blessed Kaśyapa said:
"Indeed, there are only two types of diseases: endogenous (nija) and exogenous (āgantu); these two are further expanded into many varieties.
This is according to the meaning of their causes, primary nature, substratum, classification, and locus.
Diseases are to be known as innumerable due to the vastness of their treatments. Their two bases are the body and the mind alone;
for mental diseases, one should apply the same therapeutic measures as for physical ones.
The disharmony among the pillars of the elements is that suffering designated as disease;
however, the harmony among the pillars of the elements is happiness, and that is primordial nature (prakṛti).
Otherwise, how could one's body and lifespan increase unhindered?
Medicine is thus declared for the purpose of pacifying disorders;
the nature of diseases is twofold, arising from either innate or external causes,
including [afflictions caused by] nails, teeth, fire, water, killing, imprisonment, and presiding deities.
The natural causes of wind and so forth that come from curses or malevolent spells are now explained;
hear from me the locations of wind, bile, and phlegm within the body, as well as their general locations and functions, even though they pervade the entire body. (9)

Below the navel, the bones and marrow are declared to be the seat of Vāta. The stomach, sweat, blood along with lymph, fat, the head, the chest, the neck, the joints, and the arms are the seats of Kapha.
The seat of Pitta is the stomach, sweat, and blood along with lymph.
Fat, the head, the chest, the neck, the joints, and the arms are the seats of Kapha. (10–11)
The heart is specifically said to be the seat of phlegm (śleṣman),

while the stomach and the large intestine are specifically the seats of bile (pitta) and wind (vāta) respectively. An exogenous disorder (āgantu) first afflicts [the heart] and subsequently reaches the [internal] humors (doṣas).
The innate [disease] is first accumulated and later, having increased, it causes affliction.
Therefore, for adventitious diseases, treatment like that for innate ones is desired; for innate diseases, purification is beneficial after observing the premonitory symptoms.
When phlegm adheres to the heart, it becomes dark-brown, reddish, or yellow;
then the vital essence (*ojas*) increases in the person, and upon its increase, [the person] thrives, while in its depletion, [the person] wastes away.
Sweet, unctuous, cold, light, and wholesome [foods] are beneficial in this state. (15)
They say these are the increasers of *ojas*; therefore, one should cause children to consume them as well.

Growth [of *ojas*] is the cause of complexion, strength, vitality, intellect, longevity, and happiness; indeed, the equilibrium of *vāta* and the other humors [is health], while their imbalance leads to disease.
Among those immeasurable transformations, we shall describe the diseases most clearly manifested by their specific characteristics according to their gross categories:
there are eighty diseases caused by vāta and forty caused by pitta.
Twenty diseases arising from *kapha* have been described; now learn from me the diseases of *vāta*. (19) They are:

drooping of the foot (*pādabhraṃśa*), pain in the foot (*pādaśūla*), cracking of the nails (*nakhabheda*), *vipādikā*, numbness of the foot (*pādasupti*), *vātakhuḍa*, *vātagulpha*, and *anilagraha*. (20)
Gṛdhrasī, piṇḍikodveṣṭa, separation and cracking of the knees, ūrustambha, ūrusāda, lameness (pāṅgulya), and vātakaṇṭaka; 21.
prolapse of the rectum (gudabhraṃśa), pain in the rectum (gudārti), and likewise vṛṣaṇākṣepaka.
Erection, pain in the hips, distension of the groins, and dysuria; 22.
upward movement of wind (udāvarta), hunchback, dwarfism, stiffness of the sacrum, stiffness of the back, pain in the flanks, abdominal cramps, and cardiac distress; 23.
Delusion of the heart, piercing pain in the chest, friction and obstruction of the chest,
stiffness of the neck, wasting of the arms, hoarseness of the throat, lockjaw, trembling of the teeth, distortion of the lips, muteness, and likewise paralysis of speech; 24.
Astringent taste in the mouth, dryness of the mouth, loss of the sense of smell, lack of awareness of odors (25), deafness,
hearing loud sounds [where none exist], earache, and absence of sound; constriction of the eyelids, heaviness, darkness before the eyes, and pain in the eyes (26).
Paralysis, paralysis of the eyebrows, splitting of the temples, headache, cracking of the scalp, and ardita (facial paralysis) occur in the Daṇḍakākṣa [type].
Hemiplegia, exhaustion, vertigo, and yawning [occur in the Pakṣavadha type]. 27.
Incoherent speech, trembling, exhaustion, roughness, loss of sleep,
a dusky-reddish complexion, instability, as well as hiccup, labored breathing, despondency, sterility, and impotence. (28–29)
Coryza and earache are primarily of the nature of Vāyu;
regarding these and other [diseases] not mentioned here, the specific nature and the function of Vāyu are now described: coldness, dryness, lightness, mobility, and movement.
Clarity, redness, roughness, numbness, contraction, and a sense of distaste;
31. piercing pain like a spear, astringency, hollowness, harshness, and trembling; burning sensation and exhilaration; emaciation, circular swelling, expansion, discharge, and splitting; 32.
Swelling, biting, breaking pain, and emaciation are the actions of Vāta;
in that case, sweet, sour, hot, and salty treatments are prescribed.
Burning, scorching, vertigo, feverish heat, vomiting, and sensations of smoke and acidity [are the signs of Pitta].
Internal burning, fever, excessive heat, profuse sweating, a burning sensation in the limbs (34),
a burning sensation in the skin, moisture of the blood, moisture of the flesh, wasting of the limbs, suppuration of the flesh, sloughing of the skin, and circular eruptions of red vesicles (35).

Hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta), skin eruptions (koṭha), armpit rashes, yellowish or bluish discoloration, jaundice, a bitter taste in the mouth, a blood-like odor from the mouth, lack of satiety, foul breath, the sensation of insects crawling on the body, darkness before the eyes, and thirst. 36.
Inflammation of the penis, anus, eyes, and mouth, along with yellow urine and feces—these (verse 37) are the primary afflictions of pitta. Its own nature will now be described:
lightness, sharpness, and heat; its colors are all except white and reddish (verse 38).

One should recognize a person afflicted by pitta disorders by foul odor, pungency, acidity, slight unctuousness, and symptoms such as burning, heat, suppuration, perspiration, itching, eruptions, and discharge; this is the clinical action [of pitta], and its treatment follows accordingly. 39.
Astringent, bitter, and sweet tastes possess the qualities of unctuousness, laxation, and desiccation.
(40) Stiffness, heaviness of the body, sleep, drowsiness, over-satiety, sweetness in the mouth, salivation, expectoration of phlegm, eructation, and loss of strength [are their effects]. (41)
Nausea, excessive accumulation of waste products, a coating on the vessels and throat, undigested matter (āma), goiter, loss of digestive fire, urticaria,
and a whitish discoloration of the limbs as well as of the urine and feces.
The primary [manifestations] among the innumerable diseases born of *kapha* have been proclaimed;

unctuousness, coldness, heaviness, whiteness, sweetness, and smoothness are the characteristics of *kapha*. Furthermore, its functions at the time of disease onset are said to be as follows: 44. [Smoothness and so forth.]
Excessive unctuousness and the like, delayed action, constriction, accumulation, numbness, and constipation—
these are the signs. In such cases, the wise physician should treat with astringent,
pungent, and bitter substances that are dry and hot, while carefully considering the proper dosage and the time.
In these cases, the application of oleation and sudation, as well as the five therapeutic procedures, are indicated;
however, among all those that subdue Vata, an oil enema (anuvāsana) is the best.
For those that subdue Pitta, purgation is best, and for those that destroy Kapha, emesis is best.
I shall now declare those diseases for whose sake this section on therapeutics has been proclaimed; for it is not concluded here. These are:
major diseases (mahāgada), then renunciation (saṃnyāsa), and thigh-stiffness (ūrustambha), each individually. 48–49.

Fever, ulcers, scrofula, sciatica, jaundice, gout, hemorrhoids, and likewise distension— these are the two types of diseases (acute and chronic). Vata-blood disorders, leucoderma, and swelling are proclaimed to be of three types.
Diseases of the stomach, disorders of the eyes, diseases of the ears, and ailments of the mouth; epilepsy, catarrh, and the intoxicants that cause wasting—
these fourfold causes have been specified, as well as fainting and various forms of impotence.
Thirst, vomiting, dyspnea, cough, abdominal tumors (gulma),
splenic disorders, loss of appetite, pain, hiccups, insanity, diseases of the head, heart diseases, and those known as jaundice—
these five types have been described; now hear from me about the six types as well.
One should recognize seventy-seven diseases: upward-moving disorders (udāvarta), diarrhea (atīsāra), along with erysipelas (visarpa) and other ailments;

the skin eruptions (piḍaka) of those suffering from urinary disorders (mehin), leprosy (kuṣṭha), the seven types of seminal defects (śukradoṣa), the seven types of milk defects (payodoṣa), urinary obstructions (mūtrāghāta), and abdominal enlargements (udara). 54–55.
They say there are eight of these [types of] *grahas*, while ten are proclaimed;
they know there are twenty for disorders of the female reproductive tract (*yonivyāpad*), and twenty for worms and urinary disorders (*kṛmimeha*).
These have been briefly stated as the causes for the section on therapeutics (*cikitsāsthāna*).

The other disease that arises due to the cause of a prior manifestation is called a complication (*upadrava*), just as diarrhea is in the case of fever; some authorities declare that the treatment for these [complications] is the same as their primary origin.
Some say [this applies] to complications; Kaśyapa says "no," it was previously stated that one should employ food, drink,
and medicine appropriate for both [the disease and its complications] for the sake of pacification, for in this way neither of the two increases.
Or, when a wise physician perceives a disease to be particularly severe through its specific characteristics,
that excellent doctor, desiring success, should treat that very disease first.
For whatever is the cause of bile-related diseases is indeed the same for those born of blood.
Blood, when provoked, afflicts a person through many manifestations:
discoloration, fever, diseases of the head and eyes, debility, foul odor, and the sensation of entering darkness;
as well as erysipelas, abscesses, inflammation of the uvula, abdominal tumors, hematuria, menorrhagia, and excessive sleepiness. (62–63)
Dimness of the digestive fire,
putrefaction of the channels, loss of voice, excessive sweating, intoxication, wind disorders, blood disorders, thirst, anorexia, skin diseases, and scabies.
For itching eruptions accompanied by urticaria, pustules with itching,
and various other unmentioned diseases, emetic therapy is beneficial at the very outset.
In this context,
they say that for one suffering from *vaisarpapaccha* (erysipelas), bloodletting and drying therapy (*viśoṣaṇa*) are effective;
however, drying therapy is certainly not beneficial for a child.

Neither excessive purification nor bloodletting should be performed; rather, treatment for this condition consists of food, medicinal pastes, and affusions that are unctuous, very cold, sweet, and non-acrid. 66
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, on Diseases.
Chapter Twenty-eight.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on characteristics (lakṣaṇādhyāya).
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
"Blessed One, by what characteristics do children become long-lived?"
By what means does a physician recognize those who are happy, those who are suffering, and those whose life-span has ended?
How many types of beings are there among mortals, and what is the characteristic of beings?
Let that which is praiseworthy and that which is censurable in the body be explained.
Having heard the words regarding the five types of rebirth, Kaśyapa spoke concerning the complete knowledge of the characteristics of beings, whether they be censured or honored.

In this regard, O Jīvaka the Elder, the nails of princes are glossy, smooth, and copper-colored for the sake of sovereignty; they are thick for teachers; and they are marked with lines and long for those who possess longevity. Those shaped like a depressed pearl or a husk belong to the poor; rough ones belong to those destined for suffering; flower-like ones belong to plunderers; white and circular ones belong to those lacking longevity; cracked ones belong to those who are not independent; discolored ones belong to those in misfortune; elevated and thick-tipped ones belong to those with little [to give]; and broad nails indicate a middling state, while thick ones [indicate] greatness.

White and uneven feet cause one to wander as a mendicant. Those with broad, well-established feet marked with upward lines are long-lived, wealthy, and powerful. Kings have feet marked with auspicious signs such as the svastika, plow, lotus, conch, wheel, horse, elephant, chariot, and weapons; those with copper-colored, glossy feet are fortunate; those with high-arched feet have moderate wealth and lifespan; those with white feet are poor; those without lines are servants of others; those with many lines are sickly; and those with well-rounded, smooth heels are endowed with all virtues.

Those with deficient heels have short lives; those who are flat-footed are deprived of offspring; and those with flattened feet are adulterers. Those with long toes, nails, and feet are long-lived, while those with short ones are short-lived. Those with thick toes are fortunate; those with hidden joints are possessors of enjoyments; those with thick joints become teachers; and those with hairy toes are without wealth. A heel that is rough, harsh, thin, uneven, cracked, or dirty is not praised. A raised, hairless, and smooth upper part of the foot is commended, whereas one that is uneven and contrary to these qualities belongs to thieves.

The ankles are praised when they are hidden, small, and have few hairs or veins; when prominent and broad, they lead to the loss of wealth and great suffering. A slender lower leg (prajaṅghā) is praised, whereas a thick one causes the destruction of husband, sons, wealth, and happiness, and leads to thievery. The shanks (jaṅghe) are praised when they are not protruding, without visible veins, and hairless; conversely, those that are dry, with thick veins, or hairy bring widowhood to women. The knees are auspicious when hidden. The thighs are praised when well-fleshed, with hidden veins, and smooth.

The buttocks (*sphicau*) are praised when they are well-formed, hanging down, free from sores, hairless, and symmetrical; however, if they are dry, women without offspring will have them; if they hang down excessively, they portend the loss of one's husband; if they are large, they indicate promiscuity; and if they are small, they belong to women of virtuous character. The hollows of the hips (*kukundarau*) are praised when they are deep, hairless, well-defined, and symmetrical; if they are hairy, they lead to the life of a wandering ascetic (*pravrājikā*); if they curl to the right, they bring fortune; if they are broad, they belong to those with long lives; and if they are joined together, they belong to those without long lives. Some say that the loins (*jaghana*) are praised when they are equal in size to the chest.

The chest of males is very broad, while the hips of females are so; however, neither is suitable for the waist. The testicles of a fair-skinned man are long and large, those of a dark-skinned man are black, those of a red-skinned man are fair, and those of a dark-complexioned man are reddish; they are considered hairy in the middle and fleshy, which is praised. The opposite is censured, as it causes misfortune, obesity, and loss of progeny. Those that are very small lead to a short life and suffering, according to some; whereas those shaped like a bull, a donkey, a horse, a goat, or a sheep should be known to belong to those who are fortunate and long-lived.

The male organ (*prajanana*) is praised when it is soft, long, erect, large, with a glans (*maṇi*) of copper-like hue, a great sheath (*mahākośa*), and a great urethral stream (*mahāsrotas*). That which is thin, short, pendulous, uncovered, pale or dark-brown, turned to the left, or otherwise deformed is not praised. Urine that is unobstructed, not thin, copious, and discharged in a straight stream is praised. The opposite is unfavorable: urine that is foul-smelling, painful, excessively hot, discolored, appearing at an improper time without cause, or silent; furthermore, the spraying of urine by young girls, or both these conditions, causes childlessness.

The vulva shaped like a cart brings the attainment of offspring; when plump, it brings good fortune; when pendulous, it leads to the death of children; when circular, it leads to unchastity; when raised up, it leads to childlessness; when needle-mouthed, it leads to misfortune; when excessively open, closed, or dry, or when pendulous, uneven, or lacking the characteristic marks, it leads to the acquisition of suffering; when thick in the middle, it leads to the birth of daughters; when elevated, beautiful, fleshy, and possessing the characteristic marks, it leads to the birth of sons and is auspicious; when excessively hairy, it causes widowhood; and when devoid of characteristic marks, it leads to infamy, as does one that has moles or is covered in fat.

A line of hair (*lomarājī*) that has reached the middle on both sides [of the belly] is praised for leading to renunciation (*pravrajyā*), provided it is not too thick; if it is excessively thick, it leads to widowhood. If the hair is excessively thick and dense, it leads to unchastity (*pauṃścalya*). Hair growing downwards leads to misfortune (*daurbhāgya*). A navel that is overly protruding leads to madness, while one that is moderately deep is praised. Both sides of the belly (*kukṣī*) are praised when they are elevated and hairy, leading to renunciation. If they are veiny (*sirāla*), they lead to poor food; if depressed, to poverty; if level, to moderation. If the right side is elevated, it leads to the birth of a son; if the left side is elevated, the opposite occurs.

A slightly elevated abdomen that is neither flaccid nor rigid, and not overly large, is praised. A dry and elevated belly leads to poverty; one that is broad and uneven leads to a life of irregular conduct and enjoyment; and one that is extremely parched indicates childlessness. In women, a region below the navel that is fleshy, lacking a crest (asira), not very large, and smooth leads to a short life. A region above the navel that is smooth leads to a short life. One with a single fold (ekavalika) brings fortune; two folds lead to the attainment of intelligence; three folds bring good fortune; and four folds lead to progeny and longevity.

A belly that has many folds, is heavy, and short in length leads to misfortune and a short life. A navel that is deep, clockwise, circular, elevated, and free from hair or veins is praised.
