One shaped like a pit, not protruding, brings both happiness and suffering; one that is uneven and protruding leads to a short life; one that is small in form results in childlessness; one situated too far to the side causes exile; and one that is large, deep, and elevated leads to sovereignty. The anus is explained by the same criteria as the navel. The sides of the abdomen that are circular, fleshy, smooth, and hairless are praised; those with hair and veins cause exile.

A back that is level, broad at the top, hairless, free of moles, and praised as being sunken in the middle indicates a long life; one that is bent indicates a share of suffering; one that is contracted indicates a short life; and one that is hairy indicates a lack of loving-kindness and few offspring.

One with hairy shoulders is a merchant living by carrying loads; one with hairy shoulders is a gambler or a performer. One with thin shoulders is poor; both of these types may sometimes be long-lived or even renounce the world. A farmer with smooth shoulders is prosperous; one with thick, fleshy shoulders is wealthy; one with hard shoulders is a hero; one with loose, drooping shoulders is unattached; and a man with high-set shoulders is praised. A girl with sunken shoulders is ill-fated; if the opposite is true, her qualities are diminished. High, broad, and fleshy armpits with auspicious marks are praised; the opposite is inauspicious, as is excessive hairiness in women.

Likewise, arms that are well-proportioned in their development, with hidden wrists, long enough to reach the knees, and free of visible veins, are praised for those who possess longevity; those with fine hair are for those with offspring; those without veins are for those without offspring; those with veins running crosswise belong to those who live in hardship; and those with moles belong to those who wander as ascetics. Moles on the wrists portend strife. Thick wrists are praised in men, while thin ones are for women.

For both [the king and the queen], three continuous rows of barley are praised: the first for grain, the second for preeminence, and the third for the longevity of progeny. If all are unbroken, glossy, clearly defined, and deeply incised, they lead to sovereignty. Four such lines belong to a royal seer; five or six to one who has a hundred sons; and seven to the divine hosts.
Even a single unbroken, clear line conduces to happiness.

Among women, hair that is excessively long or excessively short is censured. A scalp that is glossy, reddish, stainless, and free of sores is praised. Those with the gait of an elephant in rut, a bull, a lion, a tiger, or a swan are lords; those with a steady gait are fortunate; those with a fickle gait obtain fickle pleasure and pain; those with a horizontal gait are unfortunate; and those who stumble or have limbs that twitch are not auspicious.

Likewise, among bodies, being excessively fair, excessively dark, excessively tall, excessively short, excessively thin, excessively stout, excessively hairy, or excessively hairless is said to be unfavorable. Similarly, for children, anger, weeping, sleep, wakefulness, rage, joy, emission, grasping, steadiness, and depth—when these are appropriate and superior in quality—are praised.
Regarding this, there are these verses: [The verses follow.]
As is the face, so is the conduct; as is the eye, so is the mind;
as is the voice, so is the essence; as is the form, so are the qualities.
Thus, the threefold nature (sattva) is declared to arise from goodness, anger, and delusion.
Their superior, middling, and inferior natures have been declared in due order;
now their classification— eightfold, sevenfold, and threefold respectively— will be explained for the sake of discerning the nature of beings, which is beneficial for the preparation of medicine.

One should know that a person who delights in austerity, truth, compassion, purity, charity, and virtuous conduct; who is impartial, endowed with theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom, self-controlled, possessed of progeny, observant of rituals, righteous in character, and beloved by the world, is a Brāhmaṇa.
A wise man should designate as belonging to Prajāpati one who is free from envy, free from deceit, pure,
devoted to purity, vows, sacrifice, study, celibacy, and compassion,
and who has conquered pride, intoxication, and anger; such a person should be designated as a speaker of the truth.
They call that highly fortunate lord and sovereign Indra’s own— a wise man ever devoted to the three goals of life, a hero who acts without weariness,
one who has abandoned pride, fear, and anger, and who performs only what is appropriate for the occasion.
One who is impartial toward both friend and foe should be known as certain to belong to Yama;
one who is pure despite impurity, heroic, quick to anger and grace,
virtuous in conduct, and highly fortunate belongs to Varuṇa and is dear to Varuṇa.
They say that the powerful Kaubera [yantra] belongs to one who seeks status, honor, service, dharma, pleasure, wealth, and gain, and who yields the fruits of both anger and favor;
it is for one who knows verses, narratives, and history, and who is fond of perfumes, garlands, and fine garments.

Those who understand dance, song, and humor, and know the auspicious Gandharva arts, as well as other pure and auspicious dispositions— these too are Sāttvika. Thus, this pure Sattva, abounding in excellence, is here described as eightfold.
Health, tranquility, beauty, wisdom, discernment, and nobility; long life, happiness never forsaken, commonality, and the mark of purity;
[he becomes] a lord, yet envious, fierce, and fond of self-worship and material requisites.
The *asura* is compassionate yet fearful, fierce, a slayer, and likewise heroic;
he strikes at cruel vulnerabilities, is constantly driven by anger, envy, and impatience,
and the *rākṣasa* seeks out enmity, consumes flesh, exerts himself in toil, and desires strife.

One who hates the pure, is impure, cruel, fearless, a terrifier, turbid, fond of wine and meat, suspicious, a Piśāca-like eater of much food, sharp, full of exertion, sleepy, and having many enemies— The Piśāca [is characterized by these traits]. He is one who eats excessively.
He is fierce, possesses much toil, is prone to sleep, and has many enemies.

One should recognize a Yakṣa as being non-angry yet timid, effeminate, and constantly licking its lips; it is perpetually engaged in giving gifts, providing beds, ornaments, drinking, eating, and sexual intercourse, and is ever-rejoicing and voracious.
Proud, gluttonous, hostile, and distorted-faced;
misshapen, perverted in nature, beings who delight in the night; they consume impure and contemptible food, their speech is harsh, and they are perpetually suspicious.
One should recognize the rājasa quality as being characterized by agitation, lack of intelligence, cowardice, bird-like fickleness, homelessness, and the sevenfold manifestation of anger;
it is marked by a mixture of both qualities and defects.
One should know such a person to be like a beast— intent on food and sex, addicted to sleep, lacking intelligence, devoid of cleanliness and ornaments,
timid, lacking wisdom, gluttonous, and fallen under the sway of desire and anger.
One should know that the *mātsya* [system] is violent toward oneself and others, deceitful, and characterized by good progeny;
the *vānaspatya* [system], however, one should call upright, yet devoid of intelligence and limbs, lazy, and subject to slaughter, bondage, affliction, cold, wind, and heat.

This threefold nature consisting of darkness (tamas), which arises from delusion (moha) and is impure and inauspicious— all that is also tamasic. Know sattva to be illuminating, and rajas to be stimulating.
Tamas is said to be the regulator, which delights in mutual union;
whenever and whichever of these is predominant in a person, that embodied being is permeated by it and performs auspicious or inauspicious deeds, experiencing the corresponding fruit.
Because she shares the same nature as infants, a nurse is highly praised;
one who causes agitation and terror, being contrary [to this], is not praised.
In the case of such a contrary nurse, children either die or survive only with great difficulty.
It is equal for all; it provides nourishment, longevity, strength, and happiness to the ignorant.

Now learn from me that which is the essence of all—the tissues (dhātus) consisting of skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen, as well as the vital energy (ojas), the mind (sattva), and everything else.

One who is free from skin diseases, possesses enjoyments, has clear secondary marks and complexion, whose fresh wounds heal instantly, whose hair grows beautifully, and whose blood is of a reddish luster— such a person is one whose essence is blood.
Only this much portion of the Sūtrasthāna has been found: the third Vimānasthāna— [beginning with] "Pṛthakpākā, Hitāśana."
"The worship of the lunar days, the constellations, and the deities destroys diseases born from [neglectful] observation," so said the venerable Kaśyapa;
thus [is prescribed] the spitting into the ear for the sake of victory. This is the Vimāna [section].
The Chapter on the Initiation of Disciples.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the initiation of disciples (Śiṣyopakramaṇīya-vimāna).
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.

Then, indeed, the Guru shall initiate the student who has approached him seeking knowledge, endowed with the qualities of a disciple, according to the prescribed rule during the northern course of the sun, on an auspicious day, under the asterism of Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, the Uttarās, or another.

In an auspicious place sloping toward the northeast, having smeared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung and water, he performs there—as prescribed—the drawing of the marks, the bringing forward of the fire, the sweeping, the sprinkling, the spreading of the *brahmapraṇītā* grass, the purification of the clarified butter, the pouring of the two libations (*āghāra*), the offering of the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), and the fire-oblation (*agnihoma*). Then he offers fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *palāśa* wood smeared with clarified butter, saying: "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to Prajāpati! Svāhā to Kaśyapa! Svāhā to the Aśvins! Svāhā to Indra! Svāhā to Dhanvantari!"

Having offered oblations with the words, "Svāhā to Sarasvatī! Svāhā to Pūrṇabhaga! Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt!", he should satisfy a Brāhmaṇa with sacrificial food (haviṣya) accompanied by a gift (dakṣiṇā). Having made offerings to the gods with oblations (bali), and having given a full water-pot as a gift to the Guru, he should, facing east, consume curd while reciting the verse "Dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam. Then, having sipped water and circumambulated [the fire] clockwise, he should touch the arm of the Guru and say, "I am so-and-so, your son. Having touched the Guru's feet, he should say, "I am so-and-so, your disciple. 3.

Now, the qualities of a disciple: patience, dexterity, courtesy, compliance, purity, birth in a noble family, and abiding in righteousness, truth, non-violence, gentleness, auspicious knowledge, and realized wisdom; proficiency, acting according to what has been instructed, celibacy, lack of arrogance, and the avoidance of greed and envy. One who is otherwise should be avoided due to these defects. 4.

Now, the teacher (guru) is one who is proficient in the knowledge of dharma, wisdom, and discernment, skilled in reasoning and refutation, endowed with virtues, gentle in appearance, pure, intent on the welfare of the disciple, and an instructor; he is a physician skilled in explaining the medical scriptures, possessing the theoretical and practical knowledge of the traditions, healthy, devoted solely to this task, not distracted by other activities, and possessed of the qualities of a teacher. One who is otherwise, being devoid of these [qualities] and possessed of faults, should be avoided. 5.

Now follows the instruction for the disciple: "O, you must be gentle, favorable, righteous, and one who has conquered the senses; you must be one who studies when summoned, one who reports everything, one who shares in the teacher's sorrows, and one who knows the proper place and time; you must be steadfast. You must abstain from greed, anger, delusion, envy, laughter, enmity, intoxicants, meat, and women. You must study with the remainder of your energy devoted to service for the teacher.
You must not act without being permitted, nor without having honored the teacher, nor as long as your learning is incomplete."

Now, the rule for study: The teacher, being pure and with hands raised, in a clean place, having first uttered the word *atha* or the syllable *oṃ* to the attentive disciple, and having recited the Great Vyāhṛtis and the Sāvitrī three times, should say, "Recite, sir! When thus addressed, he should pronounce one form (word); the disciple should repeat that, ensuring it is neither clipped nor misplaced. Observing the disciple's capacity for grasping, the teacher's practice consists of listening as prescribed while enduring interruptions, demonstrations of correction, and the requirement to grasp what was not previously learned.

Blessed is the attainment of the true meaning through retention and teaching for the sake of liberation. One should not study during the forbidden periods (anadhyāya), nor when there is displeasure toward the teacher, nor on the festival days (parvan), nor at the two twilights (saṃdhyā). One should not study during lightning, meteors, thunder, rain, or when the sun is invisible; nor during a great festival, nor immediately after eating, nor upon seeing a portentous marvel. One should not study when there is injury to cows, Brahmins, the teacher, or oneself; nor during the "female" days (pakṣiṇī), nor on the Aṣṭakā days. Nor should one practice with a voice that is too high, too low, or faltering; nor without the teacher being present; nor what is unobserved or doubtful; nor while afflicted by hunger, thirst, disease, dejection, or similar conditions. (7)

Having studied and received permission, he should practice wearing white garments, with hair tied up, undistracted, looking only a yoke's length ahead, speaking first, and maintaining a pleasant countenance. He should not enter a patient’s family home uninvited; and when entering, he should observe the omens. He should not look about in all directions, except toward the patient.

He should not engage in excessive joking with women, even female servants, in the households of the four castes; nor should he address them by name without first showing honor and respect, but rather speak to them using a title of respect. He should neither conduct business with them nor cultivate excessive intimacy with them. He should not give anything to women without his husband’s knowledge, nor should he grant them anything without being informed [of his intent]. He should not speak with or sit together with a woman in private, nor should he gaze at her when she is undressed, nor laugh at her. And he should disregard a woman who shows signs of affection. Nor...

One should reveal [the teachings]. One must not reveal the secrets of the four classes (*cāturakula*) to outsiders, nor should one publicize the defects of the four classes. Even if a patient has seen signs of death (*ariṣṭa*), one should not speak of the ultimate reality (*tattva*); rather, one should always offer consolation. One should not attend to a body overtaken by death, a disease that is incurable, or a patient who lacks the necessary resources. One should not prescribe medicine without following the proper sequence, nor should one make the patient dependent on others. One should not personally administer a medicine that has been concocted [by oneself]; rather, one should be a knower of the various conditions of the body, the medicine, the disease, and age.

He should always have incense, collyrium, and medicinal herbs prepared. He should not enter into conflict with other physicians; rather, he should prescribe medicine in conjunction with them. Confident and free from hesitation, he should always speak clearly, elegantly, gently, persuasively, intelligibly, non-contradictorily, and in accordance with righteousness (dharma) when addressing those present. For the physician who desires the welfare of his subjects rejoices both in this world and the next. 8

Now, another physician might speak to him; he should tolerate that and conciliate him with gentle words. However, toward one who reviles him repeatedly, he should take up a position of opposition and from the very beginning overwhelm him with the text, giving him no opportunity to speak. Even as the other speaks, he should say, "This is not so," regarding what has been stated. He should mock him and seize upon his grammatical errors (*apaśabda*), and lead him away when he falls into difficulty regarding the meaning. He should not, however, speak harshly to him against his will; rather, he should overcome him with hymns of praise. 9.

O Physician! What is life? What constitutes the nature of Āyurveda? Why is it called Āyus? How many branches does Āyurveda have? How should it be studied? For what purpose should it be studied? What is its primary treatise? Which among these is the most important? To which Veda does it belong? Is it eternal or non-eternal? Upon what does Āyurveda depend? What are the excellent characteristics of these three constitutions (prakṛtis) and of the three types of sensations—past, present, and future? Which of these does the physician treat? What...?

And when asked, "What is the means for this Ayurveda? Is it meritorious or non-meritorious? he should reply: "O sir, therein 'āyuḥ' (life) is said to be 'jīvita' (living). The verbal root *vid* is used in the sense of 'knowing' (*jñāna*) and the root *vidl* in the sense of 'attaining' (*lābha*). Because by means of this knowledge life is known (*vidyate*), understood (*jñāyate*), attained (*vindate*), or acquired (*labhyate*), and because one does not perish (*na riṣyati*), it is called Āyurveda. And as for how many branches Āyurveda has, it has eight branches: namely, Pediatrics (*kaumārabhṛtya*), Internal Medicine (*kāyacikitsā*), Surgery (*śalyāhartṛka*), Ophthalmology and Otorhinolaryngology (*śālākya*), Toxicology (*viṣatantra*), Demonology (*bhūtatantra*), Pharmacy (*agadatantra*), and Rejuvenation Therapy (*rasāyanatantra*).

Here he says: "What is that body which these limbs depend upon, for limbs indeed have the body as their support? To this he replies: "Its body is *dharma* (righteousness), for in this [body], action (*karman*) succeeds when it has *dharma* as its support. And how was it produced? He says: In the *Atharvaveda-Upaniṣads*, it is stated that Brahmā, the self-existent, having arisen in the beginning and desiring to create progeny, first created the *Āyurveda* itself for the sake of protecting living beings; thereafter, the omniscient one [created] all beings.

Then, who bestowed upon the two Aśvins that meritorious Āyurveda—which increases infinite life, is its foundation, its nourishment, and is nectar—and they, in turn, gave it to Indra; and Indra to the four sages Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and Bhṛgu; and they gave it to their sons and disciples for the sake of welfare, and for the purpose of preserving the power of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. Thus it originated. And how is it to be studied? It is to be studied with the permission of the guru.

By whom should it be studied? Āyurveda should be studied by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. Among them, it should be studied by Brāhmaṇas for the sake of thorough understanding of its meaning and for their own merit; by Kṣatriyas for the sake of favoring their subjects and protecting the people; by Vaiśyas for the sake of livelihood; and by others (Śūdras) for the sake of service. Furthermore, it should be studied by all for the sake of dharma. For they declare that the gift of a life of happiness is superior to all other forms of dharma; therefore, Āyurveda is indeed meritorious.

Furthermore, embodied beings, satisfied by the gift of a comfortable life, share with one who is grateful and praise him beforehand; thus, this [science] becomes the means for accomplishing virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*). To the question "For what purpose, then, should it be studied?", it has been stated here: moreover, what is its primary treatise?
It is said that *Kaumārabhṛtya* is the first among the eight treatises (*tantra*).

Of this great Āyurveda, which is like the consumer of oblations for the gods, others treat what has been expanded by it. For a child, the medicine is different, the dosage is different, the therapeutic procedure is different, and the specific details are different. Which Veda does it rely upon? It says: the Atharvaveda; for therein the rules for protective rites, offerings, oblations, pacification, and remedial actions are specifically prescribed, and likewise in Āyurveda; therefore, it relies upon the Atharvaveda.

Some say that all the Vedas are based on the sciences of verse, prose, narrative, and song; however, this is not so, for the Vedas rely specifically upon Āyurveda. For example: just as among the four fingers on the right hand, the thumb exercises sovereignty and does not attain equality with them, yet it remains part of the same hand—so too, this fifth Veda, Āyurveda, exists alongside the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda.

For what reason? Just as in the Vedas the ultimate welfare of man, conjoined with the three goals of life (trivarga), is constantly contemplated by those who know Brahman; even so, in this Veda as well, the ultimate welfare of man—which is the essence of the three goals and brings about constant benefit and happiness—is contemplated through the causes, origins, symptoms, fatal signs, and treatments. And just as those endowed with various specialized sciences and knowledge, who are experts in the composition of commentaries, possessed of the intellect of the eightfold limbs [of medicine], and capable of leaping, swimming, standing, sitting, going, and coming; and furthermore—

Just as men who lack knowledge of the country always follow one who knows the country and guides them, even so those who possess specialized knowledge of the Vedas, the Śikṣā, Kalpa, Sūtra, Nirukta, Vṛtti, Chandas, Yajña, Saṃstara, Jñāna, and Samuccaya, pursue Āyurveda alone. Therefore, we say that this fifth Veda is Āyurveda, derived from the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda; for it is through this that the recovery of the diseased and the maintenance of health in the healthy are achieved, and all other activities regarding virtue (dharma), wealth (artha), pleasure (kāma), and liberation (mokṣa) are brought to fulfillment.

Is it permanent or impermanent? Why? Because of the authority of the words of the Ṛṣis, because of its indestructibility, because the probandum is not established [otherwise], and because of its commonality across space and time. What is its substratum? It has wind, bile, and phlegm as its substrata. And these are each supported by two deities: wind is supported by the Maruts and Ākāśa; bile by Agni and Āditya; and phlegm by Soma and Varuṇa—these are their respective deities. Some say they are dharma, artha, and kāma; some say they are sattva, rajas, and tamas; others say they are curable, palliable, and incurable. And what are the specific characteristics of these primary humors? To this it is replied:
In that regard, phlegm is unctuous...
this much of the Vimānasthāna has been obtained;
[now follows] the fourth, the Śārīrasthāna.

"Therefore, there are indeed only five seasons; since that [sixth] is not logically established, there is no state of six. To this it is replied: "Their state of being six is taught for the sake of the *rasas* (flavors) in the *Rasavimāna*. What is that [time] which fashioned time as a collection of *kalās* in two ways—the auspicious and the inauspicious—and which made those two equal in measure through the division of past, present, and future?

In that regard, the upward cycle (*utsarpiṇī*) is auspicious and the downward cycle (*avasarpinī*) is inauspicious; both of these are further divided into three types according to the distinction of the *yugas*: the first *yuga*, the divine *yuga* (*devayuga*), and the *kṛtayuga* constitute the *utsarpiṇī*, while the *tretā*, *dvāpara*, and *kaliyugas* constitute the *avasarpinī*. Because of their infinity, no specific measure is stated for them. Among those, in the first *yuga*, the divine *yuga*, which arises with inconceivable dimensions—where action, food, drink, movement, vigor, and lifespan are indescribable—[the following occurs].

In the Kṛta age, however, the body of embodied beings arises as a solid mass called Nārāyaṇa; therefore they say of it: its head is a solid mass without a skull, its bones are the very seat of *sattva*, and its forms are more massive than adamant; in its heart there are ten great veins, and its skin and head are impenetrable and indivisible on all sides; its semen extends for a *yojana*, its height is one *yojana*, its stay in the womb lasts seven nights, and as soon as it is born, all its functions become capable [of action], and no one can...

Hunger, thirst, fatigue, exhaustion, grief, fear, envy, unrighteous thoughts, mental anguish, disease, and old age do not afflict him; he does not subsist on breast milk, and his stability in dharma, austerity, knowledge, and discernment is exceedingly great. They say that his maximum lifespan is half a *palyopama*. Now, in the Tretā age, a bodily constitution called Ardhānārāyaṇa arises for embodied beings.

His body consists mostly of a single bone, devoid of contraction and expansion; his stay in the womb lasts for eight months, and he subsists on breast milk. There are two cranial bones, one joint on each side, three bones in the chest, twenty vessels in the back of the trunk, and semen equal to a fourth part of a hair that has turned grey. The maximum lifespan is one hundred years, and from that point, there is a gradual decline by half every subsequent period.

Then, in the Dvāpara age, a body arises with a Kaiśika constitution; its bones have hair-like minute pores, its joints are very loose, it possesses the strength of a great elephant, and its limbs are entwined with veins. Its semen resides in the joints of the limbs, its lifespan is at most one-eighth that of a grey-haired man, and it is reduced by half compared to the previous [Kṛta] age.

Now, in the Kali Yuga, a body arises with a structure of flesh and skin; it possesses three hundred and sixty bones that are extremely hollow and filled with marrow, which are as fragile as reeds; four hundred muscles rooted in the heart; seven hundred veins; nine hundred sinews rooted in the brain; two hundred arteries at the base of the palate; one hundred and seven vital points (*marmans*); three great vital points; ten seats of life; five hearts; and three [other organs].

There are eight hundred and fourteen joints, fourteen large tendons (kaṇḍarā), forty-two tufts (kūrca), six layers of skin, seven bodily constituents (dhātu), and two types of channels (srotas). For one who is born, the eruption of the teeth occurs separately; the stay in the womb lasts for ten months; after one year, he becomes established and emits speech.
His maximum lifespan is one hundred years, encompassed by pleasure and pain, mental distress and physical disease, old age, and death.

Know that the entire body—characterized by hunger, thirst, heaviness, fatigue, laxity of mind, envy, anger, falsehood, greed, affliction, delusion, and separation—is the sphere of *saṃsāra*, abounding in ailments; thus, in each pair of ages (*yuga*), there is a succession of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. This concludes the explanation of the cause of the creation of the person (*puruṣa*).

We shall now state the cause of their origination: from the Unmanifest (avyakta) comes the Great One (mahat); from the Great One, the Ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); and from the Ego-sense, the [subtle elements] beginning with space—these eight are the primary natures of the elements (bhūtaprakṛti). The five sense organs—sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch—are the organs of cognition (buddhīndriya). The five organs of action—hands, feet, tongue, anus, and genitals—are the organs of action (karmendriya). Sound, touch, taste, form, and smell are the five objects of the senses. The mind (manas), however, is beyond the senses. These sixteen are the transformations (vikāra). All this, beginning with the Great One, [proceeds from the Unmanifest].

They call the *kṣetra* (the field) the unmanifest; the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), however, is the eternal and inconceivable Self (*ātman*). Its signs are consciousness, ego-sense, the vital breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*), opening and closing of the eyes, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, memory, fortitude, and intellect; in the absence of these, it is termed "dead. Some call the person (*puruṣa*)—which is a collection of body, senses, self, and being—the Self. The non-existence and existence of cognition are the characteristics of the mind (*manas*); its two qualities are unity and atomicity. Because of the non-simultaneity of effort and cognition, it is one and distinct.

The sense organ becomes capable of apprehending its object when it is accompanied by the mind (*manas*). Space, air, fire, water, and earth—these five great elements (*mahābhūta*) are said to be the cause of the body. Sound and the others are their qualities (*guṇa*). The great elements, established through the increase of their qualities, as well as direction, the self, mind, and time, are substances (*dravya*). Qualities reside in substances. The non-obstruction of space is its mark; motion is the mark of air; heat of fire; fluidity of water; and stability of earth.

Of the six sense organs, including the mind as the sixth, three each have functions that are either remote or proximate. The mind, the eye, and the ear have remote functions; the nose, the tongue, and the skin have proximate functions. They say that all of this is characterized by touch, just as a man who has ascended a palace with windows on all sides perceives various objects through those windows; in the same way, this self, residing within the body, perceives through the unimpaired senses. [This concludes] the chapter on the body from the section on those of different lineages. As for the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it indeed divides the seed-element according to the number of bones.
As soon as the seed has entered, it is indeed enveloped by the blood; from the semen comes the bone, from both [semen and blood] comes the flesh, and from these two, the sinews,
all the sense organs of the embryo, and likewise all its limbs and members are said to arise.
In the third month, these functions arise simultaneously:
it throbbs, it becomes conscious, and it perceives sensations; however, in the third month, the mind becomes predominant as the subtle sense-faculties become manifest.

In the fourth month, the embryo becomes stable within the womb and free from disease; at that time, the pregnant woman experiences excessive heaviness of the body. O Jīvaka, however, there is an increase of flesh and blood in the fifth month.
Therefore, in the fifth month the pregnant woman suffers from emaciation;

in the sixth month there is an increase in the mother's fatigue, as the fetus becomes complete in all its elements and limbs, endowed with wind, bile, and phlegm, and increases in strength, complexion, and vitality.

Therefore, in the seventh month, the pregnant woman there is constantly exhausted; and in the eighth month, the fetus and the pregnant woman draw strength from one another due to the fullness of the flow of *rasa* (nutritive essence), and she may even suffer a miscarriage.
Therefore, in that state, the pregnant woman is repeatedly distressed and repeatedly joyful;
she meets with calamity, and for that reason the eighth month is not counted [as the time of birth].
His birth occurs, in due order, during the ninth and subsequent months.

"The karma performed in a previous body, as well as the pleasure and pain experienced during residence in the womb, one who has been born remembers for as long as he does not enter into a livelihood," so said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the chapter on the descent of the embryo, titled "The One with a Different Gotra," from the Section on Anatomy.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the anatomical section concerning the descent of the embryo. 1.

Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa: "Indeed, O venerable one, the *jīva*—because it is omnipresent and endowed with the qualities of the Lord—departs from a previous body and enters another body simultaneously; it has never been separated from the seed, blood, wind, space, mind, and intellect, and because of its omnipresence, there is no womb into which it does not enter for the sake of experiencing the fruits of its own karma."

"Furthermore, O Blessed One, which parts of the body of the embryo are produced from space, which from wind, which from fire, which from water, and which from earth? Which arise from its mother, and which from its father? What comes from the self (*ātman*), what from suitability (*sātmya*), what from the essence of food (*rasa*), and what from the vital principle (*sattva*)? Upon what are all these states dependent, and toward what end do they look? Being thus questioned, the Blessed Kaśyapa replied:

Indeed, O venerable one, sound, the ear, lightness, subtlety, discernment, the mouth, the throat, and the digestive cavity of the embryo are composed of space (ākāśa). Touch, the sense of touch, roughness, propulsion, the arrangement of the bodily constituents (dhātu-vyūhana), the vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna), and bodily movement are composed of air (vāyu). Form, the eye, radiance, bile (pitta), digestion, heat, and the growth of the body are composed of fire (tejas). Taste and the sense of taste... [are composed of water].

Coldness, softness, fluidity, unctuousness, moisture, phlegm, fat, blood, flesh, and semen are the watery elements; odor, the sense of smell, heaviness, stability, and form are the earthy elements. Therefore, the person is said to be commensurate with the world.

Blood, flesh, the navel, the heart, the *kloman*, the liver, the spleen, the kidneys, the bladder, the receptacle for feces, the stomach, the upper rectum, the small intestine, and the large intestine—these are derived from the mother. Hair of the head, body hair, beard, nails, teeth, bones, veins, ligaments, arteries, and semen—these are derived from the father. Longevity, self-knowledge, the mind, the sense organs, the out-breath and in-breath, maintenance, and propulsion—[these are derived from the Self].

Furthermore, physical form, specific variations in voice and complexion, pleasure and pain, desire and aversion, memory, ego-sense, effort, transition through different states, existence, and rebirth in various wombs—these are born of the self (*ātmaja*). Health, vitality, contentment, clarity of the senses, excellence of voice, complexion, and seed, intelligence, and abundance of joy—these are born of suitability (*sātmyaja*). The formation of the body, the growth of the body, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), binding, and function—these are [born of the body].

Nourishment (*puṣṭi*) and enthusiasm (*utsāha*) are born from *rasa*. Furthermore, *sattva* is said to be threefold—consisting of goodness, anger, and delusion—as explained previously. Among these, the *sattva* that is produced (*aupapādika*), as well as the mind (*manas*), are eternally dissolved; this is called the contact with states that are auspicious, inauspicious, or mixed. All those states depend upon one's own karma and await the proper time. For it is the wind (*vāyu*), conjoined with time, that divides and reconstitutes the body.
Regarding this, there are these verses: "From the blood the heart is born; from the heart the liver (*yakṛt*) is produced."
From the liver the spleen is born, and from the spleen the lungs are said to arise;
O Bhārgava, all these are interconnected with one another.
Beneath them lies a vast channel situated in the form of a coil.

That which is surrounded by the *jarāyu* (chorion) is called the *garbhāśaya* (uterus); within it are the *āma-āśaya* (stomach) and *pakva-āśaya* (large intestine), which serve as the receptacles for food and drink, as well as the anus (*guda*).
From that [anus] the bladder (*basti*) is produced, and it is filled by the *pariṣyanda* (urine).
The two channels situated at the openings of the vessels are also said to be below;

furthermore, these— the receptacles for feces, urine, worms, digested food, undigested food, phlegm, and bile— exist separately within the abdominal cavity of embodied beings, while the uterus is the eighth in women.
Some declare that the body consists of six sheaths: semen, marrow, and bone from the father; and flesh and blood from the mother. — Chapter 10:
The Discourse on the Investigation of the Body.

The teeth are considered to be thirty-two, and there are just as many sockets; the bones of the fingers and toes of the hands and feet are sixty, and the nails are twenty; furthermore, the metacarpals and metatarsals of the hands and feet are proclaimed to be twenty.
Regarding the four bases of the longitudinal bones of the hands and feet:
it is taught that there are two bones in the heels, four "tufts" (kūrca) in the feet,
two at the wrist-joints (hastamaṇika), and four in the forearms (aratni).
The two knee-bones are counted as two; there are four bones in the two shanks;
the two thigh-bones are known as two, and the two kneecaps are likewise two;
the two shoulders and the two shoulder-blades are also two, as are the two collarbones.
There are two arm-bones, two each for the hips and the pelvic sockets; likewise, there is one collarbone, one pubic bone, and the neck consists of fifteen bones;
the Bhārgava bones are forty-five in number.
One should point out fourteen bones in the chest and one bone in the jaw;
the wise say there are four cranial plates in the head,
twenty-four ribs, and an equal number of sockets.
They say there are exactly twenty-four *sthālaka* and *arbuda* [bones];
two *śaṅkha*s are enumerated; two are the *hanumūlabandhana*s;
and one should point out that the bones of the forehead, nose, and cheeks (*gaṇḍakūṭa*) constitute a single unit.
Thus, due to the commonality of the enumeration of bones, increase and decrease are produced by external causes;
they say there are exactly ten bases for the vital breaths—listen to them from me:
the head, the heart, the bladder, the throat, vitality, semen, and blood.
The two temples, the anus, and then the first three great vital points (mahāmarmāṇi);
the navel, spleen, liver, kloma, heart, kidneys, anus, bladder, small intestine, large intestine, the stomach (āma-āśaya) and the receptacle for digested food (pakva-āśaya), and the omentum.
The wise declare these to be the major limbs (koṣṭhāṅga); learn from me the minor limbs (pratyaṅga):

the two eyes, the two nostrils, the two ears, the two breasts, the two lips, the two hollows of the armpits (kukundara), the two hands, the two feet, the two eyebrows, the two temples (kūṭa), and the arms, shanks, thighs, and calves.

One should identify all of these in pairs: the two corners of the mouth (*sṛkkiṇī*), the two ear-lobes (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), the two ear-pits (*karṇaputra*), the two pupils (*akṣitāraka*), the two testicles (*vṛṣaṇa*), the two gums (*dantaveṣṭa*), the two temples (*śaṅkhaka*), the two sublinguals (*upajihvikā*), and the two roots of the teeth (*dantaloha*).
The bladder, the head of the bladder, the penis, the back, the chin along with the abdomen,
the forehead, the mouth, the gojihvā, the head, and the heart— each of these is one [marman]; however, there are four hearts located on the palms and soles of the hands and feet.

One should know that there are five known as the branches and the heart, and four as the supports of consciousness; the joints of the eyes are twenty, and they say the channels are of two kinds: subtle and large.
One should know that there are nine great [openings]: two below and seven above;
one should point out the navel, the pores of the skin, and the subtle channels.
From the heart, ten mothers of the vessels (sirās) extend forth.
Four vessels (sirās) flow upwards, two flow transversely, and four flow downwards;
they pervade the body, and as they branch out again and again like the veins of a leaf, they are known as "sirās" because of their flowing nature.
Just as a wooden figure might be wrapped with grass and rope and smeared on the outside with clay, so too is this thing called a body:
bones bound together by sinews, and the sinews plastered over with flesh.
Everything of his is constantly nourished by the channels (sirās) and spread over by the skin;
from the two roots of the ears, there extend a hundred vessels (dhamanīs) each,
within which the wind (anila), residing eternally, sustains the fires of Agni and Soma.
If there were two hundred thousand pits, slightly more than that, both outside and inside,
corresponding to the pores of the skin, each one arising individually through growth and decay from conception, by natural law, or by the agency of Viśvakarman;
Know that, by their very nature, women possess [these] diminished by one-fourth;
furthermore, one should know that in every pore there is a minute opening of a vessel (sirāmukha),
and through these vessel-openings, while perspiring, she releases sweat.
As the embodied being grows— from infancy through youth to old age—
we measure his fluids by the capacity of his own joined palms:
namely, marrow, fat, grease, urine, bile, phlegm, and feces.
One, two, three, four, five, six, and seven handfuls (añjali) are prescribed for blood;
eight handfuls for the muscle-fat (vasā); nine for the marrow (majjā);
and ten handfuls are declared for water residing in the skin.
By that water, the bodily constituents such as blood and the rest are nourished;
from it, urine flows in a person suffering from diarrhea,
and from it, lymph, pus, and mucous discharge flow from a wound.
When that [dosha] is vitiated, there occur ringworm, itching, eczema, skin diseases,
leucoderma, scabies, and hair loss; this condition,
agitated by fire and wind, is called sweat-pustules (pakasveda).
The quantity of *ojas* is equal to the quantity of *śleṣman*;
in the body, the semen and the brain are likewise half-an-āñjali each;
this is declared to be the maximum measure for all of them.
From that, the flesh is designated as middling, and from that, the semen is the lowest;
however, the semen begins to flow fully in the sixteenth year.
They say these elements are mutually dependent and possess mutual qualities.
The great elements (mahābhūtas) are visible, like wood and fire or sesame seeds and oil; the enumeration of the body has been specified according to its gross types.
However, the subtle divisions of the limbs of the body are infinite and extremely difficult to describe.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the chapter on the body named "Investigation of the Body," within the Section on the Body, specifically the chapter on the anatomy of birth.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the rules for birth (Jātisūtrīya).
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa:

"In each and every species, it is indeed inherent nature (*svabhāva*) that brings about the differentiation of form. For by its very nature, the wind-atoms (*vāyu-paramāṇu*) of this [embryo], being governed by the activity of conjunction, disjunction, and motion, differentiate the channels of contraction and expansion, as well as the cavities, limbs, minor parts, elements, consciousness, and the vital currents. Just as molten metal, when poured, takes the shape of the mold, so too does a human produce a human, a cow a cow, a horse a horse, and so forth. Among humans, however, there occurs the formation of the embryo."

In that regard, the increase of progeny for a couple occurs either by their very nature or from the ripening of their own past karma; those two are blessed, whereas otherwise they must be treated medically. One should treat them sequentially with oleation, sudation, emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enema, and unctuous enema, using milk and ghee prepared with sweet medicinal herbs for the man, while some say the woman should be nourished with oil and meat; however, Prajāpati [the Lord of Creatures] maintains that they should be nourished only with things that are wholesome to them (*sātmya*).

Just as a very subtle fruit exists within a flower before it has fully developed yet is not perceived, and just as fire pervades wood but is not perceived due to its latent state, so too do the blood and semen of a woman and a man exist, dependent upon time and their own past karma. For these two become potent within the blood and semen at sixteen years of age; even before that, through specific food and health, they may become full.
Thus ends the fourth assembly.

If conception occurs on the first day of menstruation, they call that a "wind-conception" (*vātagarbha*); it is as fruitless as the flowers of climbing plants. If it miscarries or falls away on the second day, or dies in the lying-in chamber on the third day, or does not live long, or is born with deficient limbs; beyond this, the fertile period (*ṛtu*) lasts twelve days for Brāhmaṇa women, eleven days for Kṣatriya women, ten days for Vaiśya women, and nine nights for others.

"The great seers say that one should observe the season (*ṛtu*) and the time for sowing; beyond this, they say [the offspring] is born out of season (*akālaja*). For what is born out of season becomes inferior, weak, unstable, unfirm, thin, fragile, and like grain [that has not ripened].
It is established that one desiring a son should approach his wife on even days, while one desiring a daughter may do so at other times, being joyful, satisfied, and full of longing."

Then, on the fourth day, having bathed and being pure, the woman, veiled with a white garment or another [clean cloth], not looking about, enters a temple while remaining pure. Having worshipped the uncovered fire that is blazing with clarified butter and parched grain, and having gazed upon and saluted a Brāhmaṇa, as well as Īśvara, Viṣṇu, and Skanda, she departs. She does so thinking, "I am beholding the Sun and the Moon," and not ghosts, goblins, or demons; for a woman who has merely bathed for purification sees whatever she looks at with her eyes or whatever she contemplates in her mind.

One generally produces a body characterized by such conduct; therefore, one should look upon the gods, cows, Brahmins, elders, and teachers as being truly existent, and one should be of virtuous mind. Furthermore, during the two twilights, one should not engage in bathing or sexual intercourse, nor should one be distracted in mind.

Then the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) should perform the *putrīyā* sacrifice. The two *ājyabhāga* offerings consist of cooked meat-rice and a preparation that wards off wind; there is a cake (*puroḍāśa*) on eight potsherds made of barley and a sacrificial porridge (*caru*) made of rice. Both are joined with the *āyuṣmat* formula. Having consecrated the sacrificer’s portion with the mantra "O Brahman, [protect] the Brāhmaṇa," the husband and wife should eat the remainder.

A white bull, a horse, or gold is the fee for the physician; this very same rite applies even for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, having performed the daily oblation in the domestic fire (*śālāgni*), and the couple should eat the remains of the offering with that same mantra.

On a bed well-spread with soft coverings, her husband—having stirred water with *lakṣmaṇā* grass and recited over it a hundred times the *Sāvitrī*, the *Vyāhṛtis*, and the mantra "The divine waters flow" (*apo devīr upasṛja*)—should administer it as a nasal drop (*nasya*). Then, having muttered the *Vāmadevya* hymn, he should have the woman lie on her right side; the man, on his left side, should lie upon her, facing upward toward the north. He should proceed slowly for the sake of progeny. Once the seed has been infused, she should remain still and not move about.
One should perform purification with cold water; thereafter, one must avoid fire-rituals, heating, exertion, physical exercise, grief, and so forth. 8.

If she should desire, "May I give birth to a son who is fair-complexioned, vigorous, pure, and long-lived," then from the time of her ritual purification and bathing, one should always have her drink a stirred potion (*mantha*) made by mixing white barley flour with honey and clarified butter, using the milk of a white cow that has a white male calf; this should be served in a silver or bronze vessel. Furthermore, at the proper times, she should eat in moderation a diet consisting primarily of *śāli* rice, white barley, milk, curd, and clarified butter. She should wear white flowers, ornaments, and garments, and [she should look upon] a white horse every morning and evening.

If she should see a bull, she should sit with pleasant, beneficial, and agreeable conversation; and if she has favorable attendants, she will give birth to a desired child. However, for one who desires a son who is dark-complexioned, red-eyed, broad-chested, or black, there should be a corresponding regimen regarding food, clothing, flowers, and ornaments, as well as contemplation of such places. One seeking a daughter should give gruel, while those desiring a son should be offered rice prepared with milk, water, and sesame seeds. Complexions other than fair, dark, and black are censured. 9

Food is of four kinds and is based on six tastes; it has twenty variations due to the distinctions of heavy, light, cold, hot, unctuous, dry, dull, sharp, stable, mobile, soft, hard, clear, slimy, smooth, rough, subtle, gross, dense, and liquid. By means of this, the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) beginning with the skin and ending with semen are nourished. Their equal growth results from consuming food that is not antagonistic to them.

However, when the flesh being consumed nourishes the flesh, the blood the blood, and so forth, other elements (dhātu) of the wind and other constituents become replenished. Out of fear of unrighteousness, one should avoid what is undesirable and instead replenish the depleted elements with pure foods possessing wholesome qualities.

In the case of depletion of semen (*śukra*), the consumption of milk and ghee, as well as other substances that are sweet, unctuous, vitalizing, and non-burning, is recommended. Furthermore, in the case of depletion of urine (*mūtra*), sugarcane juice, *vāruṇī* wine, the scum of wine (*maṇḍa*), liquids, sweet and sour items, salts, buttermilk (*takra*), jaggery (*guḍa*), and moistening vegetables such as *trapusa* are beneficial. In the case of depletion of feces (*purīṣa*), the use of preparations of barley, fermented grain-gruel (*kulmāṣa*), black gram (*māṣa*), sixty-day rice (*ṣaṣṭika*), barley meal (*yāvaka*), cow's milk, sour and salty items, and unctuous vegetables is advised. In the case of depletion of *vāta*, the use of pungent, bitter, astringent, light, dry, and cold barley-based foods is prescribed. In the case of depletion of *pitta*, pungent, salty, sour, sharp, hot, and alkaline substances are used; and in the case of depletion of *kapha*, unctuous, sweet, heavy, thick, and similar substances are employed. (10)
One should present to the pregnant woman substances that are meritorious, auspicious, pure, new, unbroken, uncracked, masculine in name, and pleasing, as well as garments and ornaments; however,
she should not wear nor accept anything designated as feminine or neuter.
A dwelling that has been fumigated, honored, and swept clean; one that is free from mosquitoes and other pests;

and one where the sound of the Vedas and musical instruments resounds—is praised for one who, having risen at dawn and completed their purification, is devoted to the worship of the Guru and the gods.
A pregnant woman should never look at the rising sun when it is curved,
nor at the waning moon, nor at the setting sun;
she should likewise not look at either during an eclipse.
Having heard that the Moon and the Sun, along with the planets, are in the house of the womb of a pregnant woman,
she should remain intent on peace-offerings and burnt oblations (śānti-homa) and request a time when the planetary conjunction has passed.
She should not show hostility toward a guest, and she should give alms without refusing them.
When the fire has ignited by itself, one should offer clarified butter into it for the sake of pacification;
[one should also present] a full water-pot, clarified butter, a garland, a full vessel, clarified butter, and curd.
One should not obstruct anything, nor should one restrain a pregnant woman.

She should always avoid being pinned down by a thin cord or rope and avoid various bindings; she may release herself from bonds at her own will. Now, one should observe these physical signs of a pregnant woman.
Upon seeing these signs, one should initiate the treatment for a newborn infant:
drooping of the face, exhaustion of the limbs, loosening of the eyelids,
sagging of the abdomen, and heaviness of the lower body.
The back, sides, waist, bladder, and groin are excessively tormented; there is discharge from the vagina, distension, aversion to food, restlessness, and exhaustion.
Having observed these symptoms, one should perform the recitation by Brahmins.
Women who are elderly, skilled, and well-washed should enter;
being pleasant-spoken, they should console and gladden the pregnant woman,
and they should reassure her by invoking Prajāpati as he urges [her] toward dharma and artha.
They would proclaim the worlds belonging to those with sons, their various pleasures, and the sufferings of those without sons in the hells and other realms;
[they would praise] Aditi, Kaśyapa the god, Indrāṇī, Indra, and the two Aśvins.
The recitation of the names of long-lived, prolific, and auspicious beings;

a sound like the resonance of a lute-string; slight discharge that is slimy; and a flow resembling the water of the *kiṃśuka* flower at birth, portends the birth of a son, while [the latter] indicates the birth of a daughter.
However, those discharges that occur after delivery which are censured, one should regard them as such;
in this state, one should pray to the deities while the woman's womb is not yet closed, but is open and turned away from the exterior.
If the *grāhi* (obstructive) humors are present, that pregnant woman may experience complications;
however, she does not give birth quickly during acute *grāhi-śūla* (obstructive colic). When the *āvi* (expelling) humors are delayed, the fetus causes distress to the woman.
In this state, some physicians declare that physical exertion with clubs and the like, as well as yawning, walking, and so forth, are beneficial; however,
the Blessed Kaśyapa stated that all such things must be avoided.
For at the time of childbirth, a woman's body is indeed tormented; the three humors become aggravated and the bodily constituents are disturbed.
A pregnant woman in such a state must be supported with special effort.
For the excessive delicacy and moisture of a pregnant woman, especially at the time of delivery, provide a basis for despondency and fear;
one foot is in the family of Yama, while one foot remains here.
Seeing her suffering, the women speak thus among themselves:
"In her current condition, physical exertion is not recommended;
for if practiced, exertion would swiftly destroy the pregnant woman."
Even by walking too much, she may destroy the fetus that has been conceived;
she would incur a terrible transgression that brings about the end of her body.
Therefore, she should sit down repeatedly, remaining undiscouraged and free from shame.
A woman desiring offspring who is advanced in age, yet endowed with wealth and beauty,
shall quickly give birth if she sniffs the powder of *vacā*, *lāṅgalikī*, *kuṣṭha*, *cirabilva*, *elā*, and *citraka* from her nostrils.
Or one should smell the smoke of *bhūrja* bark, or likewise of *nameru* or *guggulu*;
then the fetus enters [the womb] and is quickly released.
The sides, joints, hips, and back should be anointed with warm oil.
Wise women, being gentle and pleasant, should gently massage and pull her [hair];
some say that one who is weak should be made to drink wine, but Kaśyapa says "no.
One who has been previously afflicted should likewise drink barley-gruel when thirsty.
When the amniotic fluid issues forth from the womb accompanied by pain,
and the fetus, impelled by time, is released, it assumes the position for birth by withdrawing from the heart and abdomen and grasping the lower part, including the bladder and head.
Excessive exhaustion occurs, as does the bursting pain from pressure upon the birth canal;
by these causes one should recognize the turning of the fetus, and then its delivery— thereafter she should ascend the bed.
A cloak or a pillow—
only this much portion of the Section on the Body (Śārīrasthāna) has been recovered; [the remainder is] the Section on the Senses (Indriyasthāna).
The fifth section on the faculties (indriya), the chapter on medicinal herbs and drugs.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the faculty concerning medicinal herbs and drugs.
Thus said the Blessed Lord Kaśyapa.
Medicine (*oṣadha*) and therapeutics (*bheṣaja*) are declared to be the two-fold treatment;
I shall now describe the distinction between these two, medicine and therapeutics.
(3) They say that medicine is the combination of substances that produces digestive stimulation and other such effects.
When both sacrificial rites, ascetic penance, charity, propitiatory ceremonies,
and medicinal treatment fail to produce their effect for a living being,
the wise physician, recognizing that his lifespan is exhausted, should not attempt further treatment.
He upon whose head a powder resembling cow-dung dust appears, and which then falls off while oily, has but one month left of his life.
Furthermore, he whose belly dries first after he has bathed and been anointed with unguents [shall likewise perish].
If all his limbs are moist, his life lasts for half a month.
There is the destruction of the lords of dreams and the falling of celestial bodies;
there is the extinguishing of fires and the collapsing of houses and trees.
Entering a cave or a forest, and seeing in a dream a woman who is censured in dreams— black, holding a staff, naked, shaven-headed, and red-eyed—
one should know from the very sight of her in a dream that the messengers of Yama have arrived.
Having seen in a dream a dark woman with long hair, breasts, and nails, wearing discolored flowers and garments— one who uses red perfumes, flowers, and clothes— one should announce her as Kālarātri.
When a child in a dream even mounts a peacock, a cock, a goat, or a ram,
or is smeared with blood along with them, there too is fear from Skanda. (12)
He who sees in a dream a bell or a banner shattered upon the ground,
or a bed smeared with blood, will likewise experience fear from Skanda;
[he will see himself] wearing red flowers and garments, and stained by red sandalwood paste.
If he dances together with the *bhūtas*, there is fear from Skanda and Apasmāra;
when, having reached a grove of red lotuses, he worships himself as Dhātrī,
or worships a child with garlands of lotuses, then there is fear from the father of Skanda.
When a woman enters a grove of red flowers or fire in a dream, or when a child is burned by fire, then there is danger from Pauṇḍarīka;
if they are submerged in waters such as the ocean, there is danger from Revatī. (16–17)
Seeing a dry well or a dried-up river, one is struck down by Śuṣkarevatī;
having seen flesh-eating birds, a child is killed by Śakunī. One who is bitten by an Avaḍīna bird meets with immediate death.
Adorned with colors such as yellow orpiment and wearing yellow garments, he appears full-bodied and well-ornamented in a dream; such a person is killed by a Mukhamaṇḍikā.
The stars, planets, moon, sun, and constellations serve as the pupils of his eyes.

Having seen these falling down in a dream, there will be fear from the *pūtanās*; one perceives all these forms in the vision of *naigameṣī*. Or, if bitten by insects, scorpions, or snakes, there may be a death caused by poison.
If one goes toward the south shaven-headed, being dragged or trampled by wicked dogs or even donkeys,
that is said to be the end of the fever—
whatever has been prayed for, imagined, seen, experienced, or heard.
One who has cultivated [the mind] sees in dreams what was seen during the day, whether short or long;
all these are fruitless and are said to arise from the [unwholesome] causes of the humors (doṣas).
But listen now to how a dream becomes fruitful, O Vṛddhaśīvaka.
A dream that is unseen, unheard, unspoken, unimagined, and unuttered, and which consists merely of an effect, is fruitful at its conclusion;
however, having seen these and other such bad dreams, the sick person perishes. 25–26.
One who is healthy, having fallen into doubt, is liberated if he possesses a virtuous character;
however, whatever sight one has in a dream of twice-born men and others who are cold and emaciated, or of those with soiled garments and flowers, is not praised. 27.
For those very same joyful ones, who consist of pure flowers and garments,
a vision in a dream is commended, as is an auspicious conversation with them; [and likewise, seeing] palaces, trees, mountains, elephants, cows, bulls, and men.

For those who ascend [these] in a dream, a blessing has been performed for them, as well as for men who perform meritorious deeds, for cows, and for the sun, moon, fire, and brahmins (verse 30). Furthermore, the sight of fish, meat, and the blue jay is said to be auspicious.
The seizing of white flowers, a mirror, or an umbrella; crossing water; seeing one's own blood; drinking liquor;
and riding on a cow, a horse, a chariot, or a vehicle toward the northeast are all commended.
Weeping, rising from a fall, the subduing of enemies, and likewise emerging from mud, wells, and caves, as well as from a journey—
sages have declared that such things and others like them lead to success.
The mildness of diseases, the availability of physicians and medicines, fortitude, birth under favorable conditions, mental strength, and righteousness lead to prosperity,
whether one has seen terrible dreams or otherwise.
Having bathed and become purified, one who offers mustard seeds the color of fire, along with sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter, while reciting the Sāvitrī mantra,
is purified and liberated from sins and diseases. 35.

Thus has been declared the *Kaumārabhṛtya*, which increases growth; for having understood that the sense organs residing within the body are of primary importance, you should avoid those intent on medical treatment [of external symptoms] alone, and you who are devoted to righteousness (*dharma*) should protect the scripture.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the section on the Sense Organs (*Indriyasthāna*) in the *Vṛddhajīvakīya-Kaumārabhṛtya* concerning the unrefined [child].
The faculty named *auṣadhabhaiṣajīya* is completed;
thus, the faculties are finished,
and this is found to be the final chapter of the section on the faculties (*indriyasthāna*).
The Sixth Section on Therapeutics: The Chapter on the Treatment of Fever. Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of fever. 1.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa:
"The learned Vṛddhajīvaka, out of humility, questioned Kaśyapa as he sat together with the ṛṣis of meritorious deeds. (2-3)
In the Sūtrasthāna, fever was taught by the Blessed One to be of two kinds;
furthermore, in the Nidāna, it was declared by the Seer of Reality to be of eight kinds.
Among those fevers, which one arises in a newborn?
What are its premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa), its clinical form (rūpa), and what is its treatment?

What are the premonitory symptoms and the characteristics of the other fevers, and what is their treatment? And what is the treatment for fevers caused by undigested matter (āma) and indigestion (jīrṇa)?

What is wholesome for one who drinks milk, what is wholesome for one who eats grain-food, what is wholesome for one who eats both milk and grain-food, and what is beneficial for a feverish child? And what is the proper regimen— ?
In the chapter on the treatment of pregnant women:
cold milk enriched with sweet substances, combined with honey,
sugar, honey, oil, and the inspissated juice of liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhuka-phāṇita), [should be administered].
Indeed, these red-colored substances— parikartikā, molasses, sesame paste, sugar, licorice (madhuka),
and rice-water combined together— immediately destroy dysentery (pravāhikā).
One should drink a gruel prepared with the paste of *kāśmarya* bark and likewise the root of *śyāmā*, along with the whey of curd and a small amount of ghee;
as well as *kirātatiktaka*, *lodhra*, and *yaṣṭīmadhuka*.
A decoction of *varṣābhū* roots combined with *devadāru* should be drunk mixed with honey; it instantly cures dysentery.
A woman suffering from swelling should drink a decoction of *mūrvā* combined with honey.

The roots of *pippalī* and *aṅkoṭha*, as well as the juice of *vājīlaṇḍa*, should be drunk with buffalo curd; this is the treatment for jaundice (*kāmalā*). The juice of *mātuluṅga* should be drunk, well combined with rock salt (*saindhava*).
Kaśyapa has said that the paste of long pepper root, along with the leaf of *gandhapriyaṅgu* and the juice of *mātuluṅga*, is the best medicine for heart pain. This is the remedy for heart pain.
Priyaṅgu, pippalī, bhadramusta, hareṇu, honey, and the powder of jujube (badara) constitute the six-component heart-medicine (ṣaḍaṅga-hṛdayauṣadha).
A fatty meat broth seasoned with rock salt and trāvaṇa is wholesome.

In cases of upward-moving wind (ūrdhvānila), a linctus consisting of sixty-day rice (*ṣaṣṭika*) with buffalo meat, or else *bhadradāru* and *harītakī* with sour substances for the skin and wind disorders, along with rock salt (*saindhava*), *kuṣṭha*, sugar-candy (*saphāṇita*), and ghee, removes this upward wind.
Pippalī, gairika, bhārgī, hiṅgu, and likewise karkaṭakī,
combined with honey, form a linctus that destroys hiccup and dyspnea; [so too do] pippalī, pippalīmūla, mustā, and nāgara.
She should drink this digestive stimulant with milk mixed with sugar;
constantly bathing, joyful, wearing white garments, pure,
devoted to the gods and Brahmins, gentle, such a pregnant woman shall be blessed with a son.
"One should not hold the teacher too high nor too low, nor for too long;
likewise, one should avoid causing agitation, laughter, and crowding," so said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the treatment for pregnant women. Now, we shall explain the chapter on the treatment for difficult labor (duṣprajātā). 1.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa:
"I shall indeed declare by name those diseases that arise in women who have had difficult births, as well as their medical treatment."
For those women who give birth with great difficulty or who suffer from ailments after delivery, the wind (vāyu) is quickly pacified by means of oleation and sudation; therefore,
a wise physician should administer a digestive stimulant gruel (yavāgū).
Just as a healthy woman sleeps soundly on a comfortable bed at night,
so too [the practitioner] [sleeps] due to the sudden arising of fear from departing during the night,
and from the suppression of various impulses such as envy, grief, terror, and anger.

Indeed, these and other diseases arise in women who have recently given birth due to sleeping during the day, indigestion, and overeating; [these include] a splitting sensation in the vagina, back, and hips, as well as disorders of the lateral channels, wind, and menorrhagia.

Vātāṣṭhīlā, gulma, pain in the heart, dysentery (pravāhikā), retention of feces and urine, flatulence, and indeed colic; the vagina swells and becomes morbid, and there is severe pain in the vagina (yoniśūla). 8–9.
Trembling, vomiting, delusion, stiffness of the neck, lockjaw, fever with diarrhea, erysipelas, ringworm,
scabies, eczema, kiṭibha eruptions, pustules on the body, and pain in half the head.
Heart diseases, eye diseases, splenic disorders, edema, and jaundice—
these and many other ailments arising from difficult births afflict the body; therefore, the medical treatment follows next.
The two *pañcamūla* groups, *bhārgī*, *madhuśigru*, *śatāvarī*, *uśīra*, *candana*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, and *madayantikā*;
the two *bale*, *vasuka*, *pāṭhā*, *payasyā*, and likewise *amṛtā*.
Vṛṣādanī, sugandhā, and likewise kāryā, punarnavā (14),
mūrvā, gṛdhranakhī, mustā, moraṭa, and tilvaka— one should collect the roots of these according to their availability (15).
Then, the best of physicians should boil three equal *prasthas* each of barley, jujube, and horse-gram in eight times that amount of water;
once it has been reduced to one-eighth, he should strain it thoroughly and set it aside.
In that case, one should add this supplementary powder of medicinal herbs:
long pepper, long pepper root, leadwort, elephant pepper, cumin, the two types of turmeric, ginger, sweet flag, and chebulic myrobalan. (17–18)
Kuṣṭha, rāsnā, ajamodā, viḍaṅga, marica,
bhadradāru, elā, bhārgī, and the seeds of kuṭaja— one karṣa each of these parts, with one pala of salt. (19)

One *prastha* of oil, one *prastha* of fat, and a decoction that is double that amount [two *prasthas*] should be used; likewise, one *prastha* of milk, one *prastha* of curd, and one *prastha* of water,
combined with half a *prastha* of the juice from the pulp of *mātuluṅga* and mango fruits.
Once it is prepared slowly over a mild fire, one should then remove it from the heat;
it is excellent for use as an unguent, for drinking, and for enema therapy (bastikarma).
As for those complications arising from wind (vāta) that afflict women in childbirth, [this is the remedy].
This excellent three-fold preparation (traivṛta) is the best for pacifying all [diseases].
Having boiled the paste of all these very same ingredients, one should have it drunk;
whatever disease of the postpartum woman (sūtikā) there may be, it shall cure it within three nights.
The two groups of five roots, bhārgī, rāsnā, the two types of punarnavā, śigru, and haṃsapadī—
[these are mentioned] in the chapter on the treatment of childhood seizures (bālagraha-cikitsita).
And despite being angry due to their lack of devotion toward Brahmins, she spoke with words full of favor in response to their entreaties:
"O Revatī, may you receive the fruit of these transgressions."
You alone shall be the foremost among all the grahas, equal to them in vigor, strength, and splendor;
you shall be invincible even to the gods and honored by them,
and people on earth shall call you "Nābhi" because of your many [qualities].
Vāruṇī, Revatī, Brāhmī, Kumārī, Bahuputrikā, Śuṣkā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Yamikā, Dharaṇī, Mukhamaṇḍikā, Mātā, Śītavatī, Kaṇḍū, Pūtanā, and Niruñcikā.
Rodanī, Bhūtamātā, Lokamātā,
Mahī, Śaraṇyā, and Puṇyakīrti— these are your twenty names,
O you whom faithful people on earth shall worship.
No fear shall ever arise for these from any living beings,
for that man who, being pure and free from sin, recites these twenty names morning and evening; his progeny shall increase.
Then, having propitiated Skanda again with fierce ascetic penance,
Guha, knowing her desire, spoke to Revatī:
"Nandikeśvara shall indeed be the fifth among your four brothers."
"You shall be known in the world as Bhaginī Ṣaṣṭhī;
just as they will worship me, so shall all embodied beings worship you. Possessing power equal to mine, you shall always remain in the midst of your brothers."
"Six-faced, eternally graceful, bestower of boons, and able to assume any form at will—
this sixth lunar day shall be honored by you and shall become meritorious in the world.
Thus was the sister Ṣaṣṭhī born to the wise Skanda.
Therefore, she should always be worshipped, for she is indeed the root of happiness and long life; for that reason, one should worship the Sūtikā-Ṣaṣṭhī and the Pakṣa-Ṣaṣṭhī,
dedicating them to the six-faced Ṣaṣṭhī, and thus one rejoices in the worlds.
Thus was Revatī born, she who is honored by gods and asuras.
O Vṛddhajīvaka, hear now her primary functions:
fever, dysentery, erysipelas, affliction, and the impairment of the sense organs.
Constipation, colic, loss of appetite, fainting, dyspnea,
cough, thirst, insomnia, excessive sleep, inflammation of the mouth, the appearance of ulcers, paralysis of a single limb, hemiplegia, exhaustion from lactation, and cholera.

Hiccups, fainting, intoxication, delusion, weeping, fixedness of the eyes, impairment of voice, complexion, and digestive fire, paleness, jaundice, restlessness, corruption and destruction of breast milk, headache, and a sense of melting in the heart.
Diseases of the nose, eyes, and ears, as well as trembling, contraction, and weeping—
whatever other various diseases have not been specifically mentioned are for the most part declared to be born from the wrath of Revatī.
Therefore, a wise person should perform its treatment as a common procedure;
for some say it is Revatī, while others call it Graha.
[The herbs used are] Aśvagandhā, Ajashṛṅgī, the two types of Sārivā, and the two types of Punarnavā.
A decoction of *kṣudrā*, *sahā*, and *vidārī* is used for sprinkling; likewise, *palankaṣā*, *sarjarasa*, *kuṣṭha*, *girikadambaka*,
*devadāru*, *samañjiṣṭha*, *surā*, oil, and *suvarcikā*.
One should prepare equal parts of *nalada*, *tumbaru*, and cinnamon bark;
by anointing the body with this, one subsequently becomes comfortable.
[Likewise, one may use] the flowers of *aśvakarṇa*, *dhātakī*, and *tinduka*.
One should boil the flowers of *kakubha*, as well as those of *dāḍima* and *dhava*, along with *tvakṣīrī* and *madhuka*, together with milk; then,
if a child drinks an appropriate dose of this, he becomes healthy and happy.

Ghee cooked with these very [substances] destroys diarrhea and anorexia; when combined with sugar and honey, it cures thirst, loss of appetite, and vomiting. Furthermore, the feathers of an owl and a vulture, bitter bottle-gourd, and ajaṭī [are used for this purpose].
White barley, cow’s ghee, and this drink for one afflicted by the Revatī star— both Varuṇa and Ariṣṭaka, as well as Putrañjīvaka and Citraka—
their bark should be held by the infant, the mother, and the nurse.
One should pacify the complications by means of their respective medical treatments;
when the child is under the asterism Revatī, one should perform rites for prosperity.
Hereafter, I shall explain the treatment for Pūtanā.
One should administer all those aforementioned medicines;
for the asura named Dundubhi, who causes terror to both gods and asuras,
fought with Skanda out of delusion, and having seen the six-faced one enraged, [he fled].

Skanda entered the cave of his maternal uncle, the great mountain Krauñca; and with a spear, he struck that great mountain, his maternal uncle, and that Dānava simultaneously— therefore he is called Guha because of his slaying of Guha.
Having fallen from his caste, Guha was approached by the gods and asuras,
the quarters, the oceans, the rivers, the great elements, and the clouds,
who then fumigated him for the sake of purification; thereupon, Guha became purified.
In the very place where the blessed and pure Skanda of great strength was born, Pūtanā, who causes terror to all the worlds, appeared;
there Guha spoke to that auspicious Pūtanā as she stood before him.
When she was told, "You who have transgressed the bounds of propriety," she replied, "So be it.
She is known by five names: Malajā, Pūtanā, Kauñjī, Vaiśvadevī, and Pāvanī. Listen now to her treatment.
Karañja, śobhāñjanaka, āsphoṭā, āṭarūṣaka,
saptaparṇa, nimba, and bhārgī are for sprinkling;
along with surā and sauvīraka, there are yellow orpiment and realgar.
One should cook a medicated oil for external massage using *kuṣṭha*, *sarjarasa*, *pippalī*,
*pippalīmūla*, *bṛhatī*, *kaṇṭakārikā*, *śālaparṇī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *madhūka*, and likewise *madhuka*.
Having gathered these ingredients together, one should cook ghee in milk;
this ghee will pacify vomiting and hiccup for one who consumes it. [One should also use] the excrement of a cock, its feathers, and old skin.
One should employ this fumigation, which brings happiness at the time of twilight: an old monk’s outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*), snake-cast-off skin, and ghee,
along with *anantā*, *kukkuṭī*, *bimbī*, *ariṣṭā*, and *karkaṭī*.
One should wear these, strung together with thread, on the hands and feet;
by means of treatments for eye diseases, one should pacify Andhapūtanā,
and by means of treatments for Śītaṅkāra, one should pacify Śītapūtanā.

A wise person should cook ghee with long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), chaba pepper (cavya), leadwort (citraka), ginger (nāgara), the five roots (pañcamūlī), and rock salt (saindhava);
this medicated ghee is proclaimed by the Great-souled One as "the digestive stimulant" (dīpanīya).
A linctus made from rāsnā, punarnavā, kuṣṭha, tagara, devadāru, patra, aguru, hareṇu, guḍūcī, triphalā, and sugar, mixed with honey, should be licked to pacify śītapūtanā.
One should cook ghee with these along with the ten roots (daśamūla) and four times as much milk;
once purified, one should have the child lick it, and thus Kaṭapūtana is pacified.
[Likewise, one may use] Bilva, Aṅkoṭha, Kapittha, Arka, Kārpāsa, and Maṭarūṣaka.
One should cook oil or ghee with milk, using the leaves of uruvūka, vaṃśa, and aśmantaka, along with prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, śatapuṣpā, and punarnavā.
Having anointed the body with this [oil], one should administer this alkaline preparation;
furthermore, one should drink a decoction of *mṛdvīkā*, *payasyā*, *śrīparṇī*, *sārivā*, as well as *madhūka* and *nāgapuṣpa*, combined with *śītapākī*.
Then, combined with sugar and honey, it becomes effective for his well-being;
thereafter, one should diligently administer fumigation to him morning and evening,
using golomī, the sloughed skin of a snake, vacā, and siddhārthaka.
Having mixed it with clarified butter, the physician should fumigate [the child] at the two twilights;
this is the remedy for Andhapūtanā, consisting of bilva, aṅkoṭha, and other ingredients.
Formerly, immediately after his birth, Skanda was [treated] in the presence of Umā and Śaṅkara.

He adorned the six-faced one with perfumes, ornaments, flowers, and other such items; he applied collyrium to his forehead-eye and fashioned various decorative marks upon his nose, cheeks, chin, and mouth.
Then the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and their hosts likewise delighted him;
thereafter, out of his childhood nature, the blessed Guha said to his mother:
"Let this very mass of Mahādeva’s matted hair be my ornament."
"Give it to me," he said repeatedly and firmly, yet Guha did not obtain it.
Becoming angry, the ever-playful Guha threw everything down upon the ground, wiped his face, and spat out the entire amount.
Thereupon the three worlds became agitated, their knowledge lost and their minds bewildered;
the couple, too, being deeply distressed, gave him the nectar-born [child].
From that time forward, the moon has been seen upon the heads of the seven [Ṛṣis].
