From the face of the high-souled Nandin— Rudraskanda and the others— as well as from the face of Revatī, which had been cast off by Skanda in his wrath, there arose that terrible graha known as Mukhamandikā.
As if wishing to consume her with his wrath, Guha then said to her,
"O illustrious lady, prepare food for those whose forms and deeds are mixed.
And Skanda’s attendant replied, "So be it."
Thus was Mukhāci born; hear now her treatment:
oil prepared with *kapittha*, *bilva*, *tarkārī*, *bimbi*, and *gandharvahastaka* is beneficial as an anointing for the infant.
One should cook ghee with the minor five roots (khuḍḍāka-pañcamūla), śyonāka, madhūlikā, madhūka flowers, the bark of milky trees (kṣīrī), and long pepper (pippalī);
this should be prepared with cow's milk that has been boiled, combined with sugar and honey.
A child should drink one kola-measure [of this]; thereafter he becomes healthy.
As for fumigation, one should use kuṣṭha, resin of the sarja tree, barley, and ghee.
Alternatively, there is the wearing of a jewel made from the tongues of a snake, a vīralla bird, and a blue jay (cāṣa).
Once that has been digested, one should then administer even food to him;
after this, I shall describe [the treatment] for one afflicted by Śītapūtanā:
Nādeyī, Surasā, Bimbī, Kapittha, and likewise Jīvaka.
Having decocted this [mixture of] *nadībhallātaka*, *śyāmā*, *bilva*, and *śītaśiva*, one should sprinkle with lukewarm water;
now hear about the oil for anointing one who has been sprinkled with this.
One should cook oil for anointment using cow urine, goat urine, mustaka, devadāru, kuṣṭha, and all fragrant substances (sarvagandha),
along with khadira, the heartwood of rohiṇī, palāśa, and the bark of kakubha.
Having gathered these ingredients, one should cook ghee in milk;
when it is prepared, one should have the patient lick it at the proper time with a measured amount of sugar and honey.
One who has been seized by Śītapūtanā is liberated from it, provided they maintain a wholesome diet.
One should collect the excrement of vultures, owls, and hyenas;
and for one seized by Śītapūtanā, this is the treatment: an ointment made from goat’s hair and *picumanda* as an incense fumigation.
Henceforth, listen to the general remedy for all [these conditions]:
agnimantha, kurabaka, varuṇa, pāribhadraka, niśā, anala, poṭagala, pūtikā, and likewise rohiṣa.
Listen now to the oil for anointing one who has been sprinkled with this:
priyaṅgu, rocanā, śatapuṣpā, kuṭannaṭa, tālīsapatra, nalada, as well as candana and sārivā.
Oil prepared with equal parts of madhūka, aṅkoṭha, mañjiṣṭhā, pṛthvīkā, and bhūtikā, combined with water containing green gram and sour gruel—
when a child is anointed with this, the Pitṛ-graha spirit quickly releases him.

One should cause to be administered here a decoction of *bimbi*, *kāśmarya*, *madhuka*, horse gram (*kulattha*), jujube (*badara*), barley (*yava*), and the small pentad of roots (*khuḍḍāka-pañcamūla*),
as well as dates (*kharjūra*), *mustaka*, and coconut fruits.
Nālikā, aṅkura, mṛdvīkā, madhūka, and likewise madhuka— these, when dried and powdered, [are used];
this is the chapter on the treatment of splenic enlargement and halīmaka.
There occurs a depletion of digestive fire and strength,
along with fainting, thirst, giddiness, drowsiness, despondency, anorexia, and heaviness; the wise physician should apply a treatment for that which alleviates vāta and pitta.
Buffalo ghee prepared with the fresh juice of *guḍūcī* and milk should first be used for mild oleation;
thereafter, one who knows the proper time and strength should induce purgation by means of an appropriate dose of *trivṛt* combined with the juice of *āmalaka*.
One should always have the patient who has been purged consume sweet and non-burning foods;
however, for one who is weak, *guḍaharītakī* (haritaki with jaggery) should be administered daily,
and whatever medicine is prescribed for *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) is also recommended here.
One āḍhaka of the fresh juice of ripe āmalaka fruits should be prepared;
one prastha of ghee should be cooked with these— pippalī, madhuka, drākṣā, candana, uśīra, and bālaka— and once cooked, sugar should be added.
One who eats wholesome food in the morning with *tālīśa* and honey shall become free from disease;
this should be administered when *pitta* is predominant. Now listen: however, when *vāta* is predominant, one should employ *kalyāṇaka-taila*, *balā-taila*, or *kaumāra-taila*.

One should administer the same medicinal treatment for jaundice (kāmalā), anemia (pāṇḍu), and edema (śotha); furthermore, Agastyaharītakī should be constantly consumed by one who follows a wholesome diet.
Thus said the venerable Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the treatment of *plīhā* (enlarged spleen) and *ahalīmaka* (a type of anemia). Now, we shall expound the chapter on the treatment of *udāvarta* (upward movement of wind). 1.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa:

From the consumption of astringent, pungent, bitter, dry, cold, putrid, and dried vegetables, as well as parched grain, sun-dried meat, oil-cakes, *suniṣaṇṇaka*, *dugdhikā*, *kodrava*, *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, barley, *kaṭṭa*, the tips of *vetra* reeds, *karkandhū*, *kapittha*, *bilva*, *karīra*, *gāṅgerukī*, *likuca*, *pārāvata*, *bhavya*, sour gruel (*kāñjika*), fermented vinegar (*śukta*), *āranāla*, water boiled with husks (*tuṣodaka*), *mudga*, *kalāya*, *atasī*, and so forth; and from the suppression of natural urges by one whose self is parched and whose constitution is predominantly Vāta—the Vāyu becomes provoked, drives the body upward, and being repelled by the Udāna wind, reaches the rectum and the internal receptacle.

Having caused the downward-flowing channels to contract and having vitiated the passages of feces, urine, phlegm, bile, wind, and semen, it obstructs them; thereupon, it produces a life-threatening condition characterized by constipation (ānāha) or its specific symptoms.

In an infant who consumes milk, the milk becomes undigested due to the following causes: being carried on the hip for too long, suppression of the bladder and rectum, excessive crying, staying awake at night, lack of oiliness, not consuming milk, suppressing natural urges, fasting, eating insufficiently, irregular eating, staying awake, mental distress, jealousy, and constant physical exertion. When that milk is consumed while in such a state, it leads to *udāvarta* (upward movement of bodily humors). In this regard, there are six types of *udāvarta*: they are said to be six because they result from the suppression and non-discharge of flatus (*vāta*), feces (*viṣ*), urine (*mūtra*), semen (*śukra*), vomiting (*chardi*), and sneezing (*kṣavathu*).

Because it shares common characteristics with udāvarta, some authorities refer to this condition as that very same disorder. The symptoms and medicinal treatments for those [types of udāvarta] have already been described in the chapter on the suppression of natural urges (navegāndhāraṇīya). However, because this disease is particularly severe, we shall provide some further instruction here as well. The patient is constantly afflicted by colic, fainting, burning sensations, flatulence, distension, aversion to the urge to defecate, discoloration, loss of consciousness, stumbling, falling, lamentation, thirst, hiccups, dyspnea, excessive perspiration, and a cutting pain like glowing coals. There is pain in the bladder, rectum, heart, flanks, groin, and abdomen, along with weakness in the thighs and various aches; these are the symptoms of sudāvarta. It occurs first in five [days].
The premonitory symptoms are as follows:

first, one should treat a person who has been anointed with warm oil and salt and whose body has been appropriately fomented by means of *phalavarti* (medicated suppositories). Once the [disease] has been loosened, for the sake of strength and to prevent complications, one should provide the patient with a diet consisting primarily of warm, unctuous, sweet, and salty foods—namely, preparations of barley, wheat, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice; leafy vegetables; ghee; and the meat of animals from marshy or aquatic habitats.

One should insert into the rectum, using a probe, suppositories made from the seeds of *kośātakī*, *kaṣṭvā*, and *alābu*, along with long pepper (*pippalī*), rock salt (*saindhava*), asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), *vacā*, yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), realgar (*manaḥśilā*), and powdered black gram (*māṣa*), ground with cow’s urine; these may be smeared with clarified butter or pungent oil. The regimen of care is exactly as before. Furthermore, one should apply those same unctuous and warm treatments as ointments, coverings, washes, and foods for the patient.

One should feed [the patient] barley-gruel prepared with ghee along with vegetables such as *saktuvāṭya*, *kulmāṣa*, cakes, *vāstuka*, barley, greens, *sudhā* leaves, *trivṛt* shoots, *pañcāṅgula*, *śrīvārikā*, *śrīphala*, *suvarcalā*, *kākamācī*, *kalāya*, *pālaṅkyā*, and others. Alternatively, one should administer *trivṛt*, *pīlu*, barley, and *utkāra* with cow’s urine. Or, *trivṛt*, *harītakī*, *śyāmā*, and *sudhā* combined with milk or urine act as a breaker of constipation (*ānāha*).

One should prepare pills the size of an *āmalaka* fruit from the powders of *triphalā*, *dantī*, *śyāmā*, *trivṛt*, *kampillaka*, *pīlu*, *svarṇakṣīrī*, *vacā*, *saptalā*, *nīlikā*, and *grahaghnī*, using the milky sap of the *sudhā* plant. Then, by eating one pill and following it with a drink of warm water or urine, one is liberated from [the effects of] poisons within a day.

These same ingredients beginning with *triphalā*, excluding milk and urine, are made into a powder together with the five pungents (*pañcakaṭuka*), the five salts, *hiṅgu*, *kuṣṭha*, the two types of alkali (*kṣāra*), *śatapuṣpā*, *pāṭhā*, and *śrīphala*. This powder, taken in a dose the size of a cat's paw (*biḍālapadaka*) with either milk, wine, warm water, or cow’s urine, is called the *Nārāca* powder; it is the destroyer of flatulence, colic, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), fistula-in-ano, and hemorrhoids.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
If one should neglect these therapeutic procedures for upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*), [the result will be as follows].
One should prepare for him a Nirūha enema containing oil, heat, and salt, as well as an Āsthāpana enema. —
Chapter on the Treatment of Rājayakṣman.
This is the destroyer of the host of diseases.
Twenty excellent *pippalī* fruits boiled in half an *āḍhaka* of water,
reduced to one-fourth, [should be mixed] with an equal amount of goat's milk.

One suffering from consumption should drink this decoction daily; by that alone one should always eat, or even without food or water according to one's strength. One who is devoted to this practice is liberated after twelve years, provided they have been treated with oleation and sudation and have purified their system.
One should drink five long peppers with milk and increase the dose by five each time until reaching one hundred; then, one should decrease it in the same manner while abstaining from food and water.
This "Increasing Long Pepper" regimen is the destroyer of all diseases.
Alternatively, one hundred pippalīs should always be boiled in one āḍhaka of water until reduced to one-fourth; this should then be cooked again with an equal amount of milk.
If kapha is predominant, it should be taken with honey; if vāta is predominant, with ghee.
In a condition where pitta is predominant, one becomes comfortable by consuming [the medicine] with sugar;
however, the *pippalī-vardhamāna* regimen is beneficial when vāta and kapha are predominant.
In all cases, *pippalī* with milk is beneficial, as determined by the observation of the season and other factors.
At the onset of autumn, having uprooted the roots of *nāgabalā* and dried them while keeping them in a new vessel, one who is celibate, has conquered his senses,
and avoids women and *śūdras*, should administer the powder with milk in a secluded place.
On the first day, one should take one karṣa, and thereafter increase the dose;
from then on, the pure person should drink it daily with milk, increasing by one pala each time. When that medicine has been digested, he should drink milk, avoiding both solid food and water.
Within a month, Nāgabalā cures consumption along with its complications in men;
moreover, it bestows progeny, longevity, strength, and intelligence upon the diligent practitioner.
Within six months, one becomes a retainer of all that has been heard and is freed from all diseases.
Even an eighty-year-old man may become young again within a year by means of this procedure involving *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, *śuṇṭhī*, *brāhmī*, and *madhuka*;
it possesses those same qualities as the aforementioned method and, like the *nāgabalā* regimen, destroys all diseases.
Massaged with goat dung and sprinkled with goat urine,
he should drink nothing but goat's milk and dwell together with goats;
by living beneath a pit for goats, one afflicted by consumption is liberated.
This is indeed an elixir (rasāyana) that destroys wasting diseases and increases strength.
Two hundred of the best *harītakī* fruits, having been crushed,
[are combined with] the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *sudhā*, *dantī*, *karañja*, *adhoguḍa*, and *asanā*.
Having crushed together mayūraka, devadāru, nicula, kuṭaja, aṭarūṣaka, kaṭaṅkaṭerī, bṛhatī, rāsnā, śyonāka, citraka, and varuṇa— twenty-five palas in total—

One should boil this in six *droṇas* of water until it has been reduced to five *āḍhakas*. Once it is strained, one should add a *tulā* of jaggery and cook it further; observing that it has turned thick, one should place it in a vessel of clarified butter.
One should add long pepper (marica), embelia (viḍaṅga), bhārgī, indra-yava, cumin seeds (kuṭabīja), and one prastha of long pepper (pippalī);
having mixed these with one prastha of honey, one should administer it after a month has passed.
One who eats wholesome food in the proper measure at the right time is freed from diseases born of *kapha*;
this is known as the *Mahābhayāriṣṭa* formulated by Kaśyapa.
[The ingredients are] *apāmārga*, *aśvagandhā*, *nākulī*, and white mustard seeds.
A paste of sesame seeds and bilva is beneficial as an ointment for wasting diseases.
One hundred palas of dehusked garlic, crushed into pieces,
should be boiled in ten droṇas of water until reduced to one-fourth.

One should cook two āḍhakas of ghee there with the "life-giving" (jīvana) herbs, along with one droṇa of goat’s milk and a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla). This secret ghee should be administered after a month has passed.
This "Indrāṇī-ghṛta" (clarified butter of Indrāṇī) destroys pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣma*);
it grants the desires of barren women, eunuchs, and the elderly, provided they consume wholesome food.
Alternatively, one may administer garlic according to the prescribed method.
Having placed one āḍhaka of aged garlic into half an āḍhaka of cow's ghee within a vessel of ghee, one should store it among grains for a year,
or for six months, eight months, or four months thereafter.
By drinking [this] like *nāgabalā*, one is liberated from all diseases;
one should cook grape-ghee according to the procedure for *indrāṇī*-ghee,
and likewise, by using *pīlu*-ghee, one is liberated from all diseases.
Sacrificial offerings, the Rohiṇī-bath, the performance of auspicious rites for those two,
worship of Rudra, fortitude, purity, and celibacy are prescribed for the sake of pacification;
these are said to be the six and eleven forms of the consumptive disease (yakṣman).
"The very same complications [arise] when those [diseases] are not pacified; this is one's own medical treatment," so indeed said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the treatment for *rājayakṣman* among the treatments.
The Chapter on the Treatment of Gulma.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment for those afflicted with gulma;
thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Arising from all types of blood disorders such as wind (vāta) and others, and located in the abdomen, heart, flanks, and bladder,
these five foremost gulmas (abdominal tumors) caused by the five [doshas] have been demonstrated in the Sūtra.
When the doshas of men become aggravated due to common factors such as activities, food, and drink, [they produce these diseases].
Taking their seat in the stomach (āmāśaya), they then produce abdominal tumors (gulma).
One who is dominated by vāta, becoming attached to foods and drinks that increase vāta,
runs, leaps, floats, studies excessively, sings, and dances.
One who indulges in cold winds and water, who is fond of cold, dry, and pungent things, and who— afflicted by disease, emaciated, and parched— consumes sharp medicine,
may forcibly provoke vomiting or even cause oneself to vomit.
One who suppresses the wind (vāta) and other humors, or drinks excessively when satiated;
one who travels by fast conveyance, or indulges excessively in sexual intercourse;
or one who is young, dry-tempered, and addicted to physical exercise, study, and women—[these are causes of hemorrhoids]. 7–8.
Provoked by these and other factors, the wind (vāta) accumulates a collection of humors (doṣa-saṃcaya);
wherever it settles in that location, a gulma is formed there.
It causes the destruction of the digestive fire (agni-nāśa), loss of appetite (aruci), colic (śūla), vomiting (chardi), eructation (udgāra), and rumbling in the intestines (antra-kūjana).
The passage of feces with difficulty, emaciation, and abdominal tumors are the premonitory signs (10).
Pain, fainting, fever, pricking sensations, emaciation, thirst, a reddish complexion, and pain in the flanks, shoulders, and eyes are the symptoms of Vata-gulma (11).
One should recognize fever, burning sensations, thirst, diarrhea,
and yellowness as occurring in a Pitta-type Gulma (abdominal tumor) in those who consume Pitta-aggravating foods and hot substances.
(12) Horripilation, fever, vomiting, anorexia, and a sense of constriction in the heart [are also present].
In one suffering from a kaphaja gulma, there is whiteness of the urine, eyes, nails, and feces, as well as coldness. All these symptoms are observed in the sannipatika type.
A blood-born (rakta) gulma arises in the female genital tract, but never in men.

She who has given birth to stillborn infants, she who suffers from repeated miscarriages, she who engages in excessive sexual intercourse, she who craves pregnancy immediately after her period, she whose menstrual flow is excessively cold, she who habitually suppresses natural urges, and she who consumes food that aggravates the wind (vāta) [constitute those unfit for conception]. 15.
In a woman whose vāta has become aggravated, it enters the womb; it obstructs the menstrual flow and causes it to accumulate there month after month.
When the blood has thus accumulated, the woman thinks, "I am pregnant. (16–17)
Darkness appears on the area of the breasts, there is a line of body hair, and she experiences constant longing; she assumes all the indistinct characteristics of a pregnant woman,
while jaundice, paleness, and emaciation become even more pronounced.
Thus, they describe the blood-gulma (raktagulma) of women by these characteristics.
A mass that resembles a tumor (gulma) is called gulma because it is a collection of many doṣas;
except for that which arises from all three doṣas, gulmas that have been present for a long time are not curable.
First, the physician should treat a gulma that has been prepared with oleation and sudation using medicines that pacify the respective doshas; furthermore,
nourishing therapy should be used for excessive gulmas, and strong drying therapy for those that are excessively parched.
Furthermore, excessive purification is not recommended for those suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma).
Take one akṣa each of abhayā, pippalī, vyoṣa, yāvaśūka, citraka, sauvarcala, viḍaṅga, and vacā. (22–23)
One should drink one *prastha* of this ghee when it is properly cooked, according to one's strength;
this "ten-ingredient ghee" (*daśāṅga-ghṛta*) is a remedy for *vāta-gulma*. [The ten ingredients are:
rock salt (*saindhava*), barley-alkali (*yāvaśūka*), long pepper (*pippalī*), and elephant pepper (*hastipippalī*).
Take six parts each of one pala of ginger and *citraka*;
with an equal amount of milk, cook one *prastha* of ghee. This is called *ṣaṭpala*; physicians declare that for all types of abdominal tumors (*gulma*), it is like nectar.
The physician should cook ghee with equal parts of milk and one akṣa each of these: abhayā, pippalī, drākṣā, guḍūcī, punarnavā, lavaṇa, kṣāra, gandharvā, bhārgī, rāsnā, and rasāñjana. (27)
That ghee named Śaiśuka is a remedy for vāta-gulma (abdominal tumors caused by wind). Thereafter,
once the patient suffering from gulma has been lubricated, fomented,
and restored to health, one should induce purgation with a mild laxative or with oil extracted from castor seeds.

After the patient has been purged, one should feed them at the appropriate time with food that is not excessively dry, but rather moderately sour, salty, and hot, and containing a suitable amount of fat and meat broth; one should always feed the patient suffering from gulma while avoiding foods heavy due to their etiological factors.
Excessive eating is never recommended for those suffering from all types of gulma (abdominal tumors/lumps).
[One should instead take] pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, nāgara, bilva, kapittha, badara, vṛṣaka, and gaṇikārikā. (31–32)
One should powder equal parts of asafoetida, pomegranate, jīvantī, vṛkṣāmla, amlavetasa, puṣkaramūla, śaṭī, dantī, all types of salts,
the two alkalis, and ajamoda when they are dry. (33)
These balls, resembling jujube fruits, are prepared with the juice of citron;
the physician should prescribe them to be drunk with warm water, wine, or sour liquids.
They destroy vāta-gulma, udāvarta, and splenic pain.

One suffering from vātagulma should always eat peacocks, partridges, cranes, pigeons, and wild cocks, as well as barley, wheat, and śāli rice. However, if the vātagulma does not subside even while being treated with oleation therapy (sneha), [other measures should be employed].
For those suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma) with constipated stools, non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) and likewise unctuous enemas (anuvāsana) are beneficial;
one should also administer Abhayā (Harītakī) with jaggery, followed by a draught of milk. 37.
For those suffering from abdominal tumors with constipated stools—
The chapter on the treatment of skin diseases (kuṣṭha):
perspiration, excessive hardness of the limbs, or excessive smoothness, discoloration, dryness, horripilation, thirst, heaviness, redness, debility, and trembling.
The appearance of pustules and ulcers, excessive pain, and the spreading of wounds.

Thereafter, leprosy (kuṣṭha) arises in those who do not engage in [therapeutic] action. Among these, one should recognize those dominated by Vāta by dark-reddish discoloration, pain, itching, a stinging sensation, roughness, dryness, stiffness, and stretching; those dominated by Pitta by burning sensations, pain, fever, diarrhea, suppuration, discharge, eruptions (koṭha), and rapid onset, as well as by a craving for cold, sweet, and astringent things and for ghee; and those dominated by Kapha by white or pale, thick, elevated, heavy, numb, and stiff lesions, extensive involvement, loss of digestive fire, and a craving for things other than cold.

The *sānnipātika* (arising from the combination of all three humors) is called *kākaṇaka* because of its reddish color; it is characterized by mangled forms, extensive cracking, exudation, worms, burning sensations, and pain, with the falling off of body parts, foul odor, abundant swelling, and many complications. We shall now explain the other types born of two humors—their summary characteristics are as follows: *kapālakuṣṭha* when wind (*vāta*) predominates, *audumbara* when bile (*pitta*) predominates, *maṇḍalakuṣṭha* when phlegm (*kapha*) predominates; *ṛṣyajihva* arises from wind and bile, while *pauṇḍarīka* and *sidhma* arise from bile and phlegm. This is the summary definition.

In detail, there are eighteen types of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), which we shall explain individually: *sidhma*, *vicarcikā*, *pāmā*, *dadru*, *kiṭibha*, *kapāla*, *sthūlāruṣka*, *maṇḍalakuṣṭha*, and *visarpa*—these nine are curable; while *pauṇḍarīka*, *śvitra*, *ṛṣyajihva*, *śatāruṣka*, *audumbara*, *kākaṇa*, *carmadala*, *ekakuṣṭha*, and *vipādikā*—these nine are incurable.

All types of *kuṣṭha* (leprosy/skin diseases), however, reside in the skin, flesh, blood, and lymph; they impair the sense of touch and, as they progress (*vardhamāna*), cause deformity. Specifically, *sidhma* resembles a dust-covered gourd flower or a *vāraṇapuṣpī* blossom. *Vicarcikā* is characterized by dark-red ulcers with pain, discharge, and suppuration. *Pāmā* is marked by itching, swelling, suppuration, discharge, and heat. *Dadru* consists of spreading circular patches that possess dryness, itching, burning, and discharge, which increase in size and become heavy and then subside. These [lesions] are characterized by black, dark-brown, or reddish discharges that are rough, harsh, and increasing. They eventually become heavy and then subside.

Furthermore, they arise repeatedly as *kiṭibha* eruptions—black, rough, harsh, and dirty, appearing in various circular shapes (*maṇḍala*). During the seasonal transitions and in the heat, it causes great distress; shaped like a skull, it is a "skull" (*kapāla*) that involves the discharge of slimy secretions, pain, burning, itching, fever, erysipelas, and the formation of large ulcers. Resembling something both soft and hard, it is a "greatly inflamed" (*mahāruṣka*) condition characterized by circles resembling the flowers of the *bandhujīvaka*, accompanied by burning, itching, pain, and discharge; this is known as *maṇḍalakuṣṭha*. It occurs when one is bitten by spiders, insects, moths, or snakes, and the wound is neglected.

Through transgression, it becomes as hard as a donkey’s hoof; difficult to cure, born from poison, characterized by great swelling, and breaking open after a long time—this is *puṇḍarīka*, which has the color of a lotus petal. Due to its white appearance, it is called *śvitra*. We shall describe these five types later. *Ṛṣyajihva* resembles the tongue of a deer, being rough, discolored, heavy-colored, and exuding moisture. *Śatāruṣka* is afflicted by many rough, oozing eruptions that are blue, red, yellow, and black. [The type resembling] a ripe *udumbara* fruit is non-exuding (*asrāvi*).

One should recognize *kuṣṭha* (leprosy) as being dull-witted, manifold, and of the *audumbara* type; it is described as resembling a crow's foot, like an elephant's hide, rough, and characterized by increasing skin-scales. The *vaisarpa* type arises from spreading eruptions, constantly oozing, painful, and infested with worms. *Ekakuṣṭha* is characterized by cracking, oozing, and pain in the hands, feet, thumbs, lips, and shins. One should know *vipādikā* as a non-healing condition involving cracking and discharge. Indeed, all diseases, if neglected out of delusion, become incurable; those that are incurable quickly destroy men. Therefore, for one’s own welfare, one should strive promptly.

In cases of skin diseases (kuṣṭha) where vāta is predominant, the drinking of clear ghee (ghṛtāccha) interspersed with gruel (maṇḍa) several times is recommended; likewise, bitter ghee (tiktasarpiḥ) is recommended for the subsequent two types [of kuṣṭha]. This concludes the chapter on the treatment of vomiting, purgation, non-unctuous enemas, and dysuria.
When pitta becomes aggravated by excessive carrying of loads on the hips and shoulders, it follows kapha and vāta; when these then vitiate the bladder, which is their locus,
a severe dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) arises in the person at that time.
Urine that is frothy, scanty, reddish, or dark,
accompanied by continuous colic, constipation, burning sensation, pain, yellowness, excessive heat, and steaminess, is the characteristic of Vātāghāta (urinary obstruction caused by Vāta).
In the Pitta-type [mūtrāghāta], the infant passes urine with a burning sensation in the mouth;
in the Kapha-type, he passes urine that is copious, with little distress, white, and thick,
accompanied by heaviness and swelling of the bladder.

That which arises from a combination of two [humors] is known by the forms of those two; that which arises from all three combined (sānnipātika) should be understood as being like pitta, because the urine is passed with blood. Specifically, in the case of that produced by the combination of all three, there are fainting, giddiness, and delirium.
In all [types of prameha], emaciation, restlessness, loss of appetite, instability, thirst, colic, despondency, and excessive [discharge] are the complications;
the pramehas manifest slowly, whereas the kṛcchras afflict embodied beings immediately.
The specific distinction regarding painful urination (kṛcchramēha) is that there is a burning sensation in the urinary organ;
painful urinations are quickly cured, whereas pramehas are persistent.
Those pramehas characterized by a predominance of pitta and those located in the seat of vāta are difficult to cure.
Therefore, treatment shall indeed be taught by way of general principles:
having boiled the roots of the Śara grass, one should drink that water when it is cold,
strained, and mixed with sugar and honey, for the alleviation of dysuria.
Madhuka, the root of śara, triphalā, and sitavārikā,
boiled together with sugar and honey, prevent dysuria;
one should also administer the decoction of the tārṇa-pañcamūla after it has been properly extracted.
Combined with sugar and honey, it wards off all types of dysuria;
likewise, a linctus made of śatāvarī, pṛthakparṇī, kulattha, and badara,
combined with sugar and honey, removes urinary retention.
One should prescribe a treatment for dysuria that is the opposite of that for polyuria;
the medicine, drink, and food should be very unctuous and mild,
and one should administer purgatives that are sweet, such as products of sugarcane, cucumbers, ghee, and milk.
One should always consume that which is constipating and avoid that which causes burning; likewise, one should regularly take ūṣaka, the two types of bṛhatī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, both types of vasuka,
ginger, barley, darbha grass, vṛkṣādanī, and balā.

Milk boiled with these [drugs] along with long pepper (pippalī), and mixed with a measured amount of ghee, should be administered in cases of painful micturition accompanied by blood; by this, one is quickly cured.
One should also use the minor five roots (kanīyasī pañcamūlī), horse gram (kulattha), and jujube fruits (badara).
A linctus combined with sugar and honey is beneficial for urinary retention;
for obstructed urination (mūtrāghāta), a meat broth mixed with rock salt and clarified butter should be prepared,
either with the five roots including Tārkṣya or with Rāsnā and Gokṣura.
The two types of karañja, nigarbhā, kārpāsa, madhuśigruka, śvadaṃṣṭrā, the two types of vasuka, lotus stalks, blue lotuses,
long peppers, rock salt, small cardamom, and black pepper.
The child should drink this prepared gruel along with *suvarcalā*;
or one should administer a linctus made from these same medicinal herbs combined with sugar and honey;
likewise, clarified butter cooked with these [herbs] should be used as a remedy that wards off difficult urination.
The minor *pañcamūlī* (the five roots) together with the five spices (*pañcakola*) and barley, along with horse gram (*kulattha*), sweet *śigru*, and sesame,
should be prepared as a meat broth (*rasa*) with a small amount of fat and combined with *sauvarcala* salt.
This should be administered in cases of urinary obstruction, especially in cases of gravel (śarkarā).
The painful urination (kṛcchra) arising from the three doṣas combined has symptoms identical to those of gravel;
the stones may resemble gold dust or be similar in appearance to mustard seeds.
Just as curd forms from the bile of cows when agitated by wind,
so too, when the urine of those of evil deeds is churned and stirred up by Vāta,
gravel (śarkarā) is formed; and when these increase, they then become stones (aśmarī).
This is their characteristic; however, in some individuals, the pain is constant and the gravel is expelled along with the urine.
But when a stone (*aśmarī*) accompanied by a foreign body (*śalyavatī*) develops in the bladder, it remains there.
As it is being diminished, it wastes away; as it is being nourished, it thrives.
Therefore, it does not cause constant pain; its extraction is desired.
The extraction of the stone involves a sharp medicinal procedure for the purpose of clearing the urinary channel.
"Kaśyapa does not desire anything [administered] with force to those who are very young," so said the Blessed Kaśyapa;
thus ends the chapter on the treatment of dysuria in the Section on Therapeutics.
Now begins the chapter on the treatment of the two types of ulcers.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "On the Two Types of Ulcers.
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
In the Sūtrasthāna, two types of wounds were proclaimed by the Blessed One;
I desire to hear their detailed exposition as well as their characteristics, along with the activities, diet, and medicines for the benefit of the ignorant. (3)
Thus questioned by his disciple, that Prajāpati, having honored him, spoke:
"One who proclaims the rules of this tantra without providing detail does not shine among the virtuous, like a greedy crow perched upon an offering."
This must necessarily be understood by a physician without malice;

therefore, O friend, listen for a moment out of a desire for the welfare of children. Now, indeed, there are two types of wounds: endogenous (*nija*) and exogenous (*āgantuka*). The endogenous arises from wind (*vāta*) and the others—each individually or from the combination of all two. The exogenous arises from injury, fracture, piercing, incision, burning, cutting, crushing, or from weapons, grass, wood, fire, poison, teeth, nails, curses, spells, roots, rituals, and so forth. Its treatment is exactly like that of the endogenous.

One should apply the characteristics and medicinal treatments according to one's own reasoning. One should recognize the Vātika [type] by stiffness, hardness, scanty discharge, piercing pain, pricking, throbbing, and an astringent taste in the mouth; one should recognize the Paittika [type] by fever, burning sensation, delusion, thirst, rapid suppuration, redness, cracking, loss of appetite, and foul odor; one should recognize the Kaphaja [type] by numbness, coldness, softness, mild pain, unctuousness, pallor, slowness of action, and excessive discharge; that which possesses all these features is Sānnipātika; and that which possesses two sets of symptoms is to be known as Saṃsṛṣṭa (combined).
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"The nature of all ulcers has been explained through the observation of the *doṣas*;
for indeed, no ulcer exists in an embodied being without depending upon the *doṣas*. (9)

For these [wounds], the treatment consists of: the application of measures such as nursing by a wet-nurse, restraint of the child, pacification (saṃśamana), binding, washing with warm water, application of medicinal pastes (kalka), purification (śodhana), healing (ropaṇa), and restoration of the natural skin color (savarṇīkaraṇa). Furthermore, for a vāta-wound, one should employ the drinking of fats (sneha), specific diets, poultices (upanāha), fomentation (sveda), and applications of warm affusions along with sweet, sour, and salty substances; whereas for other types, one should use cold water and milk affusions, cold plasters, the drinking of ghee with sweet, astringent, and bitter pastes, and the consumption of mung beans, śāli rice, and meat from wild animals, while avoiding hot, sour, pungent, and salty substances, as well as binding and filling the wound.

One should pacify a Pitta-type ulcer with heat, sharpness, bitter, pungent, and astringent [substances], alkalis, purificatory measures, poultices, fomentation, affusion with warm water, fasting, bandaging, and drainage; and one should treat Kapha-type ulcers with the opposite [measures]. Therefore, one should apply these [therapies] according to reason. One should not perform drainage, incision, cauterization, suturing, probing, or forceful procedures on those who are excessively young.
Regarding this, there are these verses: [The verses follow.]
One should place it bound with worn-out, washed cloths in such a way that the medicine does not fall out and does not cause pain to the child.
From this binding, erysipelas, swelling, burning, fever, and thirst [arise]. 11.
If [the bandage] is too loose, it does not remain in place; therefore, a medium [tightness] is recommended.
A bandage protects the wound from the dangers of wind, sun, grass, wood, water, flies, and so forth; it heals quickly and prevents [the animal] from licking or biting it.

One should not bandage a wound that is afflicted by fever, erysipelas, or burning sensations, or one in which blood and pitta are predominant; however, one should wash such a wound twice a day. Two types of turmeric, sesame seeds, ghee, rock salt, madhuka, and trivṛt [are used for this].

This paste known as *ariṣṭapatra* is both purifying and healing (15). For purification and healing, a medicinal preparation of honey (*kṣaudrarasakriyā*) is appropriately used; for cooling, the application of ghee, water, and roasted grain flour (*saktu*) is prescribed (16).
A paste consisting of *samaṅgā*, *dhātakī* flowers, the bark of fresh *āmalakī*, ghee, long pepper (*kṛṣṇā*), sesame seeds, and spikenard (*māṃsī*) is a healer of wounds.
One may likewise cook ghee or oil with all these same medicinal herbs.
They say that *kaṭphala* powder, when applied as a dusting, promotes the healing of wounds.
One should declare a wound to be "ripening" (suppurating) when it is afflicted by fever, burning sensations, and thirst;
once these have subsided, one should know it to be ripe if it has become thick and elevated in appearance.
If it is located on a vital point (marman), it should be neglected; however, one should fill the wound with curd from a cow and bind it after smearing it with salt.
Some say that if it does not arise from a vital point, one may incise it, but others say no, based on previous observations.
Due to the loss of blood and its diminished state, a foolish physician might harm the child;
[or] having opened it,
[he applies] madder or realgar.

An ointment consisting of Triphalā, Jātī flowers, Kāsīsa, and Lohapatrikā, mixed with ghee and honey, is an excellent means for restoring one's natural complexion; likewise, an ointment of these same ingredients mixed with cow-dung juice is supremely effective for making the skin uniform in color.
If the ground is smeared with oil and sprinkled with the skin, hair, hooves, horns, bones, and ashes of quadrupeds, it will cause hair to grow again.

Now, indeed, eight types of pustules arise in children due to the bodily humors (*doṣas*) and their own specific defects; having stated their causes and symptoms, we shall now describe their names, forms, and treatments: *śarāvikā*, *kacchapikā*, and *jālinī* are dominated by phlegm (*kapha*); *sarṣapikā*, *alajī*, and *vidradhi* are characterized by an excess of bile (*pitta*); *vinatā* is dominated by wind (*vāta*); and *aruṃṣikā* arises from all the humors combined.

Among their characteristics: *Śarāvikā* is depressed; *Kacchapikā* is smooth and elevated; *Jālinī* is covered with a network of vessels like the pores of the skin; *Sarṣapikā* consists of small, quickly suppurating pustules resembling mustard seeds, whether numerous or few; *Alajī* is characterized by many complications, quick suppuration, and spreading (*vaisarpa*); *Vinatā* is sunken in the abdomen or on the back, deep-seated, dark blue, and painful; and *Māṃsavidradhi* (flesh abscess) arises from the provocation of *pitta*, or it occurs at joints or vital spots (*marma*) as a "boil" (*vidradhi*), so called because it quickly burns and tears the limb. This is that [abscess].

It arises both externally and internally; for the ignorant, both types are difficult to cure. Aruṃṣikā (scabies/eruptions) born of the three doṣas is of four kinds, according to the distinction of the doṣas—being caused by one, two, or all three in equal measure. The symptoms of Vāta are piercing pain, pricking, flatulence, throbbing, distension, and itching. The symptoms of Pitta are fever, thirst, burning sensation, delusion, intoxication, and delirium. The symptoms of Kapha are coldness, sliminess, excessive moisture, anorexia, and a sense of heaviness or numbness. When all [doṣas] are present in equal measure, it is caused by all three. Furthermore, these aforementioned characteristics apply to other ulcers as well. Regarding this, there are these verses:
In cases such as sarāvikā and others, purgation is recommended for one who has been well-lubricated;
furthermore, the physician should perform the appropriate wound-treatment on those [lesions],
and one should employ measures for resolution in the case of unripened pustules (piḍakās).
In cases of aruṃṣikā, constant head-shaving is beneficial, along with affusions, plasters, the drinking of ghee, and wholesome diets; furthermore,
frequent bathing and anointing with wound-healing oils (vraṇataila) are recommended.

Two types of *haridrā*, *trikaṭu*, *saindhava* salt, or *manaḥśilā*, *suvarṇaja*, *japā*, *jātī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *aśvagandhā* root, *udakā*, *kaṇā*, *daśamūla*, and the three fruits (*phalatraya*)— these constitute a medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*).
One should rub the *aruṃṣikā* with these [herbs] combined with cow’s urine;
one should also cook oil with these very same [herbs], and that too destroys *aruṃṣikā*.
If, however, it should cause pain, one should then apply a massage with sesame seeds.
The physician should cauterize an aruṃṣikā that has been cut with a razor using either sweet wound-oil or fresh butter; furthermore,
he should apply a plaster of milk and urine, which have been prepared together and made lukewarm.
If they do not stop in this way, then after that, one should perform emesis; when the child is repeatedly smeared with the powder of baked bricks,
he dries up in his limbs while eating the seeds of *trapusa* or *vāru*.
In one who consumes food that increases fat and indulges in daytime sleep, the fat becomes aggravated and is carried to the skin by the wind; then,
enclosed within the skin filled with fat, it produces *aralkīlikā* (cysts).
When these [fleshy growths] are seen here and there after being lanced and incised, appearing like jujube fruits or cow's udders, they continue to increase; therefore,
their cauterization with heated fats or molasses is the primary treatment.
Having cut [the flesh] bit by bit for the benefit of the patient, or having applied an alkaline caustic,
or having bound it with alkaline threads, one should thereafter perform the treatment of the wound.
[One must avoid] incompatible food, putrid, stale, excessively hot, or irregular eating, which leads to illness...

From the crushing, leaping over, and shaking of seeds—specifically those of *kodrava*, hemp, radish, linseed, cotton, *tuvarī*, *kulattha*, and so forth; from smelling the smoke of these when being burned; likewise, from the cutting of cloth, and from the [smoke of] *āla*, *bhallātaka* stones, and so on;
[and] prepared with rice-flour.
One should have the patient lick cold butter mixed with sugar and honey, or lick butter accumulated during the heat;
however, one should maintain the digestive fire— whether it be blazing or depressed— by means of breast milk alone.
If fickle children, while crawling about excessively,
should suffer a wound from grass, wood, bricks, weapons, or other such objects,
their injury will be as severe as that of cutting raw flesh, and their resulting calamity will be agonizing.
One should join it together after cleansing it and sprinkle it with warm water.
Furthermore, in the case of excessive bleeding, one should arrest it with cold water;
however, if the flow persists, one should apply cauterization or alkali.
One should administer it mixed with honey and ghee to a patient who eats wholesome food;
one should also prescribe the drinking of ghee for both [mother and child], and perform treatments as in the case of a wound,
especially during cold seasons for infants who lie on their bellies.
For those whose limbs are defiled by their own urine, whose clothes are soaked with urine,
who sleep on grass, and who are deprived of bathing and anointing,
there arises the presence of worms, bedbugs, and lice, and from being bitten by them.
The body develops an eruption of lichen-like patches, especially in the region of the waist; in such cases, massage, dry rubbing, bathing, the application of perfumes, the use of incense,
and the preparation of a special bed are recommended for children.
Massaging with oil at night is always beneficial for children;
it induces sleep, is strengthening, promotes growth, and destroys fatigue. Therefore, regular massage is highly recommended for children.
For the sake of pleasing Mahāsena, the wise Śakra created an elephant named Dussaha, possessing the strength and splendor of Airāvaṇa;
he was made the mount for Skanda and assigned to Śākha and Viśākha.
Being highly pleased by these two, he was made a village headman with stones and granted the sovereignty over all subordinate officials;
yet when he was not honored at times of worship, he became angry with the person.
In the gaps between the fortnights, at the twilights, in assemblies, and at festivals,
a great four-tusked elephant terrifies the child in his dreams;
being thus terrified, he suddenly awakens, trembling with fear.
Wherever this limb is touched, a swelling arises there;
they become filled with fat and marrow, many of them appear,
some of which ripen, while others burst open.
On the fifth day, one should worship Duḥsaha, the best of nāgas,
according to the custom appropriate for one's family; likewise, those [afflictions] perish even for one who constantly eats ghee and milk and over-eats due to a phlegmatic constitution.
While sleeping, this disease increases through the growth of flesh, fat, and blood;
therefore, both mother and son should be treated here with emetics,
and one should administer rice gruel and mung-bean broth for seven days.
When [the afflictions] do not subside but continue to increase, even the "autumnal fever" (śaradāha) is recommended;
for them, the root is severed like the treatment for a ripened ulcer—
thus the Sage taught the medicine for various diseases.
Having observed this, the wise physician Kaśyapa spoke for the benefit of children; therefore,
a learned doctor should always maintain this for the welfare of infants.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the chapter on the two types of wounds in the Section on Therapeutics; [this is followed by] the chapter on the treatment of catarrh.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the medical treatment for catarrh (pratiśyāya).
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.

Due to the constant consumption of heavy, sweet, cold, and dry foods; from repeatedly drinking breast milk; from sleeping constantly while digesting heavy meals; from bathing while suffering from indigestion; from drinking cold water or immersing oneself in it while afflicted by phlegm; from drinking excessively after eating; from the suppression of natural urges; from constantly suppressing one's urges; from always lying on an unsuitable bed, or lying on one's side excessively, or sleeping with the mouth open; and due to other such causative factors, the wind (vāta) becomes aggravated in those with weak digestion or irregular eating habits.

Having vitiated the upper receptacle of *kapha* and the channels, it causes rhinitis (*pratiśyāya*). When it vitiates the channels of the mouth, oral diseases arise; when it reaches the ear, ear diseases arise; and when *kapha*, *pitta*, or blood causes the *kapha* to congeal toward the root of the nose, it is called rhinitis. In that condition, the head, mouth, and nose feel as if they are obstructed; pleasant, unpleasant, and indistinct odors are perceived—these being due to obstruction from *vāta*, lack of clarity from *kapha*, and excessive moisture from *rakta*.

From the bile (pitta), a foul odor arises in the channels. Being in this state, for the sake of counteracting dullness, anorexia, nausea, and obstruction, he becomes excessively addicted to things that are very hot, sharp, sour, and salty; consequently, his bile becomes aggravated. Due to the increase of its strength, it produces fever, thirst, internal burning, restlessness, a foul odor in the channels, suppuration, and a sun-like dizziness (divākarāvarta).

Therefore, the sages describe this [catarrh] as being of four types: vātika (wind-born), paittika (bile-born), ślaiṣmika (phlegm-born), and sānnipātika (arising from the combination of all three humors). They are as follows: one should recognize the vātika type of catarrh by the following symptoms—the patient cries out, finds no pleasure, remains constantly awake, sneezes frequently, and even when lying on his back, there is only a slight discharge of phlegm from the nose; furthermore, it is relieved by unctuous, warm, salty, and sour treatments. One should recognize the paittika type by fever, burning sensations, thirst, delirium, dryness of the palate, and inflammation of the mouth, nose, and eyes, accompanied by the rapid maturation of phlegm.

One should recognize kaphaja pratiśyāya by its delayed onset, lack of clear manifestation, nausea, heaviness of the head, excessive discharge, slow sneezing, stiffness of the neck, a coating over the heart, indigestion, and aggravation by hot, pungent, astringent, and dry things. One should recognize sannipātika pratiśyāya when it possesses all these symptoms along with foul-smelling secretions from the channels and the presence of worms.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
Pratiśyāya arising from the three doṣas is generally characterized by a predominance of vāta and śleṣman.
It pacifies the loss of strength, digestive fire, and complexion, and it is a destroyer [of disease] when neglected;
therefore, fasting is recommended for it at the very outset.
Alternatively, one should drink lukewarm water that stimulates digestion or water boiled with the five roots (pañcamūla).
According to one's capacity—
whether in water or even in gruel— one should take warm rice of the red *śāli* variety mixed with the three salts.
Or, having observed the relative strength and weakness of the humors (doṣas), one should drink barley-gruel;
provided with a covering for the digestive fire, staying and sitting in a windless place,
and eating light, warm food, one is liberated from the condition, provided one does not drink it excessively.
Bandaging, inhalation of smoke, and the consumption of guḍaharītakī are recommended; furthermore,
drinking clarified butter at night after having eaten is praised when [the previous meal] has been digested.
If it is not pacified by that [treatment] as well, one should administer ancient ghee,
or the *ṣaṭpala* ghee, or *pañcagavya*, or *kalyāṇaka*, or *abhaya*. Furthermore, barley-based food (*yavānna*) should always be given very hot, enriched with salt and unctuous substances.
Or one should drink pippalī mixed with black pepper;
or one should constantly hold black pepper in the mouth until it is completely consumed.

One who knows the true nature of diseases and understands what is wholesome for his constitution is liberated from illness by drinking long pepper (*śuṇṭhī*) combined with rock salt and warm water, or by employing the "increasing dose of long pepper" (*pippalī-vardhamāna*), or by taking *abhayā* with jaggery while maintaining a diet of wholesome food.
One is freed from catarrh by [using] patola leaves and triphala;
one should always foment the apāna region after anointing it with ghee, in a place free from wind.
One should avoid food that is obstructive, heavy, and cold, as well as sleeping during the day;
all this treatment which has been prescribed for coryza,
a wet nurse should administer to a very young child without hesitation.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa;
thus ends the chapter on the treatment of urōghāta, within the treatment of pratiśyāya in the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsā-sthāna).
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of urorghāta (chest affliction).
Thus said the venerable Kaśyapa.
The doshas, provoked by their own specific causes, produce the fourfold urorghāta.
They cause greed and indigestion in those who indulge [in them];
cold fever, catarrh, a throat as if covered with bristles, and weak coughing.
This is declared to be the Sameti, which destroys all diseases.
This very same formulation, when combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa), cures heart disease and dyspnea.
When mixed with honey and licked, it leads to health in cases where phlegm is predominant.
A disease characterized by an excess of *pitta* and *kapha*, known as *uroghāta*, is born from the three *doṣas*.
Therefore, one should constantly employ treatments that subdue *pitta* and *kapha*, such as the *dhātrī* (emblic myrobalan).
Thus ends the treatment for *uroghāta* in the Section on Therapeutics (*Cikitsāsthāna*).
Now begins the chapter on the treatment of swellings (śopha).
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of swellings.
Thus said the venerable Kaśyapa.

In those who habitually consume excessively salty, sour, pungent, alkaline, and hot substances after emesis, purgation, fasting, illness-induced emaciation, or unwholesome food and indigestion; or who indulge in such things as salt and the like at the end of a journey; or who deviate from their regimen by bathing, drinking, sleeping, sexual intercourse, and physical exercise with cold water whenever they please; or whose milk possesses similar qualities—in such cases, a severe disease called *śvayathu* (edema) arises, which is of four types.

Indeed, its defects are as follows: the ulcer is blackish-red in color, small, dry, as if filled with ants, painful, and when pressed, it becomes depressed; it is hot without apparent cause and subsides through cooling measures and oleation;
one should know that to be the Vātika type. [The chapter on the treatment of worms follows the description of] blue, red, and yellow [ulcers].
One should bring these together according to their availability;
when one *droṇa* of water remains as a quarter-part after boiling, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with it,
adding rock salt (*saindhava*), for that is a supreme destroyer of worms.
This Viḍaṅga-ghee, to be licked together with sugar,
drives away all worms, just as the thunderbolt [destroys] the Asuras;
it is [the remedy] for bitter, hot, pungent, and dry substances, for urines, and for salt.
The application of oleation and sudation, as well as wholesome diet for the destruction of worms,
and bathing and other measures for external parasites, have been proclaimed in the chapter on the two types of wounds (Dvivraṇīya).
However, for a very young infant, the wet-nurse should perform all these treatments herself.
Milk that has been purified by cleansing therapies, lightened by wholesome foods,
and processed with medicinal herbs conduces to immortality.
However, having applied very hot mustard oil mixed with rock salt to the rectum—
"One should apply fomentation to the anus with a finger; thus one quickly obtains relief," so said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the treatment for worms in the Section on Therapeutics.
The Chapter on the Treatment of Alcoholism (Madātyaya). Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of intoxication from excessive drinking (Pānātyaya).
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa. 1–2.
When the consumption of liquor occurs, three types of disease are said to afflict men:
*pānātyaya*, *vibhrama*, and *pānāpakrama*.
Among these, when a man drinks while the previously consumed liquor is still undigested (*ajīrṇa*), [it results in *pānātyaya*].
That drinking leads to an excess; therefore, it is considered *pānātyaya* (excess from drinking).
From the consumption of excessively disordered drinks comes *pānavibhrama* (confusion from drinking).
The sudden cessation of drinking is called *pānāpakrama* (withdrawal from drinking). 4–5.

Wine, when consumed in moderation—especially by those of a *sāttvika* temperament—is illuminating, appetizing, aphrodisiac, and produces clarity in sexual pleasure; it removes emaciation and mental fatigue, is exhilarating, and increases strength. (6)

The consumption of food is the root of joy, health, and nourishment; it is also essential when there is a deficiency of breast milk in nurses, or when afflictions such as wind-pains and cold-fevers or irregular fevers have arisen. 7–8.
For delicate women, in various diseases, for those who have recently given birth, for those with difficult labors, in cases of prolapse of the womb or excessive sexual indulgence,
and for children suffering from the eruption of teeth or afflicted by thirst.
In cases of dryness of the palate, throat, and lips, during weeping, and from excessive staying awake,
as well as in diseases characterized by wind and phlegm, they say that wine is like nectar; yet that very same wine, when drunk excessively and repeatedly, [becomes poison].
It is said that [excessive drinking] opens the door to all diseases; it acts like poison,

causes alcoholism (madātyaya), produces disorders of wind (vāta), or makes [the condition] difficult to cure— this applies to one who consumes intoxicants excessively while young or when suffering from indigestion.
One of weak constitution who abstains from food suffers a loss of bodily essence (rasa).

Due to its dryness and sharpness, the wind (vāyu) is provoked; due to its heat and post-digestive transformation (vipāka), the bile (pitta) is provoked. Consequently, these two doshas become simultaneously aggravated and reach the stomach (āmāśaya).
When the great vessels (mahāsirā) are overwhelmed by obstructed phlegm, they become disordered; then,
as those vessels rooted in the heart become disordered,
the body suffers excessively— of that, I shall now describe the symptoms.
One becomes deluded, agitated, cries out, is burned, and suffers intensely from fever;
there is cardiac distress, trembling, horripilation, pain in the sides, headache, loss of appetite, perspiration, constipation, prostration, and diarrhea. (16–17)
He becomes emaciated, faints, and even laments;
one should recognize this as *madātyaya* (alcoholism), and I shall now describe its symptoms:
pain in the heart, the sides, and the joints, delirium, and excessive wakefulness. (18)

In the fever caused by pitta, one appears like a madman during a delirium stirred up by wind; there is suppuration of the channels, burning heat, diarrhea, perspiration, yellowness, vomiting, or a disturbance of the blood, and one perceives everything as yellow. (19–20)

In the case of a kapha-type [poisoning], there is vomiting, cold fever, lassitude, drowsiness, stiffness, loss of consciousness, and despondency; furthermore, there are dyspnea, cough, vertigo, exhaustion, diarrhea, and trembling. (21)
Pain and delusion are common [symptoms], yet the omniscient one [the physician] recognizes all forms [of the disease]. 22.
They declare that intoxication (madātyaya) most frequently arises from undigested matter (āma);
therefore, in cases of intoxication, fasting (laṅghana) is indeed beneficial first. 23.
Appetite, lightness, stability, clarity of the senses,
the subsiding of diseases, and purity of speech— these are the signs when [the body] is properly dried out.
Having produced these, however, it undergoes a morbid transformation through excessive drying.
Then, one should recognize their non-attainment [of the desired effect] when that [dose] has not been surpassed;
having observed these reasons, and seeing the patient afflicted by the intoxication of digestion, one should at the proper time administer a refreshing drink (tarpaṇa) cooled with pomegranate water.
One should administer for drinking the very same liquor that caused the intoxication to arise, mixed with a large amount of cold water;
for his bodily fire consists of that [liquor], as do the rasa-carrying vessels.
And since his mind has been cultivated by that [practice], therefore that indeed is his medicine. Or else, having bathed with water that is pleasant according to the season,
being cleansed and anointed, pure, and having gone to a pleasing seat and dwelling— (28–29)
One should skillfully administer a refreshing drink (*tarpaṇa*) that is pleasant to the heart and easy to digest;
for breaking the fast (*pāraṇā*), roasted barley flour (*saktu*) is pleasing to the heart, or alternatively, parched grain flour (*lāja-saktu*).
[These may be taken with] rock salt, black salt, cumin, and very cold pomegranate water.
That wine, along with a small amount of buttermilk, and roasted barley flour (saktu) in small quantities;
as well as kuṭhera, bhūstṛṇa, honey, jambīra, sumukha, and others—these sour preparations (ṣāḍava), both cooked and uncooked, are excellent when fragrant. 31–32.
The filaments of citron fruits, fresh ginger, living pomegranates, sugar, jaggery, and candied sugar, as well as the meat of wild animals—
sour, non-sour, prepared, and seasoned according to their respective categories. (33)
The physician should cause one afflicted by alcoholism (pānātyaya) to drink upodikā prepared with buttermilk, or that which is prepared with jaggery and sugar; such an avakṣīrī preparation,
provided it is available, should be administered for the sake of recovery.
A wise man should taste some of the foods here and savor others;
he should smell, look at, and drink some for the sake of generating faith.
He should also permit her pleasure in due order, according to what is appropriate for the season.
Whatever [element] he is habituated to, that very thing one should administer to him.
Gradually, one should introduce him to contact with food and drink, and he should use garments of fine silk, linen, plantain leaves, and the like. (37-38)
Various types of sandalwood, both cool and warm, as well as foods and drinks that are parching or heavy;
the application of fire and sun, sleeping during the day, and emaciation. 39.
One should avoid grief, travel, sexual intercourse, fatigue, and physical exercise (40). Gruels, thin rice-gruels, and soups are not recommended in cases of alcoholism;
if the condition is not relieved by these means, then one should employ this following treatment (41).
Uśīra, tintiḍīka, the fresh juice of pomegranate, and honey—this refreshing drink is excellent for quenching thirst caused by pitta-type pānātyaya.
Kāśmarya, pomegranate, grapes, dates, and parūṣaka [are also beneficial]. 42.
One should appropriately give one *kuḍava* each of the lodhra-group substances (43). Having finely ground lodhra, āmalaka, and mañjiṣṭhā,
they should be steeped in one *āḍhaka* of water and set aside, along with *jātī* or *keśara* (44).
This [mixture] dispels thirst, vomiting, diarrhea, intoxication, fainting, delirium, instability, loss of appetite, and exhaustion.
[It consists of] lāmajjaka, lotus stalks, bark, madhuka, and likewise utpala. 45.145–146ab.
One pala each of guḍūcī and two palas each of sugar,
along with saffron, should be kept in a new vessel containing one āḍhaka of water;
this cures intoxication accompanied by complications arising from an excess of vāta and pitta in men.
One should prepare other beverages well-known in the world, and one should provide food and drink that are generally intoxicating in abundance.
Then, one should ensure continuity [of treatment], so that the patient may become strong. 48.
Then, the wise physician should administer purification (saṃśodhana) for that [condition] according to the specific dosha involved.
Trivṛt powder mixed with wine should be drunk to facilitate downward movement of the humors;
alternatively, it may be prepared as a beverage (pānaka) combined with wine and jaggery.
Thus has the treatment for erysipelas, burning sensations, and fever been described;
that same [treatment] should be applied in cases of thirst, fever, and burning pain caused by intoxication (madātyaya).
51 Thus indeed said the venerable Kaśyapa. 52

Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of intoxication (*pānātyaya*) within the Section on Therapeutics (*cikitsāsthāna*). Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of urinary disorders (*phakka*). 1.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa:
"A child who does not walk on his feet by the end of one year is to be known as a *phakka*; I shall describe his characteristics."

A nurse whose milk is dominated by phlegm (ślaiṣmika) is known as one with "cooked" (phakka) milk; a child drinking her milk suffers from many diseases and, due to emaciation, may reach a state of being "cooked" (phakkatva).
One whose nature is characterized by bile and wind (pittānila-prakṛti) has sharp milk and gives birth to sharp offspring.
Whence do those who are lame, dull-witted, or mute arise? [They arise] from consuming milk that aggravates the three humors (doṣas).
From the heart proceed the sense-faculties of embodied beings, preceded by the mind; and the senses, being under the control of the mind, bring about what is beneficial.
In that regard, the organ of speech alone is divided into two parts, just as the hands; with one half it utters sound, and with the other half it grasps.
For this reason, men who are mute are for the most part also deaf.
For the ear is known to have its root in speech; indeed, when speech fails, the ear fails as well.
The ear is the root of speech, and a man who is deaf speaks from that very root; for when the root is destroyed, the speech is destroyed.

Phlegm (phakkatva) is said to be of three types: that born from milk, that born from the womb, and thirdly, that arising from disease. Among these, the type born from milk is described as occurring quickly due to the cessation of breast milk in a nursing mother who is pregnant.
Either he perishes or dies, that wretch tormented within the womb;
or else, the helpless child, with his flesh, strength, and luster wasted away, suffers from diseases such as fever, whether innate or adventitious.
With his buttocks, arms, thighs, great belly, head, and face completely withered, with yellowed eyes and bristling body-hairs, his skeletal frame was visible;
his lips and body were shriveled, and he constantly discharged urine and excrement.
Either his lower body becomes motionless, or his hands and feet follow one another;
due to weakness he is slow in movement, and because of this slowness he is despised. He becomes accessible to flies, worms, and insects, and suffers as death approaches. (14–15)
With shattered and bristling hair, his body hair stiffened, possessing large claws,
foul-smelling and filthy, wrathful, and stammering, he pants and faints;
he is produced from excessive excrement, urine, rheum of the eyes, snot, and impurity.
By these causes, one should recognize the swelling caused by disease in an infant,
especially in those who are unprotected and particularly those whose mothers were pregnant at the time of birth.
Those with a severely impaired *grahaṇī* generally become afflicted by *phakka* due to eating in excess;
consequently, their food is rendered useless because of weak digestive fire, the discharge of undigested fluid, and the excessive production of urine and feces.
One should have medical treatment performed; the patient (phakka) should drink the *kalyāṇaka* ghee or the *ṣaṭpala* ghee as if it were nectar (*amṛta*).
After seven nights, one should purify him with *trivṛt* mixed with milk.
Then the pure chamber becomes corrupted;
however, a Śūdra must not drink Brāhmī-ghee, for that is his destruction.
Those Śūdras who drink Brāhmī are joined with the loss of their progeny.
The deceased do not go to heaven, and their merit is destroyed,
[if this occurs] by means of a lamp, or by *rāsnā*, or by *madhuka*.
One should administer milk boiled with punarnavā and ekaparṇī, or with eraṇḍa and śatapuṣpā, or with drākṣā, pīlu,
and trivṛt; or, the wise physician, having collected all of these together, [should do so].
One should eat meat,
or else well-prepared broth or even milk,
together with śāli rice; and one should also drink that [milk] constantly.

By that one gains vitality and is liberated from all diseases; by that very [mixture] one should cook oil, as it is declared in every way for those suffering from swellings (*phakka*): *rāsnā-madhu*—[and so forth].
One should administer ghee, oil, milk, broth, or meat-soup that has been doubly processed; by doing so, one is liberated from all diseases.
If one perceives an excess of phlegm (kapha), one should drink milk mixed with urine.
By this practice, one who eats wholesome food is liberated from urinary disorders;
ten palas each of castor root, aṃśumatī, bilva, and so forth,
should be prepared separately.
One should add one *prastha* each of barley, jujube fruits, and horse gram;
boil them in four *droṇas* of water until the decoction is reduced to one-fourth.
Then, one should cook one *prastha* of oil, one *prastha* of curd, and the decoction together once again.
One should protect that proven remedy with effort and employ it in every way;
it was used by Bandī, Paṅgu,
Ikṣvāku, Subāhu, and Sagara.
By means of this, Nahuṣa, Dilīpa, Bharata, and Gaya obtained sons, as well as long life, strength, and happiness;
and because it was taught by former kings, it is remembered as "Rājataila" (the King’s Oil).
For when kings are intent upon bestowing favor,
a wise man praises a three-wheeled, curved chariot constructed by a craftsman.
One should administer this slowly; once it has been grasped, one should practice movement.
Enemas, internal oleation, sudation, and massage are especially indicated for children suffering from combined Vāta disorders.
"Comfortable beds, seats, and enema applications are for the benefit of a person," so said the Blessed Kaśyapa;
thus ends the treatment of phlegm (phakka) in the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsāsthāna).
The Chapter on the Medical Treatment of the Nurse-Mother (Dhātrī).
Now, therefore, we shall explain the medical treatment of the nurse-mother.
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
"O Sage, you ought to explain to me the entire science of the treatment of nurses;
for the happiness and suffering of children undoubtedly have their root in the nurse.
Thus was the one of great asceticism questioned by his aged disciple.
The best among speakers expounded the entire medical treatment for wet-nurses:
a nurse with a *puṣpikī* complexion has a sharp digestive fire (*tīkṣṇāgni*);
one who is *vātapaittikī* has balanced humors (*samadhātu*); and one with a *viṣama* complexion has an irregular digestive fire (*viṣamāgnikī*).
The equilibrium of the digestive fire (samāgni) is the root of longevity, health, and progeny for living beings;

an irregular fire (viṣama) is the root of all diseases. For one with a sharp fire, nourishing therapy (bṛṃhaṇa) should be practiced constantly; for one with a weak fire (mandāgni), the action of stimulating digestion (dīpana) is required.

A diet of wholesome food is always conducive to the well-being of one with irregular digestive fire; furthermore, either the *Kalyāṇaka* or *Ṣaṭpala* formulations are employed according to strength and suitability, or the *Pañcaka* [formulations].
Thus, one should not employ alkali or drugs predominantly containing alkali according to the prescribed rule;
for alkali is destructive to offspring, and its use by wet-nurses is not recommended.
Anointing with unguents, massaging, bathing, wearing white garments,
delicious food,
comfortable beds, and nurses— these are the causes of happiness for [the infant].
For obese nurses, venesection is recommended after they have been treated with oleation and sudation; subsequently, purification by both upward and downward means should be performed,
whereby the fat is diminished and the channels are opened.
Whatever juice nourishes a woman who is emaciated and has lost her menses, by that she attains success; [specifically,] one *tulā* of *balā* root washed clean, along with *daśamūla* and *śatāvarī*.
Guḍūcī, rohiṣa, rāsnā, vṛścikālī, punarnavā, vṛṣa, sahacara, uśīra, sārivā,
sūrva, kākajaṅghā, and aṃśumatī.
Aśvagandhā, mṛgairvāru, kālā, navamālikā, atimuktaka, śārṅgeṣṭā, kapittha, and triphalā— these,
starting from daśamūla, are recorded as having portions of ten palas each.
Barley, horse gram, and black gram—
having boiled these in one droṇa of water until reduced to one-fourth, one should strain that decoction and place it back on the fire.
Now, one should have these medicinal herbs placed here in portions of one pala each:
two types of medā, two types of haridrā, the two types of kākolī, vṛṣa, jīvaka, and māṣaparṇī.
Cinnamon bark, leaf, and sandalwood; uśīra; the two types of bala; the two salts; mūrvā; śvadaṃṣṭrā; śārṅgeṣṭā; śyāmā; drākṣā;
surāhva; madhuka; hastipippalī; kuṣṭha; vyāghranakha; and vacā.
Small cardamom, agallochum, gambhari, dill, parushaka,
conchflower, visalya, scorpion-plant, and madhulika.
Sour pomegranates, fragrant substances such as guggulu,
walnuts, jackfruit, bhavya, and prācīnāmalaka;
as well as śatāvarī, vidārī, madhuparṇī, and triṣāṇikā.
One should cook half an *āḍhaka* of the decoction with one *āḍhaka* each of cloves, camphor, *spṛkkā*, and *kaṭukā* fruit,
along with one *droṇa* of milk and sesame oil.
Having set that aside until it is prepared, one should store the *balā*-oil in a firm, well-burnished earthen vessel;
it is highly recommended for use as an ointment.
It affects the limbs, the viscera, the bones, the marrow, and the vessels;
it causes external and internal extension, lockjaw, vertigo, hemiplegia, emaciation, pallor, facial pain, and abdominal tumors.
Deafness and trembling,
epilepsy, insanity, and the kaṭapūtana spirit; earache, headache, hernia, and the mārutakuṇḍala affliction.

Balā-taila removes eighty wind-related diseases, twenty disorders of the female reproductive tract, all defects of the semen, and all planetary afflictions; it is [prescribed] for the treatment of senility.
In chronic fever, in tertian and quartan fevers,
in women who have had difficult births, in vaginal pain, in various types of fatigue, in diarrhea and fever, and in all diseases of phlegm (kapha).
One should not employ it in cases of indigestion, emaciation, fainting,
or vomiting; however, one may prepare Rāsnā oil according to this very same procedure, for it destroys most of those diseases which have been enumerated above.
Of śatāvarī, badarī, guḍūcī, and madhuka; of punarnavā, drākṣā, pīlu, and sahacara; and of vṛṣa, nāgavīryā, anantā, and śatapuṣpā.
This same procedure is prescribed for oils known by their own names:
one should add the cooked substance to the oil while it is still hot and churn it thoroughly; this is the constant distinction in this case.
The same procedure as previously described is proclaimed for śyonāka oil;
one should add thirty palas of honey and meat to the decoction.
The same procedure as previously described is proclaimed for kapittha oil.
One should give one *tulā* of ripe *kapittha* fruits;
O Lord, it is proclaimed that here one should use only the fresh juice, four times the amount of oil.
Fish oil, cooked with the decoction and meat-broth of fish,
is recommended for wind-related diseases (vātavyādhi), just like Bala-oil;
this applies also to the oils of crane, swan, gallinule, curlew, and sarasa crane.
They say that the oils of the *āṭī* and *śakunaka* birds are known by their respective names;
this procedure is proclaimed as a remedy for foul odors, a commodity that produces offspring even for the impotent and the barren.
In cases of foul odor from the vagina, mouth, or ears, and when they are slimy,
women should always apply kapittha oil using cotton swabs;
likewise, oil mixed with the juice of the mango (sahakāra) is recommended.
And the consumption of various oils that are pleasing and fragrant;
hereafter, I shall explain the remaining treatment for the bodily constituents (dhātus).
In children who have undergone the drinking of medicated fats (*sneha*), or who have consumed *ṣaṣṭhīmallaka*,
or due to eating in excess, or from the consumption of incompatible foods or undigested matter (*ajīrṇa*),
the seizure known as *ṣaṣṭhika* arises, which destroys the body.
Incurable and persistent— this woman, who wears a limited number of necklaces, is virtuous in character, ascetic,
and always eats only what is left over, surpasses even the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī.
When deception has occurred, one should have five rites performed;
alternatively, one should propitiate Śiva and Skanda through severe austerity.
Furthermore, indigestion among the nurses is never commended.
Indeed, the humors corrupted by indigestion in wet-nurses produce—
loss of appetite, exhaustion, intoxication, delusion, scabies, ringworm, leprosy, erysipelas, abdominal tumors, heart disease, dyspnea, and cough.

Hiccups, drowsiness, fatigue, dyspnea, vomiting, epilepsy, and physical debility; hemorrhaging, bilious fever, vertigo, insanity, colic, emaciation, throat-obstruction, stiffness of the thighs, as well as cataplexy (saṃnyāsa) and other such great maladies.

Because of eating moderate and wholesome food, there is no such occurrence [of complications] for the mother’s son; furthermore, it results in the well-being of the nurses. Therefore, one should provide that [diet]. O Vṛddhajīvaka, in this world, there are three who perform difficult tasks.
The physician, the nurse, and the child themselves experience pleasure and pain;

for without thorough knowledge, [the physician acts] regarding the application of medicines for wind and other humors through actions following the scriptures, by observing the infant's gestures and constant appearances.

Medicine must be administered to the child; how then could that physician, a specialist in pediatrics (*kāumārabhṛtya*), not commit an error? For those reasons, he is constantly distressed, yet he performs what is difficult by applying common therapeutic measures.

The drying up of her own body for the sake of the body of the nurse’s son— along with the embryo in the case of the pregnant woman and along with the child in the case of the nurse— is to be understood as non-defiling.
Out of affection, one encounters very many other extremely terrible afflictions;
and for the sake of protection, out of the duty of longing, affection, and compassion, mothers endure all sufferings, as is celebrated here regarding the proud woman.
From the very moment of conception, even as a child,
one is afflicted by sufferings even though one does not cause them oneself;
therefore, the nurse must always maintain pure conduct, diet, and posture.
"The mother becomes [the provider] for her sons and enjoys the fruits of her sons' success," so said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of the wet-nurse in the section on pediatrics (*kumārabhṛtya*) within the *Vṛddhajīvakīya*.
The treatises on therapeutics are completed.
Now begins the seventh section, the Siddhisthāna;
its first chapter is titled "The Success Relating to the Princess."
Now, therefore, we shall explain the accomplishment regarding the princess;
thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa. [The question was asked:
"O Blessed One, [regarding] princes or other great-souled ones..."
