For how many years is the administration of enema therapy (bastikarma) prescribed? What is the quantity of oil (sneha) for an enema, what types of enemas are there, and which ones are beneficial?
For which diseases are enemas recommended, and for which are they contraindicated?
In which condition should the non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) be administered, and for which diseases? What is the dosage for the enema procedure?
What is beneficial and what is harmful? What are the complications, and what is their treatment?
Thus questioned in the midst of the sages, Kaśyapa spoke these answers: "Listen attentively; you have raised a matter of great importance.
Indeed, the procedure of enema therapy (bastikarma) is difficult to master, especially in children."
Enema therapy is like nectar for both children and non-children;
it brings wealth and fame to physicians, while ensuring longevity for the child and progeny for the father.
However, medicine that is poorly administered destroys these three at once.
"Therefore, for embodied beings afflicted by diseases primarily consisting of *vāta*, one should administer enema therapy (*basti-karma*) to children from birth onwards.
Thus said Gārgya; "No," said Māṭhara, "because of their childhood and so forth."

"It is recommended [to administer it] after one month, for by then the child would have become stable. Punarvasu Ātreya replied, "No, because the difference is slight; rather, the child should be given an oil enema after four months."
He said: After consuming breast milk and ghee, as the child grows both upward and downward, he may become afflicted by diseases arising from over-nutrition;
if seized by these, he becomes difficult to cure, therefore [this regimen] is beneficial for one year.
Then the child, being capable and able, goes and speaks with a mind that has not yet experienced [the world].

But Pārāśarya said, "No," for he was indeed difficult to manage at that time; Bhela, however, told him that it would be beneficial even for a three-year-old, because the difference [in age] was slight, there would be no contradiction, and because of the inability to endure delusions.
But for those aged six years and upwards, Bhela—
[in order to reach] certainty regarding even the subtle [matters] within the fortnights, they all then urged Kaśyapa again and again.
He declared his decision to them regarding the enema treatment for children:
"The one who eats food below and [the one] who is like a forest fire during the accumulation..."

On an auspicious day, the physician should have a vessel made from one of the following materials as they become available: gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, tin, lead, iron, ivory, wood, bamboo, horn, bone, or reed; it should be smooth, free of flaws, straight, with a globular mouth like a cow’s tail. [The patient] shall gradually obtain comforts such as sprinkling with warm water, perfumes, white garments, flowers, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), amulets (*pratisara*), ornaments, food, and diversions. Daily, prior to the oil enema (*anuvāsana*) and other procedures, massage, rubbing with unguents, sprinkling with warm water, and meals are prescribed.

After the non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), there should be the administration of lukewarm water and the observance of celibacy, as in the case of one who has undergone purgation; thus ends the section on the assembly.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
By this method, the physician should administer enemas at intervals of one day; daily administration of enemas leads to destruction [of strength], for oil is heavy by nature due to its abundance.
Because colic, fever, loss of appetite, constipation, flatulence, worms, diarrhea, the onset of skin diseases, epilepsy,
and mental dullness arise from it, [the use of ghee] every other day is beneficial.

Even when the time has arrived for administering an enema to living beings, it should be given at intervals of one day; it must not be given during an imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), for that would cause the wise physician to ruin those very constituents.
In practice, however, one should administer non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) with gradual reduction and increase;
for if they are administered repeatedly after the application of unctuous substances (sneha), the channels become obstructed.
Therefore, for the purpose of opening them and for purification, the unctuous enema (āsthāpana) is beneficial.
When the time for a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) has arrived, the child who is not given the enema—
[having been treated with] sudation, staying overnight, digestion of food, and lying in a windless place— is [neglected].
The physician should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) to a child who has been well-anointed with oil but has not yet eaten;
a properly administered nirūha quickly restores to their natural course the wind, urine, and feces that have become disordered within embodied beings.
It produces rawness, dullness,
and stiffness; it even destroys the luster of the skin, just as washing does for a garment or scrubbing does for a mirror.

Similarly, for men, the non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana), when administered by the wise at the proper time, is praised for its entire procedure just like the unctuous enema (anuvāsana). However, one should not suppress the urges that recur after a nirūha enema has been administered.
Bathing is prescribed for those who are free from affliction and have recovered,
as well as in cases of disorders of the humors, heart disease, pains in the flanks, skin diseases, and intestinal worms.
In cases of urinary disorders, abdominal enlargements, and gulma; in colic associated with vāta; in diseases where the doṣas are combined; in those that are localized or deep-seated;
and when blood or phlegm is vitiated, one should prepare a non-unctuous enema (nirūha).
Yet,
from the tips of the hair to the tips of the nails, the enema nourishes men;
it bestows complexion, luster, and strength, promotes longevity, and increases semen.
The enema treatment, when administered at the proper time, is auspicious for clearing the female reproductive tract, bestows sons even upon barren women, is like nectar for children,
and [cures] those with Vata disorders or those afflicted by Vata.
Enema therapy removes all the seeds [of disease] for those women whose fetuses miscarry, or whose children, though born,
are weak or delicate; and it is beneficial for women who are very tender, fortunate, and constantly engaged in sexual intercourse.
Those youths who have many wives, those who are lords yet not in their prime, and those who waste away through excessive attachment— for them,
the nectar [of this teaching] is most highly praised.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the first chapter, named "The Success of the Princess," in the Section on Success (Siddhisthāna).
Chapter Two, named "Success with Three Characteristics" (Trilakṣaṇā Siddhi).
Now, therefore, we shall explain the accomplishment characterized by three marks.
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa:
one should observe the threefold mark of men in five types of actions.
And the wise Duryodhana [maintained] the sustenance of the body, the bodily fire, capacity, complexion, strength, and voice.
Having observed the humors in their state of vitiation, one should purify them according to the specific humor involved; thus all the humors are pacified, and strength, lifespan, body, youth,
digestive fire, and progeny are restored.
Through purgation, one is cleansed, the sense faculties become serene,
and the bodily constituents (dhātus) are purified; the seed becomes fit for the bow [of yoga],
and one is freed from diseases born of fat, foul odors, and phlegm, as well as from vomiting.
There is alleviation or reduction of disease, along with purity and lightness; however,
there is fullness of the stomach, heaviness of the heart,
the onset of cold fever, flatulence, and frequent spitting.
Headache, loss of appetite, lethargy, impairment of the digestive fire, excessive sleepiness, laziness, and the aggravation of disease— these should be known as the signs of improper vomiting;
moreover, pain [in the chest] is the sign of one who has vomited excessively.
But when one afflicted by colic vomits bile, blood, or feces mixed with these, or vomit that is undigested, he does not recover while undergoing treatment;
for [the humors] have reached the stomach, the small intestine, the rectum, the uterus, and the blood.

Purgation is characterized by the downward movement of hunger, flatus, and urine, as well as lightness of the body, stimulation of the digestive fire, and a sense of relief. These are the signs of successful purgation.

Difficulty in passing stool and urine, eruptions on the skin, the onset of fever, loss of appetite, heaviness, and flatulence are the signs of one who has been improperly purged; fainting, colic, and prolapse of the rectum [are signs of] Vāta...
The procedure of nasal therapy (nasya) is of two kinds: nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa) and reducing (karśana).
Nourishing therapy is indicated when there is a predominance of wind-related pain, while reducing therapy is for cases of excessive phlegm (kapha).
Nourishing therapy is performed with various unctuous substances (snehas) processed with sweet medicinal herbs.
Emaciation is said to be achieved through subtle or pungent-succedaneous (kaṭusiddha) oleation therapies;
those qualities [of nourishment] are called br̥haṇa (nourishing),
and nasal medication is called nasya.
Know that the pacification of disease, joy, the maintenance of bodily functions, the attainment of memory, intellect, strength, and digestive fire, as well as clarity of the senses,
result from a properly administered nasal therapy (nasya); whereas the opposite effects indicate its improper application.
It cures insanity, disorders of vāta and pitta, heart-disease, abdominal dropsy, sūryāvarta, and lack of satiety when administered as a nasal drop for those excessively afflicted by heat.

Vigorous digestive fire, maintenance of youthfulness, nourishment, complexion, fortitude, strength, downward movement of flatus, tranquility— these are the characteristics of one who has been properly treated with oil enemas;
whereas dejection, satiety, and loss of appetite [are signs of improper administration].
Obstruction, hard stools, increase of disease, discoloration,
trembling, and an aggravation of wind are the symptoms of improper oil enema (duranuvāsita).
When phlegm, resembling pure crystal, is expelled without urine or feces—
accompanied by freedom from complications and hunger— one is said to have been properly purged by a Nirūha enema.
Suppression of feces and urine, colic, flatulence, the onset of disease,
drowsiness, sleep, anorexia, and a sense of satiety are the signs of a poorly administered non-unctuous enema;
furthermore, there is a powerful aggravation of Vata throughout the entire body.
"The enemas designated for therapeutic action should be administered during the intervals; beyond that, one should not give them.
Thus spoke the venerable Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Failure of the Three Characteristics," in the Section on Success (Siddhisthāna).
Chapter Three: The Success of Emesis and Purgation. Now, therefore, we shall expound the success regarding emesis and purgation. 1. Thus [we shall explain] the success regarding emesis and purgation.

Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa: One should administer emetics according to the specific characteristics of the patient and the prescribed method, having first prepared the patient with oleation (*upasnigdha*) while observing the strength of the digestive fire (*agni-bala*). Or, after the patient has been properly sudated (*svinna*), allowed to rest, and has passed the previous day's meal, on the following morning—once the food is digested—the physician should have the patient brush his teeth and so forth. Then, having obtained the sprouts of *kaṭaphala*, *nicula*, *śirīṣa*, and other such plants, or all of them together, he should boil them in a *droṇa* measure of water (or more). To this decoction, he should add *grahaghni*, *kṛtavedhana*, *vacā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), long pepper (*pippalī*), *vatsaka*, *trapusa*, and seeds of *madana*. Once the mixture is ready, the physician, facing east, should stir it while the patient is seated upon a seat.

One should have the patient drink that decoction—mixed with a paste of *grahaghni* and other drugs, neither too thick nor too hot or cold—up to the neck according to their strength, or alternatively, an *ariṣṭa*. After five or six periods of time have passed, one should not suppress the urge that has arisen from the blue lotus (*utpala*), the white lotus (*kumuda*), and so forth; nor should one allow the patient to rest between urges. The patient should be supported at the sides and slightly bent forward. Regarding emesis, Kautsa says that two or three urges are the minimum, four or five are middling, and six or seven are the best. Śaunaka says this is suitable for those who are large-bodied, while Pārāśarya says it is appropriate for those who are lean, middling, or strong. However, the majority of authorities hold that it must be determined by observing the specific disease.

Then, having made him rinse his mouth with warm water after he has vomited, and having laid him down in a windless place with his head toward the east, one should administer [emetics] such as *apāmārga*, *pippalī*, or *śirīṣa* seeds to draw out the phlegm that is stuck in the throat. Standing by, for conditions such as catarrh, headache, ocular congestion, earache, otitis, stiffness of the neck (*manyāgraha*), stomatitis (*dantapuṣpuṭaka*), swelling of the gums, and constriction of the throat or larynx, the regimen of consuming thin gruel and the like, staying awake during the day, and using warm water is prescribed as the most wholesome treatment.

One who is thirsty should drink water boiled with *śṛṅgavera* (ginger), slightly warmed. For even cold water, when drunk in small quantities, aggravates his catarrh and other ailments; it produces skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), nausea, fever, loss of appetite, sleepiness, and lethargy. Therefore, we shall prescribe this for those aged six years and so forth. Indeed, a very young child is incapable of performing this regimen; he does not understand the benefit [of] the treatment for the eyes. Having grasped [the medicine], a dose that pacifies the affliction—just the size of a *viḍaṅga* seed or a jujube stone—should be given.

All medicinal substances, whether the size of a jujube fruit (*badara*) or an emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*), should be collected. Vṛddhakāśyapa states that all these, whether adjuncts for emesis or adjuncts for purgation, should be prepared with sugar during the months of Caitra, Vaiśākha, and Āṣāḍha.

From those [juices], the physician or a skilled nurse, having determined by reason the appropriate amounts of one and a half, two, or three *palas* for mixing, should insert them into the nostrils using a finger whose nail-portion has been trimmed; however, Gautamī says that if the finger is deficient in length, it should be done with a single [application of] *nasya*. According to Vṛddhakāśyapa, for a very young child, two or three grains of *apāmārga* seeds mixed with honey and sugar should be used, as stated by Janaka Vaideha.

Then indeed—O Bhagavān, a physician who administers emetics and other treatments while being ignorant of the proper time, dosage, age, and the strength or weakness of the disease, results in the destruction of the fool and the destruction of his own dharma. Thus he said: "Miti," says Vāryovida; "On account of the heaviness or lightness of the *dhātrī* (wet-nurse)," says Vātsya; "May the child be as happy as the *dhātrī*," say the majority.
Then the venerable Kaśyapa said: "All this is incorrect and ineffective—Miti."
Regarding this, there are these verses:
When a disease arises in a child, the purification of the nurses alone is sufficient for the child's well-being; who in the world does not understand this?
But for one in whom [the disease] resides in the body, how can his previously accumulated defects be pacified as long as that [disease] has not been extracted?
When the physician properly performs the purification of both the future obstruction and the [existing] humor so as not to increase it,
then health is quickly restored to the child, just as a scratch on a stone.
The seat of the humors is the nurse, just as the earth is the source of rivers;
when the humor becomes aggravated, it afflicts the child,
and the established principle is that there is no relief for these two without purification.
The infant who vomits up the milk as soon as it is drunk, him no diseases— whether divine or human— ever afflict; [he is protected by] the breast-milk...
It causes inflammation of the mouth and, when administered by a wet-nurse, likewise induces fever in children;
therefore, one should administer medicine to an infant using a spoon made of *balā* or similar materials.

Then, indeed, for one who has been properly oleated, sweated, rested comfortably, and whose food is digested—having obtained a karṣa portion each of the previously mentioned drugs such as dantī, śyāmāka, kampillaka, nīlikā, saptalā, vacā, viṣāṇikā, and so forth, or half-pala portions each—one should administer them in water measuring two or four prasthas, boiled down until a quarter remains, combined with urine, neither too thin nor too hot or cold, having regard for the time, strength, and age of the patient.

For a child, however, one should cause [the medicine] to be drunk as before with *āḍūka* or together with fresh butter; one should have this licked daily in two or three doses, or four, one, two, or three *prastha*s. Beyond this, they call it excessive administration (*atiyoga*). In that case as well, the entire regimen of care is the same as for emesis.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
One should administer emesis until bile appears and purgation until phlegm appears; however, it is best when they cease spontaneously, being free from complications.
One should not suppress the natural urges.

One should administer hand-sudation (*hastasveda*) for colic in children from six years of age onwards, while cloth-sudation (*paṭasveda*) is recommended for those older than that. Now, indeed, [vomiting may occur] due to excessive nourishment, excessive dryness, excessive emaciation, excessive flesh and fat, because the medicine is too small in quantity, or because the medicine is too thick, too liquid, too hot, too cold, too sweet, too pungent, too salty, too astringent, too sour, too alkaline, or because of its extremely loathsome form, taste, or smell— whether after eating food or having drunk medicine— while the patient is moving about, sleeping, or has a distracted mind.

From the use of cold winds, cold dwellings, cold water, and cold clothing; from the avoidance of footwear, sandals, and fire; and from the suppression or excessive stimulation of natural urges—improper application (*duryoga*) and excessive application (*atiyoga*) of emetics and purgatives arise. Their symptoms are as follows: flatulence, catarrh, constipation, cardiac oppression, colic, piercing pain, vomiting, stiffness of the head, dysentery, hiccup, labored breathing, cough, dryness of the palate, hoarseness of the throat and mouth, salivation, fainting, fever, depression, and the appearance of impurities in the bodily channels.

The complications characterized by improper administration (*duryoga*) include: exhaustion, debility, despondency, delusion, loss of memory, impairment of hearing, emaciation of the body, incoherent speech, the sensation of being lifeless, colic in the colon (*pakvāśaya*), a sense of floating, dryness of the mouth and heart, convulsions of the neck and sides, trembling of the heart, roughness of the hair, face, and limbs, pain in the waist, bladder, groins, and penis, burning in the scrotum, pain and suppuration in the anus, prolapse, diarrhea, tremors in the thighs, striking of the knees, and lameness in the calves—these are the great diseases that arise from excessive administration (*atiyoga*). Furthermore, when an emetic is used for purgation, or a purgative for emesis, that is called the reversal of excessive administration (*atiyoga-viparyaya*).

In one with a cruel digestive tract (krūrakoṣṭha) who has not been lubricated, the administration of a mild medicine in a small dose causes coryza, distension, and excessive salivation of kapha. When administering medicine during fever or diarrhea associated with phlegm, constipation arises due to the mildness or small quantity of the medicine. From excessive laxation, there arise prolapse of the rectum, aggravation of wind (anila), loss of consciousness, and cutting pain in the anus (parikartikā). For one who lacks oleation and sudation and drinks medicine while suffering from indigestion, there occur dysentery, colic, vomiting, hiccups, flatulence, asthma, cough, anorexia, nausea, and seizure-like symptoms.

In one who is excessively unctuous, there arise colic, lassitude, sleepiness, discharge from the anus, burning of the head, contraction of the lips, loss of digestive fire, and consumption. From the suppression of natural urges, there occurs the provocation of the three *doṣas*, as well as fainting, seizures, insanity, and vertigo.

If one administers a large quantity of medicine even to a patient who has undergone oleation and sudation and possesses a soft bowel, that medicine results in the taking of life; it may produce beneficial effects but also provokes the *vāyu*, and once provoked, it leads to delirium, insanity, hiccups, dyspnea, cough, dryness of the palate, thirst, colic, deafness, facial paralysis, impairment of the reproductive seed, and the affliction of *timira* and *puṣpa* eye diseases. This occurs when the medicine is excessively salty, excessively astringent, administered at an excessively hot time, not properly prescribed, or remains as a residue.

That which is prepared for emesis results in purgation; or when there is indigestion accompanied by phlegm (*saśleṣman*), or if the purgative is too liquid or too cold, such that the purgative results in emesis—this reversal of the medicinal action is called *atiyoga* (excessive administration). Furthermore, in the case of oleation (*sneha*) and non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*), the upward movement of the humors (*doṣas*), weak action, or lack of action constitutes *duryoga* (faulty administration) and *ayoga* (non-action), respectively. In these two cases, either purification (*śodhana*) or the non-unctuous enema is intended.

This [ghee] serves to pacify his cutting pain, flatulence, discharge, distension, colic, sleepiness, excessive dejection, and disease. One should administer this ghee prepared with *triphalā*, *citraka*, *urupūga*, *dantī*, and *śyāmā* according to the prescribed method; or else, one should give *sarpis* (clarified butter), oil, or milk prepared with *jīvanīya* drugs as an enema (*basti*) for the pacification of constipation, distension, colic, discharge, dysentery (*pravāhikā*), and wind disorders. Or, for constipation and discharge, one may apply milk boiled with *triphalā*, *kāśmarya*, *mṛdvīkā*, *gandhatvak*, and *mūla* into the rectum as an enema.

It is praised. Gandharvataila is recommended for its use as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana), as it pacifies all disorders of Vāta. Alternatively, an enema prepared with a decoction of Gandharva [wood] along with a paste of Hiṅgu, Dāru, Bilva-shalāṭu, Pathyā, and Pūtika, processed with sour kāñjika, is said to pacify all complications, just as described previously; this is called Gandharvataila, an unctuous enema. Regarding this, there are these verses: [omission of text]. Likewise, licking [the medicine] with cold water in the proper measure is wholesome.
Likewise, one should quickly drink cold decoctions of both [medicines], and having smeared the head and body with ghee, one should sprinkle them with very cold water;
the feet also should be washed with cold water.
[This is] the eighth [chapter].
With *kaṭphala*, *padmaka*, *yavāsa*, *moca*, along with *keśara*, *uśīra*, and *samaṅgā*—these being well-ground into a paste combined with cold water—as well as [the paste] of cooling trees; |||
When the house, including its head and foundation, is being smeared [with fire], and when it is being overwhelmed by beds, seats, drinks, and foods,
the wise man should quickly extinguish that danger, just as one would a house with one part already ablaze.
When water boiled with those same substances as they are available, mixed with half the quantity of goat’s milk,
is prepared and used to cook the finest *lāja-peyā* (gruel of parched rice),
vomiting is indeed induced when it is quickly consumed.
One should drink a very small amount of *variṣṭha* (a type of fermented liquor), which is slightly delayed in action and cold, and is astringent;

or one should drink the juice of sour fruits, tree bark, *rasāñjana*, and *lodhra* mixed with rice-water. When purgation has increased excessively, one should administer emesis; by this means, the child indeed quickly attains relief.

They declare that its preparation is excellent: a decoction prepared with wood-apple (*kapittha*), honey, and the tender shoots of *jambu*, mango, cane-leaf fig (*vetasa*), and *payodruma*, boiled with water and then mixed with milk.
They say that this [decoction] is most excellent when boiled repeatedly; likewise, when used for drinking or in the administration of enemas, it destroys [the excess].
Water or milk boiled with dhātakī and these [other ingredients], as well as gruel, are beneficial in cases of excessive application.
Having prepared choice meats from wild animals, one should administer soups, sour gruels, meat-broths, and milk with clarified butter to pacify excessive [administration of emetics];
that [excessive administration] results in purgation, anal pain, and inflammation.
Furthermore, those complications which have not been mentioned all subside, and the patient becomes free from disease; indeed,
physicians desire that for one whose limbs have been well-anointed in the case of vāta-śūla, sudation (sveda) should be administered as appropriate,
and that he should drink digestive (dīpana) gruel.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the third chapter, named "Success in Emetics and Purgatives," in the Section on Success;
and [now begins] the fourth chapter, named "Success in Nasal Therapy."
Now, therefore, we shall explain the successful application of nasal therapy (*nastaḥkarma*).
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa:
"Nasal therapy is said to be of two kinds: purification (*śodhana*) and filling (*pūraṇa*)."

In cases where *kapha* and *vāyu* predominate, one should take any one, two, or three of the following—*ṣaḍgrantha*, *vṛścīkā*, *pippalī*, *ikṣvāku*, *kṣavaka*, *pravaraka*, seeds of *śigru*, seeds of *śirīṣa*, seeds of *apāmārga*, seeds of *naktamāla*, garlic (*lasuna*), seeds of *mayūraka*, *saindhava* salt, *sauvarcala* salt, bark of *varāṅga*, *jyotiṣmatī*, or *viśvabheṣaja*—and having ground them on a clean stone slab, mix them with the fresh juice of *bījapūraka* or the fresh juice of *ārdraka*, or one of those two, combined with honey and *mṛdvīkā* grapes; this should be administered while warm.

Having prepared the patient who is lying down facing east with his nose elevated, the physician—or one authorized by the physician—should apply fomentation to the neck, the openings of the vessels, the forehead, the nose, the facial hair, the face, the neck, and other regions as required. Then, having bent the tip of the nose downward with the left thumb, he should extract phlegm from the head through the right nostril, administering it drop by drop in small quantities; furthermore, he should repeatedly apply fomentation to the heart and other limbs, and massage them after the discharge of a small amount of phlegm.

Or, having prepared three, four, or five [substances], they become dry powders for insufflation (*pradhamana*), tied in small cloth bags to be sniffed; when combined with honey, however, they constitute an *avapīḍa*. It is called *pariṣat* because it completely destroys the phlegm in the mouth and nose. With those same [substances], [an oil] is prepared with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*), marrow, and urine.

One should administer [medicine] by force to an infant held in the lap of a nurse; for a disease, if neglected, develops like poison. Therefore, one should perform the treatment neither too quickly nor too slowly, neither too thickly nor too thinly, neither too hot nor too cold—nor for one who is hungry or thirsty, nor after drinking [liquids], nor during undigested mucus (pratiśyāya), nor during indigestion (ajīrṇa), nor during wind-disease of the head or fever, nor when fatigued, nor for one wishing to bathe the head, nor immediately after bathing the head, nor for a woman in her menses—except in cases of emergency.

If medicine is administered to him too quickly, it obstructs the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and his bodily orifices (*khāni*) become inflamed; moreover, dyspnea, cough, hiccups, salivation, obstruction of speech, and exhaustion arise. Alternatively, if it is excessively hot, it produces a burning sensation and causes the wounds to resemble the whirling of the sun. If it is excessively cold, it causes constipation (*viṣṭambha*). If it is too much [in quantity], it returns suddenly all at once. If it is too little, it causes constant agitation. If it is given too frequently, it provokes the wind (*vāta*) and other humors. If it is too sharp, it incessantly agitates the loss of memory, insanity, wind disorders, and so forth. By this very [explanation], the method of treatment is explained.

Furthermore, for one who has drunk [the medicine] or undergone nasal therapy (nasya), there may arise nasal discharge, diseases of the head, heaviness, and excessive salivation of phlegm; in cases of chronic catarrh (pakva-pratiśyāya), injury to the nose, fetid nose, nasal swelling, and nasal polyps; in cases of catarrh due to indigestion (ajīrṇa-pratiśyāya), obstruction of the sides, hoarseness of the throat, cough, dyspnea, vomiting, fever, anorexia, and restlessness; after bathing the head, [diseases such as] hemicrania (ardhāvabhedaka), fever, and loss of digestive fire; in cases of wind-fever (vāta-jvara) and the like, it aggravates those very same diseases; and for a woman in her menses, the menstrual flow becomes disordered.

The vagina of a woman who has bathed after her menses becomes parched; for a pregnant woman, there is loss of limbs; for one suffering from indigestion, there is vomiting and anorexia; for a hungry person, exhaustion and anorexia; for a thirsty person, cough, dyspnea, phlegm, and vomiting. Now, indeed, we shall prescribe the appropriate medicine for these conditions. For nasal therapy (nastaḥkarma), whether dry, oily, or both, each has its own respective treatment that is non-contradictory.

And here is the specific distinction: in cases of vomiting, one should cause the patient to drink a decoction prepared by boiling grapes (*mṛdvīkā*), pomegranate (*dāḍima*), rose-apple (*jambu*), mango (*āmra*), and *musta*; this should be cooled, strained, filtered, and mixed with honey and sugar. As before, it is highly commended. Furthermore, a meal consisting of red *śāli* rice, green gram (*mudga*) broth, and rock salt (*saindhava*), along with sudation (*sveda*), fasting (*laṅghana*), gargles (*kavalagraha*), nasal drops (*avapīḍa*), spitting out secretions (*ṣṭhīvana*), fumigation (*dhūpana*), and inhalation of smoke (*dhūmapāna*), as well as fasting, are recommended for coryza (*pratiśyāya*). Thus concludes the assembly.

When the food is digested and there is excessive salivation due to *kapha*, one should lick a powder of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) with rock salt (*saindhava*) and honey. For the eyes, rock salt, black pepper, *rasāñjana*, and realgar (*manaḥśilā*), ground with goat’s milk and made into suppositories (*varti*), alleviate itching, blurred vision, discharge, and eye-secretions. Alternatively, medicinal extracts (*rasakriyā*)—along with head-purgatives, smoking, nasal drops, emetics, purgatives, non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*), and a wholesome diet—are recommended.

Oil cooked with the pastes of *devadāru*, *tālīsa*, *māṃsī*, *musta*, *śigru*, *gandharvā*, *vāsaka*, and *punarnavā*, along with honey, should be applied frequently to him. For one who suffers from excessive nasal administration (*atinasya*), thirst, coldness, or shivering, a strong head-purgative (*śirovirecana*) produces wind-disorders such as *śaṅkhaka*, *hanustambha*, *divākarāvarta*, and extreme delusion, or it may cause fever with its complications; in these cases, *kumārataila*, *yaṣṭīmadhukataila*, *punarnavātaila*, or clarified butter (*ghṛta*) prepared in a similar manner [should be used].

The meat broth of wild animals (*jāṅgala*) prepared with spices is recommended. In cases of insomnia, fish, meat, curd, barley, wheat, *śāli* rice, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice, prepared with molasses and combined with fats, salts, and pungent spices as side dishes, induce sleep. For a woman who has bathed after her menses and for a pregnant woman, one should prescribe medicine according to the chapters on flowers and the chapters on medicinal soups (*puṣpādhyāya* and *yūṣādhyāya*). Alternatively, milk processed with the *jīvanīya* (vitalizing) drugs may be used as an enema (*pariṣeka*).
Regarding this, there are these verses: [The verses follow.]
Kumārataila is the supreme remedy for these diseases;
likewise, aged ghee is beneficial when used as nasal drops, for drinking, or for massage.
Furthermore, fasting, medicated smoking, fumigation, sudation, and warm affusions are recommended.
Enmity, oppression,
and [other such factors]— barley-food, *śāli* rice, mung beans, *dhātrī*, pomegranate,
and rock salt are beneficial as a nasal medication (*nasya*) for one suffering from the disorder at that time.
In the administration of nasal therapy (nasya) for infants, especially those who are breast-feeding,
one should employ either pungent oil (kaṭutaila) or ghee mixed with rock salt (saindhava);
one drop, two drops, or three drops, according to the observation of the disease.
One should place one's finger on the two nostrils and close them for a moment;
by this, the phlegm is digested and one is no longer afflicted by phlegm.
One should also observe the prescribed avoidances, such as bathing and other such activities.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, named "Success in Nasal Therapy," in the section on Success within the Siddhisthāna.
Now begins the fifth chapter, named "Success in Therapeutic Procedures."
Now, therefore, we shall expound the "Success of Treatment.
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa:
"A physician who desires the success of his treatments should always speak thus:"
One should regard oneself as if holding a vessel of oil— out of fear of seeing [the resulting] disease.
One should avoid sexual intercourse during indigestion, riding in vehicles, speaking loudly, sleeping during the day, excessive walking or standing, unwholesome food, and the like.
When there is indigestion, disease increases and emaciation arises again;
through sexual intercourse during medical treatment, one incurs impotence and pallor. He who constantly indulges excessively in sexual pleasure suffers from wind (vāta) disorders due to travel.
From sleeping during the day, there occurs impairment of the digestive fire (agni-sāda), an increase in phlegm (kapha), fever, and loss of appetite (aruci).

From speaking too loudly, there results stiffness of the neck (manyā-stambha), headache, constriction of the speech organs, sides, and jaw; as well as hoarseness of the throat, fatigue, exhaustion, and fever.
Diseases of the wind (vāta) affecting the waist, groins, feet, thighs, knees, and bladder;
gravel, stones, lameness, and other such conditions arising from excessive walking;
numbness of the lower body, as well as lethargy, stupor, and various delusions—[these result from the suppression of natural urges].
Vāta-śoṇita (gout), nausea, discoloration, loss of appetite, exhaustion, itching, jaundice, fever, vertigo, as well as jaundice, skin diseases,
erysipelas, scabies, and other such ailments are born from unwholesome regimens.
One should administer their respective treatments without contradiction:
those who are emaciated one should nourish, and those who are over-nourished one should cause to lose weight.
[One should avoid treating] those who are excessively tall, excessively obese, decrepit, cracked, or thin.
And one should avoid that which is crooked.
(12) Excessively short, hard, thick, thin, long, slow-acting, perforated, too large, and damaged—these nine types of enema bags (*basti*) are to be rejected. (13)

Not reaching the rectum, being carried too far, the intellect being misplaced, causing pain, leaking, becoming stuck, being loose, obstructing the flatus, and being administered either too late or too early—
these are the defects arising from errors of judgment on the part of the practitioner performing the enema procedure.
For fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇdara), one should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) with ghee prepared with Jīvaka and Ṛṣabha;
or one should perform a decoction enema (nirūha), or induce purgation (sraṃsana); thereafter, the patient becomes comfortable.
"One should feed the child milk, barley-based foods, leafy vegetables, and the meat of wild animals, combined with fats, when hemorrhoids arise;
thus said the venerable Kaśyapa. (17)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, named "Success in Treatment," in the Section on Success (Siddhisthāna).
Now begins the sixth chapter, named "Success in the Procedure of Enemas" (Bastikarmīyasiddhi). Herein we shall explain the success regarding the procedure of enemas. 1.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa:

When the rectum is overwhelmed by impurities, or when wind has arisen in the rectum, or when feces have accumulated, or when phlegm is present, or when the nozzle is crooked, or when it is flaccid and not properly pressed, the unctuous substance does not reach the colon (*pakvāśaya*). One should recognize this as "inadequate application" (*ayoga*).

One should recognize as *atiyoga* (excessive administration) when a person who is overwhelmed by wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*kapha*), feces, or urine either moves upward while passing [the enema] or does not return at all—this being the case for one who has been purged, drained, desiccated, thirsty, hungry, exhausted, anxious, envious, fatigued, afflicted by grief, or stricken by fear. From these two [types of excessive administration], diseases such as thirst, fainting, nausea, fever, burning sensations, heart disease, swelling, colic, hemorrhoids, anemia, and excessive numbness arise. In those cases as well, relief is attained through oleation, sudation, emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enemas (*āsthāpana*), and the use of fruit-purgatives, along with wholesome, measured, and appropriate diet, according to the specific humor involved.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"The enema, being excessively compressed or due to its excessive quantity, becomes overwhelmed by *vāta*;
even when it has reached the mouth, it may be mixed with *pitta* and *kapha*."

One should observe these symptoms when it ascends upward: it causes severe obstruction, or it suppresses the vital breaths (prāṇas), or there is thirst, fainting, perspiration, nausea, burning sensation, heaviness, and giddiness.
Having perceived these signs—
and having rested again and again—
one should repeatedly press [the area] with strength once power has been generated, and one should sprinkle it with cold water.

One should terrify, frighten, and cause him to weep; one should tell him that his own dear kinsmen and relatives have died, or likewise that they are bound, slain, or mistreated. Then, having sprinkled him with cold water and fanned him, one should drink well-ground kuṣṭha together with kumuda and cow's bile mixed with water.

One should drink *abhayā* mixed with cow’s urine, or combined with *trivṛt*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *saptalā*, and other such substances; or, for one whose morbid humors have been eliminated, the elders highly recommend a non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) prepared with a decoction of purgative drugs, mixed with oil, heated, and seasoned with salt, along with the five roots (*pañcamūla*).
One should feed him with *śālī* rice accompanied by meat juice prepared from wild animals (*jāṅgalaka*) seasoned with ghee; furthermore, one should avoid all [excessive] bathing and such activities.
Then, having observed his suitability, digestive fire, strength, and other factors, one should nourish the child using enemas (*basti*) alone.

One who suffers from abdominal distension and is afflicted by colic pain, whose body is well-lubricated, and who eats wholesome food, should be treated with the application of medicinal suppositories (phalavarti) as prescribed,
as well as with powders of yeast (kiṇva), white mustard (siddhārthaka), and black gram (māṣa).
One should prepare fruit-suppositories (phala-varti) resembling barley-corns, prepared with oil, jaggery, and rock salt;
these should be administered into the rectum for one suffering from abdominal distension (ānāha), six, seven, or five times according to the patient's age.
By means of these, once the patient has been purged, he attains relief; however, if this is not successful, one should purge him with sharp (tīkṣṇa) drugs.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, named "Success in Enema Therapy," in the section on Success in the Siddhisthāna.
The seventh chapter, titled "Success in the Five Procedures.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the success in the five procedures (pañcakarmīyā-siddhi).
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.

Then, O Blessed One, among the diseases of embodied beings, which ones are curable by emesis and which are not; which ones are curable by purgation and which are not; which ones are curable by oil enema and which are not; which ones are curable by decoction enema and which are not? [The Blessed One: The Blessed One said: "O son of noble family, listen attentively and bear it well in mind; I shall explain to you how the diseases of embodied beings are curable or incurable by means of emesis and so forth. In this regard, O son of noble family, those diseases of embodied beings that arise from an excess of phlegm (*kapha*) and wind (*vāta*), and which are characterized by heaviness, coldness, numbness, and a lack of appetite, are curable by emesis. Those that are characterized by a burning sensation, thirst, heat, and a downward movement of the humors are not curable by emesis. Those diseases that arise from an excess of bile (*pitta*) and wind, and which are characterized by a downward movement of the humors, abdominal distension, and a lack of appetite, are curable by purgation. Those that are characterized by upward movement, fainting, and a burning sensation in the head are not curable by purgation. Those diseases that arise from an excess of wind and phlegm, and which are characterized by stiffness, heaviness, and a lack of movement, are curable by oil enema (*anuvāsana*). Those that are characterized by excessive heat, thirst, and a burning sensation are not curable by oil enema. Those diseases that arise from an excess of bile and phlegm, and which are characterized by pain, fever, and the expulsion of feces and urine, are curable by decoction enema (*nirūha*). Those that are characterized by a lack of heat, weakness, and the absence of morbid humors are not curable by decoction enema."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, thus have I explained to you how the diseases of embodied beings are curable or incurable by means of emesis and so forth."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, furthermore, there are four types of diseases of embodied beings: those arising from the primary humors (*doṣaja*), those arising from exogenous causes (*āgantuja*), those arising from a combination of both (*sannipātaja*), and those arising from mental afflictions (*āhārasamutthita*). Among these, those arising from the primary humors are curable by the aforementioned methods. Those arising from exogenous causes—such as injuries from weapons, poison, or fire—are curable by external treatments such as surgery, ointments, and bandages. Those arising from a combination of both are curable by a combined application of these methods. Those arising from mental afflictions—such as grief, fear, anger, or desire—are curable by means of counseling, consolation, and the cultivation of wholesome thoughts."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, thus have I explained to you the fourfold classification of diseases and their respective treatments."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, furthermore, there are three grades of severity for diseases: mild, moderate, and severe. Mild diseases are curable with simple remedies. Moderate diseases require more intensive treatment. Severe diseases require the most comprehensive and urgent intervention."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, thus have I explained to you the three grades of severity and their corresponding management."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, furthermore, there are two types of patients: those who are compliant and those who are non-compliant. Compliant patients follow the instructions of the physician and take their medicine at the proper time; they are easily cured. Non-compliant patients disregard the physician's advice, do not take their medicine, or take it at the wrong time; they are difficult to cure or incurable."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, thus have I explained to you the two types of patients and their prognosis."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, furthermore, there are five factors that determine the success of medical treatment: the physician, the medicine, the attendant, the patient, and the nurse. A physician who is learned, experienced, and compassionate; medicine that is pure, effective, and appropriate; an attendant who is skillful, attentive, and kind; a patient who is self-controlled, patient, and follows instructions; and a nurse who is diligent, clean, and devoted—when these five factors are present, the treatment will be successful."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, thus have I explained to you the five factors essential for successful medical treatment."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, furthermore, there are three types of physicians: the ignorant, the half-learned, and the truly wise. The ignorant physician lacks knowledge of the scriptures and clinical practice; he is like a blind man leading the blind and brings about harm rather than healing. The half-learned physician possesses some theoretical knowledge but lacks practical experience; he is hesitant and often errs in his diagnosis and treatment. The truly wise physician is proficient in both theory and practice, possesses great compassion, and acts with skill and precision; he is the one who truly heals."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, thus have I explained to you the three types of physicians."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, furthermore, there are three types of medicines: those that are potent but harsh, those that are mild but slow-acting, and those that are balanced. Potent but harsh medicines may cure the disease quickly but can cause side effects. Mild but slow-acting medicines are safe but may not overcome a severe illness. Balanced medicines are both effective and gentle; they are the best choice for most patients."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, thus have I explained to you the three types of medicines."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, furthermore, there are three types of attendants: the unskilled, the skilled, and the highly skilled. The unskilled attendant does not understand the physician's instructions and fails to provide proper care. The skilled attendant understands the instructions and performs his duties competently. The highly skilled attendant anticipates the needs of the patient and physician, acting with foresight and wisdom."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, thus have I explained to you the three types of attendants."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, furthermore, there are three types of patients: the easy to treat, the difficult to treat, and the incurable. The easy to treat patient has faith, follows instructions, and has a favorable constitution. The difficult to treat patient is stubborn, ignores advice, and has a complex condition. The incurable patient has exhausted their lifespan, is afflicted by a terminal disease, or lacks the necessary conditions for recovery."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, thus have I explained to you the three types of patients."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, furthermore, there are three types of nurses: the negligent, the attentive, and the devoted. The negligent nurse is careless and fails to administer medicine or care. The attentive nurse is vigilant and ensures the patient's comfort and health. The devoted nurse is selfless, compassionate, and treats the patient as her own kin."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, thus have I explained to you the three types of nurses."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, thus have I fully explained to you the various aspects of medical science, including the nature of diseases, their classifications, the types of patients, the qualities of physicians and medicines, and the roles of attendants and nurses. By understanding these principles, a physician may bring relief to suffering beings and fulfill the purpose of the sacred teachings."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, this is the chapter on the 'Classification of Diseases and Their Treatments' within the Great Treatise on the Eight Branches of Medicine."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, if a physician masters this chapter, he will possess the wisdom to diagnose and treat all ailments, thereby becoming a true benefactor to the world."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, therefore, you should study and uphold this teaching with diligence, and share it with others to ensure the welfare of all living beings."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, thus have I spoken. Having heard these words, the son of noble family and the entire assembly rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had taught."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, furthermore, there are three types of therapeutic procedures: palliative (*śamana*), eliminative (*harana*), and restorative (*bṛṃhaṇa*). Palliative procedures alleviate symptoms without removing the root cause. Eliminative procedures expel the morbid humors from the body. Restorative procedures nourish and strengthen the body when it is depleted."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, thus have I explained to you the three types of therapeutic procedures."* *The Blessed One said:* "O son of noble family, furthermore, there are three types

Kaśyapa states: Phlegm-born fever, anorexia, bad taste in the mouth, excessive salivation, phlegmatic heart disease, choleraic vomiting (visūcikā), cough, asthma, throat obstruction, tonsillitis (galaśuṇḍikā), goiter (galagaṇḍa), cervical adenitis (gaṇḍamālā), scrofula (rohiṇikā), scrotal enlargement (vidārikā), severe internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), nausea, urinary disorders (prameha), chlorosis (halīmaka), the Skanda-graha, Skanda-epilepsy (skandāpasmāra), Skanda-pitṛ-graha, Naigameṣa-graha, heaviness of milk, increase of milk, thickening of milk, indigestion (ajīrṇa), cutting pain (parikartikā), nausea, colic, flatulence, excessive purging, diarrhea (arśita), and those afflicted by poison or drinking [poisonous substances]—these are curable by emetics.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"And those diseases in which phlegm predominates..."

An elderly person, one who has recently flowered, one in her menses, a pregnant woman, one confined to bed, one with scanty milk, one with light milk, one whose milk has ceased, one who has lost her child through vomiting of breast milk, one prone to vomiting, a woman desiring offspring, one who considers herself wise, one suffering from abdominal disease, one with fever caused by Vāta, a corpulent person, one with eye disease, one afflicted by thirst, one with fainting, one who has undergone a Nirūha-vasti or an Anuvāsana-vasti, one wounded, one emaciated, one suffering from hemorrhoids, a very young child, or an extremely old person.

Those suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic disorders, upward discharge of blood, hair diseases, ear ailments, head tremors, facial paralysis (ardita), hemicrania (ardhāvabhedaka), sūryāvarta, revatī, pauṇḍarīka, śakunī, pūtanā, or mukhamaṇḍikā fevers; those who are not pregnant but desirous of conception; those with discolored milk, leaking milk, or weak digestion; and those with erysipelas (vaisarpa), hemorrhoids, irregular digestion, leprosy (kuṣṭha), edema, vitiligo, upward discharge of blood, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, diabetes (madhumeha), halīmaka, jaundice (kāmalā), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), heart disease, intestinal worms, abdominal epilepsy (apasmāra), rigidity, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), phlegmatic insanity (kaphonmāda), abscesses (vidradhi), elephantiasis (ślīpada), or vaginal disorders—these should not be administered emetics. Furthermore, those who are not pregnant but desirous of conception, those with discolored milk, leaking milk, or weak digestion; and those with erysipelas, hemorrhoids, irregular digestion, leprosy, edema, vitiligo, upward discharge of blood, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, diabetes, halīmaka, jaundice, anemia, heart disease, intestinal worms, abdominal epilepsy, rigidity, upward movement of wind, phlegmatic insanity, abscesses, elephantiasis, or vaginal disorders—these should not be administered emetics.
Thus it is said.

Regarding this, there is a verse: One should treat those [fevers] that are agitated, arising from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta), those of bilious origin (paittika), those involving phlegm and bile (kaphapaittika),
those resulting from the mixture of humors, and those rooted in phlegm, by means of purgation (sraṃsana).

Those with a non-unctuous or empty digestive tract, those who are emaciated or obese, those suffering from heat, the weak, the indulgent, the very delicate, those whose wealth has perished, and those afflicted by thirst, dryness of the palate, stiffness of the thighs (ūrustambha), lockjaw (hanugraha), wind-disease of the heart (vātahṛdroga), revatī, or pure vāta disorders, should not be purged.

Those suffering from catarrh, cough, asthma, consumption, hiccups, dryness of the mouth, epilepsy, throat-obstruction, thrush, tumors of the mouth, *adhimantha*, nasal discharge, hemorrhoids, *alajī*, inflammation of the uvula, goiter, scrofula, tonsillitis, ophthalmia, and other such conditions should be treated with nasal purgation (*nastaḥ-virecana*).

Furthermore, those suffering from tooth-ache, lockjaw, stiffness of the neck, headache, deafness, earache, hemicrania, *sūryāvarta*, facial paralysis, hoarseness, speech impediment, trembling of the lips, blindness, foul odor of the mouth or nose, premature graying of hair, baldness, and various ailments caused by Vāta, should be treated with nasal oleation (*nastaḥ-upasnehana*).
Regarding this, there is a verse:
One should administer oleation via the nose (nasal enema) for those with Vāta disorders, but one should purgative those with Kapha disorders;
for diseases located above the clavicle, this is indeed the supreme remedy.

Those suffering from emaciation, disorders of the vital organs (marmans), Vāta, splenic enlargement, Vāta-gulma, dysuria, pain in the colon (pakvāśaya), abdominal Vāta, uterine colic, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), stiffness of the joints, twisting of the limbs, breaking pain in the body, apatānaka, facial paralysis (ardita), scanty menstruation, absence of menstruation, failure of conception, or being surrounded by sterile seeds—these should be treated with unctuous enemas (anuvāsana).
Regarding this, there is a verse:

"Those suffering from wind disorders, those most afflicted by wind, wasting diseases, diseases characterized by stiffness, as well as those with deformities and fractures— these should be given an oil enema (anuvāsana) by one who desires their welfare."

One should not administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) to those suffering from heart disease, pallor, edema, abdominal enlargement, urinary disorders, skin diseases, hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, pulmonary consumption, erysipelas, or other diseases caused by *kapha*. Likewise, one should not administer a decoction enema (nirūha) to those afflicted with heart disease, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), abdominal tumors caused by wind, abdominal enlargement, constipation, retention of urine, twisting pain in the bladder, urinary disorders, blood-tumors, obstruction of the female reproductive tract, pain in the flanks, diabetes, leprosy, vitiligo, fistula-in-ano, stiffness, or complications arising from combined humors;

nor to those whose hearts are agitated, who are emaciated, who are overwhelmed by disease, who suffer from bloody diarrhea, fainting, swelling, or exhaustion from sexual intercourse, physical labor, fear, anxiety, jealousy, or sleeplessness.
Regarding this, there are verses:
"The quantity of oil used in an enema (basti) is such that a decoction enema (nirūha) should be three times that amount;
however, some say they should be equal, depending on the observation of age, season, and other factors."

The great sages praise the non-unctuous enema (nirūha) when administered in very small quantities; however, those who are ignorant praise it in large amounts, for from such abundance, harm is certain. These diseases born of phlegm (kapha) arise from over-nutrition (saṃtarpaṇa).
They should be treated with fasting (apatarpaṇa), and they alone are those who should be treated with lightening therapy (laṅghana);
for those diseases which are caused by vāta are known to arise from fasting,
yet they themselves become subjects for nourishing therapy (bṛṃhaṇa) once [the vāta] has been further combined with other factors.

"For those who have undergone oleation and sudation, purification by the upper and lower routes is indicated for all combined diseases; however, oleation should not be administered via enemas," so said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, named "The Success of the Five Procedures," in the Section on Therapeutics (Siddhisthāna).
Now begins the eighth chapter, named "Success through Auspicious Rites" (Maṅgalasiddhi). Hereafter, we shall expound upon the success through auspicious rites. 1.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa:
"One should always cause auspicious things to increase for all people;
all householders should practice both acts of charity and ascetic penances."
For those who are endowed with auspicious conduct, who are always self-restrained,
and who give gifts and offer oblations, no downfall is found.
Whether raw or cooked, the oily substance [is used] for an enema.
And regarding the permanent enema (nitya-basti),
it has been stated that the oil should be prepared by mixing various decoctions with fats,
and combined with honey, urine, and salt; this non-unctuous enema (nirūha) facilitates the movement of the humors (doṣas).

Saindhava salt, madhuka, grapes, śatapuṣpā, mahāsahā,
the seeds of ātmaguptā and of cucumber (urvāruka), viḍaṅga, kuñcikā, vacā, vṛṣaka, and śirivārikā.
One should administer all the vitalizing (jīvanīya) drugs as well as kharabuṣā;
that oil known as śaiśuka is recommended for enema therapy (bastikarma),
as it destroys all diseases in children and was prescribed by the performer of meritorious deeds.
One should administer emesis and purgation using the ten roots (*daśamūla*); having strained that decoction and combined it with cow’s urine, salt,
half-parts of ghee and oil, one should prepare a warm non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*).

By this, his defects go to dissolution and his digestive fire blazes up. One should boil one *āḍhaka* of the best *madana* seeds, freed from their husks, in a *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-fourth.
Upakuñcī, kharabuṣā, pippalī, rock salt (saindhava), vacā, trapusa,
śatapuṣpā, and yavānī— this decoction, when combined with milk, cow urine, and kāñjika, [is used for treatment].
This non-unctuous enema (nirūha), containing half its volume of oil, cures all diseases caused by Vāta.
It consists of Triphalā, Sārivā, Śyāmā, the two types of Bṛhatī, the bark of Vatsaka, Trāyamāṇā, Balā, Rāsnā, Guḍūcī, Nimba, and Kūlaka.
One should prepare [a formulation] with mahāsahā, śakrayava, śatapuṣpā,
vatsaka, madhūka, aṃśumatī, drākṣā, samudrāntā, and bālaka.
A non-unctuous enema (nirūha) combined with milk, honey, and ghee destroys pitta.
[One should take] triphalā, dāru, bhūtīka, the two types of karañja, citraka, ekāṣṭhīlā, and viṣāṇī.
One should purify [the patient] with the roots of *kaṇā*, *trivṛt*, and *dantī* according to the previous procedure.
A non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*) consisting of these pastes combined with salt and oil,
slightly warmed and mixed with cow’s urine, purges both upwards and downwards and destroys *kapha*.
This Nirūha enema, beginning with Kattṛṇa, destroys all disorders;
it consists of kattṛṇa, uśīra, bhūtīka, triphalā, rāsnā,
aśvagandhā, aśvadaṃṣṭrā, śigru, ayāmā, and śatāvarī.

One should boil three palas each of ela, punarnavā, bhārgī, paṭola, and guḍūcī in one droṇa of water; when it has been reduced to one-fourth, one should then add these following substances to be ground into a paste to that decoction.
Vacā, jamodā, madana, and pippalī—
only this much of the Siddhisthāna has been obtained; [the remainder is] the Kalpasthāna.
The Section on Rituals, Chapter on Incense Preparations:
Kuṣṭha, pūtika, ambara, vacā,
mustard seeds, goat’s hair, and asafoetida combined together constitute an incense.
Ghee, the horn of a ram, the hooves of a horse and an elephant,
and the hair of a monkey, a porcupine, and a mongoose constitute an excellent incense.
Ghee, resin of the *sarja* tree, black pigment, *bhallātaka*, and *śilājatu* [are also used].
Two types of *haridrā*, *jatu*, *uśīra*, mustard seeds, *puṣpārjaka*,
*viḍaṅga*, *tagara*, *patra*, *vacā*, asafoetida, and *bālaka*— this incense, named "Kaumāra," when prepared, increases progeny.
Clarified butter, the sloughed skin of a snake, the excrement of a vulture and an owl, *vacā*, and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) constitute an incense that removes epilepsy and planetary afflictions;
likewise, clarified butter, *guggulu*, *bilva*, *devadāru*, and *nameru*.
This incense, mixed with barley, belongs to Maheśvara and wards off the planetary spirits (grahas).
The incense of Agni is said to consist of cow-hair combined with ghee;
it is especially recommended for Brahmins in all diseases.
Ghee from horses, donkeys, and camels; hair, locks, and the maternal lineage [hair];

and the nails of quadrupeds—when obtained, this incense is remembered as "Bhadraṅkara" (the auspicious-maker), effective against piśācas, yakṣas, gandharvas, bhūtas, Skanda, and those afflicted by kapha.
One should employ this incense for whomsoever one desires to become free from disease in an instant:
ghee, white mustard seeds, asafoetida, the remains of offerings to the gods, unbroken grains, snake-skin, and the patched robe of a monk; this incense is said to be a destroyer of demons.
One should employ here ghee, white mustard seeds, honey, ram's horn, goat’s milk, donkey urine, hair, and soma;
this is the supreme incense known as the "Supreme Exorciser of Pretas."
For those overcome by *para* spirits and *pretas*, as well as for *pūtanā*, the following is prescribed:
ghee, white mustard seeds, *kuṣṭha*, *bhallātaka*, *vacā*, goat hair,
*tagara*, *bhūrjāvarta*, and *guggulu*.

This incense, known as the "Ten-Ingredient Incense" (daśāṅga-dhūpa), should be employed for all types of diseases, especially for epilepsy, planetary afflictions, and secondary seizures; it consists of ghee, white mustard seeds, white *coraka*, and *palāṅkaṣā*.
Śūkarī and Jaṭilā constitute the incense known as Moha; one should also include Śrīveṣṭaka, Rāla, Lakṣā, Padmaka, Candana,
Devadāru, Surasa, and that which is born of Śāla.
This incense, named Vāruṇa, is recommended for the summer season; it is used when Śakunī, Pauṇḍarīka, or Revatī are predominant, or when there is an excess of phlegm (kapha).
This four-ingredient incense consists of ghee, marrow, fat, and lac.

This medicated ghee should be administered for mild afflictions, emaciation, or in children suffering from seizure disorders (grahavaikṛta). A fumigation consisting of *vacā*, the excrement of a hyena (*tarakṣu*), its hair, its skin,
and the dung of carnivorous animals (*prasaha*) is called the "Delighter" (*nandaka*).
Ghee, long pepper, rice husks, the skin of a tawny animal, *vacā*, mustard seeds, costus, and cardamom constitute the "long-pepper incense," which dispels the influence of the *grahas*.
Ghee, snake-skin, *bilva*, lake-foam, white mustard, and lac [are used for fumigation].
This is designated as "Śrīdhūpa"; one should employ it for those who desire prosperity.
Dog excrement and urine, peacock feathers, *vacā*, ghee, and mustard seeds—this incense is renowned as the "Graha-ghna" (the destroyer of planetary spirits).
Ghee, elephant tusk, the hair of a goat, a ram, and a sheep, and cow horn— this incense is meritorious and brings about auspicious beings.
Ghee, sthauṇeyaka, māṃsī, tagara, and paripelava [are also used].
One should prepare hrivera, śatapuṣpā, yellow orpiment, realgar, musta, hareṇukā, and cardamom for the purpose of incense;
this incense is named Śiśuka, and it removes all diseases and malevolent planetary influences.
O Bhārgava, in the primary incense, the secondary incense, and the counter-incense, ghee, white mustard seeds, parched rice, and *kuśa* grass—
all these being equal in measure— this is the *brāhmī* incense, which is called the "Brahma incense."

This ghee should be administered by a physician constantly for all diseases among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas; it quickly expels all ailments. [The ingredients are: Śvadaṃṣṭrā, Vasukā, the two types of Haridrā, and Paripelava.
Vacā and bhārgī constitute this incense, which brings comfort as a counter-incense (pratidhūpa).
Ghee, padmaka, uśīra, vālaka, keśara, and rasā are known as pratidhūpa and are recommended for all diseases.
Clarified butter, monkey fur, a hen’s egg, *vacā*, barley, and white mustard—
this incense brings great success against every kind of fumigation.
[Likewise,] clarified butter, neem leaves, root, flower, fruit, and bark.
This incense, named Ariṣṭa, brings about safety (freedom from misfortune) in an instant.
Ghee, neem leaves, donkey urine, vacā, lac,
and mustard seeds— this is the incense, and it is recommended as a counter-incense as well.
Ghee, neem leaves, lac, resin of the sarja tree, unbroken grains of rice, and the excrement of a bat and an owl— this incense destroys epilepsy.
Likewise, ghee, neem leaves, and the leaves of the surasā and aśvaghna plants [are used].
Goat, sheep, goat’s hair, and wool— this king [of remedies] destroys all diseases.
Ghee, unbroken rice, jasmine flowers, honey, white mustard seeds,
and *vacā* are known as "Gaṇadhūpa," which removes the ailments caused by all spirits.
Clarified butter, the incense of the śallakī tree, and the flowers of the jātī and śirīṣa trees,
combined with nameru, is called the svastika incense; likewise,
clarified butter mixed with guggulu and devadāru wood combined with clarified butter [is another].
Black aloe-wood, clarified butter, and mustard seeds with clarified butter; likewise, grass, earth, leaves, heartwood, flowers, fruits, and bark—
these five incenses, when combined with ghee, are declared to be destroyers of the planetary afflictions.
One should also include guggulu and the others, as well as the ten-ingredient incense;
known as "household incense," it is never obstructed.
These incenses, including the siddhārthas, are declared to be forty in number.

These [medicines] bring success to physicians for men, bestowing sons and destroying diseases; with these, the physician should fumigate children who have been afflicted, as well as the lying-in chamber, and the clothing, beds, seats, and other items belonging to the children.
The physician should first collect the medicinal incense during the Puṣya conjunction;
having fasted, being pure and bathed, and under the asterisms of Maitra (Anurādhā), Āgneya (Kṛttikā), or Uttarā,
he should have it recited, offer the oblation, and listen to sounds that are agreeable to the mind.
Four pure maidens, unwearied, should pound it;
one should place that incense in a new vessel and keep it well-sealed, employing it at the proper time.
Even if one has fallen into that state, one should quickly employ the accumulated [remedies];
for indeed, success is certain in that case, just as when [a fire] was previously prepared,
provided that, having smelled the smoke of another, one does not inhale [that same] smoke again.
He quickly contracts that disease; for that purpose, he is fumigated again.

Jīvaka, fumigation (dhūpa) is declared by physicians to be of three types according to the distinction of their application: primary fumigation (dhūpa), secondary fumigation (anudhūpa), and counter-fumigation (pratidhūpa).
Others, however, who follow the tradition of Kaśyapa and are experts in pediatrics (kaumārabhṛtya), declare that incense has two origins based on its dependence upon the mobile and the immobile.
From what have incenses arisen? What are their presiding deities? What are their substrates?
By what names are they considered, and while they are being burned, what should one recite?
Thus is the physician who has attained the status of a great man described by physicians;
therefore, hear the definitive conclusion regarding these questions according to the truth.
Whenever the daughters of the sages were born, they were carried off by Rākṣasas;
then all the great seers, devoted to burnt offerings and ascetic penance, sought refuge in Agni. Thereupon, Agni, being gratified, spoke:
"Offer these incenses and employ them as dedicated to me;
you shall have no fear from Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, or Piśācas. When diseases arise and increase, apply them indeed to the nurse."
Then those sages, being pleased and recognizing Kaśyapa as the benefactor of the world and the well-wisher of the realm of seers, joined him in that ritual;
having received oblations from the presence of Agni, he became even more exalted.
Those Kumāras, invincible to all beings, have protected them;
thus these incenses have arisen out of a desire for the welfare of living creatures,
and they are declared to have Agni as their deity, residing in both mobile and immobile things.
Having consecrated everything with the *Vidhūrava-anuvāka*, one should employ it for the protection of the child; and while [the child] is being burned, one should recite this.

May Agni fumigate you; may Brahmā fumigate you; may Śiva fumigate you; may the Vasus fumigate you; may Rudra fumigate you; may Āditya fumigate you; may the Maruts fumigate you; may the Sādhyas fumigate you; may the divine Ṛbhus fumigate you; may all the gods fumigate you; may all the deities fumigate you; may the meters fumigate you; may the earth fumigate you; may the intermediate space fumigate you; may the sky fumigate you; may the quarters fumigate you.

May the lords of the quarters fumigate you; may the divine waters fumigate you; may the auspicious Pavamāna fumigate you; may Mitra, Savitṛ, and Sūrya fumigate you; may Candra and Soma fumigate you; may the constellations fumigate you for the sake of good progeny; may the deities of the constellations fumigate you with a benevolent mind; may the days and nights fumigate you for the sake of peace; may the Ṛbhus fumigate you for the sake of meritorious action; may the years fumigate you for the sake of long life, spiritual luster, and strength.

May Prajāpati fumigate you for the sake of good progeny; may the Aśvins fumigate you for health, long life, strength, and well-being. May the Mothers fumigate you with affection; may the Fathers fumigate you for the non-severance of the body and for the *svadhā* offering. May Kumāra fumigate you for childhood; may Śākha fumigate you for youth; may Viśākha fumigate you for middle age; may Naigameṣa fumigate you for old age; may all the gods fumigate you for the celestial realm.

May all the seers fumigate you for the sake of spiritual luster; may all the rivers fumigate you for the sake of well-being; may all the mountains fumigate you for the sake of stability; may all the herbs fumigate you for the sake of food; may all the trees fumigate you for the sake of preeminence among those of good vows; may all the animals fumigate you for the sake of power and peace. I fumigate you with truth; I fumigate you with cosmic order; I fumigate you with both cosmic order and truth. Homage!
One should mutter "To the gods. Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa. This concludes the ritual procedure for incense in the section on rituals; it is the chapter on the ritual for garlic.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for garlic (laśunakalpa).
Thus said the venerable Kaśyapa:
[He spoke] to Prajāpati, who was seated at Gaṅgādvāra after having performed the Agnihotra sacrifice.
At the proper time, the Elder, desiring the welfare of living beings, asked:

"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the origin of garlic, its application, and its administration; as well as the times [for its use], and the diseases for which it is and for which it is not indicated. (3-4)
"What are his afflictions, and what is their treatment? What is the diet there, what is the avoidance, and what is the result?"—
thus questioned by his disciple, the Sage spoke for the welfare of all beings.
Listen, gentle one, to how garlic originated along with its ultimate purpose:
when Indrāṇī did not conceive even after a hundred years, Śakra devoured her, thinking it was nectar; such is the tradition. (6–7)
Embracing her with his beautiful left arm out of affection, the husband, consoling his bashful queen, made his wife drink [the water].
Due to her extreme delicacy and her modesty in the presence of her husband, [she drank it].
Because it was the essence of nectar, when the vomit emerged,
Indra happened to come to the earth and fell into an impure place;
then he said to Śacī, "You shall have many sons."
And this nectar shall become an elixir on earth;
however, due to the fault of its location and because it is not approached by the twice-born, it will become foul-smelling.
By name it shall be called garlic (laśuna), yet it remains nectar upon the earth.
Thus has this arisen; hear now the procedure for its preparation:
its juice is pungent in the seed, salty and bitter in the stalk, its leaves are astringent, and it is sweet in its post-digestive effect.
In this regard, garlic possesses sweet, bitter, and pungent tastes, each succeeding one being more predominant than the last.
Due to its sweetness, it is heavy, unctuous, and supremely nourishing.
Furthermore, because its tastes are balanced, it alleviates common ailments.
It promotes longevity, stimulates the digestive fire, acts as an aphrodisiac, brings prosperity, and maintains health and vitality.
It clarifies memory, intellect, strength, complexion, and vision;
it generates fragrance of the mouth and purifies the bodily channels.
It causes the production of semen, blood, and the embryo; it promotes modesty and self-restraint, brings about delicacy, is beneficial for the hair, and is the supreme stabilizer of youth.
Arisen from nectar, garlic is an elixir of immortality.
The teeth, flesh, nails, beard, hair, complexion, age,
and strength of men who eat garlic never decline once they have been attained;
nor do the breasts of women sag as long as they constantly consume garlic.
Their beauty does not fade, nor do their offspring, strength, or lifespan;
their good fortune increases and their youth becomes firm.
The diseases arising from worldly passion do not afflict her;
she never falls under the sway of the hips, the loins, or the roots of the limbs;
she is never barren, nor is she ever unpleasant to behold.
A man shall possess firm intellect, long life, and beautiful offspring;
he shall be untiring in worldly duties and a preserver of his vital seed (śukra). Furthermore, as many women as he approaches shall conceive.

One becomes fragrant as a blue lotus and gains the complexion of a lotus (24). One attains softness of body and sweetness of voice; it pacifies disorders of the digestive tract and greatly kindles the bodily fire (25).
In cases of wasting, fractures, and chronic diseases; in all wind-related disorders (vāta-roga); in seminal confusion, cough, and all types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha);
in worms, abdominal tumors (gulma), leucoderma (kilāsa), itching, and eruptive boils.
In cases of discoloration, darkness of vision, dyspnea, night-blindness, and eating too little;
in chronic fever, burning sensations, and tertian or quartan fevers; and in the impairment of the bodily channels, as well as stiffness and emaciation of the limbs. (27–28)

One should consume garlic for the increase of intelligence, digestive fire, and strength, [in cases of] urinary calculi, dysuria, ear-ache, fistula-in-ano, menorrhagia, splenic disorders, consumption, lameness, and gout. (29)
One is quickly liberated from diseases and attains a superior physique.

This [remedy] should not be applied for any other disease, whether caused by phlegm (ślaiṣmika) or bile (paittika), nor for one who is emaciated, an elderly person, one with weak digestion, a woman who has recently given birth, a pregnant woman, or a child. 30–31.

In cases of undigested fever (āma-jvara), diarrhea, jaundice, hemorrhoids, stiffness of the thighs, constipation, and diseases of the throat and mouth; likewise, in one who has just vomited, undergone purgation, received nasal medication (nasya), or been treated with drying therapies— 32.

One should not administer garlic to those afflicted by thirst or vomiting, nor to those with excessive hiccups or dyspnea; nor to those who lack self-control, those without companions, the poor, or those of evil character; nor to those who have already been administered enemas or purgative suppositories. (33–34)

For those whose digestive fire and strength are undiminished, the use of garlic is recommended in all diseases during the months of Pauṣa or Māgha; it should be fresh, palatable, dehusked, and unrefined. (35)
The dosage and the restrictive regimen should be determined according to the individual's digestive fire, age, and suitability.
The smallest dose of garlic is four *pala*;
the medium is six *pala*, and the best is eight, ten, or even twelve *pala*. (36–37)
There may be one hundred, sixty, or fifty measures even for dry plants that have set seed; however, for green plants with leaves, it should be as much as one can consume, even if it causes fainting.
Or rather, one should eat as much as one has the strength for, even if it leads to a swoon.
