On an auspicious day, a wise man should have garlic administered;
he should remain in a place free from agitation and protected from the wind, comfortable with plenty of fire, and clothed in garments of silk, cotton, wool, deerskin, or woolen blankets. (39–40)
He should be provided with spotless garments that are thoroughly perfumed with agallochum incense; he should always be provided with incenses and powders, and he should always wear sandals.
Another person should bring garlic, while yet another should prepare it.
One should discard the petals of these [lotuses] and prepare the seeds and stalks;
having cut them into fine pieces, one should thoroughly soak them in ghee—specifically fresh *haiyaṅgavīna* butter, oil, or what is suitable for a child. 42–43.
They should remain immersed with as much enthusiasm as possible,
even for two, three, five, ten, or eight days; [the body] should be well-anointed with oil, and one should avoid self-reflection, sleep, and the use of a tooth-stick.
Having digested his food and risen comfortably, he should cause the Brahmins to pronounce auspicious blessings;
having sat down, he should eat those [medicinal substances], always using warm water as an adjunct.
Even as a side dish (upadaṃśa), fresh ginger and Viśvabheṣaja (dry ginger) should be administered.
One may also give the filaments of citron fruits or "life-giving" pomegranates, as well as green vegetables, provided one avoids radishes (47).
Furthermore, a powder of fried meat parts may be used as a dusting agent.

One should powder cinnamon bark, ginger, black pepper, small cardamom, and cumin, along with all available salts, and mix them therein; one should also appropriately procure well-prepared liquor for it. 48–49.
One should eat garlic at intervals and likewise drink liquor at intervals;
sitting comfortably while the digestive fire is active, one should slowly consume it for the sake of satisfaction.
Afterwards, one should drink warm water, liquor, boiled milk, or plain milk.
One who knows the nature of the digestive fire, diseases, and suitability should not consume a second meal;
then, having washed his hands, mouth, and lips with warm water and the powder of *kalāya*, he should remain near the fire, wearing heavy clothing. 51–52.
One should hold in the mouth betel leaf together with lime, nutmeg, and katuka fruit, combined with cloves, flowers, camphor, and kakkola fruit;
one should not spit while holding it, nor should one indulge in sleep during the day.
By this, his phlegm dissolves and his fainting fits subside;
a pleasant fragrance arises for him and his foul odor perishes.
Being thirsty, he should drink warm water boiled with digestive stimulants.
One who is excessively afflicted by pitta may drink it lukewarm, boiled with mustaka and śuṇṭhī, or with śuṇṭhī and bālaka;
or, having drunk it simply with śuṇṭhī while slightly warm, one may sleep peacefully at night. (56)
By this method, one who has conquered the senses should consume [the medicine] for a fortnight, a month, a season, or even three or four months;
having obtained the appropriate substance and considering the disease, one should administer it according to the time.
But those dry foods must not be eaten out of fear of aggravating the bile;
listen now to what kind of food should be given in small quantities for one's benefit:
cakes made of barley and wheat, roasted on a skull-shaped pan.

Dry, fragrant, and heart-pleasing *pūpaṭas* mixed with salt; warm *polikās* of *śāli* rice; preparations of green gram and boiled grain (*kulmāṣa*); balls of parched grain flour (*saktu*) well-seasoned with salt; and five-layered pastries (*pañcapaṭṭita*) with a small amount of oil. (60–61)
Lāva, eṇa, tittiri, śaśaka, kapiñjala, cakora,
and other wild animals and birds should be prepared for the sake of their meat—
slightly warm and seasoned with sour, salty, and fatty condiments. (62)
Meat is recommended, or sour fruits such as jujube, emblic myrobalan, and pomegranate (63).
Vāstuka leaf cooked with pomegranate, or with cāṅgerī or emblic myrobalan, or the flower of the *burbura* or *vṛṣa*, or young radish [is also beneficial] (64).
For one who consumes excessive fats, dry food (rūkṣānna) is recommended;
however, for one who eats little fat, one should provide very unctuous food.
This applies to those suffering from skin diseases (kuṣṭha), asthma (śvāsa), fainting (tamī), cough (kāsa), urinary disorders (prameha), and circular wind-pain (vātakuṇḍalī).
One suffering from spleen disease, hemorrhoids, or abdominal tumors should eat this with water;
at the end of the meal, one should provide a soup for drinking and eating made from one pala of crushed garlic and two palas of pomegranate. 66–67.
One should give two palas each of meat, ghee, and oil;
well-seasoned, well-salted, and warm, one should feed the hungry person.
He should partake of a small amount of boiled rice made from *śāli*, *ṣaṣṭika*, or *gaura* varieties.
For three days, he should provide him with soup containing curd and buttermilk;
thereafter, for another three days, he should provide it with fermented gruel (śukta) and mung-bean broth.
Beyond that, he should never eat food kept overnight, but should always prepare fresh soup.

One should avoid incompatible foods, those that cause burning sensations, leafy vegetables, cow's milk products, and grains that increase secretions, as well as meat, sugarcane products, travel, sexual intercourse, anxiety, grief, physical exertion, and emaciation. (71)
One should avoid everything that is unwholesome and remain in a sheltered place for sleeping and sitting (72).
One should abandon cold treatments and instead consume garlic;
for from cold treatments and from oleation, one may incur dropsy (jalodara) (73).
From excessive oleation and the application of physical force, there arises fear of anemia, edema, and pain;
from oleation and the consumption of heavy food and drink, there occurs the disorder of the *grahaṇī* and jaundice (*kāmalā*).
By means of mushrooms, fish, and beef, there is affliction by fever, leprosy, and consumption (*kṣaya*).

From dry substances and during the hot season, there is fear of all pitta-related diseases (75). Colic, diarrhea, flatulence, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, hiccups, cholera, dyspnea, and sleepiness— these and other complications may also arise here (76).
Complications should be treated with their respective medical therapies;
in cases of vomiting, indigestion, burning sensations, and heaviness arising from kapha,
one should administer fasting as appropriate and then resume a wholesome diet.

One should administer purgation, emesis, nasal medication (nasya), and gargles (kavalagraha), taking into account the strength of the body and the disease; however, one should avoid sharp [therapies] for this patient.
The wise person should be full of faith, and should neither hasten nor feel fear.

Then, once the regimen of wholesome food has been completed, after seven days, one should have the patient— who is now eating all kinds of food, free from complications, comforted, and strong— drink ghee mixed with triphalā and salt for three days, along with garlic and other such items.
One should not cause exhaustion; rather, one should feed him cooked food.
By this, whatever disorder in his body was latent is quickly pacified, and no disorder caused by the unctuous substance (sneha) will subsequently afflict him. 81–82.
Eczema, boils, itching, deafness, numbness, and loss of sensation—
these indeed afflict him if he does not undergo purgation.
Therefore, a mild purgative should be administered, such as *trivṛt* with *triphalā* and ghee.
One should administer it with warm salt; thereafter, one should drink warm water.
While consuming [the medicine], the wise person should avoid honoring heavy foods, the gods, and the sacred fires.
Having bathed, with a fragrant and pleasing mind, one should worship the gurus and the deities.
Hereafter, I shall explain the remaining ritual procedure for garlic (*laśuna*).
One should throw one *āḍhaka* of seeds, having crushed them, into a *droṇa* of water.
It should be kept either in a place where the water does not dry up, in fire, or among sixty-day-old grains.
Free from disease and resembling an immortal, the man shall live for a hundred years;
as long as he eats [this], for that many hundreds of years he shall live,
casting off his worn-out skin just as a serpent sheds its old skin.
One should regularly consume one *pala* of garlic, or two *palas*, along with clarified butter;
there should be only a small amount of honey. Having licked this, one should afterwards drink milk.
For a year, at the end of each period of indigestion, one should eat rice with milk.

He too, freed from all diseases, lives for a hundred years. For one who is unable to digest raw grains, one should administer them roasted in clarified butter and prepared like leaf-cakes (patrapūpalikā). 90–91.
These are prepared successfully with meat, or with barley gruel (yavāgū), or with curd;
they are also recommended as *nimandakas*, seasoned with various ingredients.
[92] One hundred palas of garlic [should be boiled] in five droṇas of water.
One should boil that [mixture] until one *droṇa* remains, and then cook it again with one *āḍhaka* of ghee and one *āḍhaka* of milk; one should add this internal essence (*garbha*),
consisting of one hundred palas of garlic seeds finely prepared.
One should add whatever is clarifying, vitalizing, and aphrodisiac;
having boiled it like the *akṣa* preparation together with the ten roots (*daśamūla*), one should remove it from the heat once it is ready.
This, when taken as a drink or added to food along with honey and sugar, is beneficial. 95.
By that same procedure, oil is recommended for the administration of enemas (basti);
it bestows virility and progeny even upon the impotent, the barren, and the very aged.
When processed with purgative and emetic substances, it serves as an ointment for leprosy (kuṣṭha).

When applied to food, drink, and ointments, this unsurpassed fragrant ghee (gandhasarpis) brings health to those suffering from vitiligo, sinus ulcers, and worms. Now, that which is called Great Fragrance (Gandhamahat) is prescribed for the wealthy.
Upon seeing which, even the Wind-god himself would quickly break down;
one who is beset by a host of diseases and accompanied by the hosts of Maruts should eat garlic according to the prescribed rule and even fashion it into a crest-ornament. 99–100.
One should wear a garland of garlic on the head and even on the ears;
one should also wear a woolen blanket of garlic as an outer garment.
One should likewise bind clusters of garlic upon the hands, the feet, and the neck.
One should also place [the offerings] beneath the garments on the beds and seats;
one should give garlic and onions at all the doors of the house for the wives,
brothers, sons, female slaves, and attendants.
When the excellent incense has been offered, the wise man should treat everyone as he would himself;
he should provide all kinds of food and drink containing garlic, and let musical instruments be played and songs be sung according to one's desire. 104.
Let actors, archers, and wrestlers display their respective skills (verse 105).
One should provide perfumes, garlands, food, and drink as is appropriate;
for upon seeing the great fragrance, the wind turns back even from the very doorway (verse 106).

While wandering for alms in the Devadāru forest in a disguised form, Rudra disregarded the wives of the sages as he gazed upon them. Consequently, they had no offspring; thereupon, they sought refuge with him.
The Lord, being pleased, spoke these words to Bhadrakālī and Umā:
"O wives of the sages, you must establish this place named Gandhamādana for the destruction of all diseases and for the production of strength, beauty, and progeny."
"Like a fixed line upon a stone, the offspring shall certainly come to pass— destroying madness, poison, and curses, and dispersing the host of winds.
Then those women who discourse on Brahman performed a great festival of perfumes.
They obtained their desired objects and composed this treatise.
This supreme secret must not be spoken by a physician anywhere out of negligence, even to the son of a teacher. 111–112.
O Sage, I have been well-adorned by you with this [knowledge], having obtained which a physician in this world does not falter in his medical practices.
Garlic is known to be of two kinds: that grown on a mountain and that grown in a field. (113)
It is equal to nectar; in its absence, it is the next best thing for one's welfare.
It should be administered by physicians of the gods and the foremost of the twice-born for the sake of success.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa. 114–115.
Thus, in the Kalpas, the chapter on the preparation of garlic and the preparation of pungent oils;
now, therefore, we shall explain the preparation of pungent oils. 1.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa:
"I shall now explain the instruction on pungent oil which destroys the spleen;
for there is indeed no medicine superior to this for the pacification of the spleen."

First, however, one should cause a strong patient with *plīhodara* (enlarged spleen) who is free from complications to drink oil— either *kalyāṇaka* ghee or *ṣaṭpala* ghee— in an appropriate dose, provided he maintains a wholesome regimen of conduct, diet, and lifestyle.
Five applications for this [medicinal preparation] have been described: by means of measured doses (mātrā), continuous administration (sātatyā), and eating (bhojana).
The superior dose is twelve palas; the middling is recorded as six palas;
the inferior dose is four palas; or it may be according to the strength of one's digestive fire.

The physician should administer the entire regimen for one who has drunk medicated fats (sneha), provided they avoid staying awake at night, exposure to wind, fire, and sunlight, and remain in open air.
One should know that when the fat has just been drunk, there may be pain and drowsiness as it is being digested.
When the purgative has been digested, there is clarity of eructation, lightness, and purity;
however, one who is emaciated or excessively purged should be treated with rice-scum (*maṇḍa*) and similar remedies.
A strong patient who has been mildly purged should eat soft boiled rice.
One should always prepare *kāmbalika* according to one's strength, using a slightly oily and sour broth seasoned with *rohita* and *moca* fish,
enriched with sour fruits, digestive stimulants (*dīpana*), and prepared with pungent oil. 10.
One should feed him constantly with that [milk] until his vital breath is restored;
once his life-force has been regained, one should then always give him castor oil in measured doses according to his strength, either prepared or fresh.

One should cook mustard oil with grapes, *kāśmarya*, *madhuka*, *bālaka*, *uśīra*, and sandalwood in milk for men whose splenic enlargement (pleura) is characterized by excessive burning. When the [previous meal] has been digested, one should apply an unguent in the afternoon and bathe in lukewarm water.
One should eat *abhayā* fried in pungent oil and prepared with curd, along with *śāli* rice and *kāmbalika*. If that causes a burning sensation, one should then drink *kalyāṇaka* ghee.
One should apply this prepared oil— consisting of fish, pungent oil (kaṭutaila), curd, mung beans, ghee, and milk, cooked with the alkaline ash of the pārijāta tree.
This oil and ghee are said to cure splenic enlargement and abdominal tumors (gulma).
It is digestive-stimulant, unctuous, strengthening, and cures disorders of the *grahaṇī* and the flanks.

(17) One should boil one *tulā* of *kaṇikāra* bark in four *droṇas* of water until reduced to one-fourth; then, one should cook [medicinal substances] in that decoction together with an equal amount of milk. (18)

One *prastha* of pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*), two *prasthas* each of curd and black gram (*māṣa*), and the juice of *rohītaka* prepared with the ten roots (*daśamūla*) should be added; as well as the group of alkalis and life-promoting herbs (*jīvanavarga*), rock salt (*saindhava*), and whatever is digestive (*dīpana*). 19.
This excellent *karṇikārīya* unguent has been proven effective through practice.
Celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the use of pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*), comfortable beds, seats, and sleep, along with the avoidance of anxiety, envy, and fear [are required]. (20–21)
Lying on the left side, the consumption of curd and fish, and the intake of light, non-unctuous food pacify splenic enlargement (plihodara).
Alternatively, the paste or the powdered powder, or even the expressed juice of karṇikāra [is effective].
When consumed with pungent oil or buttermilk, it destroys the spleen disease (23). Alternatively,
mustard oil mixed with red dye (rāga), when consumed daily in the prescribed dose by those who eat curd, black gram, and water, destroys the spleen disease as before (24).
One should drink a handful of *rāgasarṣapa* seeds ground and mixed with *kāñjika*, along with salt and alkali; the food should be accompanied by *kāmbalika*.
Within seven days, even a greatly enlarged spleen is pacified.
"If there is burning pain that afflicts excessively, one should feed [the patient] milk processed with medicinal juices.
Thus spoke the venerable, aged Jīvaka, honored by the world, regarding the cure for splenic enlargement (plīhodara) in both children and adults. (26–27)
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa;
thus ends the chapter on the six preparations, the preparation of pungent oil, in the section on preparations.
"Now, therefore, we shall explain the Six Kalpas.
Thus indeed said the blessed Kaśyapa, concerning the seer Mārīca, who was seated and possessed the splendor of the sun and Vaiśvānara.
Having approached with due decorum, the Elder Jīvaka said:
"O Blessed One, when the eye is afflicted by an ocular disease, when should a remedy be administered, and what remedy would be beneficial?"
When asked, "What is the prescribed treatment there, and what therein is beneficial or harmful?", the Blessed One spoke this auspicious answer:
[The treatment] for children afflicted by eye disease consists of eye-drops and other such measures.

After six days, once the redness, swelling, pain, and discharge have ceased— or when these symptoms such as redness and the rest have subsided slightly, or are only mildly distressing— one should administer beneficial pacifying (saṃśamana) treatment at the appropriate time. (6–7)

Upon observing these symptoms— discharge of rheum, secretion, turbidity of vision, aversion to light, swelling of the eyelids, headache, and residual discharge on the eyelashes— one should employ a palliative treatment regimen.
One should place the infant at the breast along with the nurse on a wholesome diet.
Now, listen to me regarding the ritual preparations for these six: *cakṣuṣyā*, *puṣpaka*, *rocanā*, *rasāñjana*, and the fruit of the *kataka* tree as the sixth.
For those suffering from eye diseases, for four, five, or six months from birth,
one should rub [the medicine] with breast milk and fill the eyes with it.
[One should place] a piece of gold along with breast milk and honey inside a bronze vessel.
Or, having rubbed [the medicine], one should fill the eyes; this conquers all eye diseases.
These two, known as Kalyāṇaka and Yāvana, proclaimed by the great seers, were declared by the great ṛṣi Kaśyapa to be the foremost for the preparation of anointment.
In autumn and winter, the physician should have the ripe, eye-pleasing fruit collected and cause it to be stored well protected in a new water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
Then, one should prepare thirty fruits along with ten barley grains.

Having tied up putika in a shallow dish, soaked it in cow dung, and boiled it until cooked, one should then remove the husks and apply it ground with breast milk; a specific instruction will also be taught. 15–16.
In cases of inflammation with redness, this fresh medicinal preparation (rasakriyā) combined with *rocanā* should be used; in cases of discharge, it should be combined with rock salt (*saindhava*).
For eye-secretions, impurities, and swellings, the fresh medicinal preparation should be applied.
[The recipe is: with *puṣpaka*, cow's urine, and rock salt, along with the fresh medicinal preparation.

One should apply Cakṣuṣyā in cases of cataracts (pillī), swelling, and stiffness of the eyes. Furthermore, copper and brass rubbed together with sour liquids and black pepper, when combined with Cakṣuṣyā, pacifies ocular diseases arising from the humors.
One should bring together *cakṣuṣyā*, *rocanā*, *stanya*, and *puṣpaka*; this formulation is proclaimed as a pacifier for all eye diseases.
Even a single [ingredient], when combined with *stanya*, is highly praised for the eyes.
This concludes the ritual for the eyes; now learn from me the ritual for flowers (puṣpakalpa).
One should apply purified flowers in a windless place during the afternoon, or at night, having filled the eyes with the dried powder, one should sleep. 21–22.
Puṣpaka, combined with either rasāñjana, honey, or breast milk, conquers all eye diseases.
These same three formulations [are effective] when combined with breast milk, honey, and rasāñjana.

These three formulations of *rasāñjana* with water are praised for the pacification of all eye diseases; likewise, there are four such formulations of *rocanā*, and four formulations of the fruit of *kataka*. 24–25.

These [medicines] alleviate eye diseases and clarify the vision; they have been described according to the Sūtras out of a desire for the welfare of children. They are sweet, clarifying, cooling, pacifiers of the three doṣas, and auspicious. (26)
Astringent, constipating, unctuous, beneficial for the eyes, and wholesome for vision;
dry, hot, bitter, salty, digestive-stimulant, slimy, thick, auspicious, destructive of sins, pleasing, and increasing the eyelashes. 27–28.
Puṣpaka is sharp, hot, and removes impurities; it alleviates blood-bile and phlegm, quickly clarifies the vision, and is cold at the end.
It pacifies the three doṣas, is dry, possesses all six tastes, and is pervasive. 29.
Rasāñjana is purifying, promotes the growth of eyelashes, and is beneficial for the eyes (30).
They know that kataka is astringent and sweet, cooling, quickly clarifies vision, causes dilation, is refreshing, unctuous, and beneficial for the eyes (31).
I shall now describe this oil, called the *pāñcabhautika*,
which has been proclaimed by all the Tīrthakaras as a promoter of the five sense organs.
[Its ingredients are] *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, grapes, *madhuka*, long pepper (*pippalī*), and *balā*.
Prapauṇḍarīka, bṛhatī, mañjiṣṭhā, tvak, punarnavā,
śarkarā, aṃśumatī, medā, viḍaṅga, nīlotpala, śvadaṃṣṭrā, saindhava, rāsnā, and also nidigdhikā. (33–34)
One should cook either oil or clarified butter with these ingredients in equal parts and four times as much milk; when properly prepared, one should store it.
One should employ this as a nasal medication (nasya) according to the instructions shown in the Siddhisthāna.
By means of this nasal medication (nasya), one is liberated from long-standing eye diseases;
it destroys cataracts (timira), films (paṭala), opacities (kāca), pilla, blindness, turbid vision, discharge, redness, swelling, and pain. (36–37)
Baldness, graying hair known as *indralupta*, diseases of the head, facial paralysis (*ardita*),
loosening of the teeth, disorders of the jaw, and even the putrefaction of the bodily channels; (38) sleeplessness, delirium, loss of speech, muteness, and dullness of the senses.
It destroys deafness, lockjaw, and loss of memory.
Through this auspicious unguent composed of the five elements, the sense organs become clear, and memory, intellect, physical form, and strength increase. 39–40.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa;
thus ends the sixth chapter on the ritual procedures for Śatapuṣpā and Śatāvarī within the section on ritual manuals (Kalpasthāna).
Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for *śatapuṣpā* and *śatāvarī*.
Thus spoke the venerable Kaśyapa.
*Śatapuṣpā* and *śatāvarī* are identical in their taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation.
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear [this] in its true essence according to its application.
Thus questioned by his aged disciple, Prajāpati spoke of Śatapuṣpā and Śatāvarī according to their qualities and actions.
It is sweet, nourishing, strengthening, and increases nourishment, complexion, and digestive fire;
it regulates the seasons, brings prosperity, and purifies the female reproductive tract and semen. It is hot [in potency], pacifies Vata, auspicious, and destroys evil.
The Śatapuṣpā is shown to bestow sons and increase virility (6).
It is cooling, astringent-sweet, unctuous, aphrodisiac, and a rejuvenative;
it destroys disorders of Vāta and Pitta, and increases complexion, vitality, and strength (7).
Śatavīryā and Śatāvarī enhance memory, intellect, and understanding; they are wholesome, promote the growth of flowers and progeny, and destroy the afflictions and curses of malevolent spirits.
Having first performed the purification of the bodily humors (doṣas), physicians prescribe the administration of these two.
For those who consume fortifying food and drink during the rains, autumn, and spring,
there are women who do not menstruate, or whose menstruation is fruitless,
or who have it excessively, or too little, or who experience it prematurely or belatedly. (9–10)

Those who are incapable of action, those whose limbs are not firm, those born of such causes, those who have died, those who are weak, those whose sons are not steadfast, those who are emaciated in body, those who suffer from discharges, those who are discolored, and those who possess excessive physical bulk.
Those women who do not experience sexual contact and those who are of "dry" origin—there, *śatapuṣpā* and *śatāvarī* should be used like nectar;
even a man using them obtains the aforementioned qualities. 12–13.

One hundred palas of this powder should be placed in a new vessel. Having risen in the morning and digested one's previous meal, one who has consumed [the medicine] should lick half a pala, a quarter of a pala, or one pala of that *śatapuṣpā* powder with clarified butter.
Or, according to his capacity, at the end of its digestion, he should eat rice with milk.
In this case, the wise man should provide a relaxed regimen of care;
when one hundred palas have been consumed, he obtains sons as desired.
Even a barren woman and a eunuch shall give birth by means of the *śatapuṣpā* plant;
even an old man becomes young, and he shall obtain strength and complexion,
as well as brilliance, vitality, intelligence, long life, and wisdom.
One becomes endowed with progeny, fortitude, and is free from wrinkles and grey hair.
(18) Therefore, one who is intelligent should lick *biḍālapadaka* soaked in honey and ghee; after a month, he shall become a retainer of sacred learning (*śrutadhara*). (19)
One desiring digestive fire should take it with honey; one seeking beauty, with milk and ghee; one desiring strength, with oil; and one suffering from splenic enlargement, with pungent oil.
In cases of jaundice, anemia, and swelling, it should be taken with buffalo milk and urine.
One suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma) should take [the medicine] with castor oil, and one suffering from skin diseases (kuṣṭha) with a decoction of khadira.

A patient with skin disease should drink it with the fat of a dried dung-fish or with meat broth; once the meat broth is digested, the sufferer of skin disease should eat with a thin gruel of mung beans.
One hundred palas of śatapuṣpā should be boiled in five droṇas of water until one-fourth remains; having strained it, one should boil it again.
This is the general group mentioned in the treatment of dhātrī.
One should slowly cook one āḍhaka of oil with four times as much milk; once cooked,
this oil is recommended by the Sage for use as nasal drops, for drinking, as an unctuous massage, and in enemas, in order to constantly obtain the aforementioned qualities.
Whatever procedure for *śatapuṣpā* has been seen here in its entirety, that same one is stated for *śatāvarī*; however, ghee is recommended for the cooking process.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.

Thus ends the chapter on the pharmaceutical preparations of Śatapushpā and Śatāvarī in the Section on Formulations (Kalpasthāna). Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the pharmaceutical preparations of Revatī. 1.

Thus spoke the venerable Kaśyapa: "In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was indeed this entire universe. He first created Time; from that, he created the gods, the asuras, the ancestors, and humans, as well as the seven domestic animals, wild beasts, plants, and trees. Then that Prajāpati reflected, and from that hunger was born. That hunger entered Prajāpati himself; he became exhausted. Therefore, when one is hungry, one becomes exhausted. He saw plants as the means to ward off hunger; he ate the plants."

Having consumed the plants, he was released from hunger; therefore, living beings, having consumed the plants, are released from hunger and are engaged in their activities. Because Prajāpati took the very first essence (*rasa*) of these [plants], he alone should be satisfied. Living beings consume the *ṛjīṣa*—the dregs—of the essence of the plants; therefore, they hunger day after day.
The progeny—Prajāpati indeed extracted their essence. That Prajāpati, being satisfied, deposited that hunger at the proper time.
Then that Time, being hungry, began to devour both the gods and the asuras.

Those gods and asuras, being consumed by Time, went for refuge to Prajāpati. He told them of the nectar (*amṛta*); they churned it, and it came into being. [They asked: "Who indeed shall consume this first? The gods alone consumed it. Thereupon the gods became ageless and immortal. Those gods, by means of the nectar, drove away hunger and Time.

That Time drove away these beings; therefore, it takes them away. From that, the gods and the asuras were born; they fought with one another. Now, there was an asura-maiden named Dīrghajihvī (Long-Tongue), and she wasted away the army of the gods. Those gods said to Skanda: "Dīrghajihvī is wasting away our strength; subdue her! He said, "Choose a boon. The gods said, "Om. He said, "May I be one among the Vasus, one among the Rudras, and one among the Ādityas."

Those gods said, "Om," and it became so. Soma, Dhara, Agni, Mātariśvan, Prabhāsa, and Pratyūṣa—these were the seven Vasus in ancient times; Dhruva by name was their eighth. He who knows this becomes firm (dhruva) among these worlds.

Aja Ekapād, Ahirbudhnya, Hara, Vaiśvānara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, Viśvarūpa, Sthāṇu, Śiva, and Rudra—these were the ten Rudras in ancient times; Guha became their eleventh, named Śaṅkara. He who knows this becomes equal to him among the worlds. Indra, Bhaga, Pūṣan, Aryaman, Mitra and Varuṇa, Dhātṛ, Vivasvat, Aṃśa, Bhāskara, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu—these were the twelve Ādityas in ancient times.

Of those, the thirteenth was Guha, named Āṅgirasa; his is this thirteenth month as an intercalary month. Therefore, he burns there [in that month]. He who knows thus is released from all afflictions. Therefore, among all worlds, all meters, and all deities, Skanda is called the King and the Overlord. Having said "Salutation, salutation to him," one should undertake all undertakings; they succeed for him who knows thus. 6

Then he sent Revatī to Dīrghajihvī. She became a female jackal and attacked the army of the Asuras; she devoured Dīrghajihvī first. Having slain her, she became a bird, accompanied by firebrands and lightning, raining down stones and a rain of all kinds of weapons; in many forms, she conquered the Asuras. While being slaughtered by her in her many forms, those Asuras caused embryos to be placed within both human and non-human women.

Then Revatī beheld those Asuras within the wombs of both human and non-human women. Thereupon, becoming a *jātahāriṇī*, she slew them. Therefore, the *jātahāriṇī* destroys the flower [the embryo], destroys the form, destroys the embryos, destroys those already born, and destroys those being born and those yet to be born—especially that which is Asuraic, the offspring of the unrighteous, struck down by unrighteousness.

This very Revatī, O Vṛddhajīvaka, is called Bahurūpā (the many-formed), Jātahāriṇī (the child-stealer), Pilipicchikā, Raudrī (the fierce one), and Vāruṇī (the goddess of the waters). By the command of Skanda, this female spirit exists among all classes of beings; she bewilders the unrighteous for the sake of destroying the wicked. Vṛddhajīvaka, we shall now explain her origin, her arrival, her premonitory symptoms, her departure, and the remedy. For when these wicked Asuras associate together, even the virtuous are slain.
Indeed, through such association, Jātahāriṇī perceives with her divine eye.

It is observed that for her, dharma alone is said to be the cause of cessation. Now, furthermore, there is a woman who has abandoned dharma, auspicious conduct, purity, and divine rites; who hates gods, cows, Brahmins, teachers, elders, and the virtuous; who is ill-behaved, arrogant, and unstable; who is fond of enmity, strife, meat, violence, sleep, and sexual intercourse; who is fierce, piercing, venomous, and talkative; who is devoid of fear, laughing suddenly, weeping suddenly, grieving suddenly, and speaking falsehoods; who is gluttonous, or as they say, a devourer of all things, acting according to her own whims, and abandoning wholesome speech and food.

Utterly lacking in faith, intent on harming those born of other lineages, devoted to her own interests while neglecting the welfare of others, and hostile toward her husband and sons, she is devoid of affection for them and constantly curses them. She shows contempt for her father-in-law, mother-in-law, brothers-in-law, priests, and others in their place, or even for great men; thus, burning them with her wrath, she reviles them. Or, being ill-behaved and possessing an evil eye, she covets her co-wife and practices sorcery against her through spells, herbs, and rituals, or strikes her on the head, or [harms] the child.

Furthermore, she becomes one who knows only pleasure and pain, treacherous toward her friends, and a speaker of inauspicious words. She is devoid of peace-rites, fire-oblations, recitations, gifts, offerings, auspicious ceremonies, spitting, kissing, and embracing; she is present even in improper places. Because of these actions of hers, as well as other inauspicious deeds performed previously, and due to excessive drinking, eating, sleeping, and indulgence in physical exertion, she clings to these vulnerabilities—these gateways of unrighteousness—to seize those born [into the family]. Moreover, her husband likewise comes to possess such a character.

One should know that when these two [conditions] are incurable, it carries away the newborn child. Furthermore, if one of the couple is unrighteous, it becomes difficult. However, when both are righteous, upright, free from pride, and healthy, their offspring increase.

Or when a woman who has recently conceived dies, and [the patient] associates with her female attendants or others who are impure, inauspicious, unchaste, possessed by non-human spirits, or addicted to taking away newborn infants; or when he eats together with them, bathes together with them, or gives them clothes and ornaments; or when he steps upon their bathing grounds, urination sites, or places where offerings are made—especially those defiled by menstrual blood—and steps upon hair, body hair, nails, medicinal pastes, discarded clothes, rags, and the remnants of food.

If she carries away the remnants of drink, the remnants of medicine, the remnants of perfume, the remnants of flowers, or worn-out sandals, then she becomes a "seizer of newborns" (jātahāriṇī). Furthermore, when she sees a woman who is pregnant for the first time, beautiful, well-proportioned, free from disease, with full hips, breasts, thighs, arms, and face; whose good fortune is manifesting; who has beautiful hair and large eyes with red corners; whose line of body hair is growing; whose hands, feet, nails, gaze, and skin are glossy; and who is exceedingly delicate, unable to endure hardship, and incapable of exertion.

Seeing a woman who is pregnant—whose fetus grows with the passage of time, whose body increases in bulk, and whose vital fluids swell—the evil-minded ones watch her; yet no rite for pacification (*śāntikarma*) is performed for her, and then a spirit that seizes newborns (*jātahāriṇī*) attaches itself to her. For this reason, the *Putrīyā* sacrifice, which is desired for the sake of obtaining a son, is prescribed to be performed day after day; for it indeed drives away her sin. Therefore, a pregnant woman ought not even to eat together with her mother, and especially so in the first pregnancy; one should avoid negligence in this matter.
The wife of a learned Brahmin who performs many sacrifices and is constantly engaged in officiating at them may, through her own fault, become a child-stealer;
so too does she who reviles others in debates, who is hypocritical, and who is full of egoism.
All those, including the officiating priests, became food for Jātahāriṇī when the husband,
with dust-covered feet, went out upon the road at night;
then Revatī enters either during the menstrual period or into the embryo.
The husband who, having enjoyed a woman seized by Jātahāriṇī,
approaches his own wife at that same time, becomes possessed by Jātahāriṇī;
he must always avoid the house seized by Jātahāriṇī.
Then, taking a little bit from here and there, she seizes what is born;
In this very way, she causes the destruction of the offspring of buffalo-herders, camel-herders, and goat-herders (15).
Born of unrighteousness, she is addicted to and carries away those born; she belongs to those in the world who seize the property of Brahmins, who are wicked and evil-minded (16).
The fierce Revatī destroys the subjects of thieves and rogues;
those of evil deeds are of low birth and have broken the moral barriers—those who are mostly unjust and merciless toward all classes of beings. (17)
Those who provide no protection yet wield harsh punishments, who transgress the commands of their elders, who disregard established conduct, and who promote unrighteousness—
by the weakness of such a king, the subjects here go to ruin. (18–19)
Jātahāriṇī especially slays the cow and the Brahmin;
likewise, when wicked-minded royal officials oppress the subjects by the king's command, Jātahāriṇī slays them.

The merchant who destroys his merchandise, he who obstructs it, the usurer beyond measure, and he who [wrongfully takes] a maiden, land, gold, horses, or garments— all these are slain by the many-formed [Goddess]. 21–22.
Those who speak untruths,
and those who out of delusion engage in sexual intercourse during the two twilights, in water, in dust, or in deserted temples— the Jātahāriṇī slays them. (23)
When Revatī enters a woman by way of the gateway of unrighteousness, O Jīvaka, then these characteristics of hers appear:
her body withers and these features of hers decline.
Her vision becomes clouded and she does not thrive at the proper time;
deprived of strength and lacking energy, she is tormented by pains in her belly. She becomes unpleasant to behold and is afflicted by various such diseases. (26)
One who undertakes contrary actions, one who pursues contrary goals— unclean, deformed, and audacious— she engages in all matters;
yet for her there is no accomplishment of purpose, and her prosperity is destroyed.
If she does not live with the calves among the cows, goats, and buffaloes, she incurs terrible infamy or falls into widowhood;
or, being addicted to taking life, she brings about the destruction of her family. (29)

According to the scriptures, the sages declare that there are three types of women who carry the fetus to its destruction: the curable, the manageable, and the incurable. Their characteristics are now described: a woman who has reached sixteen years of age but has not yet seen her menses [is incurable].
They call her Śuṣkarevatī who has withered arms and no breasts;
and that woman who, being without menses, perishes at the proper time,
is emaciated, weak, and irritable— she too is called Kaṭambharā.

That woman who sees her menses at an improper time has flowers that are in vain; she whose cheeks are covered with thick hair is a destroyer of flowers, and she is called Revatī. She who experiences irregular menses due to the color and size of the period is likewise [unfortunate].

That which is known as Vikuṭā is characterized by weakness due to the power of the *animitta* (signless) wind; it is so called because the vagina of that emaciated woman constantly discharges [fluid].
It should be known as *parisrutā*, a condition among women that carries away the newborn.
That woman from whose womb the embryo falls away while still unformed and barely attached is called *Aṇḍaghnī*;
she is said to be cruel and a destroyer of her offspring. That woman whose embryo perishes before the limbs of the body have fully developed is likewise [so described]. (36–37)
She should be known as Durdharā (the Unstoppable), most terrible, and a destroyer of newborns;
when she carries off the fetus with all its limbs complete, she is called Jātahāriṇī (the Seizer of the Born).
She is declared to be Kālarātrī (the Night of Doom); a woman survives there only through great suffering.

That [curse] by which the embryo becomes attached, or by which it is released once conceived, is called *mohinī*; it is said to cause the destruction of women and to carry away the newborn. That [curse] by which the embryo does not move is known as *stambhanī*. 39–40.
That which, residing in the abdomen, causes one to cry out is known as Krośanā.
These ten are the destroyers of newborns while their mothers are still living; those that destroy flowers are incurable, whereas those that destroy the embryo are curable.
But that woman whose child dies at every birth should be known as a *nākinī*, a terrible spirit who carries off newborns;
for her, each offspring perishes immediately upon being born. 42–43.
That terrible one named Piśācī, who eats flesh and seizes newborn infants,
is a Yakṣī on the second day, an Asurī on the third day;
on the fourth day she is named Kali, and on the fifth day she is Vāruṇī.
On the sixth day, Ṣaṣṭhī is remembered; on the seventh day, Bhīrukā;
on the eighth day, Yāmyā; on the ninth day, Mātaṅgī;
on the tenth, Bhadrakālī; and on the eleventh day, Raudrī.
In the twelfth [month] Vardhikā is proclaimed, and in the thirteenth Caṇḍikā.
In the fourteenth she is named Kapālamālinī, and thereafter, in the period following the fortnight, Pilipicchikā is to be known. 46–47.
These sixteen have been specified individually by name and by their functions;
they are cruel snatchers of newborns, yet they can be appeased through the performance of religious rites for those who practice dharma.
But for that woman, O Sage, whose fetal forms number five, six, or seven—
Those who are subject to her die immediately; she is incurable and a snatcher of newborns.
(49) The children of that woman die, while her daughters live without effort;
she is named Kula-kṣaya-karī (the destroyer of the family), and she is incurable and a snatcher of newborns. (50)
That woman whose offspring dies as soon as it is born is known as the terrible *puṇyajanī*; she is incurable and is called a "child-taker.
She is one from whom offspring that has reached maturity dies before the age of sixteen.
She is said to be "pauruṣādinī" (one who devours the male child), and she is incurable, taking away the newborn.
When she bears another fetus, then the previous one dies; they call her "saṃdaṃśī" (the pincher), incurable, and a taker of the newborn. 52–53.
One is joined with [death] by means of the womb, one by means of a planet, and one by means of death;
this is called Karkoṭakī, a terrible bringer of the destruction of newborns. One whose twin-born child dies—whether one or both—[is afflicted by her].
They call her Indravadavā, the unassailable one who carries away those who are born.
If, of two things originating from a single navel, one dies first, the other likewise dies; they call her Baḍavāmukhī.
Then Vṛddhajīvaka once again asked this great question of the seer Kaśyapa, who was honored by the world, as he was speaking thus:
"Why is it that for those with a single navel, death and life are the same?"
Sickness and health, pleasure and pain—satisfaction is not born of these alike. (58) Then, indeed, the Blessed One Kaśyapa said:
"For that very same seed is split apart by the power of the wind."

Because their actions are identical, the unity of the channels, birth, and growth from conception are equal; likewise, from birth until the enjoyment of breast milk, their age is said to be the same, as are their pleasure and pain, and their existence and non-existence. (59–60)
There is equality in terms of marks, form, color, limbs, strength, and natural constitution, but there is no equality in satiety and emission because these two are distinct states. 61.

Now, O Vṛddhajīvaka, she who carries away at birth is said to be of three kinds according to the distinction of the worlds: divine, human, and animal. Therefore, the three worlds are pervaded by the blessed Revatī, who possesses many forms. For this reason, Revatī is recited as the one who causes fear to all the worlds. The gods worshipped her; consequently, their progeny flourished, and their progeny did not suffer interruption. His progeny does not suffer interruption for him who knows thus.

Then Kaśyapa alone first obtained that Revatī, the teacher of all the worlds, the all-pervading one, through fierce asceticism among all the sages. To him she granted abundant progeny—long-lived and unbroken—and he became superior to all. Being uniquely knowledgeable of Revatī, he imparted the *Revatī-kalpa* to his disciples for the welfare of the world. 62

Therefore, O Vṛddhajīvaka, having explained the divine Revatī, we shall now expound upon the human [Revatī]. In this regard, we shall follow whichever woman she enters here through the aforementioned gateways of unrighteousness.
At what age, at what time, or in what activity, O Sage, does the wrathful and illustrious Jātahāriṇī enter a woman?
Then the Blessed Kaśyapa said:
"The enraged Revatī enters a woman who is menstruating, pregnant, or has recently given birth, while she is confined within her hut; she does so at three times."
Without unrighteousness, that which carries away the newborn does not enter a woman;
through unrighteousness, she brings about the destruction of the mother, the father, and their sons,
as well as the ruin of all progeny.
And this [demoness] brings about the exhaustion of the lifespan of children born of her own karma.

Now, O Vṛddhajīvaka, these four kinds of women—namely, the *jātahāriṇī*, the *varṇā*, the *varṇāntarā*, the *liṅginī*, and the *kārukī*—enter here by taking possession of a woman. We shall now explain them in detail.

Furthermore, O Vṛddhajīvaka, if a man approaches a Brāhmaṇī woman who has been possessed by a spirit, comes to her house, stands before her, greets her, converses with her, speaks with her, touches her, eats with her, strikes her, reviles her, lies with her, or steps upon her footprint, her menstrual flow, her flower-offering, her garment, or her ornaments, then that Brāhmaṇī becomes a "child-stealer" (jātahāriṇī). Now they say: "That very Brāhmaṇī herself should sprinkle her when she is in her courses; that indeed is the expiation in this case."

By means of its own portion, he makes it possessed of offspring. A Brāhmaṇī woman who knows this does not become a "child-stealer" (jātahāriṇī) toward her. Furthermore, if a Kṣatriyā woman who is a child-stealer has entered into a union and come to one's house, a man may stand against her, salute her, deal with her, converse with her, touch her, eat with her, strike her, revile her, lie with her, or step upon her footprint, her menstrual flow, her used garlands, her clothes, or her ornaments; by doing so, she becomes a child-stealing Kṣatriyā.

Now they say: "Only a Kṣatriya woman should sprinkle her when she has reached puberty; that alone is the atonement for that occasion. By means of her own portion, he makes her possessed of offspring. For one who knows this, no Kṣatriya woman becomes a destroyer of her children."

Furthermore, O Vṛddhajīvaka, if he approaches, salutes, transacts business with, converses with, touches, enjoys, strikes, reviles, or lies with a Vaiśya woman possessed by Jātahāriṇī, or a Mahāśūdrī woman; or if he steps upon her menstrual blood, her discarded garlands, clothes, or ornaments—then that Vaiśya woman becomes Jātahāriṇī, or she becomes a Śūdrī, or even a Mahāśūdrī. Furthermore, they say: "That very Vaiśya, Śūdrī, or Mahāśūdrī woman should sprinkle a menstruating woman."
That itself is the atonement for it. By means of its own portion, he makes it prolific. For one who knows this, no Vaiśya, Śūdra, Mahāśūdra, or Jātahāriṇī shall exist.

Moreover, the Vṛddhajīvaka, Sūta, Māgadha, Venapukkaśa, Ambaṣṭha, Prācyaka, Caṇḍāla, Muṣṭika, Metaḍa, Umvaḍava, Akadrumiḍa, Siṃhala, Uḍra, Khaśa, Śaka, Yavana, Pahlava, Tukhāra, Kamboja, Āvantya, Nemaka, Ābhīraka, Hūṇa, Pāraśava, Kulinda, Kirāta, Śabara, and Śambara—these are the Jātahāriṇīs.

Moreover, they say: those women of the *stika*, *niṣāda*, and other such mixed castes (*varṇasaṃkara*) who seize children at birth—whichever woman is possessed by such a spirit, she approaches those women, salutes them, greets them, interacts with them, converses with them, touches them, shares food with them, strikes them, reviles them, lies with them, and steps upon their footprints, their seasonal offerings, their garlands, their clothes, and their ornaments; for her, these [spirits] born of mixed castes become "child-seizers" (*jātahāriṇī*).

Moreover, they say: one should sprinkle that very woman who is in her courses with this [mixture]. That itself is the expiation in that case. By means of her own portion, he makes her possessed of offspring. For one who knows thus, there is no woman among her kin who is a "destroyer of offspring" through the mixture of castes; she does not become a destroyer of offspring.

Furthermore, if a woman who is an old Jīvaka, a female ascetic (liṅginī), a wandering nun (parivrājikā), a female Śramaṇaka, a female Kaṇḍanī, a female Nirgranthī, one wearing rags or bark garments, an ascetic woman (tāpasī), a female Carikā, one with matted hair (jaṭinī), a member of the Mātṛmaṇḍala, a female attendant of a deity, a female Vekṣaṇikā, or a spirit that seizes newborns—or if she is possessed by such a spirit—should enter his house, and he should attend to her, salute her, engage in business with her, touch her, eat with her, strike her, revile her, lie with her, or step upon her footprint, her menstrual discharge, her flower-garland, her clothes, or her ornaments; [of him...]

A woman with bodily marks becomes a destroyer of children. Now they say: "That very woman with marks should sprinkle that menstruating woman; that indeed is the atonement there. By her own portion she makes her possessed of offspring. For one who knows thus, a woman with marks does not become a destroyer of her children."

Furthermore, O Vṛddhajīvaka, one possessed by Jātahāriṇī approaches for honor with iron; a wood-worker with wood; a potter with earthenware; a shoe-maker with leather; a garland-maker with loose flowers; a weaver with woven cloth; a tailor with sewn garments; a washerwoman with well-dyed cloth; a dyer with bleached cloth; a cowherd-woman with buttermilk; and a low-caste woman with her own [washed] garment. When she has approached the house possessed by Jātahāriṇī, a woman stands up before her and greets her.

If she engages in social intercourse with him, speaks with him, touches him, eats with him, strikes him, reviles him, lies with him, or steps upon his footprint, his season, his floral offering, his garment, or his ornament, she becomes one whose offspring are carried off by a female artisan. Now they say: "The female artisan herself should sprinkle that woman when she has reached her season; she alone is the atonement for that. By means of her own portion, she makes her possessed of offspring. For her who knows thus, no offspring is carried off by a female artisan."

Henceforth, O Vṛddhajīvaka, we shall explain the *tiraścī* and the *jātahāriṇī*. For this [latter] is said to be fivefold: namely, *śakunī*, *catuṣpadī*, *sarpā*, *matsī*, and *vanaspatī*. These generally afflict only those who are virtuous. O Vṛddhajīvaka, for those who kill or cause to be killed a growing *śakunī*, a great seizing spirit (*mahāgraha*) in the form of a bird (*śakunī*) that carries away newborns (*jātahāriṇī*) afflicts them.

Having become a female crow, a female vulture, a hen, a peahen, a blue jay, a maina, a female oil-drinker, an owl, a *bholantikā*, a female vulture, a female hawk, a female *bhāradvājī*, or any other such bird, she manifests unprecedented sights in dreams; she terrifies the pregnant woman and the woman who has recently given birth, and she strikes terror into the child. Possessing great speed and great power, of terrible form, fierce, with outspread wings, and with a beak, claws, teeth, and fangs like adamant, her eyes resembling blazing lapis lazuli, and bearing many various large feathers upon her neck— [She appears] thus.

Bearing the various qualities of gold and jewels, adorned with diverse flowers, perfumes, garments, and radiant pestles; decorated with excellent crowns, anklets, bracelets, earrings, armlets, circular earrings, left-side bells, banners, parasols, torches, and garlands of clouds like flashes of lightning—she, the sister of the Lord, the most excellent youth, having appeared in a dream and overcome him, immediately thereafter brings about the onset of disease for him.

Then, at midday, at midnight, during the twilights, or while [the mother] is asleep, she hides in the child’s chamber from one of those aforementioned [spirits]. Thereupon, the child cries out loudly, weeps, trembles, shakes, fears, becomes feverish, becomes distraught, groans, faints, stumbles, pricks with pain, feels empty, falls apart, and is afflicted by diseases and other calamities. Furthermore, if a woman repeatedly sees a *śakunī* (bird-spirit) in her dreams, then that *śakunī*, having seized the child at birth, clings to her.

With the dung of that very *śakunī* bird, or with its wing-fluid, an old woman should sprinkle that woman there, as if she were a female bird. That itself is the expiation for this case. By means of her own portion of fortune, she makes the woman possessed of offspring. For her, no *śakunī* bird becomes a destroyer of newborns—provided she does not harm the *śakunī* and knows this [rite].

Furthermore, O Vṛddhajīvaka, those who kill a cow, cause one to be killed, or consume beef—their mother-cow becomes a "seizer of newborns" (*jātahāriṇī*). This cow pursues them in their dreams, appearing either as a cowherd or as a young calf-keeper; thus, that mother-cow becomes a seizer of newborns for whom there is no remedy. Now they say: one should bathe her in the midst of cows while she is fasting on cow-urine and cow-dung; that itself is the atonement in that case. By its own allotted portion, the cow makes her [the patient] possessed of offspring.

The cow-mother of one who knows this does not become a "killer of offspring," provided she does not injure the cow. In this very same way, this rule is declared for female buffalo, goats, sheep, donkeys, female mules, female camels, sows, female mice, bitches, female galla-golikas, cows, *viṣvambharās*, and deer and other such animals.

Furthermore, if a woman—whether she lives in a house or not—kills or causes to be killed a female snake, a snake that seizes her newborn child becomes attached to her; they say her offspring will meet a violent death. One should pour [milk] upon an anthill or into a nest of snakes; furthermore, they say it should be poured into the midst of a hundred anthills. That itself is the expiation therefor. By means of its own portion, one makes her possessed of offspring; a snake that seizes her newborn child shall not befall her.

She who does not harm snakes—for one who knows this, no death by poison occurs among their offspring. Furthermore, O Vṛddhajīvaka, she who destroys the creatures that move in the water—fish, crocodiles, *timiṅgila*, sharks, conchs, *śambūka* snails, *sukhanaka* crabs, and so forth—is struck by that unrighteousness (*adharma*). Enraged, Revatī destroys the offspring; having become a fish, a female crocodile, an oyster, or a female conch, she first gladdens them in a dream and then destroys them. For the most part, their offspring perish in the water through the terror of the waters.

Or [it may be afflicted] by each of the diseases individually. Now they say: "One should drive it away by means of the Rohiṇī-bath; that indeed is the expiation for this. She who knows thus does not harm fish, nor does her female fish take away her offspring. Furthermore, those who harm trees—whether they are cultivated or wild—the deities of the trees become enraged at them.

Agni is named Vaiśvānara; Soma is named Pitṛmat; the axe is named Śiva; the waters are named Varuṇa; the earth is named Nirṛti; the cow is named Vyoman; the cow is named Śloka; the divine wind is named Devapavana; the sun is named Pūṣan; the quarters are named Kāṣṭhā; Indra is named Varuṇa; and Vāyu is named Prāṇa. These indeed are the twelve deities of the trees. They strike down the one who strikes down these very trees.

Now they say: "In the midst of the forest trees, when they have turned away, one should sacrifice to those very deities with cooked messes (*sthālīpāka*): to Agni with clarified butter, to Soma with *śyāmāka* grain, to Śiva with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), to the Waters with curds, to the Earth with seven kinds of food, to the village-smoke with offerings of smoke, to the Cow or to Agni Pavamāna with meat, to Pūṣan with various foods, to the Quarters with intoxicating drinks, and to Indra with sacrificial food. Furthermore, the forest-tree deities grant progeny to her who does not harm the forest trees; for her who knows this, the forest-tree deities do not become snatchers of her offspring. Regarding this, there are these verses: 69. There are these verses: [The verses follow.]
Through the excessive growth of unrighteousness, Revatī finds an opportunity;
having found that opportunity, she becomes exceedingly enraged and strikes down these creatures with various forms as previously described, and with others even more terrible.
Hear from me the forms of one seized by Jātahāriṇī: either wives die simultaneously, or they die one by one;
and first among them is the form of one who has suddenly eaten while terrified. 71–72.
First, there is corruption of the breast milk itself, followed by fever, drowsiness,
lethargy, headache, discoloration, or extreme pallor and yellowness;
thirst, diarrhea, hoarseness, dryness of the palate, and restlessness.
There is inflammation of the mouth, eruptions on the face, erysipelas, anemia, and jaundice (74).
The patient remains awake, weeps excessively, and is afflicted again and again;
he pants, coughs, sneezes, and becomes cold in an instant (75).
Motionless and as if dead, he remains still for a while and then moves again;
he does not thrive in due time, nor does he take pleasure in the breast.
Upon seeing a person previously unknown, the infant becomes greatly agitated.
At the sound of cats, mongooses, and mice, he weeps immediately;
even from a mild illness, he experiences agonizing pain;
he trembles constantly, and while asleep, he finds no comfort or ease.
He who, having observed these forms, does not provide medicine, accomplishes his purpose through offspring as if with wealth obtained in a dream. (79)

Henceforth, we shall describe the binding of the *prajāvaraṇa* (the protective amulet for progeny). For the binding [of such an amulet] causes the loss of the fetus before the eighth month; therefore, its binding is prohibited after that time, except in other cases. A physician who is pure and has fasted, for those who are faithful to the teachings of Vṛddhajīvaka, who perform their religious duties, and who have fasted for three nights, should bind the *prajāvaraṇa*. Once it is bound, he should honor her with desirable sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*), for that indeed bestows progeny upon her. Regarding this, the necessary materials are as follows: she must have bathed after her menstrual period (*rohiṇī-snāna*).

Some say that if one performs the ritual bathing at night, it should be done in the house; if during the day, it should be done in a secluded place in the forest. Having performed the binding of the directions and established protection for oneself, one should begin that rite.

Then, having smeared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung and water in a clean place, the physician—having bathed, being dressed in unwashed garments, adorned, and facing east—should perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*). With his hands raised, he should sip silently with water that is not noisy, free from foam, and not hot, using the *brāhma* part of the hand; he should swallow it three times, wipe his lips twice (though some say three times), and touch his eyes, ears, nostrils, and anus.

When the two suns have risen, having sprinkled the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), the one with golden hands takes a *darbha*-grass tuft containing a seed-vessel; having scratched a mark with it and sprinkled the *darbha*-grass tuft, he throws it outside and then brings the fire to that spot.

Having swept around as previously described, having thoroughly cleansed [the area], and having strewn sacrificial grass (barhis) clockwise, one should place a representation made of gold, silver, uśīra-root, or darbha-grass in front of the fire. To the south, one should establish Kumāra, Ṣaṣṭhī, and Viśākha; to the north, the Brahman priest; and a water-pot. Having purified the clarified butter (ājya) with two darbha-blades that have uncut tips, are equal in length, and are tied together as a seat (viṣṭara), he recites: "Thou art clarified butter; thou art the food of the gods; thou art splendor; thou art sight."

"Thou art the ear; thou art the sense-organ; thou art life; thou art truth; thou art the oblation. Then he offers the sacrifice: having offered the two *āghāra* libations with a *darbha*-blade serving as a spoon, he causes a pregnant woman—who has bathed, stayed overnight, is dressed in white garments, adorned, and facing north—sit upon a comfortable seat to the south. Having placed two *darbha* blades in her hands, she remains silent. Then, permitted by the physician, having performed the daily *homa* and the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, he should offer the oblation with the *Mātaṅgī* mantra.

The sacred lore named Mātaṅgī destroys evil dreams, strife, and Rākṣasas; it annihilates sin, defilement, curses, and great transgressions. Worshipped and honored by sinful ones, Brahman-sages, royal sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas, it was obtained from the Grandfather (Brahmā) by the great seer Mataṅga, the younger son of Kaśyapa, through his great and fierce asceticism. It destroys all fear, brings all the worlds under one’s control, bestows well-being, grants peace, produces progeny, binds [enemies], is stainless, and is unfailing auspiciousness for whoever, being pure, recites this lore.

He who recites this daily, remaining pure day after day, becomes purified at the two twilights; no fear from any living beings shall come upon him. He becomes possessed of many sons, great wealth, long life, freedom from disease, and the fulfillment of his aims. He who invokes this knowledge during a *śrāddha* ceremony ensures that his ancestors descend into the *śrāddha* offering in an inexhaustible manner. He who recites this in the midst of cows will have many cattle. He who causes a woman who has bathed after her menses to hear this shall become pregnant.

Whoever causes this [mantra] to be heard by a pregnant woman becomes possessed of a son. Whoever causes it to be heard by one who is having a difficult labor is quickly delivered. Whoever causes it to be heard by one whose son is dying becomes possessed of a living son. In whatever house one might know there are snakes, *rakṣas* demons, or *guhyaka* spirits, there one should scatter mustard seeds over which eight hundred recitations have been performed; all of them perish. Or, if someone should hate another, one should scatter [the seeds] at that person's door; whoever enters first encounters misfortune.

For one who recites it in difficult places, there is no fear of thieves, wild animals, or predatory beasts. In every form [of this practice], one obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. One becomes as if bathed in all sacred fords (tīrthas). All fasts have been performed. All gifts have been given. One should not conceal this knowledge of its purpose.

Homage to Mātaṅga, the best of seers, the perfected one; homage to Āstīka! Having paid homage to them, I employ this spell: may this spell of mine be successful! Sattha va hili mili mahāmili kuruṭṭā aṭṭe mamaṭe tumvipase karaṭe gandhāri keyūri bhujaṅgami ojahāri sarṣapacchedani alagaṇilagaṇi paṃsumasi kakikākaṇḍi hili hili biḍi biḍi aṭṭe maṭṭe ajihaṭṭe kukkukukkumati svāhā!

With this *mataṅga-vidyā*, one should prepare eight hundred fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made of *śamī* wood, eight hundred of *pālāśa* wood, eight hundred of *aśvattha* wood, eight hundred white flowers, and eight hundred mustard seeds the color of fire; having prepared ghee, oil, and fat, and having mixed them together with honey and clarified butter (*ājya*), one offers three fuel-sticks simultaneously and at the end of the mantra offers the clarified butter. Having thus offered eight hundred oblations, [one prepares] a protective cord (*pratisara*) from *lakṣmaṇā*.

Having empowered *putrañjīva*, *phala*, sea-foam, *pratigrathita*, *ālambā*, *agraha*, *ghnī*, *vāsu*, *śukti*, and *jīvorṇā* with the *vidyā* of Rudramātaṅgī, one should fasten them around the neck. Now, this is the *vidyā* of Rudramātaṅgī: "Homage to the Blessed One, the Mother of Rudras! O tawny one, matted-haired one, subduer of Rudra! Protect, protect this one who desires protection; command! Svāhā! With this *vidyā* of Rudramātaṅgī, one should bind an amulet.

When the *pratisara* amulet is bound, a protection for offspring is established. She shall have no fear from any living beings; her hopes will be fulfilled, and she shall have living sons, be fortunate, and remain a non-widow.

Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, having recited the peace-chant (*śānti*) as previously described, having offered with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, having worshipped and dismissed the deity, and having made the sacrificial offering (*bali*), he sprinkles the fire with water. He then silently honors virtuous, long-lived Brahmins who have sons by means of food, clothing, and sacrificial fees. Thereafter, he should fast. Having collected all that [remains] from the sacrificial ground, he deposits it at a crossroads, in water, or at the foot of a milk-tree (*kṣīravṛkṣa*). "In this manner, by this rite, the obstruction to offspring is severed; her progeny shall not cease," so said the venerable Kaśyapa.

Thereafter, for seven nights, one should offer a *prājāpatya* oblation of *caru* cooked in milk to Prajāpati; some say it is the previously mentioned cow-ghee. Or rather, [it is prescribed] for those desiring progeny, those desiring cattle, and those desiring long life.
Thus, this has been cited as the supreme [rite] for the sake of the primary purpose.
For the benefit of humanity and to bring glory to physicians,
one who is pure should employ this supreme, inviolable secret, but must not disclose it to others. 81
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa. This concludes the chapter titled the Revatī-kalpa within the Kalpasthāna; it is the chapter on the ritual for food (bhojana-kalpa).
Now, therefore, we shall explain the rules for eating,
as the Blessed Kaśyapa spoke them to the ancient sage Mārīca as he sat.

The aged disciple questioned that great man— who was like a blazing fire or the sun because he had offered the agnihotra sacrifice, and who was a treasury of austerity, self-restraint, and right conduct— in a favorable manner.
O sir, what are the characteristics of a being who is hungry, or likewise one who is thirsty, or both?
And how indeed should one recognize them when they are intense or mild?
What would be beneficial there for thirst and hunger?
What would be the beneficial sequence of foods?
And in which region is rice cooked?
O Great-souled One, what are the characteristics of one who has eaten;
what are the qualities and defects of eating too little and eating too much; and what are the effects of consuming food that is excessively hot or cold?
What are the defects that arise from the opposite [conditions], namely from the application of food and drink to hunger and thirst? And for whom is the scum (maṇḍa) considered commendable?
"O Blessed One, for whom is the *maṇḍa* recommended?
What are the benefits and the faults when the *maṇḍa* is properly consumed, and what are they in the opposite case?"
For whom is gruel unwholesome or wholesome? Also, for whom are prepared or unprepared lentil broths indicated? And for whom is a tasteless soup prescribed?
Whether it be with roots or with pomegranate (8), or with meat broth, or rice with meat soup— where is the benefit in such food and bathing?
Having spoken thus, Prajāpati became silent; then he spoke these words:
"Indeed, one who possesses only the eye of flesh is not all-knowing."
One might venture to answer these questions;
however, there is a loss of enthusiasm, complexion, voice, and gaze, as well as despondency, emaciation, fatigue, and vocal distortions. 10
There is intense affliction of the heart for a living being,
exhaustion of the face due to extreme hunger,
and the drying up of the palate, lips, tongue, throat, and cheeks.
For one who is thirsty, there is weakness of the ears and eyes, despondency, delusion, loss of memory, digestive fire, intelligence, happiness, and speech, as well as enlargement of the tongue.
One should recognize these symptoms as occurring in both the thirsty and the hungry;
in that state, there is parching of the mouth and pain from headache.
Retention of urine and dysentery after eating—
those who know the truth say that in such cases, food and drink should be consumed according to one's pleasure and suitability. 13
However, when one is severely afflicted by thirst and hunger, filling [the stomach] even once is not recommended;
for the vital energy (*ojas*) is consumed by the fire and the wind.
Furthermore, it repeatedly dries up what has been drunk,
just as heated iron quenched with water;
how, then, could there be any passage for food and drink therein?
Some physicians, considering the matter, declare that for one who has drunk [the medicine] once, satiety is praised;
for by drinking it once, hunger is indeed destroyed.
Just as when the earth has been drenched once,
the wind, having taken up the heat (pitta) and being stirred up, indeed produces thirst that burns away one's vital energy (ojas). 16
When its force is obstructed in its location, it reaches the head; thereafter, thirst torments the heart and the kloman, along with pain,
exhaustion, flatulence, and affliction of the anus.
Fever, burning of the limbs, exhaustion, delusion, and thirst, along with a lack of interest in beds, seats, women, and sensual objects— these are the symptoms of one who is undernourished.
But he who desires to take even more, yet maintains impartiality toward his desired objects and resorts to the appropriate place and time with skillful means— 18.
Those who know the truth declare that to be "insufficiently eaten";
for those who have overeaten, emesis is recommended, whereas for those who have eaten insufficiently, food should be taken with due moderation. 19
Having duly considered the time, the place, the age, and the strength, as well as the complication and the medicine,
[there arise] clarity of vision and success in speech.
One should recognize the depth of voice, lack of dejection, vigor, joy of mind regarding desired sense-objects,
and an oily complexion as signs of one who has eaten well.
Lustre, strength, memory, intelligence, vigor, joy, stability of mind, growth of the limbs,
firmness of the senses, and steadiness of life— these are [the results]. 21.
The sages declare that for a man who has eaten well,
hunger is the proper time for food, and thirst is the proper time for drink. 22
I shall now explain the proper sequence of foods as it is beneficial; listen, my child!
If thirst and hunger should arise simultaneously, [one should first address the thirst].
The physician should treat that [thirst] first; the wise one should first alleviate thirst with drinking regimens appropriate to one-third of the patient's constitution.
Then one should gradually fill one-third of the stomach and leave one part remaining; for one who eats and drinks in this manner, (there will be no disease). 24.
Thus indeed, while eating and drinking...
One who has conquered the senses and is free from rashness attains health,
longevity, strength, a bright digestion, excellent progeny, and happiness. 25
If one who is hungry drinks first,
or eats while suffering from thirst,
terrible diseases quickly arise within him.
From the opposite [of these], there arise the states of non-giving and existence, which lead to the lower realms:
fever, burning of the limbs, exhaustion, emaciation, leprosy, vomiting, vertigo, abdominal distension, cholera, and thirst.
Consumption, diarrhea, dryness of the throat and palate,
and the loss of the body, the senses, their objects, and the complexion— these afflict one who eats irregularly and has lost his appetite. (27)

The digestive fire of one who drinks too much water, eats excessively large meals, consumes incompatible foods, or overeats even when suffering from indigestion, becomes extinguished even at the time for eating food. 28.
Therefore, one should not drink water before [the medicine], nor after an oily substance, nor after eating too much;
for when drunk at the proper time, it immediately pacifies abdominal diseases.
From that, diseases such as fever arise; having assailed the bodily humors with various kinds of food,
one drinks water like a mid-course drink between meals.
Even after eating, one of a pitta constitution should drink [liquids] in the proper measure; everywhere, that which is wholesome and congenial is beneficial.
[It nourishes] the tongue, lips, palate, intestines, throat, abdomen, and vital energy.
The consumed food is burnt away and one knows no satisfaction;
there is constipation, abdominal tumors, dropsy, blood disorders, erysipelas, thirst, and pain in the eyes and head. 31
By the consumption of excessively hot drinks and food, the semen, blood, and lymphatic tissue (rasa) become impaired;
the digestive fire (agni) undergoes depletion and fails to process the nutritional essence (rasa).
Phlegm and bile accumulate in him;
however, from the excessive indulgence in cold food and drink,
there arise phlegm, wind, loss of appetite, colic, and disorders of the wind-humor.
Hiccups, stiffness of the head, eyes, and throat, and so forth;
lethargy, heaviness of the feces and urine, and their increase—these occur when food that is first unctuous and sweet is consumed. (33)
In the middle, liquid, cold, and variegated foods; and finally, pungent, hot, dry, and light foods—this is indeed the sequence of meals according to suitability. 34.
One who has a predominance of bile (pitta), whose phlegm (kapha) is diminished, who is healthy yet afflicted by fainting, fatigue, or excessive travel,
and who consumes excessively hot drinks and food— [for such a person, this is prescribed].
Vision is destroyed by the habitual consumption of intoxicants; he who spits out dry phlegm with difficulty, and he who suffers while spitting without any apparent disorder [is also affected].

The woman who gives birth from affliction and thirst, the man whose senses are wasted and who suffers from the excess of intoxication, and those who eat sparingly yet remain wakeful with women— [these are the causes]. 36.
Those mortals who have been cleansed by purificatory rites,
those afflicted by erysipelas and burning sensations, and those distressed by coughing, anger, and intoxication— 37.
He who is driven mad by eating areca nut, or he who is deluded by *madana* poison,
or those afflicted by the poisons of *kiṃpāka*, *bhallātaka*, and other toxins— [these are the ones who fall].
Those who eat honey, those afflicted by poison,
and those who consume liquor, milk, buttermilk, or curds, as well as pork or fish; 38.
Those who have their mouths cleared by betel-leaf and nutmeg,
those for whom a thirst appropriate to the time has arisen, and others of that same kind— 39. [these are the ones who should not be questioned].
They declare that water is wholesome and cooling for those afflicted by constipation, thirst, and weak digestion; likewise, such persons obtain the nourishment of strength and vitality. 40
The Kaurukṣetras, Kurus, Naimiṣeyas, Pāñcālas, Māṇīcaras, Kausaleyas, Hārītapādas, Cāraśaurasenas, and others.
The Matsyas, the Daśārṇas, those born in the Śiśira mountains, the Sārasvatas, those known as the Sindhusauvīrakas, and whatever men dwell in the region between the Kurus; ||| 41 ||
Those born in Udaka, Vipāṭ, Sindhu, and Vasāti;
the Kāśmīras, Cīnas, Aparacīnas, and Khaśas; the Bāhlīkas, Dāśerakas, and Śātasārās. 42.
For those who possess a digestive fire that is either equal to or greater than their strength,
the aforementioned dry food and other such items should be prescribed by the physician, as they are habituated to them and are beneficial for their constitution. (43)
For it pacifies his intense thirst and bestows strength, nourishment, and relish;
it ensures the downward movement of wind and the maintenance of natural constitution.

It produces [disorders] arising from feces, urine, the body, and the sense organs; however, because it quickly provides satisfaction through its gentle qualities and suitability, it is considered beneficial.
One should eat from pleasant vessels adorned with beautiful flowers, in a place that is agreeable to the mind;
[and one may consume] buttermilk, fermented gruel, curd, whey, and jaggery. 45.
Grapes are foremost among wholesome foods, as are well-prepared groats;
cold water is beneficial, as is pomegranate juice, rock salt, and the tender shoots of *bhūstṛṇa* grass. 46

The juice from *trivṛt*, *vāsaka*, and *kāravṛnta*, along with *kuṭhera* and other herbs together with *mātuluṅga*, as well as roasted barley flour (*saktu*) combined with fresh ginger— these [should be used].
Ghee is the best; light are the six flavors (ṣāḍava),
as well as the finest foods when cooked, soups, meat gravies, syrups, and preparations mixed with wine.
Therefore, having considered the arguments regarding groups and so forth, those who know the procedure should prepare *avakṣāri* from what is habitually wholesome;
likewise, [the preparations] of Kāśī, Puṇḍra, Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Kāca.
[He conquered] those born on the shores and islands of the ocean,
as well as those who dwell by the eastern sea,
