the Kirātas, and the people of the eastern mountains. 49
One should treat them with potherbs, fish, meat, rice, sesame oil, and pungent substances;
for their phlegm (kapha) is accumulated due to their very nature.
When doubled, it produces thinness [in the year];
and [it likewise affects] the inhabitants of Kaliṅga and Pāṭṭana,
as well as those of Dakṣiṇāpatha and Narmadā.
One should treat these patients with drinks endowed with various high- and low-quality substances, as well as with oils, *kaṅgu* grains, *āḍhakī* pulses, and *yavaka* barley. 51.
Roots, tubers, chickpeas, and peas—these are wholesome for them; likewise, their gruels should be warm and well-prepared. 52
For a prepared gruel, warm with pomegranate, buttermilk, sour gruel, or water,
and containing rock salt, quickly destroys thirst.
For one of a bilious temperament, [the gruel] should be prepared at the proper time with fresh black pepper and ginger, or processed in ghee,
or combined with milk, water, and sugar.
Gruel (peyā) destroys fever, diarrhea, exhaustion, delusion, cough, hiccup, and thirst—provided it is wholesome and agreeable to the individual. 54.
If it is both suitable and beneficial as food for that person.

And whatever is situated according to the individual's body, location, and constitution, the physician should always prescribe that for him at the proper time— being pleasing to the heart, light, and in the correct dosage. 55
Beneath the left breast is the āmāśaya; there the food is digested, and as its essence spreads,
it nourishes the bodily tissues.
They are the source of all waste products and impurities;
they possess a keen digestive fire, excellent complexion, strength, and stature;
they are constantly engaged in physical exercise and are prolific speakers.
Those addicted to women become consumptive, sleepless, freed from diseases yet emaciated and weak,
Those afflicted by irregular fevers,
as well as those suffering from disorders of wind (vāta), should drink meat broth before their meal. 58

With bodies oozing with secretions, afflicted by diseases of the throat and mouth, wounded, and tormented by bile, phlegm, and other humors; [stricken] by fever, dysentery, planetary seizures, grief, and sleeplessness.

Those afflicted by urinary disorders (prameha), anemia (pāṇḍu), or jaundice (kāmalā); those possessed by poison or intoxicated by liquor; or those who have been struck by various types of spells (gāraka).
Furthermore, those men who suffer from vomiting, enlargement of the thighs, or chronic wasting should not drink meat broth;
however, for them, buttermilk is recommended.
Or it may be combined with rock salt and sugar;
or joined with sauvarcala or viḍa salt, along with clarified butter, both in the middle and at the end. 61
For buttermilk, when freshly churned, provides fragrance,
relish, strength, and nourishment; it is sour, warm, clear, light, and beneficial for the voice.
When consumed by one who has vomited, purged, suffered from fever, become emaciated, or is afflicted by the exhaustion of a long fast, it causes the digestive fire to blaze up.
62. And [it does so] in one tormented by the fatigue of a great fast.

In those afflicted by the disorders of thirst and diarrhea, or tormented by the defects of fever; in those scorched by erysipelas and bile diseases; and in those with combined diseases who have a great appetite. 63.
One should administer the scum even in cases of burning sensations in the abdomen,
in women who have recently given birth, and also in cases of jaundice. 64
In cases of constipation arising from undigested matter (āmātisāra) and fever, in disorders born of phlegm (kapha), in dyspnea and throat diseases,
and in hiccups, upajihvā, and swelling of the uvula (galashuṇḍikā).
In cases of cough, eye disease, heaviness of the head, vomiting, exhaustion, insanity, choleraic dysentery, disorders of the female reproductive tract, enlargement of the spleen, and chronic catarrh;
In cases of abdominal tumors, heart disease,
halīmaka, and disorders arising from the provocation of vāta alone, when the milk of a dhātrī has become excessively increased and vitiated; 66.
In a child, when there is an increase of kapha and vāta during sleep,
when there is an increase of urine, when there is fluid in the heart, and in cases of spitting, lethargy, and despondency. (67)

In all types of diarrhea, as well as in planetary afflictions (*graha*), back-aches, consumption (*yakṣman*), heart disease, and the torments of anxiety, exhaustion, insanity, intoxication, and fever;
A wise physician should not prescribe *maṇḍa* (scum).
For if *maṇḍa* is drunk by one afflicted with a disease of the *kapha* type, it increases that very *kapha*.
Thus, by extinguishing their fire and further provoking those diseases, he makes them even more painful;
therefore, [one should avoid] those men who are afflicted by phlegm.
Physicians do not recommend the scum [of boiled pulses];
for them, the water from boiled mung beans, combined with rock salt and trikaṭu, is beneficial for comfort. 70
Indeed, the broth of mung beans (mudga-maṇḍa), being astringent and bitter and possessing a pungent post-digestive effect, quickly destroys phlegm (kapha).
Therefore, [it is used for one whose body is] emaciated and freed from disease.
Or one who has a burning fever with lingering illness,
or one who is exhausted yet strong but diseased, or one who is accustomed to cow's milk, meat, and fish; ||| 71 ||
One should mix it with a flavorless broth, or with blood, or with a preparation made from cow's milk; it should have been strained three times and processed with digestive-stimulating water. 72.
It may be made with rice that has been thoroughly parched, or likewise with mung beans, barley, or fried grain;
it should be warm, fragrant, pure, and yellow. (73)
Within a moment, the medicinal extract (maṇḍa) bestows strength upon him; likewise, his disease becomes mild,
and all his sense faculties return to their natural state.
The sequence of foods should likewise be prepared as follows:
for one who drinks the *maṇḍa* as prescribed, these benefits arise;
in the case of the opposite, the opposite results.
Those very things that are suitable for the *maṇḍa*— namely,
thin gruel that is light, does not cause a burning sensation when warm, and promotes the downward movement of the bodily humors (*doṣas*)— are likewise suitable here.
Pitta is countered by the quality of sweetness,
and one should employ the sequence of food items in due order;
for one afflicted by Vata and Kapha, [a meal] with pomegranate is always beneficial.
For one afflicted by pitta and kapha, it may be prepared with sugar;
or it may be cooked with the meat-juice of wild animals, or with milk, or with pomegranates. (77)
Beneficial for men afflicted by wind (māruta), as well as in cases of abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic enlargement (plīhan), and chronic catarrh (pīnasa),
[this applies] along with food, bathing, recreation, and vehicles.
They say that physical exercise, conversation, singing,
and wholesome food are beneficial for one who is healthy,
when a disease has subsided, and when the digestive fire is weak.
When the disease has subsided and the fire blazes brightly,
those freed from illness— though emaciated and weak, with failing senses and deficient in complexion, strength, and digestive fire— [recover]. 79.

Those afflicted by travel, those oppressed by bile (pitta), and those tormented by fever, diarrhea, abdominal diseases, anal disorders, anxiety, and ailments from drinking or traveling on foot— [these are relieved]. 80.
Constantly oppressed by coughs, weapons, and poisons, and struck by grief,
they are afflicted by the exhaustion of physical exertion, singing, and study.
Afflicted by the earth, fire, wind, heat, and lack of sleep (81), with their eyes, throats, mouths, and noses burning,
they become despondent and lose their memory and intelligence.

Those suffering from constipation, dry feces, or urinary retention; those afflicted by fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, or intestinal volvulus; and those with crushed limbs, fractures, dislocations, or jaundice—[these should not be treated]. 82. [Nor should one treat] those with emaciated limbs.
In cases of clean wounds devoid of flesh, in chronic fevers, in quotidian, tertian, and quartan fevers, as well as in constant fever— 83.
Those struck by *rakṣas*, *piśācas*, serpents, *bhūtas*, *yakṣas*, hunger, thunderbolts, thirst, fire, or cold;
those [afflicted] with women, children, or sons, and those whose milk has become scanty or dried up.
If her fetus does not develop, or if the infant who drinks from the breast does not thrive, and remains constantly awake and weeping excessively; 84.
And for one whose vision is impaired by sharp nasal medications or drying treatments or by medical procedures, they should consume boiled milk. 85.
One who requires purgation should drink milk boiled with medicinal herbs;
for milk instantly bestows strength and quickly fortifies the sense organs. 86
It bestows intelligence, longevity, health, and happiness; they call it the foremost elixir (rasāyana),
and through it the embryo attains nourishment and firmness.
The *bandhyā* and the *ṣaṇḍha* give birth to old age; it cleanses the anus, purifies the milk, moves the wind in its natural direction, and produces lightness in men. 87.
Therefore, they declare that among all elixirs (rasāyana), milk is the best at the end of a disease; they say milk is wholesome and pure. 88.
Milk is auspicious; milk is said to promote longevity. Milk improves the complexion; they say milk is beneficial for the hair. Milk is a restorative; they say milk is youth-preserving. (89)
Milk permeates all embodied beings;
disease does not afflict one who drinks milk.
There is nothing else in this world superior to milk as an aphrodisiac.
There is nothing more life-sustaining than milk (90).
Due to its coldness, milk increases wind;
because it is [mildly] bitter, it first breaks up the feces for one whose constitution is dominated by bile.
Due to its heaviness, it causes slight pain;
due to its unctuousness, it purges both during digestion;
and because of its sweetness, it nourishes the body.
Likewise, it quickly clarifies the sense faculties;
through its density it brings stability to water, and through its sliminess it purifies the internal channels. 92
Furthermore, due to its astringent nature, it obstructs the wind (vāta), and by that means it produces colic;
moreover, because of its unctuousness and sweet quality, it causes pain.
Milk, being digested, excretes its own waste; because of its unctuousness, heaviness, astringency, and coldness,
it loosens [the body's impurities] and immediately bestows strength.

Because it possesses unctuousness and coldness and is associated with sweetness, it increases *kapha* in those whose nature is *kapha*; furthermore, this [milk] is wholesome because of its inherent state of being a natural habituation (*sātmya*) and an astringent (*kaṣāya*). 94.
It produces satisfaction from digestion and not distress;
it makes the complexion fair due to its whiteness, and it provides oiliness through its unctuousness. 95
Due to its coolness, astringency, dense and thick consistency, contact, and fermentation within the vessel,
[the spirit] is gradually obstructed by the accumulation of heat.
Milk slowly approaches the state of curd; for milk that is afflicted by wind and heat quickly turns to curds—
this indeed is the cause therein.
Through heat, density, and then through the swelling,
moistening, and churning of the curd, the fire within the milk produces sourness. 97.
Likewise, as it passes beyond the marrow, it flows upward by its own nature and rises up; meanwhile, the waste matter (kiṭṭa) settles downward for him. 98
And having previously perceived through the power of divine knowledge that this [ocean] was being churned by the gods with skillful means,
he then obtained the ghee, the curd, and the water.
Cows are the foundation of all that moves and is stationary.
Therefore, for men who are afflicted by long-standing diseases, who have fallen into a swoon, or who are falling [from a height]...
Physicians declare milk to be the ultimate refuge;
for milk indeed produces sleep, happiness, longevity, and strength. However, one who is foolish regarding the seeds of passion [should avoid it]. 100.
The wise physician should prescribe milk with *bhallātaka* nuts, betel nut (*pūgaphala*), and other such ingredients;
or he should drink cold jaggery-water. 101.
One should always feed him milk with jaggery,
or food prepared with clarified butter; likewise, the same should be done even when using *dhānvīraka* ghee.
Indeed, milk is said to be its digestive medicine.
Among deer, those from marshy lands are inferior, while those from arid regions are superior; likewise, one born in good soil, heavy, firm-eyed, and steady is best.
Among the bamboo species of the Sāmudraṣaṇḍha forest,
the *kṣukavaṃśaka* bamboo is highly praised; it is increasingly superior as one proceeds further [along the series],
being sweet, cooling, nourishing, and digestive.
When consumed as a liquid, it is unctuous, aphrodisiac, improves the complexion and the eyesight, and increases phlegm;
however, when drunk, it causes a burning sensation. 104
One whose constitution is dominated by phlegm (kapha) should drink sugarcane juice after eating;
those with a predominance of bile (pitta) or wind (vāta) should drink it before the meal;
however, for one in whom the humors are combined, it is beneficial to drink it during the meal.
For thus all obtain happiness (105); therefore, I shall describe the types of diseases as being like sugarcane juice by nature, for the sake of their welfare.
In cases of fever, diarrhea, diseases of the throat,
cholera, leprosy, rheumatism, and cough; in anemia, colic, and dropsy.

In cases of vomiting characterized by an excess of phlegm, after purgation or emesis, following nasal therapy (nastaḥkriyā) or non-unctuous enema (nirūha), and in disorders of hoarseness, wasting, and chronic catarrh (pīnasa). 107

One should not consume milk in cases of urinary disorders (prameha), edema, pain, or diseases, nor in conditions arising from internal secretions (abhiṣyanda); it is likewise forbidden during all planetary afflictions and in cases of excessive growth.
For children, those who are excessively drowsy, and those afflicted by phlegm diseases (kapha),
the use of sugarcane is not beneficial; however,
listen from me as to who it is beneficial for.
In cases of chronic fever, anorexia, internal hemorrhage (rakta-pitta), cough, wasting from chest injury, depletion of phlegm, thirst, impaired digestion, erysipelas, and alcoholism. 109.
In cases of urinary disorders, ear diseases, and wind (vāta) affecting the head and eyes;
in the wasting of skin, flesh, complexion, luster, intellect, semen, sleep, strength, vitality (ojas), and blood. 110
For those for whom milk is said to be beneficial, sugarcane juice is likewise wholesome for children;
it cures excessive salivation, anorexia, satiety, and fainting caused by *kapha*.

If consumed in excess, this meat-juice causes pain from piercing headaches, catarrh, and throat diseases, as well as urinary disorders, nausea, loss of consciousness, loss of digestive fire, and fever.
Thus, this auspicious and excellent chapter concerning the inquiry regarding food has been declared for the benefit of men and for the sake of the elders among physicians. 112.
"They declare that which is in accordance with the Dharma to be the root of happiness.
Thus spoke the Blessed One Kaśyapa.
This concludes the section on food within the *Kalpasthāna*.
The Chapter on Specific Preparations: Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "Specific Preparations.
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa. 1–2.
To Kaśyapa, who was seated after having offered the agnihotra sacrifice and was honored by the world, an elder— standing in humility and seeking specific instruction—
questioned him: "In the Sūtrasthāna, two types of fever were pointed out by the Blessed One."
"Through my knowledge of causes, symptoms, and medicines, I have treated him accordingly.
Yet, O Blessed One, there remains a doubt regarding this fever of combined humors (sannipāta-jvara); please dispel my doubt through your specific expertise and defining characteristics."
O Sage, is this combination (sannipāta) one, or are there many?
If it is one, is it by means of equal humors (doṣas), and how then could there be multiplicity?
[This concerns] the three—wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha)—when they are all provoked.
O Great Sage, which of these humors (doṣas) becomes aggravated first?
Do the humors become aggravated simultaneously, or in succession? Or do they become aggravated irregularly, one by one at a time? (7–8)
O illustrious one, what are the specific varieties [of diseases] in detail and in brief?
How many types of *sannipāta* are there, and what are their individual names?
What are their complications, and what is the method for their avoidance?
When asked by his aged disciple, "What are their treatments, and which among them are curable or incurable?", Prajāpati spoke these wonderful words regarding the specific types of *sannipāta*.
Listen, O Bhārgava, to the true nature of this specific type of *sannipāta*, which many physicians of unrefined intellect do not understand.
It arises from cold treatments, from sexual intercourse, and from the consumption of incompatible foods. (12)
Due to staying awake at night, sleeping during the day, anxiety, envy, and emaciation;
likewise, due to giving birth with difficulty, various kinds of misconduct, the infant’s drinking of spoiled milk, and eating contaminated food. (13–14)

For those people who constantly consume incompatible actions, drinks, and foods— due to fasting, eating before the previous meal is digested, eating during indigestion, and the sudden change of food and drink, as well as the change of seasons— (15)
From consuming wind and water tainted by poison, from being defiled by poisoned food, especially in mountain valleys that are unfavorable,
and from the improper application of the five types of unctuous substances and their therapeutic procedures.
And when the aforementioned causes combine,
O Bhārgava, the three humors (doṣas) become aggravated as life-force wanes;
consequently, diseases such as fever afflict a person most severely.
Furthermore, because it is antagonistic to all [other] defects, this great disease is difficult to treat.
Just as a tree would not be destroyed by fire, thunderbolt, or wind, so too a person does not survive when the wind, bile, and phlegm are provoked. 19–20.
Just as those struck by poison, fire, and weapons do not survive simultaneously, so too do those who lack ascetic merit not survive when afflicted by the derangement of the humors (sannipāta).
Furthermore, both of these [poison, etc., and the humors] are like a house set ablaze from above.

Just as three hunters with poisoned arrows, having surrounded a deer, cannot spare it, so too the three humors (doṣas), like incurable diseases, cannot spare an embodied being when they have converged upon men.
Because they inevitably cause the body to fall when combined,
and because another [disease] quickly falls together with them, this is called *sannipāta* (a combination). Furthermore,
there is the sudden appearance of sensory functions and the sudden appearance of urine.
A sudden change in one's character is the primary symptom of *sannipāta*.
O best of physicians, its varieties have been described as thirteen,
arising from the deficient, moderate, excessive, balanced, dual, and single-predominance of the humors.
In one whose *sannipāta* (combined derangement) is aggravated by a predominance of *vāta* and *pitta*,
there occur fever, aching of the limbs, thirst, dryness of the palate,
blurred vision, loss of appetite, drowsiness, diarrhea, dyspnea, cough, exhaustion, and vertigo. (27)

When a *sannipāta* (combined derangement) characterized by an excess of *pitta* and *śleṣman* becomes aggravated, there occurs internal burning with external coldness, and thirst increases; the right side of the body is pricked with pain, and there is stiffness of the chest, head, and throat. (28–29)
One spits phlegm mixed with blood, the throat is pained with difficulty, and diarrhea, dyspnea, and hiccups increase along with pramīlaka;
these two are declared by name as the sannipāta fevers Vidhu and Phalgu. 30.
For one in whom the *sannipāta* (the simultaneous derangement of the humors) becomes aggravated with a predominance of phlegm (*śleṣman*) and wind (*anila*),
that *sannipāta* is extremely severe; it is the sovereign [disease] characterized by a predominance of wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*).
Sannipāta with an excess of pitta and śleṣman is *phalgu*;
sannipāta with an excess of kapha and vāta is *makarī*;
sannipāta with an excess of vāta is *visphāraka*.
Sannipāta with a predominance of pitta is "quick-acting" (śīghrakārī);
sannipāta with a predominance of kapha is "intense" (ulbaṇa).
When sannipāta occurs with [humors] that are diminished, increased, or moderate, it is as follows:
His diseases are said to be those very same ones, arising according to the strength of the respective doṣas;
however, his raktapitta becomes aggravated, affecting all the channels,
and he is covered on all sides by eruptions resembling burns from fire.
The mantra for the heart and stomach, as well as the liver, spleen, and lungs,
is cooked within the body; pus flows upward and downward,
the teeth decay, and death follows— this is its specific characteristic.
When there is a combination (sannipāta) of the humors that are moderate, increased, and diminished,
the diseases arising from it are said to depend on the strength of the respective doṣas;
such a person has stiff limbs and a fixed gaze, and lies down as if slain.
When there is excessive evacuation of feces even in one who eats much,
it indicates a maturation (pāka) of all the channels; this is the specific characteristic here when the *sannipāta* occurs in its increased, diminished, or moderate states.

The diseases of that [wind] are said to be those very same ones, arising according to the strength of the respective humors (doṣas): yawning, wakefulness, exhaustion, delirium, headache, stiffness of the neck, and even death; this is its specific characteristic.
The names of these three are Yāmya, Krakaca, and Pākala. Understand from me that Sannipāta is provoked when the three doṣas are in equilibrium;
in this condition, one should observe the symptoms of all three doṣas.
They say that those symptoms described in the treatment of fever which are equal in strength like three staffs, or like three legs,
constitute this extremely severe *sannipāta* known as *kūṭapākala*.
When a great disease called *kūṭapākala* arises— which instantly slays from terrible illnesses, thunderbolts, weapons, and fire—
one seized by *kūṭapākala* neither hears nor sees.
He does not move, he does not speak, he neither praises nor blames; intent solely on breathing, with limbs rigid and eyes fixed,
the life of such a person lasts for at most three nights.

Seeing him in that state, the deluded people spoke: "He has surely been overpowered by a *rākṣasa* while wandering at an improper hour in the night"; and some further asserted that he had been seized by a *yakṣiṇī* or by *brahmarākṣasas*.

It may be inhabited by Piśācas or Guhyakas, or likewise by others residing in that region; it may be one where cries have been raised or curses uttered, or where others have struck the head [of an image];
it may be one where the worship of the family deity has been interrupted, or which has been assailed by the household deities.
Some say it is the affliction of the constellations, others speak of the effects of poisons (*gara*), while physicians call it a derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*); it is known as *kūṭapākala*,
occurring when those three [humors] are simultaneously provoked in a healthy person.
Then, due to incompatible food, the passage of time, and the ripening of karmas, a pustule known as *viṣa* arises in the body;
the wind (*anila*) quickly becomes aggravated and subsequently impairs his digestive fire (*agni*).
When that person, whose digestive fire has been impaired, consumes the fourfold food as before, it becomes predominantly phlegm;
then the wind (vāyu), taking up that phlegm, courses through his channels.
Having filled and blocked all his channels, both subtle and large, the wind (pavana) becomes obstructed;
it then provokes the bile (pitta) in him, and that bile is impelled by the wind.
Obstructed on all sides by phlegm through mutual association and dependence,
it afflicts the embodied being by producing fever, nausea, loss of appetite, pain in the joints, choleraic disorders, and various other diseases.
Whether due to a transformation of the *prakṛti* or by its very nature, the lords of diseases become aggravated; and according as they attain a state of being one,
two, or many-fold in their intensity, they are described as weak, moderate, or excessive.
When the humors are equal and fixed, "Kūṭapākala" arises;
thus these thirteen types of *sannipāta* are to be described.
However, when the rasa of this [patient] is impaired, it flows away, driven by the wind (*anila*).

A wise physician should not be confused regarding the specific characteristics of the doshas, for they may manifest as despondency, heaviness, fainting, and pain in the limbs, whether they are excited individually,
combined, weakened, or arising from a single dosha.

If one were to sprinkle cold water upon a patient suffering from the burning pain of a *sannipāta* disorder, how could that afflicted person survive, and how could he even be called a physician? Likewise,
[if one gives] ghee to one who is trembling and lamenting during a *sannipāta*...
How could those two [the physician and the patient] both survive if he were to cause one suffering from *sannipāta*— who is thirsty, afflicted by pain in the flanks, and parched throat—
to drink cold water? He who gives such water is death itself in human form.

For physicians say that crossing this ocean is like fighting with a stone against death itself; he who rescues an embodied being submerged in the ocean of *sannipāta* is truly a healer of *sannipāta*.
What dharma has not been performed by Kaśyapa, and what worship does he not deserve?
When a medical emergency arises, what should one undertake first? Having asked these questions, listen now to the commencement of medical treatment.
In this matter, physicians fall into great delusion when they are uncertain;
by administering medicine at the wrong time—either at the onset or at the end—they kill the patients.
In a case of *sannipāta*, one should observe whichever *doṣa* is most powerful by its specific characteristics.
"Others, such as physicians, know that one should apply suppression (nigraha) in his presence;
but we, O Vṛddhajīvaka, do not treat in this manner. Those physicians who know thus are indeed of improper vision."

In a disease born of the three doṣas, one should first effect the suppression of phlegm (śleṣman). For when the phlegm has been removed and the channels have been opened, lightness arises immediately and thirst is likewise pacified.

Pain in the head, heart, ears, and sides subsides, as does heaviness and numbness of the tongue; moreover, vision becomes clear. Therefore, one should repeatedly perform the depletion of phlegm (śleṣman) with medicinal remedies.
On the first day, one should cause a person whose humors (doṣas) have been aggravated to vomit;

however, once the body has become desiccated, one should not induce vomiting, for such a person might vomit impure matter. Furthermore, in all cases of *sannipāta* (combined humors), one should not administer honey.
For honey is a cooling treatment, and coldness here is contraindicated;
one suffering from *sannipāta* is always praised for using warm treatments. One should avoid sleeping during the day and should rely upon fortitude and mental strength.
One who is skilled in application should first employ fasting, sudation, nasal medication, massage,
and gargling in cases of *sannipāta* for three nights, five nights, or even ten nights.
In cases of *sannipāta*, however, one should administer fasting (*laṅghana*) until health is observed.
The signs of proper fasting are: a desire for food, lightness, debility, clarity, cheerfulness, and the cessation of complications.

As stated in the chapter on sudation (sveda-adhyāya), all forms of whole-body sudation produce, when not properly performed, lack of perspiration, heaviness, lack of faith, and physical distortion; whereas when overdone, they cause delusion, emaciation, flaccidity, and wind-pain (vāta-ruj).
One should generally apply fomentation to that very place where his pain occurs;
for phlegm, driven by the wind (vāyu), obstructed in the flanks or the heart,
and hardened by bile (pitta), afflicts a person like a piercing splinter.
For that [patient] who is unemaciated, yet sluggish, obstructed, and physically debilitated,
there is no remedy other than something sharp to effect the removal of suffering; for him, sharp nasal drops (nasya) and sharp gargles (kavalagraha) are required.
For one suffering from pain in the sides, one should prescribe fomentation and staying awake during the day;
or else, one should administer a sharp nasal medication (nasya) prepared with warm juice of *mātuluṅga* and *ārdraka* combined with the three salts, or another preparation prescribed for success.
By that, the phlegm is broken up and, being sweated, is discharged; his head, heart, neck, and face become clear, and his vision brightens;
drowsiness, dryness of the palate, dyspnea, and cough are all pacified.
Furthermore, during sleep, a pungent nasal drop (nasya) and collyrium (añjana) are beneficial;
alternatively, lukewarm gargles (kavalagraha) prepared with sharp substances, salts, and the juices of mātuluṅga, combined with sour liquids, should be employed.
One should hold a wick soaked in rock salt (*saindhava*), fresh ginger juice, and the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*) in the mouth, and spit it out again and again;
by this, the phlegm from his heart, neck, sides, head, and throat [is expelled].
When the kapha is stagnant, it is drawn upward; lightness occurs in the dry state,
as well as joint pain, fever, sleepiness, dyspnea, cough, throat ailments, heaviness of the mouth and eyes, numbness, and nausea, which then subside.
One should administer [the treatment] once, twice, three times, or four times, having observed the relative strength and weakness of the humors;
for this is said to be the supreme medicine for one suffering from a *sannipāta* disorder who is constantly being drawn away by *śleṣman*.

Thirst occurs when the mouth, heart, throat, and palate become parched; for such thirst, water shall be prescribed as a remedy that is digestive-stimulant, subdues phlegm and wind, or even alleviates all three humors.
By this means, his phlegm is cooked; once cooked, it abandons its site.
When the phlegm has been released, the wind (vāta) then moves in its natural direction.
Through the downward movement of phlegm and wind, the bile (pitta), its strength diminished, follows suit.

For him, the disease becomes easy to treat, because his *kapha* is secondary; then, knowing him to have undergone fasting (*laṅghita*), to be free from much affliction, and desirous of food, one should offer him a gruel (*peyā*) prepared with digestive (*dīpanīya*) decoctions.
A gruel made from old grains of *śāli* or *ṣaṣṭika* rice, fried and strained three times, dry, lukewarm, and mixed with salts,
is recommended; it should not be too thick, nor should one eat a large quantity of it.
If it is digested without obstruction, one should know that the man’s life is saved;

however, in a case of excessive phlegm (*śleṣman*), a decoction of mung beans (*mudga*) with fresh ginger, black pepper, *sauvarcala* salt, and *saindhava* salt is beneficial when added to that same water.
Having first consumed grapes mixed with sugar and honey,
and if pitta is predominant, the physician should administer only gruel (peyā) combined with sugar; however, he should not prescribe unctuous substances, food, drink, or other heavy items.
In cases of *saṃnipāta* (combined humoral disorders), one should feed him, for that [heavy food] would be like poison to him;
the physician should always give *peyā* (gruel) with pomegranate to one suffering from anorexia—
neither too hot nor too salty— or even vegetable soup seasoned with sour fruits.
One should feed him at dusk, and as soon as he has eaten, one should have him sleep in a private,
windless room provided with fire and a comfortable covering;
for seven days, one should feed him small amounts of food, gradually increasing the quantity.

Then one should administer *virasikā* prepared with buttermilk and pomegranate, as well as decoctions that alleviate *sannipāta* fever according to the specific dosha involved; once the food has been properly digested, one should provide the meat broth of wild animals.

For three days, one should have him consume that [broth] seasoned with dry, hot, pungent, and salty substances; thereafter, for another three days, he should be given that same broth in a quantity equal to a jujube fruit (*badara*),
prepared in a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) and other ingredients, and refined with the addition of quail (*lāva*) and similar meats.
In a disease where Vāta is predominant, the soup should have its sourness, saltiness, and oiliness made manifest;
it should be prepared with ghee and refined by the addition of mung bean broth as a counteragent.
In a disease where Pitta is predominant, the soup should be made with mild oiliness, sourness, and saltiness.

Likewise, when there is an excess of phlegm, one should administer a decoction of *kulattha* beans prepared with the meat of rabbits and other such animals, along with *bāla*, *mūlaka*, and *vyoṣa*, and a small amount of fat;
this should be done upon seeing that the patient's strength has been restored and he is only slightly supported by his illness.
After making the patient eat soft, unctuous food with mild laxatives, one should administer a purgative;
for the remaining morbid humors (doṣas) are pacified once he has been purged—this is the prescribed sequence. Now hear from me also regarding the medicinal decoctions (kaṣāyas).

Pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, and nāgara constitute the group known as the digestive (dīpanīya); it removes diseases caused by kapha and vāta, is appetizing, stimulates digestion, is beneficial for the heart, light, and an excellent astringent.
Śaṭī, pauṣkara, pippalī, bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārikā,
śuṇṭhī, karkaṭakī, bhārgī, durālambhā, and yavānikā constitute the śaṭyādi group; it destroys colic, distension, and constipation, and alleviates kapha and vāta.
Musta, parpaṭaka, uśīra, devadāru, mahauṣadha, triphalā, durālabhā, nīlī, kampillaka, trivṛt,
kirātatiktaka, pāṭhā, vacā, and kaṭurohiṇī.
Madhuka, pippalīmūla, and the group beginning with mustā are said to be the "Mustādi" group; it is purifying, pacifying, a destroyer of the three doṣas, and a stimulator of the digestive fire.
Alternatively, this may consist of eighteen ingredients including water and pārvata.

In a *sannipāta* disorder where *pitta* is predominant, the founders of the medical tradition recommend drinking light water boiled with either the *pañcamūla*, the *śaṭyādi* group, or the *pañcadaśamūla*. This prepared decoction serves as a digestive stimulant (*dīpana*).

Having observed the relative strength and weakness of the bodily humors (*doṣas*), one should administer water boiled with *pārvatī*, *pañcamūlī*, or *dīpana* herbs, along with *mustaka*, *parpaṭaka*, and *durālabhā*. This water should be either lukewarm or very hot.
In a disease where pitta is predominant, all [medicines] are recommended lukewarm as a drink;

in a condition with undigested matter (āma) and kapha predominant, a decoction of the pippalyādi group combined with vacā, devadāru, vayasṭhā, and sara should be drunk, along with hiṅgu, kṣāra, and saindhava salt.
By this, the doshas are quickly digested and constipation is relieved.
[The following are used: Abhayā, Kaṭphala, Bhārgī, Bhūtīka, Devadāru, Vacā, Parpaṭaka, Mustā, Dhānyaka, and Viśvabheṣaja.
A decoction of śaṭī, hiṅgu, and honey should be drunk in a disease where vāta and kapha are predominant;
likewise, durālabhā, vacā, dāru, pippalī, bhadrarohiṇī, mahauṣadha, karkaṭakī, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā [should be used].
This decoction, taken with salt, cures fever caused by the simultaneous derangement of all three humors (sannipāta-jvara).
It consists of triphalā, rohiṇī, nimba, paṭola, the three pungents (kaṭutraya),
pāṭhā, guḍūcī, the tips of vetra, saptaparṇa, and vatsaka.
Kirātatiktaka, mustā, and vacā, boiled together as one,
destroy excess kapha when drunk and kindle the digestive fire;
so too do āragvadha, vacā, nimba, paṭola, uśīra, and vatsaka.
This decoction of śārṅgeṣṭā, ativiṣā, mūrvā, triphalā, durālabhā,
bhadramusta, balā, pāṭhā, madhuka,
and bhadrarohiṇī quickly pacifies fever born of the three doṣas.
It removes stiffness, swelling, distension, and heaviness;
one should apply warm poultices containing salt for the treatment of torticollis (manyāstambha), chest constriction (uroghāta), and pain in the chest, flanks, and head.
Due to prolonged fasting, the heart, flanks, throat, lips, and palate of a person are afflicted by the application of nasal drops and warm gargles;
consequently, with a wounded chest, he spits out thick phlegm mixed with blood.
When drunk, the person is stretched out and faints; by that [poison], the creature perishes.
His stomach burns and he makes some indistinct moaning;
having drunk it, he falls asleep quickly, and once digested, he wakes up in water.
In persons with a predominance of pitta in their disease, pitta becomes aggravated by the administration of jumping exercises, hot treatments,
and the application of sharp medicinal drugs; having recognized this pitta-predominant *sannipāta* through these causes, [one should treat it accordingly].
One should have the patient drink water boiled with the *mustā* group of drugs, cooled and mixed with honey and sugar, at the appropriate time; by this, he shall obtain relief,
and even if [the disease] has spread slightly, he will quickly become comfortable through that very treatment.
This bolus (modaka), consisting of triphalā, pippalī, śyāmā, kesara, sugar, and trivṛt mixed with honey, indeed dispels disorders where pitta is predominant;
[it is prepared] with barley, jujube, horse-gram, and the two groups of five roots (pañcamūla).
A wise physician should cook clarified butter in a decoction of triphalā,
having added these well-ground pastes prepared in their proper proportions:
mustā, pāṭhā, vacā, śuṇṭhī, rohiṇī, cavya, and citraka.
Śṛṅgī, durālabhā, śigru, kairāta, the two types of rajanī (turmeric and yellow turmeric), tejovatī, somavalka, saptaparṇa along with kevuka,
vayasthā, pippalīmūla, pippalī, and gajapippalī.
Chinnaruhā, ativiṣā, the leaves of nimba and paṭola, kaṇḍū, apuṣpī, gojihvā, the fruits of naktamāla,
tumburu, the root of puṣkara, and the roots of madana and arka.
Clarified butter prepared according to the prescribed method with alkaline substances, the five salts, and a measure of asafoetida, known as *kaṭuka-ghṛta*,
should be administered in the proper dose and at the right time to one afflicted by *sannipāta* fever.
It pacifies residual defects of suppressed [doshas], affliction by irregular fever (viṣamajvara),

heart disease, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), abdominal tumors caused by vāta (vātagulma), splenic enlargement (plihodara), dyspnea, and cough; it also kindles the digestive fire and increases strength.
In cases of combined disorders (sannipāta), even when the complications have mostly subsided, phlegm and pain in the flanks may persist for one who eats; therefore,
the physician should rekindle that patient's digestive fire again, as it tends to become sluggish over time.

A physician should not place excessive trust [in his success], thinking, "The disease has been conquered by me. For in one who is emaciated, the *doṣas* become aggravated after a long time due to the consumption of incompatible things; once provoked, they strike back and kill again, just like a *sannipāta* poison.
If a man survives having emerged from a *sannipāta* disorder, his vital energy, strength, and flesh are exhausted; his beard and hair are withered;
he is deprived of voice and memory; his semen is depleted and his sense faculties are impaired.
He becomes one with indistinct speech, discolored, and having weak digestion;
yet, once freed from the *sannipāta*, that man regains his strength after a long time.
Having seen this, he should be given nourishing food, for that indeed is his rebirth.
If, remaining in that state, he suffers from complications such as fever, emaciation, anorexia, splenic enlargement, consumption, or jaundice, he will not survive,
even if he was previously endowed with all favorable signs and possessed of all his vital functions.
Even if neglected for three nights, a *sannipāta* disorder does not resolve;
however, once the *sannipāta* has subsided, whatever disease persists and whatever complications arise, one should treat them with their respective specific therapies.

Consuming a single meal a day, practicing celibacy, and partaking of light drinks and food; avoiding labor and exertion; remaining on a comfortable bed, seat, or standing position; staying awake during the day; and sitting together with virtuous friends.
Variegated ointments and garments, or sometimes even oil alone;
and the meat-broths of wild animals served lukewarm, or those prepared with the soup of *kulattha* beans;
and seasoned *vāstuka*, *taṇḍulīya*, and tender radish.
One who desires long life should follow this regimen according to the rules for two months;
or, if due to the crooked nature of this consumption (yakṣman), he continues for three or even four months,
he should eat with milk boiled with ghee, especially if he has a bilious temperament.
Furthermore, for thirst, one should always hold camphor powder in the mouth with cow’s milk mixed with sugar and honey;
one should also constantly wear excellent fragrant flowers and oils.
Meat from aquatic or marshy animals, preparations made from mung beans,
flour, and sesame, newly distilled wines, heavy or fresh foods, milk-rice, rice-and-pulse porridge, sour gruel, fried cakes, barley-meal, and curd.
One should avoid all of these, as well as eating with faith [in the donor], the fatigue of exercising horses, cold water, wine and spirits,
frost, the east wind, and excessive heat.
O Jīvaka, listen to me as I describe those foods and drinks that are praised for him— those which are fit to be eaten with faith and are wholesome according to his specific needs:
namely, long peppers prepared with molasses and ghee, and those cooked with curd.
Likewise, primary foods prepared with jaggery, those made of mung beans, preparations of barley and wheat, curd-based dishes, dried radish,
and soups of mung beans and āmalaka, as well as bitter soups seasoned with ghee.
In this way, the physician should effect conversion through faith;
the wise physician seeking the Dharma should treat with diligence those suffering from anorexia.
Furthermore, O Sage, that which I shall speak regarding the treatment of puerperal fever in the *Khila* section, you should apply here as well.
"Therefore, the treatment for combined disorders (sannipāta) should also be applied here," so said the Blessed Kaśyapa;
thus ends the "Specific Formulations" (viśeṣakalpa) in the Section on Formulations (kalpasthāna).
The Chapter on the Ritual of the Saṃhitā.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual of the Saṃhitā.
Thus indeed said the Blessed Kaśyapa. 1–2.
One who is devoted to the study of the *Saṃhitā*, pure, virtuous, and has conquered his senses;
a physician born into a family of physicians, firmly established in both the text and its meaning—
when questioned by another physician, he should explain the rules of the *Saṃhitā*.
How many locations are there in this tantra? Why is it remembered as a "tantra"?
What are the names of the locations, and what are the chapters on ritual action?
I wish to hear, in accordance with reality, the sequential order of the names of these locations.
Eight topics are to be declared; therefore, the tantra is spoken of.
He who studies the one hundred and twenty chapters is a master.
[The sections are] Sūtrasthāna, Nidāna, Vimāna, and Ātmaniścaya.
The Indriyas, Cikitsā, Siddhi, Kalpa, and Saṃhitā; the Sūtrasthāna and Cikitsā each consisting of thirty chapters; the Nidānas, the Vimānas, and the eight Śārīras. 7–8.

The twelve chapters on accomplishments (*siddhi*), the ritual manuals (*kalpa*), and the senses (*indriya*), along with the eighty supplementary chapters (*khila*), constitute the Tantra together with its supplements.
Indeed, the retention of this Tantra is like the retention of the Vedas.

It is meritorious, auspicious, and life-prolonging; it destroys evil dreams and strife. It is the great, righteous abode for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; it constantly bestows happiness upon men and brings wealth, honor, and fame.
One who has mastered [the science] does not become unrighteous, nor childless, nor ignorant, nor censured;
he is never unhonored or unknown in this world.
Furthermore, the physician who studies constantly and teaches correctly [attains these qualities].
Having attained fame in this world, one is honored in the realm of Śakra.
During Dakṣa’s sacrifice, as the divine sages fled out of fear of slaughter, all diseases arose from the torment of both body and mind. 13–14.

Fever arises from excessive weight; abdominal tumors (gulma) from running; enlargement of the spleen (plīha) from swimming; vertigo from poison; diarrhea from suppressing the natural urges while running;
thirst and internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta) arise from exertion and from running in the heat.
Hiccups and dyspnea arise from an excess of phlegm in those who run or drink water [excessively].
Thus has the origin of these and other diseases been proclaimed, as they manifested among men due to the transition between the Kṛta and Tretā ages.
Since they steal away knowledge, power, fame, and the goals of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa,
the great seer Kaśyapa— acting on the command of the Grandfather (Brahmā) and having perceived this with his eye of wisdom— acted for the benefit of the worlds.
The sages obtained the system (tantra) fashioned through austerity. Jīvaka, the son of Ṛcīka, who was pure and free from darkness,
first received that great system and then condensed it.
All those sages did not approve of that childish speech;
then, in the presence of all the ṛṣis, the pure Jīvaka,
having been submerged in the Gaṅgā lake at Kanakhala for five years, [reappeared].
Overcome by wrinkles and grey hair, he emerged after a moment.
Then, having witnessed that miracle, the sages were filled with wonder and gave the child the name Vṛddhajīvaka, even though he was but an infant.
They received the treatise and made the best of physicians out of him;
thus, this treatise which had been lost in the Kali Yuga was, by chance,
preserved without effort by Yakṣa for the welfare of the world.
Then, by the wise Vātsya, a descendant of the lineage of Vṛddhajīvaka,
this great treatise was obtained without effort after he had thoroughly studied the three Vedas— Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma— as well as all their auxiliary sciences (aṅgas).

Having propitiated the yakṣas Śivaka and Kaśyapa through austerity and wisdom, he [re]composed that treatise originally created by Vṛddhajīvaka for the sake of Dharmakīrti’s happiness and for the prosperity of all beings. (27)
"Whatever purpose has not been stated regarding the eight locations in the *Śākhā*,
I shall explain each of those to you again in their entirety within the *Khilas*," so said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, named the Saṃhitā-kalpa, within the Kalpas of the Vṛddhajīvakīya-tantra on Pediatrics (Kaumārabhṛtya), revised by Vātsya;
and the Kalpasthāna is completed.
And this collection is completed; hereafter follows the section on supplements (khilasthāna), namely, the ninth section on supplements.
The First Chapter: On the Description of Intermittent Fevers (Viṣamajvara-nirdeśīya).
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "On the Description of Intermittent Fevers.
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Bhārgava, who was observant of his vows, questioned Kaśyapa— the knower of all scriptures, the teacher of all the world, and his own guru— regarding a doubt he held.
[Kaśyapa] had previously declared the medicinal treatment for irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*) within the context of the treatment of fever.
The Blessed One has not specified the cause of irregularity.
It is logical that constant [fevers] and the others are irregular because they arrive at irregular intervals; why then is a non-remitting fever considered "constant" yet "irregular"? (4–5)
By what cause do fever caused by a *preta*, that arising from a seizing spirit (*graha*), and irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*) occur?
This should now be explained at the proper time according to its components and so forth;
you ought to speak of it in truth, with its specific distinctions and in detail.
Thus questioned by his disciple, Kaśyapa spoke this answer: "A fever that has few causes, an external course, is modified (vaikṛta), is free from complications,
has a single site, is easily remedied, is light in its digestion, and is balanced (samo jvaraḥ)."
The "Irregular" (*viṣama*) is the opposite of that; it is considered "Continuous" (*saṃtata*) because of its intensity.
Likewise, those four arising from the possession by *pretas* are called "Irregular" due to their difficult conquest and because they are seized by fierce spirits (*ugra*). 9.
The irregularity of the *saṃtatika* and other fevers has been illustrated due to their severity;
likewise, I shall now explain how the irregularity caused by time (*kāla*) arises in the four types of fever beginning with the *satataka*. 10–11.
When all the rasa-carrying vessels, whether individually or in pairs,
are reached by the aggravated *doṣas*, they produce irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*).
This occurs in a man who is either currently afflicted with fever, one who is being freed from it, or one who has just been released from it.
Excessive physical exertion, heavy food, unwholesome food, and water in excess;
milk-rice, rice-and-pulse porridge, flour-based foods, minced meat, and thin curd;
oil-cakes, preparations of black gram, and likewise the flesh of domestic and marshy animals—[these should be avoided]. (13–14)
If one indulges in such other incompatible and heavy foods, as well as sleeping during the day, eating before the previous meal is digested, or overeating,
his fever will increase or become acute and irregular.
He who consumes astringent decoctions while the humors (doṣas) are not yet ripened;
or who, out of greed, drinks unctuous substances, milk, or nourishing foods; or [who acts] through the invocation of deities or even by contact with planetary spirits (grahas). 16–17.
In one who has just vomited or purged, or who has drunk oleaginous substances or received an oil enema, if he suddenly indulges in cold treatments, heavy food, or sexual intercourse,
his vāyu will likewise enter between the bones and the marrow.
When aggravated, it quickly provokes both phlegm (śleṣman) and bile (pitta).
Thereupon, due to this imbalance of the bodily constituents (dhātu), an irregular fever arises— whether continuous (satata), quotidian (anyedyuṣka), tertian (tṛtīya), or quartan (caturthaka).
It does not fail to reach subsidence, nor does it fail to become provoked again;
it does not overstep the proper time for tranquility and provocation. Furthermore, that which consists of latent tendencies (anuśaya) does not depart from its inherent nature of subsidence.
For there is no arising of entities that are quiescent by their very nature (22). Just as a person is regarded as liberated when the onset of a fever has subsided,
even so, in this state, one is not yet truly liberated from these [remaining] signs (23).

Understand from me how this [disease] arises again and again due to a slight bitterness or pungency in the mouth, or sweetness and so forth, as well as from excessive desire for food, exhaustion, and heaviness of the head. (24)
The path having been blocked by the disorder that is the cause of the irregular fever,
the wind (vāyu), once that disorder has subsided, regains its passage and, taking up the remainder of that disorder, returns it to its proper place in due order.
That remnant of the dosha, having dissolved into its own site and relying on the power of time, reaches the seat of rasa and once again produces fever (27),
due to the specific nature of the treatment and the exhaustion of its own strength.
It undergoes both decay and growth by depending on qualities that are equal to itself.
Having attained cessation, it flares up again and again by its own nature, just like a lamp even when its oil and wick have been exhausted. (28–29)

Resorting to its own substrate, a fever that has become pacified yet remains pacified manifests its strength at the proper time, even though the fuel of the humors (*doṣa*) has been exhausted. That which is constant and occurs by necessity, depending upon its own causal humor (*doṣa*), [is called *niyata-jvara*].
It manifests over a day and night, demonstrating the power produced by the cause of time (31).
This fever, occurring at two times [daily] according to the specific dosha, is known as *satataka*. Its location is the stomach (*āmāśaya*), depending upon which it persists (32).
When the dosha, having fallen from its location in the chest on the day of the tertian fever and having reached the rasa, manifests its power,
then the tertian fever arises as a persistent condition at its own time.
Having fallen from that third location, the throat, after one day and night, it reaches the chest after another day and night in due order;
the dosha, having taken refuge in the rasa-dhatu, becomes intensified along with the internal heat (ushman). 34–35.
On the third day it produces relief; that is the tertian fever (tṛtīyaka).
The head is the fourth location, which is declared to be the quartan fever (caturthaka).
When the dosha has fallen from its station after a day and night, it remains in the throat.
Then, after another day and night, it returns to the chest;
on the third day and night as well, it becomes aggravated in the rasa-dhatu (lymphatic/humoral constituent).
That should be known as the quartan fever (*caturthaka*), a great fever that persists for a long time.
Arising from a deep-seated location and corrupted by the mixing of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), it manifests its power at the proper time and then dissolves into the head of the living being.
This occurs because it originates from the three *doṣas* and through contact with the primary elements (*bhūta*). 39.
For this is most difficult to treat; therefore, one should apply treatment to it.
By means of powerful pacificatory fire-offerings (śānti-homa) and perfected mantra-words, as well as the removal of its evil, one who desires success must act. 40–41.
One should take refuge in Bhūteśvara, the blue-throated one who has the bull as his emblem;
for a fever that persists for a long time and is difficult to cure increases at its own appointed time—
whether after one day, two days, three days, or likewise four days.
Why is this [embryo] not born on the fifth or the sixth day?
Its abode, its place, is the chest, the throat, and likewise the head;
there is no other place for it beyond that, and due to the absence of such a place, it is not born.
The first [fever] belongs to Agni, the second indeed to Vāyu, the third would belong to Viśvedevas, and the fourth to Īśāna.
Why? Because [the patient's] strength is exhausted, and his bodily constituents (dhātu), power, and vitality (ojas) have diminished.
The fever of the living being increases, especially at the time of liberation (death).
Due to the absence of movement, its course is struck by the external wind;
following the wick that has been consumed, it is overwhelmed by the oil and the wind.
Just as a lamp, though its fuel is exhausted, does not shine,

so too when the strength of the elements has declined, the fever— though its own power is diminished— is especially extinguished at the time of liberation due to the absence of any further substrate for its defects.
Burning away the remainder of the cause without exception, it displays its power;
through the excellence of the counter-measures, it either subsides or destroys [the disease]. Whether by ripening, pacifying, or purifying, it removes what is excessive. (49)
When the *doṣas* are situated in their own locations, the person is released with purified channels (50).
Beyond these three causes— namely, the ripening (*pāka*) of the *doṣas* and so forth— as previously specified,
there is no other cause for liberation from fever elsewhere (51).
Why is it that, when the humors are agitated by a defect, fever generally first manifests with coldness in a living being, and subsequently a burning sensation arises?
(52) Because the Vāyu is pervasive, clear, cold, dry, mobile, and rough.
Pitta is fiery, hot, sharp, small in quantity, light, and liquid.
Kapha is lunar, cold, heavy, unctuous, and abundant; it is powerful, causes slow digestion, and its onset and subsidence are long-lasting.
And because of the common quality of coldness, Vāyu is the secondary strengthener (anubala) of Kapha;
for a Soma-like (cooling) quality is considered strong, whereas a fiery (āgneya) one is weak.
By this great reason, Kapha is indeed more powerful.
Therefore, in the initial stage of fever, cold occurs first, followed by burning heat.
When the phlegm (kapha) is pacified through its own transformation of momentum and by means of hot treatments, then the bile (pitta) becomes aggravated.
Or, through the processes of transformation, one may become happy once that [fever] has subsided;
this great cause has been explained correctly regarding that which is preceded by cold.
Now, why does fever arise in a living being preceded by burning heat?
That same reason is cited here as well because of its superior strength:
when the excessively aggravated *pitta* is combined with a small amount of *vāyu*, and is further joined by *śleṣman* of weak power in the seat of *rasa* (the stomach). 59–60.

At first there is a burning sensation for the person, and at the end, coldness sets in, accompanied by shivering, delirium, and the loss of memory and intellect. These two fevers, characterized by coldness and burning, arise from the combination [of doshas].
For those two, a fever preceded by a burning sensation is either incurable or difficult to cure.
(62) How is it that the doshas—vata and the others—though possessing qualities that are mutually antagonistic, combine to produce diseases and yet do not neutralize one another? (63)
Because defects are known not to pacify one another by their own nature or through their specific faults,
they therefore produce various diseases when combined.
Just as the qualities of *sattva* and the others are mutually opposed in their functions, so too are these defects.
Why does the head of one suffering from fever, especially when there is a burning sensation in all the limbs, become specifically cold?
It is because the pathways are obstructed by the *doṣas* and because the bodily heat (*tejas*) moves upward. (65–66)
Due to the predominance of the sense organs, the head suffers excessively;
oppressed by that excessively increased heat, the *soma* constituent descends downward, whereby coldness occurs in the feet. (67)
When one is thoroughly scorched by the heat of fever, why is the procedure of applying heat and so forth performed first, and not the other? Because cold is the subduer of heat,
just as in a heated room that is closed off with its door-panels.
Just as an excessive heat that causes burning on all sides subsides instantly once the door is opened,
so too does the heat in the channels of embodied beings subside when those channels are obstructed by defects.
The heat of fever increases in the body according to the strength of its causes;
for the purpose of opening [the channels], a warm treatment is prescribed for them,
for the quality of cold is known to be constricting, while the warm is considered liquefying.
Therefore, warm water is given to the fever patient for drinking;
by this, his humors (doṣas) are matured and the digestive fire (kāyāgni) is kindled.
The heat of the fever subsides and the constipation is relieved. (73)

Thirst is quickly allayed and a desire for food arises. (74) Except in the case of fever caused by pitta, every warm regimen removes fever; even in that case, treatments such as non-warm and cold measures are prescribed. (75)
Thus, the seven types of irregular fevers (viṣamajvara) have been described according to the questions; hereafter,
listen as I describe the treatment for those beginning with the quotidian (satataka),
for one whose tissues, strength, and vital essence (ojas) have been depleted and exhausted by these preliminary measures.
Chronic fever persists in an embodied being due to dryness;
therefore, a wise person should strive to restore its strength by means of delightful, varied, and pleasing foods served with faith. (77–78)
One should treat irregular fever (viṣamajvara) by means of drinking the first-pressed liquor (surāgra), eating the flesh of birds that scratch for food (vaiṣkira),
and the application of ghee, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), milk, and garlic,
as well as through the administration of medicinal herbs.
One should treat it with offerings to the deities, incense, unguents, and collyrium;
with the drinking of fats, massages, and immersions in water; and with unctuous, warm, and strengthening foods, drinks, and therapeutic procedures.
One should conquer [the condition] predominant in pitta with bitter and cooling pacifying treatments, along with purgatives, milk, clarified butter, and cooling ointments;
as well as with emetics, digestive stimulants, fasting, and light meals. 82
In a fever where Kapha is predominant, one should treat it with dry and hot decoctions (kaṣāya).
In a fever where Vāta and Pitta are predominant, characterized by horripilation and body aches,
one should drink Mahākalyāṇaka ghee or Pañcagavya ghee.
Or, after drinking a large dose of ghee, one should vomit it up again;
or on that very day or the following day, one should drink rice-gruel (peyā) mixed with black pepper.
Alternatively, one should drink a decoction of rājamūla or clarified butter (havis) that subdues fever.
This aforementioned application removes the fourth [type of fever].
Having drunk milk that is warm from the udder, one may vomit it at will, or otherwise drink cold milk with honey, or non-cold water infused with nimba leaves. 86–87.
Or, having drunk buffalo ghee mixed with a small amount of asafoetida,
one should eat food with curd only after that [ghee] has been fully digested;
or else, finely ground roots of the *nīlaspanda* plant with rice-water.
On the day of Jvara-tithi, the fat of a lion should be administered as a nasal drop (nasya).
Harītakī, vacā, kuṣṭha, nimba leaves, guggulu, white mustard seeds, and barley, mixed with clarified butter, constitute an incense that removes chronic fever.
The roots of sahadevā, along with kaṭukā, rohiṇī, and vacā,
ground with rice-water, form a paste that removes burning sensations and fever.
(91) One should cook oil for anointment with wine and all the fragrant substances.
Mustard seeds, garlic, asafoetida, the three pungents (trivyoṣa), yellow pigment (rocanā), sweet flag (vacā), bear bile, goat urine, and the fruits of the karañja tree—
these are beneficial as nasal drops (nasya) and collyrium (añjana) for those overcome by fever caused by planetary spirits (graha). 92–93.
This unexcelled medicinal paste is recommended for obstructions caused by the combination of humors (sannipāta), for those bitten by venomous snakes, for hemorrhoids, and for vaginal pain;
it acts through terrifying, exhilarating, and various wonderful sights. 94.
The physician should distract the mind of this patient at the onset of fever. This drink should be administered to the person after they have been treated with oleation and sudation,
consisting of trikaṇṭaka, ajagandhā, nīlinī, and kaṭurohiṇī.
Or one should drink the paste of *kaṭurohiṇī* saturated with cow’s urine;
and the one who knows the procedure should also perform whatever has been prescribed in the treatment.
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Khilas, titled "Instruction on Malignant Fevers.
Now begins the second chapter, titled "Specific Instruction. Hereafter, we shall expound the chapter named "Specific Instruction. 1.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa: Vṛddhaśīvaka questioned the great seer Kaśyapa, who was aged, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, seated comfortably and composed.
O you who are free from fever, you have already explained in detail and with all its variations,
exactly as it is and in its entirety, everything that was to be said regarding irregular fevers from the very beginning; yet, this has been done in a general manner for all fevers.
"You ought to explain in its entirety what remains beyond this.
Thus urged, Prajāpati spoke these words,
which were beneficial, both that which had been stated in brief and that which had not yet been stated.

I shall speak further concerning fevers and those afflicted by fever; listen to that, according to the sequence of the specific introduction regarding the description of the characteristics of their stages.
In a state of instability, even wholesome medicine, when administered, [is ineffective].
It produces no quality at all, but rather leads only to defects.
When applied at that [proper] time, it leads to immortality;
yet through external wind, injury, anger, grief, fear, or depletion, it leads to harm.
When fever has arisen in a person due to exhaustion, possession by malevolent spirits, or the suppression of natural urges, one should not administer emetics;
if administered, it quickly produces a severe fever accompanied by complications.
When fever has arisen from over-saturation (pūraṇa), one should indeed employ [emetics] in moderate measure; however,
when the doshas have increased excessively and are likewise highly agitated,
the physician should quickly induce emesis out of fear of a sannipāta fever.
After he has been treated with emesis and other such procedures in the proper sequence, one should then administer head-purgation (śirovirecana) following the emesis;
in this way, the headache and heaviness of the head are quickly pacified. 13.

Obstruction of the eyes and other senses, as well as loss of appetite, are relieved. Furthermore, in cases of chronic fever (jīrṇajvara) or when these disorders are present, one should administer [the treatment]:
the strong [dose] for those with many doṣas, and the medium [dose] for those with moderate doṣas.
In a fever of slight morbidity, a mild treatment should be administered by the wise physician,
especially when one observes that the specific symptoms of the disease are present in their entirety, along with intense pain and affliction of the body. (16)
One should know that [the condition] then has many defects; otherwise, it has few defects. Likewise, when these [doshas] are of moderate strength, one should discern that the defect is moderate.
Constipation, anorexia, thirst, fainting, breaking pain in the limbs, and headache [occur]. 18.

In fever caused by *āmaja* (undigested toxins), one should recognize the symptoms as: delirious speech, laziness, nausea, drowsiness, burning sensations, fatigue, vertigo, excessive urination, exhaustion, constipation, a sense of nausea, and heaviness of the abdominal cavity. (Verse 19)

When their cessation has mostly occurred and the softening of the fever has arisen, and after eight nights have passed, one should declare the fever to be free from *āma*. The heat becomes pale-red in appearance and attains softness at that very moment. (20–21)
When fever has moved to the external channels, there is lightness within, enthusiasm, digestion of the humors, clarity, and mildness of thirst and other symptoms;
in that state, one should administer massages, medicinal pastes, and affusions.
If one's humors (doṣas), whether undigested or digested, have not been eliminated;
if there is no subsiding of the disease, nor energy, nor lightness; and if there is neither excessive emaciation nor a lack of desire for food—[then the treatment is ineffective]. (23–24)
Or, if the time is not far advanced, the patient is weak due to the [excessive] doshas; conversely, due to the opposite conditions, the embodied being becomes weak due to the [inadequate] medicine.
In the case of a patient weak from doshas, when the doshas have not been ripened by digestive (pācana) measures, [the medicine fails].
One should properly bring about pacification through purgatives for those [diseases] that have matured;
however, for other [acute] diseases, the strengthening of the body's strength is desired when the doshas have suddenly arisen or are newly manifested. (26–27)
Whether against one who is strong or weak, he should never employ astringent medicine or any medicinal treatment if it would compromise his righteousness or reputation.
Just as in autumn, when two great bulls are enraged and locked in combat, [one must avoid harming either].
Just as a weak female elephant at the front of a herd cannot withstand the force of two elephants,
so too, when two powerful men who are stores of faults become agitated, they do not tolerate one another's strength; consequently, embodied beings are tormented by them.
The humors nourish that which is weak; therefore, astringents cause them to become stagnant. Having increased further, they swiftly destroy the life-force of the embodied being.
Or, agitated by astringents, they cause long-lasting affliction.
When the humors (doṣas) have had their force broken by the prescribed method of fasting and other such measures,
medicine administered at the proper time will lead to the pacification of the disorder.
Fasting, sudation, and the three types of digestive gruels (peyā) combined with appetizers (dīpana) [are the treatments].
Rice-gruel is of three kinds, and soup is of three kinds; decoction is of three kinds, as is taste.
Clarified butter for massage, enema, poultice, and immersion baths—this sequence beginning with fasting is prescribed as the remedy that dispels fever. (33–34)
The doshas are digested within seven nights across the seven tissues;

therefore, one should administer a digestive decoction (pācana) during the seventh day. Beyond this, depending on the condition, one should employ either palliative (śamana) or purgative (sraṃsana) measures.
Due to its dullness, stability, and heaviness, fever born of phlegm (kapha) takes a long time to reach maturation;
therefore, its medicinal treatment is prescribed after eight days or even longer, according to the stage of maturation. (36-37)

By consuming the remnants of the digested food, the digestive fire is quickly kindled and blazes forth; through the digestion of the morbid humors (doṣas) and the resulting stimulation of the digestive fire, the subsidence of fever is certain. One should administer meat soups (rasas) processed with fats suitable for that condition.

Thereafter, one should perform pacification (saṃśamana) for the purpose of alleviating any remaining traces of the disease; this involves desiccation (praśoṣaṇa) appropriate to the location, the bodily humors (doṣas), the digestive fire, suitability, and the season, in order to clarify the tissues (dhātus) and nourish the strength. 39–40.
For one suffering from fever, clarified butter that alleviates fever should be administered for three or four days, but not beyond that due to its drying nature;
by this, the feverish person is cooled, just as a blazing house is extinguished with water.
Clarified butter pacifies pitta due to its coldness and vāta due to its unctuousness;
although it possesses qualities similar to those [doshas], it overcomes kapha through processing.
Furthermore, if, despite the administration of pacification, there is still an excess of doshas due to their abundance— 43—

Heaviness and numbness of the colon (pakvāśaya), perspiration, discoloration of the feces and urine, and a lack of desire for food are observed; in such a case, one should administer a purgative to the patient who has undergone oleation and whose body is emaciated. 44.
When colic pain is located in the colon, when there is stiffness in the sides, back, and waist,
and when there is obstruction of flatus, feces, and urine, a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) along with an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) is indicated;
furthermore, when fever has moved to the external channels, massage and similar treatments are recommended.

If a person of a Vāta constitution should suffer from a Vātika fever during a season characterized by Vāta, that fever— being a triple combination— is difficult to cure. The same applies to a person of Pitta or Śleṣman constitution.
Diseases such as fevers that have contrary constitutions are easily curable (48).
Indeed, all diseases consisting of one, two, or three constitutions are generally curable with ease, difficulty, or extreme difficulty respectively (49).
When the humors (doṣas) are excessively aggravated, three types of treatment are determined:
purification (śodhana), pacification (śamana), and both pacification and purification (śamana-śodhana).
Among these, for men who are strong, possess a robust digestive fire, and are virtuous—
For those with diseases of intense onset, purification therapy (*śodhana*) is the beneficial medicine.

For those who are strong, whose morbid humors (*doṣa*) are slight, whose disorders have not excessively increased, and who cannot endure great affliction, palliative therapy (*śamana*) is said to be beneficial. (51–52)
Likewise, for those embodied beings with moderate or weak doshas who are afflicted by powerful diseases, pacification (śamana) and purification (śodhana) are beneficial.
That which expels the doshas upward, downward, or in both directions [is purificatory]. 53.
A substance is known as a *saṃśodhana* (purifier) because it possesses various potencies (*vīrya*) and thus eliminates the humors;

whereas that which does not eliminate the humors either downward or upward, but merely pacifies them, and does not possess intense qualities or potencies, the wise know that substance as a *saṃśamana* (pacifier). 54–55.
That which does not excessively purify but also pacifies the doshas is a substance possessing medium strength; it is both pacifying and purifying (śamana-śodhana).
[The group consisting of] daśamūla, śaṭī, rāsnā, vayasthā, and pañcakolaka—56.
One should prescribe *śārṅgeṣṭā*, *rohiṇī*, *pāṭhā*, *sarala*, *devadāru*, *mustā*, *amṛtā*, *vṛścikālī*, *karkaṭākhyā*, *durālabhā*, *trāyantī*,
and so forth, as pacifying agents.
Vacā, kośātakī, nimba, pippalī, and the fruit of kuṭaja (58);
the two types of alkali with cow’s urine, madana, the salts, triphalā, āragvadha, dantī, nīlinī, saptalā, and trivṛt (59).
Furthermore, other substances such as these that are said to be purifying are:
*kāśmarya*, *āmalaka*, *drākṣā*, *śītapākī*, *parūṣaka*, *madhuka*, *pippalīmūla*, *viḍaṅga*, *hiṅgu*, and *saindhava*. (60)

Pāṭhā, ajagandhā, ativiṣā, pathyā, mustā, kaṭutrika, rohiṇī, and so forth— such substances are pacifying (śamana) or purifying (śodhana). This threefold action has been prescribed for the purpose of subduing the doṣas.
When the *doṣas* are pacified, clarity arises in the *dhātus* and in all the functions of the excretory channels;
therefore, the *doṣas*, *dhātus*, and *malas* remain established in their respective activities. (63)
Health arises for human beings, and ill-health occurs in its opposite.
When one follows the proper diet and conduct as prescribed for suitability, the wise person should maintain the equilibrium of the *dhātus*, the *doṣas*, and other factors. (64–65)
The pacification of those that are provoked, the augmentation of those that have diminished,
and the elimination of those that have increased— this much indeed constitutes medical treatment.
Thus, one should understand its unity, its multiplicity, its various states, and its arising and passing away.
Having carefully considered the relative strength and weakness of the humors and of the patients,
as well as the medicinal substances according to their distinct names and forms,
and their tastes, qualities, potencies, and post-digestive effects exactly as they are.

Having understood the place, the time, the therapeutic means, the dosage, and the disease itself, the physician should administer treatment without negligence. (69) As for those formulations that have been specifically prescribed for their respective treatments:
They should be employed in that very same way; there is no deliberation required regarding them.
For who indeed is capable of knowing the specific action of various refined substances when they have attained a state of unity, as perceived by those who see reality? (70–71)
One should know that some substance has one taste, while by its qualities it is otherwise, by its potency it is otherwise, and in this regard, by its post-digestive transformation (vipāka),
it is yet otherwise; nevertheless, having attained unity in its application, it is not contradictory.
And another quality of inherence arises according to its object;
just as when a fragrance is established separately, another fragrance [arises], so too the fragrance of the constituent parts, which delights the mind, is directly perceived through inherence. 73–74.

Therefore, regarding additions or omissions in the applications of the sages' formulations, one should not be negligent without first understanding the relative strength and weakness of the doshas and the medicines;
rather, the wise physician should consider the patient's age, physical constitution, and the strength of their digestive fire.
In this matter, one should determine the dosage according to whether it is superior, inferior, or middling.
Thus has this distinction regarding fevers been described for the purpose of treatment;
knowing this, one will not be bewildered in various clinical procedures.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa. 78. Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Specific Instructions," within the Khilas;
[now begins] the third chapter, "On the Commencement of Medical Treatment."
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the commencement of medical treatment (Bhaiṣajyopakramaṇīya).
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa:
[he beheld] the Brahmanical sage of immeasurable luster, blazing with Brahmanic glory.
Bhārgava questioned Kaśyapa, the creator of the world:
"Illness is the cause of affliction; medicine is the cause of well-being.
That which is properly applied is nectar, while anything else becomes like poison."
Therefore, O Blessed One, you should explain the application of medicine:
what is the medicine, what is its basis, and how is it taught?
