Furthermore, [explain] the state of being a knower of medicine, as well as the nature of medicine and the nature of healing.
The state of being medicine, the state of being a disease-curer, and likewise the state of being an astringent—
just as these tastes are established in each respective substance through their secondary (guṇa) nature,
so too is the sweet taste observed in the *madhuka* plant through its primary (pradhāna) nature.
Sourness is in the *kapittha* fruit; saltiness is in rock salt (*saindhava*); pungency is in dry ginger (*nāgara*);
7. Bitterness is in *tiktakarohiṇī*; and astringency is in *abhayā*.
Such being the variety of tastes, every [taste] is indeed a combination [of these]. 8.
Why is it designated as "decoction" (kaṣāya), and what is the reason for this?
How many medicinal qualities are there, and how many varieties of it are recorded?
How many times is the medicine administered, and what is the procedure for each occasion?

In what state and at what stage should medicine be administered, or should it not be administered? How should it be drunk, and what must be avoided after drinking it? What is the form of the medicine while it is being digested, and what are the characteristics of its having been digested? (10–11)
Having analyzed the threefold nature of age, how is the dosage prescribed for purgatives and emetics,
as well as that which pacifies the humors (doṣas),
that which is life-sustaining, and that which is known as digestive-stimulant? 12.
O Great Sage, declare all this according to its true nature: what the dosage for purification should be, and what the dosage of oil should be,
starting from the moment of birth up to the maximum of one hundred years.
Thus, to the disciple who was desirous of hearing, the best among speakers explained, according to the proper method, the course of medical treatment:
"This is the cause, this is the symptom, and this is the remedy for it."
Thus far, they declare the knowledge of diseases to be supremely subtle.
The wise say that the knowledge of medicines is even more subtle than this;
I shall explain that to you in its entirety, so listen to me.
Health attends the man who follows a wholesome diet by virtue of its quality; disease quickly overcomes the one who indulges in what is unwholesome.
That disease is said to be of two kinds: physical as well as mental.
Mental afflictions are known there as mental diseases (ādhayaḥ), while physical ailments are known as bodily diseases (vyādhayaḥ).
The characteristic of disease is threefold: curable, incurable, and manageable.
Vāta, pitta, and kapha are the humors (doṣas) that cause bodily diseases.
The pairs of opposites— such as the pleasant and the unpleasant, and so forth— and mental afflictions are the causes of disease;
one should conquer the mental through fortitude, vigor, mindfulness, knowledge, and discernment (21),
and the physical through medicines that rely upon time, application, and destiny.
Furthermore, that disease is of two kinds: exogenous (āgantu) and endogenous (nija). The exogenous afflicts first and subsequently gives rise to the [disturbance of the] humors (doṣas);
the endogenous, however, accumulates first and later, when increased, causes affliction.
Therefore, for exogenous diseases, they observe the same therapeutic procedures as for endogenous ones; having observed the premonitory symptoms of the endogenous types, purification is beneficial.
Purification is of seven kinds, and treatment is dependent upon it. 24.

And that [success] depends upon the four pillars; and a pillar is said to be a medicinal remedy (auṣadha). A remedy consists of the basis of rational application (yukti) and the basis of destiny (daiva).
Rational application is proclaimed as the act of emesis and so forth, while destiny is proclaimed as sacrifice and the like. (25–26)
That which is called *oṣa* is a "burning" [disease]; because it is placed (*dhīyate*) within this [medicine], it is therefore called *oṣadhi*.
It bestows health by removing the *oṣa* (disease), and for that reason, it is an *oṣadhi*, an *oṣadha*.
Physicians know it as *bheṣaja* because it is to be administered according to medical knowledge (*vijñāna*).

Because it is beneficial for one who has conquered disease, they call it "medicine" (bhaiṣajya). Furthermore, for one who is disciplined, it leads to freedom from disease because ailments do not recur;
it is so called either because it scrapes the throat or because it generally attenuates diseases. (28–29)
The term "decoction" (kaṣāya) is applied primarily to all types of medicinal preparations.
Like sound, form, taste, touch, and smell, it is produced from specific substances;
a substance that is neither undercooked nor overcooked is said to possess its full medicinal quality. 30.

It is light in digestion due to its small quantity, pleasing to the heart, and promotes the downward movement of the humors (doṣas). It requires little to drink, possesses great potency, is nourishing, and preserves strength.
Furthermore, it causes little harm even when consumed improperly and produces only mild exhaustion.
Medicine endowed with the qualities of processing is considered fit for a king;
for it is manifoldly divided as prepared or unprepared, cold or hot, liquid or solid, lukewarm, oily or non-oily. (33)
It is divided into exactly seven types according to the differences in disease and age:

powder (cūrṇa), cold infusion (śītakaṣāya), fresh juice (svarasa), pressed extract (abhiṣava), hot decoction (phāṇṭa), paste (kalka), and boiled decoction (kvātha); understand these from me as they truly are.

The powder, finely ground into a subtle dust, is employed in various procedures: for disorders of the *grahaṇī*, for wounds, and for collyriums and the like. A cold decoction (*śītakaṣāya*) is prepared by saturating [the drug] with rainwater.

It removes the burning fever of bile, hemorrhaging, poison, fainting, and intoxication (37). Likewise, a well-prepared *abhiṣava* (fermented decoction) made from the root of *niśā* (turmeric) at dawn, which pacifies disturbances of the digestive fire and strength, is wholesome when combined with its own juice (38).
The fresh juice (svarasa) is known to be obtained by pressing grapes, sugarcane, emblic myrobalan, and other such fruits;
it is employed in palliative formulations for various diseases. When boiled with rainwater until reduced to one-half, [it is likewise used].
Alternatively, when a decoction (kaṣāya) is stirred once with a wooden ladle and a froth (phena) forms, it is called a phāṇṭa.
This [phāṇṭa] is recommended for those with mild doshas and strength, for children, and for minor diseases.
A paste (kalka), ground into a fine powder, should be used for drinking, external application, and electuaries. 40–41.

Because it consists solely of the substance to be drunk, that decoction is difficult to digest and acts slowly; it should be administered when the patient has moderate digestive fire. It is recommended for those endowed with youth and strength, as well as for severe diseases.

Having thus divided it into seven parts, one should examine it tenfold: first in the middle of the food, then below, and repeatedly in the *samudga* [the hollowed palms]; then with the food, between two morsels of food, and finally between each individual mouthful. 43.143-44a.
Previously, medicine taken on an empty stomach does not cause a loss of strength (44).
It quickly destroys the humors located in the stomach and is itself digested.
When the body is constricted by food, vomiting, eructation, pain, and other such symptoms arise (45).
Since they do not occur [in such a person], that food should be given even to one who is weaker;

It quickly pacifies disorders of the abdomen, chest, throat, and head (verse 47). When applied alternately as *sāmudga* (covering both sides), it repeatedly alleviates dyspnea, cough, hiccups, thirst, and vomiting when the humors have moved upward or downward (verse 48).
For those who are weak in constitution, it is beneficial to take food along with medicine in order to protect their strength and digestive fire;
this applies to women, children, the elderly, those who are indulgent, those suffering from chest wounds, those emaciated by disease, and those who are averse to medicine.
When the digestive fire is sluggish due to illness, or when it is excessively sharp, the administration of medicine between two meals is prescribed.
For those whose semen has become utterly diminished, aphrodisiac (vājīkaraṇa) medicine should be administered. A powder that increases digestive fire and strength should be taken with the meal;
between meals, emetics are recommended, and the inhalation of medicinal smoke is also praised.

Medicine taken without food quickly destroys the disease of those who are strong; yet that very same medicine, when taken with food, overcomes the disease of those who are weak. One should divide these ten periods for taking medicine into ten parts.

One should not administer medicine to one whose bodily constituents and senses are depleted, who is tranquilized, exhausted, fatigued, or hungry; nor to one whose stomach has been scorched by medicine, nor to one who is angry, despondent, afflicted by grief, or likewise awake at night. (53–54)

One should not administer medicine to one who has indigestion from improperly digested food, nor to one afflicted by excessive physical labor, nor to one who has just undergone a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) or an oil enema (anuvāsana).
One should also not administer medicine to one who has fasted, or to one who has just undergone purgation.
One should not administer medicine immediately after someone has consumed food, is unconscious, is afflicted by heat, or has just drunk water;
nor should one administer medicine that is contrary to the patient's condition.
One should not administer medicine exclusively to those under twelve years of age;

for in such cases, the medicine administered daily and consistently may lead to harm due to the inequality of their life-force (*prāṇa*), humors (*doṣa*), constituent elements (*dhātu*), strength (*bala*), and vitality (*ojas*). 58.

The strength and lifespan of princes who are extremely delicate are diminished; for those who are excessively aged, enraged, or whose bodily constituents, senses, and vital energy (*ojas*) are depleted,
medicine taken in excess is like a tiny amount of water poured upon the sun.
That which is deficient or excessive in relation to the disease, the bodily humors, the strength, and the digestive fire;

that which has never been desired before; that which is devoid of the aforementioned qualities; that which is incompatible with health or suitability; that which is improperly prepared; and that which is disagreeable to the mind—[these are the causes of harm]. 61.

If, at the conclusion of its digestion, even a subtle disorder is perceived after drinking it, and if there is no alleviation of the disease, that [medicine] should be avoided by the wise. That which destroys the strength of the patient and suppresses the potency of the disease [should also be avoided]. (62–63)

That very thing should be administered to him, because one observes that disease is not eradicated [by other means]; even when the disease has subsided, the medicine of tranquility is [obtained] through peace and generosity. That same [medicine] should be applied in small doses once, twice, or thrice, according to one's strength.

On an auspicious day, at the beginning of the forenoon, having first paid homage to the gods, the twice-born, physicians, and preceptors, the pure physician should, like a reciter of mantras, administer medicine to that virtuous patient who is seated comfortably facing the east and desiring health.
Facing north, he should offer it, saying, "Drink this, indeed!
[He should avoid] excessive walking, standing, lying down, sitting, and talking; as well as anger, grief, sleeping by day, incompatible food, cold, and the heat of the sun. (67)
One who has taken medicine should not indulge in sexual intercourse nor suppress the urge to urinate or defecate (verse 68).
Yawning, aversion to sound, dryness of the mouth, restlessness, fatigue, drowsiness, cramps, and a sense of exhaustion are the signs that the medicine is being digested (verse 69).
The passage of feces, urine, and flatus, lightness of the body,
clarity of eructation, lucidity, and purity of the heart,
as well as hunger and relaxation of the abdomen, are the signs of the proper time for food.
Having first divided age into three types, I shall hereafter explain the *mātrās*.
This age is threefold, known as fetal, infantile, and juvenile;
this is further divided into three types: youth, middle age, and old age.
During the rainy season he should subsist on milk; as long as he drinks milk, his age is considered that of a child, up until he reaches sixteen years.
During the entire period of youth, he should subsist on solid food.
Beyond this, as the elements, the constituent factors, strength, vigor,
and prowess increase for thirty-four years, the youth [reaches maturity];
and as these elements and other qualities become stabilized, the man reaches up to the age of seventy.

The middle state [of life] subsequently becomes old through the gradual depletion of the elements and so forth, in due order; this dull-witted person continues in this state of activity until the end of his lifespan.
Another conceptualization concerns that aged man as being sixteen years of age.
The dosage of medicine should be progressively reduced as [the child] grows;
for one who is a hundred years old or even more, it is said to be like that of milk and rice.
For a newborn, the dose of ghee should be equal to the stone of a jujube fruit.
It may last for five nights, or ten nights beyond that;
it may continue for as long as half a *kola*, or beyond that for twenty nights;
it may last for one *kola*, or for a month, or with an additional two months.
In the third month, ghee measured at two *kolas* is recommended;
in the fourth month, the measure is said to be the size of a dried *āmalaka* fruit;
and in the fifth and sixth months, it is the size of a fresh *āmalaka*.
That same [digestive fire] becomes somewhat more intense during the seventh and eighth months; however,
for a child who subsists on milk and rice, the digestive fire generally becomes irregular due to the mixing of foods, as the child's constitution is predominantly characterized by wind (vāta).
For that person, the dose of oil is prescribed according to the requirement for kindling the fire;
however, for one who does not eat, the digestive fire is generally moderate,
and for such a person, the drinking of a dose of ghee equal to an *āmalaka* fruit is desired.

Having observed that very digestive fire (*agnibala*), one should increase the dose for both the growing infant who subsists on milk and the child who consumes both milk and solid food. One-fourth part of the medicinal fat (*sneha*) should be administered according to the specific disease.
One should feed the child ghee until he is eight months old;
from the eighth month onward, one should administer it ground with water to the infant; thereafter, for the boy who consumes solid food, one should follow the prescriptions of the scriptures.
I shall describe the various measures of medicinal substances according to their divisions—
whether it be a *mucūṭi*, a *prakuñca*, a *prasṛta*, or an *añjali*.
In medical treatment, these must be adjusted according to the size of the patient.
A dose of powder that can be grasped by the tip of the fingers or by the hand is prescribed for digestive stimulants (dīpanīya);
for vitalizers (jīvanīya) and pacifiers (saṃśamana), the dose is double that amount. 89–90.
In the upper part [of the body], however, one should administer half a mātrā; likewise, in the case of purgation, one should provide a decoction (kaṣāya) that subdues vāta, pitta, and kapha.
One should give two prasṛtas combined with sugar and honey.
One should administer one *prasṛta* of the decoction of emetic drugs, and likewise one *prasṛta* of purgative drugs; there is no doubt in this matter.
For vitalizing (*jīvanīya*) and palliative (*saṃśamana*) drugs, the dose is double that amount.
One should administer one *akṣa* measure of the paste of drugs that are digestive stimulants (*dīpanīya*); double that amount for those that are vitalizers (*jīvanīya*) and pacifiers (*saṃśamana*);
and half an *akṣa* for those that are emetics (*chardanīya*) and purgatives (*vairecika*).
I shall now describe the dosage of unctuous substances for emesis and purgation.
When the patient has been well-prepared with emetic drugs for the purpose of emesis, one should administer ghee in the appropriate dose when phlegm (kapha) is to be expelled. 95.
In cases of emesis arising from an excess of phlegm, ghee should be given in measured quantity.
Likewise, in the case of purgation with ghee, half a measure (ardhamātrā) should be administered when pitta is aggravated by purgative drugs. Furthermore, for one of kapha constitution,
a dose that acts both downward and upward is recommended.
Even when prepared with drugs that stimulate digestion, pacify, and sustain life,
if the Vata dosha remains aggravated and localized in the colon (pakvāśaya),
purgation should be administered when it is stuck in the abdominal lumps and the flanks.
One should administer four times the quantity of ghee prepared with pacifying, digestive-stimulating, and digestive-promoting substances;
specifically, one should give four parts of *kumbhasarpis* (pounded ghee) relative to the dose [of the other ingredients], or reduced by one-quarter, one-half, or three-quarters respectively. 99–100.
One should administer ghee to children after carefully considering their age and strength;
likewise for decoctions with pastes, powders, and ghee.
Thus have the various dosages been described; treatment is rooted in dosage.

Therefore, having understood the season, suitability, the body, the digestive tract, age, strength, constitution, the medicine itself, and the increase and decrease of the doshas, one should properly administer the dose as prescribed. (102–103)
One should always be vigilant in the administration of medicines;
for those who dwell in the forests know medicinal herbs by both name and form, as do goat-herds and cowherds, yet they do not understand the properties of their actions. (104)
However, physicians who know yoga, who are experts in the scriptures, and who understand dosage, strength, and the rules of administration, recognize their [the herbs'] qualities and actions;
or, one who knows their action even if ignorant of their appearance is called a knower of their true nature. (105-106)
How much more so for the physician who understands medicinal herbs in every way— knowing that they are like poison, like a weapon, like fire, or like a thunderbolt;
for medicine that is not understood is [deadly], while that which is understood is like nectar.
Even a medicine, if improperly administered, becomes a sharp poison; yet poison, when applied according to the prescribed method, serves as a remedy—
just like a blazing fire or a provoked venomous serpent.
Just as a sharp sword-edge or a rutting elephant [is dangerous], so too is medicine that is not properly prepared and administered by an unskilled physician;
through an error in dosage, it may even take one's life. (110)

Having observed, touched, and questioned [the patient] regarding the performance of what ought and ought not to be done, the physician should then administer those well-known medicines that exist in abundance, according to their taste and potency. 111–112.

Otherwise, one who lacks knowledge of the proper dosage and is excluded from both reason and scripture destroys a patient who is emaciated, afflicted by disease, delicate, and of a *sāttvika* temperament,
by the administration of sharp medicines in an excessive dose. (113)

A physician afflicts a patient who is like one with a great disease, great hunger, great strength, and great power, by means of mild and small medicinal applications; therefore, the strong are to be treated, while the weak are beyond treatment. 114–115.
Having commenced with moderate measures, one should not withdraw from the diet; rather,

for the emaciated patient, one should sustain and increase the digestive fire by providing rest at intervals and employing wholesome foods and medicinal treatments, for it is when the fire is increased that life is maintained.
Just as wind, bile, phlegm, and blood are eternally present within the bodies of men,
so too are all these [qualities] present even in children.
But for those two, that form is indeed very slight;
just as it is very slight for one with a small body, so too the food, drink, and medicine are very slight.
"Having reflected with his intellect in this matter, the physician should administer [the medicine], for dosage is primarily dependent upon the body, the digestive fire, and age.
Thus spoke the venerable Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Introduction to Medicines," in the Khila section.
Now begins the fourth chapter, named "Instruction on Soups" (Yūṣanirdeśīya).
Herein we shall explain the chapter entitled "Instruction on Soups. 1.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa:
"Food accompanied by soups and other condiments is more wholesome for both the healthy and the sick; it especially brings about health."
Therefore, food is the cause of sustenance for all beings;
indeed, there is no other means for living beings to maintain their life-force apart from food. Furthermore, no medicine equal to food is to be found.
A man can indeed be rendered free from disease by food alone;
however, even when provided with medicine, one who abstains from food cannot be cured.
Therefore, physicians declare that food is the great medicine.
Indeed, because of the commonality of its bringing about [results], it is regarded by the wise as being of one kind;
it is of two kinds according to the distinction of potency (*vīrya*); it is of three kinds according to the distinction of the humors (*doṣa*);
and likewise, it is said to be of four kinds according to the distinction of food types such as edibles (*bhakṣya*) and consumables (*bhojya*).
Furthermore, because it consists of the five elements, it is remembered as being fivefold;
that same [element] is again designated as sixfold by virtue of being the substratum of the six tastes;
and it is further divided twelvefold through the twelve modes of discernment.
Furthermore, based on that [body], the fourfold collection of dharma, artha, kama, and mokṣa proceeds through twenty-four variations of time and so forth;
likewise, well-being, daily life, and medical treatment proceed depending upon that very same [body]. (10)
Contentment, nourishment, fortitude, intellect, enthusiasm, manly vigor, strength,
sweetness of voice, vitality, splendor, life-force, intuition, and radiance—
all such qualities of men arise from food alone. 11–12.
Then, a self-possessed person should eat food that is wholesome and moderate in quantity at the proper time, containing the six tastes.

Furthermore, I shall hereafter explain everything regarding what should be eaten, how it should be eaten, and the qualities—both beneficial and detrimental—of those things to be consumed; this constitutes the section on the classification of foods.
In this regard, O Elder Jīvaka, I shall fully describe to you various soups prepared with diverse ingredients that pacify various diseases;
they are appetizing, digestive, aphrodisiac, and they improve the voice, complexion, strength, and the digestive fire.
Soup (yūṣa) primarily induces perspiration and brings about satisfaction, nourishment, and happiness;
due to its oily and warm nature, it pacifies Vāta, and through its oiliness and astringency, it subdues Pitta, while through its slightly warm quality and processing, it subdues Kapha.
The wise say that the root *yūṣ* denotes the acts of liquefying and cooking. (17) Because it liquefies foods when cooked, it is therefore called *yūṣa*.
[It is prepared] with various kinds of ingredients, as well as other substances and non-rice grains. (18)
Soup is said to be prepared as follows:
gruel with rice, lentil soup, *virasikā* soup, pomegranate soup, and likewise two soups made from *citraka* and *āmalaka* are proclaimed. 19.
The two types of pañcakola soup are astringent and digestive stimulants (20).
Furthermore, O Bhārgava, there are grain soup, horse-gram soup, fruit soup,
flower soup, leaf soup, and likewise bark soup (21).
The primary *pallava-yūṣa* (tender-leaf soup) and likewise the *mahā-yūṣa*;
the *rāsnā-yūṣa*, the *mahā-yūṣa* of *aṅgerī* and of radish; as well as the *guḍa-kambalika* made from *punarnavā* and *atibalā*.
There is also a soup of the primary trikaṭu, or with garlic, or with vāstuka.
These twenty-five soups were composed by Kaśyapa;
O Bhārgava, these soups are astringent-sweet, as well as astringent-sour.

All [these] are prescribed as being of two kinds, and all have their origin in liquid substances; they are prepared, unprepared, or both prepared and unprepared within the realms of bile, phlegm, and wind.
Furthermore, due to their application with oleaginous substances, these soups (yūṣas) are traditionally known to be of three types in relation to diseases.
These very same factors are declared to be digestive (pācana), depleting (karṣaṇa), and nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa) [respectively],
due to their cold, hot, or mixed potencies, their reliance on various substances,
and their application through the processing of salt, the three pungents (vyoṣa), fats, cooking, and refinement.
These soups are established for the wise; I shall not describe them again and again.
According to the differentiation of the doshas, these soups are enumerated as seventy-five (28), and likewise fifty due to their being sustaining and so forth, based on the [five] tastes.
Some soups are made with meat broth, while others consist of any liquid condiment;
some are prepared by cooking in fire, while others, such as *rāga*, *khāḍava*, and syrups, are uncooked.
Furthermore, those soups cooked with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) or oil (*taila*) are known as *yamaka-sneha-siddha*.

This soup alone is recommended for those suffering from wind diseases (vātaroga), dryness of the feces (varcaḥ-śoṣa), and injuries; for those with a stimulated digestive fire (dīptāgni) who lack sleep; and for those exhausted by carrying heavy loads, travel, fatigue, sexual intercourse, falling, and similar causes. (31)
Curd, sour gruel, fermented rice-water, and the group of digestive stimulants (dīpana); 32.
The decoction (*niryūha*) is the best among all soups (*yūṣa*), other than that prepared from the five medicinal actions (*pāñcakarmika*).
Decoction, *niryūha*, extract (*ādāna*), and astringent (*kaṣāya*) are synonymous terms. 33.

The embryo, the paste, and the addition are said to be the processing (saṃskāra) of old, dehusked mung beans with digestive water (dīpanāmbu). Because it is thin, it is called mung-bean gruel (mudga-maṇḍa); when thickened slightly, it is mung-bean soup (mudga-yūṣa).
Soup prepared with mung beans, tamarind, and sour gruel is known as *virasikā*.
That same soup, when prepared with pomegranate and sour gruel, is called *rocana*; it is also known as *dāḍimayūṣa* when refined with mung beans and pomegranate.
A decoction of mung beans and āmalaka is called dhātrī-yūṣa;
these five soups are prescribed for the administration of the five-fold purificatory therapies (pāñcakarmika).
Now, I shall describe other soups intended for specific desires according to the observation of diseases.
The decoction of *citraka* prepared with its roots,
trunk, and leaves is known as *citraka-yūṣa*; it cures disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī-doṣa*) and colic,
destroys splenic enlargement, hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, and skin diseases, and overcomes heart disease, phlegm, and wind.
In the same way, the root-soup (mūlakayūṣa) also requires seasoning with śaṭī,
karkaṭakī, bilva, māṣa, pauṣkara, dhātakī, dadhittha, pomegranate fruit, cāṅgerī, and samaṅgā. 40.
This *pañcakola-yūṣa* (soup of the five spices) is considered a supreme astringent. That same soup, when combined with digestive stimulants (*dīpana*) and salts, is also digestive.
[It is prepared] from all types of unhusked grains taken in equal proportions. 41–42.
A grain-soup (*dhānyayūṣa*) prepared without black gram, sesame, flat beans, or mustard is known as *niryūha*; it is considered the best when seasoned with cardamom and pomegranate.
Alternatively, it may be prepared in whey (*dadhimanda*) or buttermilk (*takra*), depending on the specific illness observed. 43.

In diseases of the head, ears, and eyes, in heart disease, in abdominal enlargement, and in colic (ānāha), as well as in loss of appetite and diarrhea, [the soup] with sesame and black gram should be prepared;
however, when made in a decoction of horse gram (kulattha), it is called horse-gram soup (kaulattha-yūṣa). 44–45.
A parching soup made from the fruits of *kapittha*, *bilva*, *badara*, *dvāka*, *dāḍima*, and *cūta* destroys diseases caused by the combination of wind and phlegm (*sannipāta-anila-kapha*).
This fruit-soup made with unripe fruits cures chronic diarrhea (*jīrṇātīsāra*). 46.
One should prepare a medicinal broth (yūṣa) from the flowers of śaṇa, śālmalī, dhātakī, along with padma and saugandhika, as well as from kovidāra and karbudāra;
this is used for menorrhagia, internal hemorrhaging, and burning sensations in the abdomen and eyes.
A soup made from flowers, prepared with oil and sour gruel, along with pomegranate, bilva, śobhāñjana, eraṇḍa, balā, rāsnā, and mango water,
is a leaf-decoction soup; this leaf-soup (patrayūṣa) subdues vāta.
Having decocted the barks of pomegranate, mango, rose-apple, and *cirabilva*, this "bark-soup" (*valkayūṣa*), when mixed with whey (*dadhimanda*), cures diarrhea.
[Likewise, a soup made from] the barks of *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *kālā*, and *palāśa* [is used for the same purpose]. (50–51)

This principal leaf-soup, prepared with the sprouts of lotuses and seasoned with ghee and pomegranate, is beneficial in all diseases of bile (pitta), in miscarriage, and in burning sensations; it is also wholesome for those suffering from bitter-tasting disorders. 52.
Solely with curd and ghee, soups made individually from punarnavā, rāsnā, aṅgerī, and balā are declared to be destroyers of vāta. One should prepare a decoction of rohita and āpota fish in water.
One should boil that decoction again with vinegar,
sour gruel, and buttermilk; when five palas of jaggery have been added along with liquid ingredients and one kudava of seeds,
it is boiled— this is *kāmbalika*, which is parching, or it may be prepared with pungent oil (kaṭutaila).

It pacifies wind diseases, is nourishing, and increases strength; when prepared with sesame oil, it produces sexual pleasure, sleep, and relish. It also stimulates the digestive fire and includes the five roots (pañcamūla) and sweet fruits. 56–57.
As before, all types of grain, cumin, black pepper, kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, kāśmarya, parūṣaka (58),
jujube fruits, horse gram, rāsnā, castor root, and punarnavā.

Two palas each of gokṣura, śigru, and young leaves of palāśa—these one should boil in one droṇa of water until reduced to one-fourth. Then, one should add a prastha each of curd, kāñjika, and vinegar, along with a prastha each of oil and ghee. 59–60.
One hundred young, leafless radish roots,
prepared with the processing of *vyoṣa*, constitute this perfected great broth (*mahā-yūṣa*);
it is highly recommended for all diseases, especially those that are combined.
For those suffering from chronic diarrhea who have undergone digestive fire-stimulating treatments (*atyagni*), are sleepless, and have stiff limbs, jaws, and eyes,
one should administer meat-broth together with a decoction; or alternatively,
for the pacification of chronic diarrhea, a paste of sesame seeds may be prepared.
The garlic soup, which destroys wind (vāta) according to its own specific procedure, has been described;
furthermore, the three types of soups and meat broths have already been shown previously.
The Lord [Viṣṇu], having steamed the radishes in water, squeezed them out while they were still fresh.
Then, having fried it in oil, one should add the ingredients and take it up.
This radish soup (mūlakayūṣa) destroys all diseases;
it is prepared with water and ghee, being neither sour nor watery in flavor.

Fried with oil, it pacifies pitta and subdues vāta; these soups (yūṣa), arising from their own respective sources, have been described both in detail and in brief. (67) Now I shall also describe gruels (yavāgū) prepared with various ingredients.
"Listen, O Vṛddha, to these twenty-one [remedies] that pacify various diseases.
What is the difference between boiled rice, *vilepī*, and *yavāgū*? O Blessed One, I wish to hear this. Thus addressed, Kaśyapa spoke.
Rice-gruel (odana) is described as being pure, well-prepared, thoroughly cooked, drained, and soft;
it is also said to consist of rice grains that are mostly whole and not diminished.
Lack of cooking, lack of moisture, incompleteness, and failure to drain [are its opposites].
Lack of flavor, lack of clarity, and coldness are the opposites of the qualities of boiled rice (odana).
One should prepare gruel (yavāgū) with one-twentieth part liquid along with rice,
or with fifteen parts, or even with ten parts.
A *peyā* (thin gruel) consists of twenty cracked grains of rice, equal in quantity above, in the middle, and below;

it should not be removable by hand, and it is accompanied by solid ingredients (*saparigraha*). A *yavāgū* (thick gruel) is dense, broken apart, cold, and its rice grains have not been fully consumed.
If the gruel (yavāgū) is slimy, clear, or unpalatable, it causes the accumulation of the humors (doṣa). However, gruel prepared with buttermilk or curd, when thickened, seasoned,
and such that it can be lifted by the hand, is prohibited for those engaged in therapeutic procedures.
Warm, thick, and made with crushed grains that are soft,
this *vilepī* should be described as having qualities and defects similar to those of *yavāgū*.
For men who have fasted for a long time, *kṣīrapeyā* (rice gruel prepared with milk) is recommended.

A gruel prepared with digestive (dīpanīya) decoctions is said to alleviate cold-pitta (śītapitta), be nourishing (bṛṃhaṇī), bind the feces (varcabandhanī), destroy colic (śūlaghnī), and stimulate digestion (dīpanī). Furthermore, when prepared with astringent (kaṣāya) decoctions, it is described as being digestive (pācanī), pacifying (pacanī), and binding the feces (varcabandhanī). 77–78.
A gruel prepared with bilva, dadhittha, pomegranate, vyōṣa,
and cāṅgerī is constipating, digestive, and carminative.
In cases of affliction by Vāta, however, [one should use] the five roots (pañcamūla), balā, vṛṣaparṇī, śālaparṇī,
and pomegranate together with the tender fruits of bilva.
A gruel is beneficial in cases of diarrhea caused by pitta and kapha;
they say that water should also be drunk warm in such cases.
This same gruel, when prepared with curd, increases the appetite, and when prepared with sesame seeds, it cures dysentery.
It pacifies severe bloody diarrhea, menorrhagia, and uterine bleeding; furthermore, a gruel made with pomegranate, ativiṣā, and sour substances serves as a digestive for undigested āma. 81.
There may be a gruel made from kaṇṭakārī juice and gokṣura with treacle for urinary diseases (82);
or a gruel prepared with suvarcikā, kṣāra, viḍaṅga, śigru, and pippalīmūla.
A gruel prepared with *takrā* (buttermilk) is effective in destroying worms and is beneficial for abdominal tumors (*gulma*), cough, and disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*).
A gruel made with *mṛdvīkā*, parched grain (*lājā*), honey, *pippalī*, and *sārivā* alleviates thirst.
Poison is quickly destroyed by *somarājī* prepared with boar extract; it is strengthening, while *gavedhukā* is desired for the purpose of emaciation. 84.
A gruel prepared with ghee, rock salt, and balā, boiled in water containing the two sets of five roots (the ten-mūla),
destroys asthma, cough, and phlegm. 85
But a gruel made with leafy vegetables, meat, sesame, and black gram, enriched with ghee, is emollient and laxative;
however, when prepared with the stones of rose-apple and mango, along with wood-apple and bilva, it binds the stool and relieves the two types of acidity. (86)
But that same [dish], prepared with buttermilk, would be suitable for a disease of the *ghṛta* (ghee) type;
however, when combined with oil-cake, it is for a disease of the *taila* (oil) type; and when prepared with *upodika* and curd, it is likewise.
It brings about intoxication and a burning sensation, yet it also leads to clarity. One should prepare those [medicines] for those afflicted by disease using both unroasted and roasted vegetables;
whatever measure is well-known in the world, whether measured by calculation or held on a scale, [should be used].
"In this tantra, there may be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, there is nothing to be said regarding that by me.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Soup," among the Supplements (*khila*).
The fifth chapter, on the commencement of food.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "On the Commencement of Food.
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.

Now, indeed, we shall explain hereafter the specific variations of that twenty-fourfold measure of food previously stated by us in the *Rasavimāna*, beginning with time (*kāla*). For what reason? Because apart from food, we do not perceive any other basis for the life-force (*prāṇa*) of living beings.

When properly utilized, it sustains life, gladdens all the sense organs, nourishes the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), strengthens memory, intellect, and all forms of power and vigor (*ojas*), and produces clarity of complexion; however, when improperly utilized, it causes one to consume it with discomfort.

Therefore, at the proper time, one who desires health, longevity, and strength should eat that which is wholesome to his constitution, in the right quantity, warm, unctuous, and non-contradictory; served in a clean place with pure vessels by a pure attendant; facing eastward, silently and with a focused mind, tasting it; neither too fast nor too slow; neither too hot nor too cold; neither too dry nor too unctuous; neither too much nor too little; neither too liquid nor too solid; neither when hungry nor when satiated; and not consisting of only a single taste. There are verses on this subject: Health consists in the equilibrium of the *doṣas* and the removal of all afflictions.
For that purpose, the sages study the meritorious Ayurveda;
for that same purpose, they employ rejuvenative therapies (rasāyana) according to the prescribed rules; and the attainment of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation is dependent upon it.
Therefore, a wise person who possesses self-mastery should strive for that purpose:
the desire for food, the easy digestion of what has been eaten,
the proper discharge of feces, urine, and wind, and lightness of the body.
Clarity of the sense faculties, pleasant sleep and awakening, the acquisition of strength, complexion, and longevity, cheerfulness, and equilibrium of the digestive fire—
know these to be the signs of health; in the opposite case, the reverse applies.
Health depends on food; food depends on the proper method; the method depends on discretion; and discretion will now be explained.
[This applies] when the humors (doṣas) reside in their own locations and the channels (srotas) are clear.
When such a desire has arisen, the wise know it to be the proper time for food.
For one who eats at the right time, the food tastes delicious; satisfaction and nourishment increase, digestion occurs with ease, and diseases born of exhaustion or indigestion do not arise. (10–11)

They say that suitability (*sātmya*) is propriety; it is a collection of foods that, when consumed continuously, accords with one's own nature by its very essence. One who eats what is suitable lives for a hundred years due to the excellence of suitability.
Nor is it afflicted by the disturbances caused by unwholesome food;
for those who eat light food without excessive fullness, and heavy food in small quantities, what they have eaten is easily digested when consumed in the proper measure. 13–14.

It should not be contrary to one’s health, digestion, or physical activities. For food that is warm tastes well, overcomes phlegm (śleṣman), promotes the downward movement of wind (vāta), and is digested very quickly. (15)
It removes the desire for food, brings lightness to the body, and kindles the digestive fire in embodied beings.
It nourishes the body with unctuousness, invigorates manly vigor, promotes the accumulation of the bodily constituents (dhātus), and bestows strength and a healthy complexion.
One should not eat even well-prepared food that is incompatible, for it quickly destroys the life-force of an embodied being, just as honey and ghee [taken together] would;
one who eats compatible food attains health, longevity, complexion, strength, and happiness. (18)
One who eats contrary [to these rules] incurs the opposite of those very results.
But one who serves from a clean vessel, being himself pure in a clean place,
attains contentment and, by that means, achieves nourishment.
The wise man’s mind does not suffer distress from things undesirable or unpleasant;
therefore, one who desires long life and health should not eat what is undesirable.
A wise man eating while facing the east attains a long life.

In silence, one finds delight for all the senses and harmony for the mind. Therefore, being focused on this alone, attentive to the proper measure, digestion, and method, and remaining silent, one who is healthy should eat his meal.
He who eats by repeatedly tasting flavors with a pure faculty of taste perceives the diversity of tastes and attains their specific distinctions.
For one who eats too hastily would not achieve stability in his nourishment. (24)
He does not know the proper sequence of foods, nor the excellence of their flavors; yet, by eating neither too quickly, he attains all of that in its entirety,
as well as clarity of the senses and the natural downward flow of the bodily winds.
He chills his food, eats very slowly, eats excessively, and eats cold food; yet he does not attain satisfaction.
Due to its coldness, its excess, and its lack of flavor, what has been eaten is digested with great difficulty. (27)

From eating food that is excessively hot, the tongue, throat, lips, heart, and stomach are burned; one does not perceive the taste, and one contracts dreadful diseases such as inflammation of the mouth and eyes, erysipelas, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), vertigo, and fever. (28–29)
For one who eats excessively cold food, colic, weakness of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), nausea, and an increase in phlegm and wind arise, as well as cough and hiccup;
it also causes dryness, constipation, upward movement of gases (udāvarta), and discoloration. (30)
For one who eats excessively unctuous food, there arise lassitude, provocation of Vāyu, suppression of urine, drowsiness, thirst, indigestion, abdominal diseases,
as well as diseases arising from Kapha and fat, and those originating in the throat. (31–32)

Stiffness, cramps, distress, loss of physical activity, and indigestion (visūcikā) are to be known as the disorders arising in living beings from eating too much. Those who eat too little suffer from disorders of excessive digestive fire, emaciation, and vertigo.
From eating excessively liquid food, a person experiences lack of satiety, lightness of body, sleepiness, loss of strength in feces and urine,
nausea, excessive urination, piercing pain in the flanks, catarrh, and diarrhea. (34–35)
Furthermore, eating food that is excessively dry causes it to digest only after becoming obstructed;
having consumed food that has already produced its own rasa, one may cause the depletion of urine and phlegm.
He who, out of delusion, negligence, or greed, eats without any desire for the food, [suffers these consequences].
One suffers from indigestion, aversion to food, vomiting, colic, and abdominal distension (37).
For one who eats when already satiated, there occur thirst, fainting, loss of digestive fire, exhaustion of the limbs, fever, wasting, diarrhea, or dullness of vision (38).
Weakness and lack of firmness arise from eating food of a single taste;

however, for a living being who consumes all tastes, there is no aggravation of the *doṣas*, equilibrium of the *dhātus*, as well as increase in strength and lifespan, along with health and stimulation of the digestive fire. (39)
Therefore, one who desires health should avoid the practice of a single taste.
The man who eats according to this method— taking into account the season, suitability, and other factors—
attains the benefits arising therefrom and is not afflicted by the humors.
A habitual diet of sweet substances produces stability, well-being of the limbs, nourishment of the sense organs, strength, and an increase in phlegm and fat;
however, it causes weakness of the teeth, eyes, and hair, as well as the arising of diseases born of phlegm and bile.
A habitual affinity for sour tastes produces lightness and stimulates the digestive fire (agni).
An affinity for salty tastes causes provocation of the blood, visual impairment (timira), thirst, weakness of semen, premature graying of hair, and loss of strength.
A habitual predilection for pungent tastes causes the wasting of muscle tissue, emaciation, dryness, and the depletion of semen and strength;
it increases pitta and vāta, diminishes moisture, aggravates vāta, impairs vision, and depletes kapha. (45)
The habituation to the bitter taste produces the alleviation of skin disorders (46).
The habituation to the astringent taste causes the depletion of phlegm and bile, the provocation of wind, softness of digestion,
and the pacification of blood (47).
Vitality, luster, strength, complexion, longevity, intellect, fortitude, memory, and delicacy arise in an embodied being who is habituated to ghee;
likewise for one habituated to milk, which is the supreme elixir (rasāyana). 48.
One whose body is firm and well-developed, who is free from fat, and has conquered fatigue; who is strong, accustomed to oil, and free from diseases caused by diminished vāta and kapha;
who possesses keen vision, strength, abundance of śleṣman, firm fortitude, and steady senses—[such a person is fit for oleation]. 49–50.

A man whose diet has become habituated to meat will have a firm physical basis and experience little illness; however, for one to whom unwholesome food has become habitual and wholesome food has become unpalatable, he should gradually adopt the wholesome and gradually abandon the unwholesome. (51)
One who eats food that is first unctuous and sweet, varied in the middle, and ending with dry and liquid substances, does not suffer exhaustion.
Here, two parts of the meal should consist of solid food, and the third part should be water. (52–53)
One should leave a fourth part remaining for the movement of the vital air (vāyu);
then, having rested for a moment and walked slowly a hundred paces,
food eaten while sitting comfortably is digested without distress.
Listening to songs accompanied by the sounds of lutes and flutes, witnessing dramatic performances, and hearing various wonderful stories, he increases his strength after eating;
otherwise, he fails to obtain the proper enjoyment of pleasant sensations.

From the excessive consumption of very unctuous, very dry, or heavy foods; from drinking too much water; from the suppression of flatus, feces, and urine; from staying awake at night, sleeping during the day, and from irregular eating—(57) [these cause the obstruction of the channels].
Furthermore, due to the consumption of unwholesome things, [the food] does not digest properly. (58) When wholesome and unwholesome items are eaten together, that is "equal eating" (*samaśana*).
The physician should recognize "overeating" (*adhyaśana*) as occurring when a subsequent meal is taken before the previous one has been digested. (59)
When hunger and thirst have been stilled and the digestive fire has been pacified by the consumption of food, [the following are unwholesome]:
due to an imbalance of qualities, improper processing, or the violation of the sequence of suitability—such as fish with milk, or radish with jaggery. (60)

Eating when there is indigestion is known as *ajīrṇāśana*; likewise, eating excessively due to overindulgence is to be understood as *aty-aśana*. These two are declared to be the primary causes for the arising of diseases.
In whichever regions whatever dietary habits have been prescribed, they should be taught accordingly in those very places; thus,
these twenty-four variations have been fully described.
"Indeed, physicians should be instructed by a king or one like a king,
or by other wealthy persons, for the sake of accomplishing fame, dharma, and wealth.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Classification of Foods," in the Khila section.
Now begins the sixth chapter, titled "The Classification of Tastes and Humors.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "The Classification of Tastes and Humors."
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa:

"A physician who knows the classification of the tastes and the humors (doṣas) with respect to their provocation and pacification attains the status of a true physician; otherwise, he is the opposite."
Therefore, I shall explain in detail and according to the scriptures the variations of the doshas and the variations based on the tastes (rasas),
specifically regarding diseases such as fever and others according to their distinctions by dosha.
Sixty-two types of conceptualization have been taught; beyond this, however, is the gross enumeration.
[There are] three for each weapon, nine from pairs, making thirteen in total;
and ten and two others are proclaimed according to whether they are inferior, superior, or equal. (5–6)
I shall describe their classification in detail and in due order:
diseases caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha are each to be known as threefold;

those caused by the humors in equilibrium (sama) are three, those caused by combinations of two (dvandva) are six, and those caused by all three in disequilibrium (viṣama) are nine; thus they are traditionally recorded.
There are six [types] with two, one, and three [doṣas] respectively; six with deficient, medium, and excessive [doṣas];
and one with all three doṣas being equal—thus there are thirteen afflictions.
Through these increased doṣas, there are twenty-five permutations.
Thus, when the *doṣas* are diminished, twenty-five diseases are observed:
six from two being diminished and one increased; ten from one being diminished and two being of equal strength; and two other diseases from all three being diminished, excessive, or equal. (10)
Thus, this enumeration of the modifications is sixty-two when categorized by their variations.
There would be ten types [of disorders] caused by wind, bile, and phlegm remaining in their natural state;
however, the variations of the tastes are traditionally held to be six, occurring one by one.

Each preceding pair is joined with the subsequent ones; thus, there are fifteen combinations among the remaining pairs. Among the three tastes, there are three additional permutations for each of the preceding ones. Then, by adding one at a time to the three pairs starting with pungent (kaṭuka), [the combinations are formed].

Likewise, with the pungent and other tastes combined separately with the sweet, sour, and salty, there are eighteen; with two at a time, twenty; and with three at a time, twenty, formed by combining the preceding and succeeding groups, such as the sweet with the *vyoṣa* (the three pungents) and so forth, in their respective order. 14–15.
Those pairs which were joined with the three preceding [tastes] should now be joined with the three subsequent ones;
thus there are nine variations for each, while here there are six otherwise.
When sweet, sour, and salty are each combined individually with the three—bitter and so forth—they form [these combinations].
Likewise, pungent and the others—these fifteen [tastes] were mentioned by the ancients.
There are six groups of four and five [tastes], arising from the omission of one at a time;
with six [tastes] remaining, there is one [group]. This arrangement of them results in sixty-three varieties.
There are fifty-seven combinations; however, the six tastes, being uncombined, are joined with the three *doṣas* in sixty-six ways according to their association:
sometimes one, sometimes two, and sometimes all three, due to the increase of the *doṣas*. (19)
One should administer treatment according to the sequence of mild, moderate, and excessive doshas with mild, moderate, and strong rasas respectively;
likewise, for those that are doubly powerful, singly powerful, or balanced, one should use corresponding [rasas]. 20–21.
One should perform the depletion of those who are increased, the maintenance of those who are moderate,
and the augmentation of those who are diminished, according to the measure of the increase of the *rasas*.
In this matter, a specific adjustment should be made as appropriate through the reversal of the *rasas*.

Thus, by means of these sixty-two tastes, there is an equilibrium for the sixty-two defects; through those very groups of six, one [person] is employed in the regimen for health. A wise person should apply the pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes in their proper sequence.

In a disease born of phlegm (kapha), one should administer medicine according to the principles of yoga; pungent (kaṭuka) substances applied first quickly destroy the sliminess and heaviness of the phlegm, and therefore bitter (tikta) substances should follow immediately after.
It diminishes the sweetness of the mouth and also dries up the phlegm (kapha).
Astringent (kaṣāya) taste collects [impurities] and draws away the oiliness (sneha) from the mouth.
Bitter, sweet, and astringent tastes are beneficial in succession for the Pitta disorder.

Because bile (pitta) is of an acidic lineage, a bitter taste administered first quickly digests it; once it is digested, the sweet taste then pacifies it through its coldness, heaviness, unctuousness, and sweetness. (28)
A decoction (kaṣāya) is administered to counteract that liquidity;
because of its dryness and desiccating nature, it dries up the fiery element (taijasa).
In a disorder of Vāta, salt is first administered through a combination [of substances].
By its moistening nature, it overcomes constipation;
by its heat, it destroys coldness, and by its heaviness, it also overcomes lightness.
In the same way, the sour taste, when subsequently administered in that very [condition], [exerts these effects].
Having opened the channels congealed by sharpness,
the sweet taste, when administered after the sour taste, quickly brings the wind back to its natural course, as it is unctuous and warm, even though that wind has moved onto a wrong path. (32–33)
It counteracts the lightness, clarity, and dryness of the wind (vāyu) through its heaviness, sliminess, and unctuousness, according to its strength.
Thus have been described the applications of the tastes for all diseases.
Generally, the formulations mentioned for diseases such as fever and others are observed to consist primarily of pungent,

bitter, and astringent tastes, while being sweet in terms of their post-digestive effect (vipāka); this applies to vāta-type fever, starting with gruels, vegetable soups, meat broths, and so forth, in the order previously described.
The two tastes, salty and sour, are employed when combined with processing agents (saṃskāra).
Thereafter, the sweet group beginning with vidārigandhādi is administered in pitta-type fever, just as the bitter group beginning with śāṅgiṣṭhādi is administered [in kapha-type fever]. 36–37.

In fever born of *kapha*, the *madhura* (sweet) group beginning with *sārivā*, the *kaṣāya* (astringent) group beginning with *abhayā*, the *pippalyādi* (long pepper) group as previously described, and the *kaṭuka* (pungent) group [are indicated]; likewise, the *āragvadhādi* (cassia fistula) group which is bitter (*tikta*), and the *tri-phalā* group which is astringent (*kaṣāya*). (38)
In all cases, the wise physician should employ the tastes as specified by this method—
according to the disorder, according to suitability, and as desired—
by means of various additions and subtractions of substances in different ways.
Or just as a lute-player, skilled in the tones of the strings,
would properly employ the notes by both raising and lowering them (41),
perceiving them through various variations, he demonstrates the musical scales and melodies.
One who knows the reality of the circle of sounds through its many extensive conceptual elaborations;
likewise, one who knows the reality of the scriptures, is skilled in yoga, and possesses right practice;
one who knows the strength and weakness in a disease, knows its nature, and is endowed with yoga—42–43.
An expert in the scriptures, increasing and decreasing the applications according to their potency—
whether by means of substances that are purely cold in potency, or likewise hot in potency,
or by substances that are a mixture of both cold and hot— should employ these formulations.
One should employ [the practice] in its entirety, according to rule and in proper sequence (45).
One should apply the yogas in many ways— through combinations and alternatives, and through the accumulation of various aesthetic sentiments— just as one performs dance in accordance with song (46).
Having considered the relative strength and weakness of what has been stated both collectively and individually,
I shall hereafter explain in detail those sixty-two varieties of defects, having first summarized the ten locations.
Of these, three are each single [units], and those which are increased are three equal [sets].
With the equals there is one; thus these are seven. Through the increase and decrease [of these], they become fourteen;
through the increase of their positions, they become one hundred and forty-four.
Having set these aside, the remaining thirty, ten, and eight undergo division—
into hundreds and thousands— due to their immeasurability;
and among the six unequal pairs, the wise man [should choose] one or another.
One should increase from its own position until it reaches the eighth position.
These [positions] become twenty-four by being counted one by one and two by two;
and through the process of decrease, one by one, there are also twenty-nine varieties.
Thus, these fifty-three [deities] have been shown by means of a single *dvandva* (pairing);
this same logic would undoubtedly apply to the remaining *dvandvas*.
In this way, there are exactly three hundred and eighteen of them.
One should likewise specify those with two strengths and one strength.
Defects that are inferior, middling, or superior remain established in their respective places;
they move from their own place to the seventh place one by one.
Two and two, and all of them together, there are six groups of seven; one should decrease these in sequence from below as follows: 56.
Thus, they declare that there are eighty-five varieties of those [divisions].
This very same classification applies to the remaining [elements] according to their divisions.
There are seven hundred and sixty-two varieties;
thus, there are one thousand three hundred varieties as taught by the elders.
When the [three] humors are diminished in ninety-eight ways, there are exactly that many [types of fever].
When two are diminished and one is increased, there would be three hundred and six;
and as many indeed are the varieties when one is diminished and two are increased in strength.
With those that are diminished, increased, or equal, there are six, six, and six hundred [varieties] respectively;
here, the sequence of division is the same as that which was demonstrated for the duals.
Fourteen types, along with their subdivisions, are specified separately for those two.
Together with those [factors], one should analyze all these in their entirety;
there are four thousand one hundred and sixty such divisions of fevers and other ailments as they have been declared according to the scriptures.
Now, from the perspective of the action of the fourfold classification of combinations (yoga-vibhāga-gati),
a physician should know that there are one thousand and nine types of *sannipāta* (complex disorders).
Hereafter, the detailed classification of the *rasas* (tastes) will be explained.
Just as there are six locations for the increase of the humors (doṣas) according to their respective order,
so too, it is the established conclusion that one should establish six locations for the tastes (rasas).
That same action [applies] to all [tastes] from two onwards, except in the case of their depletion (kṣaya).
Thus, for the groups of two, there are one hundred and sixty-six;
for the groups of three, one should specify six hundred and twenty;
and for the groups of four, one should state one thousand and sixty-five.
There are eight hundred and one hundred and six of the fivefold [combinations];
two hundred and one hundred and eleven of the sixfold;
this is the permutation of the combined [factors], while the six single [factors] are with their own permutations.
When each of the various distinct tastes is combined together,

there are seventy-three of them; furthermore, these variations of taste and humor (rasa-doṣa) amount to exactly three thousand, beyond which they cannot be further defined due to their extreme subtlety.
"I shall not speak [further], O illustrious one, nor out of a deficiency of intellect.

(70) Beyond this, we shall now teach the varieties of *rasas* in detail. They are as follows: sweet (*madhura*), sour (*amla*), salty (*lavaṇa*), pungent (*kaṭuka*), bitter (*tikta*), and astringent (*kaṣāya*)—these are the six *rasas*. Of these *rasas*, there are now sixty-three permutations. Among them, there are six by taking each one individually; namely: sweet alone, sour alone, salty alone, pungent alone, bitter alone, and astringent alone. (71)

Each preceding [taste] combined with those following it forms pairs; these amount to fifteen. Among them, the sweet (*madhura*) is joined with the five beginning with sour (*amla*): namely, sweet-sour, sweet-salty, sweet-pungent, sweet-bitter, and sweet-astringent. Sour is joined with the four beginning with salty: namely, sour-salty, sour-pungent, sour-bitter, and sour-astringent.

Salt [tastes] with the three beginning with pungent, namely: salty-pungent, salty-bitter, and salty-astringent. Pungent [tastes] with two, namely bitter and astringent, as follows: pungent-bitter and pungent-astringent. Bitter with astringent, as follows: bitter-astringent. These are exactly fifteen.

These pairs constitute fifteen variations. Through combination with sweet (*madhura*), there are five; through combination with sour (*amla*), four; through combination with salty (*lavaṇa*), three; through combination with pungent (*kaṭu*), two; and through combination with bitter (*tikta*), one. Among the first three tastes—sweet, sour, and salty—three additional combinations are produced: sweet-sour, sweet-salty, and sour-salty.

Each one of these three pairs is to be combined with the other three tastes—pungent (kaṭu), bitter (tikta), and astringent (kaṣāya)—thereby forming triads. They are as follows: sweet-sour-pungent, sweet-sour-bitter, sweet-sour-astringent; sweet-salty-pungent, sweet-salty-bitter, sweet-salty-astringent; sour-salty-pungent, sour-salty-bitter, and sour-salty-astringent.

Regarding the three remaining tastes—pungent (kaṭu), bitter (tikta), and astringent (kaṣāya)—three combinations of two are produced, namely: pungent-bitter, pungent-astringent, and bitter-astringent. Each one of these three pairs of two should be joined with each of the other three tastes—sweet (madhura), sour (amla), and salty (lavaṇa); thus, combinations of three are produced.

Namely: pungent-bitter-sweet; pungent-bitter-sour; pungent-bitter-salty; pungent-astringent-sweet; pungent-astringent-sour; pungent-astringent-salty; bitter-astringent-sweet; bitter-astringent-sour; bitter-astringent-salty. Regarding the first and the last groups: there are three in the first group—the triad of sweet, sour, and salty—and three in the last group—the triad of pungent, bitter, and astringent. These constitute twenty triads as stated by the first [sūtra]; nine [triads] by the second, and two by the third. (73)

Among the three preceding tastes—sweet, sour, and salty—the three [qualities] previously mentioned should each be combined with the other three tastes—pungent, bitter, and astringent—by means of the previously mentioned triads and dyads, both individually and collectively; thereby, sets of four are produced.

Namely: sweet-sour-bitter; sweet-sour-pungent-astringent; sweet-sour-bitter-astringent; sweet-salty-pungent-bitter; sweet-salty-pungent-astringent; sweet-salty-bitter-astringent; sour-salty-pungent-bitter; sour-salty-pungent-astringent; sour-salty-bitter-astringent. In these, the preceding [tastes]—sweet, sour, and salty—are combined one by one with the succeeding [tastes]—pungent, bitter, and astringent.

Namely: sweet-sour-salty-pungent; sweet-sour-salty-bitter; sweet-sour-salty-astringent. The latter three—pungent, bitter, and astringent—are each combined with the preceding [three], namely sweet, sour, and salty; from this, fourfold combinations (*catuṣka*) are produced. Namely: pungent-bitter-astringent-sweet; pungent-bitter-astringent-sour; pungent-bitter-astringent-salty. These fourfold combinations are fifteen: nine as stated in the first sūtra, three as stated in the second sūtra, and three as stated in the third sūtra; thus, these fourfold combinations total fifteen. (74)

There are six groups of five. By removing one at a time from the six tastes—sweet (*madhura*), sour (*amla*), salty (*lavaṇa*), pungent (*kaṭu*), bitter (*tikta*), and astringent (*kaṣāya*)—six groups of five are produced. They are as follows: sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent; sweet, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent; sweet, sour, pungent, bitter, and astringent; sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and astringent; sweet, sour, salty, pungent, and astringent; and sweet, sour, salty, pungent, and bitter. These are the six groups of five.

One [type] consists of the six [tastes]: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent; namely, sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent. Thus, these tastes are divided into sixty-three types: fifty-seven are combined and six are uncombined. So said the Blessed Kaśyapa. (75–76)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Khilasthāna, titled "The Classification of Tastes and Defects.
Now begins the seventh chapter, titled "The Specifics of Purification.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on the specifics of purification.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa:
"Regarding the two perfections known as purification, whatever specific details have not yet been mentioned concerning the upward and downward [movements], all of that I shall proclaim hereafter."
The accumulation, provocation, and pacification of pitta occur during the rainy season and so forth;
those of kapha during the winter and so forth; and those of vāyu during the three seasons beginning with summer.
The three seasons known as the rainy, autumnal, and winter constitute the period of emission (visarga).
The dewy season (śiśira), spring (vasanta), and summer (grīṣma) are designated as the period of withdrawal (ādāna).
During the interval between withdrawal and emission (visarga), the strength of embodied beings is middling;
however, at the very beginning and end [of the cycle], there is weakness, while at the end of the first and the beginning of the last, the strength is supreme.
In the winter, even when accumulated by unctuous and cold waters as well as medicinal herbs,
the phlegm (kapha) does not become aggravated here because of the cold;
it becomes aggravated when the cold has passed and it is heated by the rays of the sun.
Therefore, in that case, purification should be performed following emesis.
Even though the essence of the bodily fluids has been depleted during summer due to the excessive heat of the season,
the wind (vāyu) does not become aggravated here because of the nature of the time.
Due to the obstruction of the sun by clouds, the digestive fire becomes aggravated at the onset of the rainy season;
in that condition, therapeutic measures following the administration of enemas (basti) are especially recommended.
This is because both water and medicinal herbs undergo an acid transformation during the rains.
Even though that pitta has accumulated here, it does not become aggravated due to the coolness of the rainy season;
however, when scorched by the rays of the sun during the autumn season, it becomes aggravated.
Furthermore, after administering a purgative, a cleansing therapy (viśodhana) should be performed here.
When there is an aggravation of the *doṣas*, treatment must be administered immediately at all times;
for a *doṣa* impelled by its cause does not wait for any period of time. Due to the suitability of the season, the aggravation of the *doṣas* is not as severe [at other times].
Therefore, since it is produced by causes, one should treat this [condition] quickly with emetics, purgatives, non-unctuous enemas, and unctuous enemas;
thus one attains health and is liberated from diseases. 14–15.
From the aggravation of kapha and pitta arise obesity, lack of luster, itching of the ears, eruptions, boils, and pimples;
as well as loss of sleep, restlessness, drowsiness, nausea, fatigue, debility, foul odor, laziness, a sense of sinking, and exhaustion. (16)
Aversion to food, indigestion, impotence, and affliction of the intellect; even for one who is satisfied by nourishing foods, there occurs a decline of strength and complexion,
as well as the sight of bad dreams— these are the signs of excessive morbidity.

The physician should administer purification (*saṃśodhana*) to one who is strong and has a stable body, while for one whose dosas and strength are moderate, he should administer pacification (*saṃśamana*). Furthermore, even for one with weak dosas and strength, drying therapy (*viśoṣaṇa*) should be applied at the appropriate time.
Then, for one who is fit for purification and has been prepared with oleation and sudation, one should duly administer emesis or purgation.
Oil, when drunk, destroys Vāta and produces softness of the body.

Sweat destroys the attachment of impurities in an oily-bodied person; it liquefies the subtle, fluid morbid humors (doṣas) lodged within the channels. When properly administered, purificatory therapy quickly removes them.

Purgation should be performed with substances that are purified by mantras, non-repulsive, and pleasant to the heart; emesis, however, should be performed with repulsive substances, as it attains its proper effect through such means.
One who has been oleated should vomit on the third day and drink a laxative on the fourth day.

In the event of a morbid transformation (vikāra), that [regimen] is appropriate; however, for one in a healthy state (svasthavṛtti), a person desiring to undergo emesis should eat food that increases kapha tomorrow morning. For purgation, the diet should consist mostly of liquids, unctuous, hot, clear, and light.
Likewise, due to the aggravation of phlegm (kapha) and the lightness of the feces, the movement of the humors (doṣas) both upwards and downwards occurs without effort;
this applies in cases of toxic erysipelas (viṣavisarpa), edema (śvayathu), gout (vātarakta), and jaundice (halīmaka). (26–27)
In cases of jaundice and anemia, one should administer purgation that is not excessively unctuous;
nor should one give a purgative combined with unctuous substances to a person whose body is already too unctuous.
For one who is unctuous, a dry (non-unctuous) purgative is appropriate, while for one who is dry, an unctuous purgative may be administered at will.
What man can endure the slipping of a smooth load from a chariot? Just as water is poured out from a jar of ghee with ease,
so too is a bodily humor expelled from an oiled body by means of purgatives.

Sudation moistens the body, just as moistened and softened fuel [is prepared]; thereafter, the medicine removes the humors from the person whose body has been sweated. For just as a soiled garment is loosened by alkaline salt and then washed with water, [so too are the humors removed].
In the same way, having provoked the humors according to the prescribed rules by force, one should cleanse them with purificatory therapies.
Once vomited, one should prescribe fasting; after fasting, one should give light food.
For that person who has undergone both emesis and purgation, the sequential regimen beginning with thin gruel (peyā) is recommended.
By that [means], the fire increases subtly, just as from fuel and friction;
once the fire has arisen and impurity has been produced in the body, it becomes stainless.
Like a dye applied to a cloth, the subsequent procedure attains perfection.
Whatever affliction may arise here through improper application or the like,
its successful resolution— whether by means of a concise or detailed method— is declared to be "success" (siddhi).
Following that, the various options for the examination of food shall be fully explained.

In all cases, three types of gruel (peyā) are prescribed for the initial stages of complications and so forth; these are prepared according to various options such as uncooked and the like. Following that, vegetable broth (yūṣa) is given, and after that, meat broth (rasa). The first [type of gruel] is salt-free and prepared with digestive-stimulating (dīpanīya) water.

The second variety, *kṣudrā*, should contain a small amount of salt and spices; likewise, the third is prepared with a measure of fat. Soup (*yūṣa*) that has neither distinct salt nor fat is considered *akṛtaka* (unprepared). 38–39.
The prepared broth (kṛtayūṣa) should be well-seasoned with a distinct amount of fat, sourness, and salt; it may be either prepared or unprepared with mild sourness, acidity, salt, and fats.
In this very manner, one should understand the sequence beginning with the liquid (rasa), such as the peya and others.
Taken once, it is the least; twice, the middling; thrice, it is the best and deserves purification.

One desiring health should consume this preparation—which consists of a mixture of gruels and so forth and serves as a universal cleanser—until health is restored, at which point one should return to a natural diet.
Having excluded incompatible foods and whatever may be unwholesome for the teacher,
hereafter I shall explain the purpose regarding the dosage and other factors;
the maximum dose of an emetic decoction is four añjalis.

In purgation, the dose is medium at three *mātrās* for those with short [stature], and two half-[mātrās] for those with medium [stature]. Having considered each individual and the relative strength or weakness of the *doṣas*, a decoction of *madana* fruits combined with long pepper (*pippalī*) and mustard seeds [is prescribed]. 44–45.

Alternatively, that same [mixture] may be used with *grahaghnī*; or it should be administered for the purpose of emesis combined with the pastes of *paṭola*, *ariṣṭa*, *vatsaka*, *priyaṅgu*, and *madhuka*, mixed with honey and rock salt (*saindhava*). 46.
However, when [the food] is undigested, it is not beneficial; in this case, plain salted warm water alone is indicated.
For that [water], having thoroughly agitated everything, quickly expels it through the mouth.
If, despite this, the undigested matter does not cease its constipation, then [further measures] should follow.
One should extract it with vacā, jagandhā, madana, and pippalī, or with other medicinal pastes made from loathsome and nauseating substances,
or by means of pleasant methods such as tickling the throat with the fingers, lotus stalks, and the like. 49.

Even by means of intense pressure on his sides, abdomen, and back, one should wait for a moment after he has vomited; when a burning sensation (vidāha) precedes and perspiration occurs all over his body, [then the procedure may continue]. 50–51.

The best of physicians should recognize that the dosha is flowing out by means of horripilation; likewise, he should know it has moved from its locations immediately upon the appearance of horripilation. Furthermore, one should indicate that it has reached the visceral cavity (koṣṭha) by means of distension and cramps.
When nausea and salivation appear, one should induce vomiting;
having drunk hot water mixed with salt repeatedly until it reaches the throat, this should be done until there are eight, six, or even four bouts [of vomiting]. (53–54)
Or until the appearance of bile, or even until the cessation of the disorder; or measured by weight, one, one and a half, or two *prasthas*—
whatever exceeds that when drunk is defective, and it should be expelled.

When the water in the receiving vessel is seen to be free from the smell of raw flesh, free from vomiting, and even when drunk, not slimy (56), and when it is clear and free from impurities after being vomited,
and there is lightness of the abdomen, chest, throat, and head, along with the alleviation of disease (57).

One should point out these as the signs of one whose morbid humors have been immediately expelled: lassitude, emaciation, lack of excessive enthusiasm, and a sense of clarity within. Then, for that person who has undergone sudation with oils, [the head] should be treated. 58. Upon the head of that embodied being who has been fomented with oils...

One should eliminate any remaining morbid humors (doṣas) by means of nasal medication (nasya) or the inhalation of medicated smoke (dhūmapāna). Then, according to the degree of purification, one should treat the patient with a combination therapy; the purgative (virecana) should consist of *harītakī* or *grahaghnī*, as prescribed in the Kalpa section.
Pathyā combined with pippalī and rock salt, or trivṛtā combined with pathyā;
or the fruit of āragvadha boiled with milk or meat broth;
or triphalā combined with trivṛtā, ghee, vyōṣa, and rock salt.
Likewise, Gandharva oil is an excellent unctuous purgative (snehavirecana),
prepared with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla), or with the meat-broth of wild animals (jāṅgala),
or with a decoction of grapes, or with water boiled with digestive stimulants (dīpana). 62–63.
Alternatively, there may be Trivṛt combined with Drākṣā and Abhayā mixed with cow’s urine; or it may be Trivṛt together with Drākṣā; or it may be Trivṛt with Aṣṭakā (64);
or Pathyā, Trijātaka, Vyūṣa, Viḍaṅga, Āmalaka, and Ghana.
In this formulation, the powders are equal in measure, sugar is six times as much, and Trivṛt is eight times as much.
This powder destroys fever, exhaustion, dyspnea, cough, anemia, and consumption;
it also cures worms, poison, hemorrhoids, and dysuria in living beings.
In the mild [purgative], there are ten urges; in the medium, fifteen; and in the strong, thirty.
