These urges, measured at two, three, and four *prasthas* respectively, should be accompanied by feces, mucus, and phlegm mixed with wind, in that order. (67)

In emesis, [the doshas] end with pitta; when combined with kapha, they are called *kaṣāya-kapha*. In proper administration, there is excessive discharge characterized by a predominance of blood (*śoṇita-uttara*); in inadequate administration, there is no discharge at all, or it may be contrary or very slight.
The failure of treatment (vibhraṃśa) is the cessation of the therapeutic action; it occurs when only the medicinal drug has been eliminated.
In a disorder arising from complications of excessive administration (atiyoga), one should administer ghee internally;
or, in that case, oil cooked with the Madhuka and other drugs should be used as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
One who has vomited or purged poorly, whose body is unctuous and endowed with strength,

who has abundant morbid humors (doṣas) and a strong digestive fire, should be given a purgative on the following day; however, one who is weak should be purified again after being gradually and repeatedly treated with oleation and sudation.

However, one should never induce emesis in those who vomit with difficulty or have a harsh digestive tract; rather, one should pacify their humors (doṣas) through palliative treatments or enemas (basti).
This applies especially when the substance is unpleasant, extremely foul-smelling, or when there is indigestion (ajīrṇa) or an excessive amount [of material].
If the medicine taken in the proper manner goes upward because it is obstructed by phlegm (kapha), one should administer emesis or lightening therapy (laṅghana) to that patient;
or, once the body has been thoroughly oleated or the stomach (āmāśaya) has been purified, one should administer purgation. (74–75)

If emesis occurs after a downward movement of the wind (māruta), purification is prescribed for him merely by means of a combined therapy (saṃsarga). For one who is weak and has few morbid humors (doṣas), a mild purification is beneficial. (76)
When the humors (doṣas) are provoked, one descends gradually, little by little;

in that case, drinking warm water is the best means for inducing downward movement. Alternatively, if the humor becomes associated with belching and moves neither upward nor downward, [this treatment should be applied]. 77–78.
If the medicine causes pain for the person, one should apply sudation (sveda) in that case;
if the medicine has been administered in an excessive dose and causes eructation, one should quickly remove it.
If there is excessive discharge after the medicine has been digested, one should treat the patient with astringent (stambhana) measures.
For an embodied being with a stimulated digestive fire, a cruel bowel, and an abundance of morbid humors (doṣas),

who suffers from upward-moving wind (udāvarta), the physician should first eliminate the feces using fruit-enemas (phala-varti); then, once the body has been well-anointed and fomented, he should administer a purgative.

When it is unattached, it proceeds quickly and easily with great force; it does not cause affliction nor excessive exhaustion, yet it purifies the humors (doṣas), possesses excellent qualities in its result, is administered in the proper measure, and is well-prepared. 82.

The yellow [rasa], when consumed with one-pointed mind, brings about perfect purification. (83) In those men who have a stimulated digestive fire, who are constant in their duties, and who eat dry food, the humors (doṣas) always go to destruction through the actions of wind and fire. (84)
They tolerate even the defects of incompatible food, overeating, and indigestion;
in their state of health, they are neither to be purified nor [excessively] protected from disorders of Vāta.
Having recognized them as such, the physician ought to perform purification only when necessary.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Specifics of Purification," in the Khilas;
now begins the eighth chapter, titled "The Specifics of Enemas."
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the specific classifications of enemas (basti).
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa:
There is no medical treatment that brings greater comfort to the body than the administration of an enema.
Regarding diseases located in the branches, the trunk, or those affecting all or half the body,
no cause other than Vāta is found for their arising;
likewise for Kapha, Pitta, the impurities, and the Rasa.
In its dispersal or its contraction, the wind alone is the cause here;
and when it has increased, there is nothing that can conquer it except the bladder-like [remedy].
Half of medical treatment, or even all of it, consists of the treatment for wind.
Karma, Kāla, and Yoga—these are the three designations in their respective order. I shall explain them according to etymology, definition, number, faults, and alternatives;
[that which arises] from the arms and so forth is designated as Karma.
When the strength [of the wind] has become excessively aggravated, it should be treated according to the prescribed rule;

for that time, when it is associated with moderate strength, should be determined by calculating half of that [period]. When the wind is conjoined with bile, it must be administered by one who possesses discernment.

Because of the small quantity of oil enemas, that application should be administered for its lightness; it is indicated when vāta is associated with kapha and is not excessively strong. There are twenty-four oil enemas (anuvāsanas) and six non-unctuous enemas (nirūhas) for this procedure.
In this [regimen], there are twelve non-unctuous enemas (anuvāsanas) at the appropriate time and three evacuative enemas (nirūhas).
Indeed, in the [alternative] formulation, there should be three evacuative enemas and five non-unctuous enemas;
thus, the total number of enemas for the Karma-ādi group is shown to be fifty-three.
There are four unctuous enemas at the beginning of the five [non-unctuous enemas], and likewise four at the end;
three are placed between every six non-unctuous enemas. Three unctuous enemas are administered at the beginning, at the end, and in between the intervals.
In the course of the treatment, three enemas (nirūha) should be administered with an interval between each, and two at the end;
such is the prescribed instruction regarding the division [of the number]. Now hear the alternative methods:
seven, five, or three [enemas] at the beginning are forbidden in the case of Vāta.

Sometimes, observing various conditions based on the strength of the doshas and the time, the physician should increase or decrease these very two— the enemas or the medicinal substances— of pitta and kapha as they are least predominant. (16)
One should apply enhancement in yoga and reduction in the administration of karma;
having observed both of these, as well as the strength or weakness of the doshas, [one should act].
In the case of vāta, a nirūha enema that is balanced, unctuous, and warm, along with the drinking of oil, is indicated. 17–18.
In cases of pitta, the six parts [of the enema] are unctuous, containing milk, sweet, and cold;
three parts contain urine, being sharp and hot for kapha; and eight parts contain oil for all [doshas]. Administered once, it expels the vāta located in the āśaya (receptacle).
If [the blood] is mixed with bile or phlegm, it should be administered two or three times; beyond that, it is not recommended.

In this case, the regimen of consuming meat broth, milk, and vegetable soup is recommended in sequence; alternatively, one should act according to the patient's strength, the time, the digestive fire, the region, the constitution, and suitability.
These methods for the application of enemas have been described, ending with the consideration of their defects;
this is another formulation known as the "Fourfold Auspicious" (Caturbhadra).
There are four enemas at the beginning and likewise four at the end.
The administration of these two [medicines] in between is this faultless procedure (kalpa).

When performed two or three times according to the requirements of the case, it brings comfort to one who is afflicted by fever and other ailments, and whose complexion, strength, and vitality are diminished. (23–24)
In the stages of *jāta*, *anuvāsana*, and *avasthā*, enemas that increase strength, virility, and digestive fire should be administered in odd numbers;
they should never be given in even numbers. Diseases are destroyed by odd-numbered enemas through the principle of odd overcoming odd. (25)

In the case of a kaphaja [fever], there is one or three [days]; in a paittika [fever], five or seven; and in a vātaja [fever], nine or eleven—or whatever [number] it attains when balanced. Thus, for the sake of subtle and manifold meanings, it has been stated both in detail and in brief. (26–27)
Having understood this, one should apply the treatment as I shall describe hereafter:
those whose impurities have become deep-seated and accumulated gradually, who are aggravated and characterized predominantly by Vāta, are especially curable by means of enemas (basti). 28.
For one who is well-nourished and patient, emesis is the ultimate remedy.
Therefore, it should be administered during the intermediate period; likewise, for one who is inferior, it should be even more inferior.
This applies respectively to one who has undergone oleation and sudation and has been prepared for emesis.

Furthermore, for one who has been lubricated and sweated, and subsequently purged, once the sequential regimen has passed and an oil enema (anuvāsana) has been administered as appropriate, then after three days,
when the patient is alert and the effects have subsided, one should administer a decoction enema (nirūha).
Therefore, for one who has been attended by the three [therapies], the period for the administration of the action [purgative] is seven days.
The re-administration (punarāsthāpana) should be performed on the fifth day; the patient’s body should be well-anointed and fomented, and he should have fasted in the morning before the meal.
Once the [unwholesome matter] has been properly expelled from the viscera and the peripheral channels, the wise physician, equipped with all necessary instruments,
should administer a Nirūha enema using a clean vessel made of gold, silver, or bronze that is level on all sides. (34)
Having added each substance one by one as they will be prescribed in sequence,
the physician, facing east and being well-composed, should prepare the nirūha enema;
in this process, two handfuls (prasṛta) of honey must first be placed therein.
Half a karṣa of rock salt (saindhava), an equal amount of oil and honey, one prasṛta of medicinal paste (kalka), four times that amount of decoction (kvātha),
two prasṛtas of meat broth, and one prasṛta of urine.
A *basti* consisting of twelve *prasṛta*s, thus stirred with a churning stick (38),
should be administered by a knowledgeable physician according to the specific purpose and the correct method;
provided there is a desire to add any particular substances [as needed] (39).

In this regard, it should be stated that honey is poured first for the sake of auspiciousness, as it is the cause of the conjunction of the syllables in their proper order; for honey possesses viscosity, abundance, and astringency.
Salt breaks [the mixture] through its pungency and then brings about cohesion;
therefore, immediately after the honey, a portion of salt is poured in. Then, the oil is added, which serves to bring about a state of uniformity. 41–42.
The paste (kalka) is quickly mixed together, and the decoction (kvātha) attains uniformity;
thus, when the blending of the oil, paste,
and decoction has been performed, the urine imparts sharpness and also enhances the potency.
When properly pressed in this manner, it causes phlegm and wind to flow out from the channels (srotas), and it quickly eliminates bile as well;
otherwise, if pressed incorrectly, it does not achieve the desired effect of clearing the phlegm.
A non-properly churned and adhering enema does not lead to the desired result; therefore, this sequence is prescribed for the administration of a *nirūha* enema.
Furthermore, the measure for a superior dose has been declared as one *prasṛta*.
Therefore, an increase in treatment is desired based on the strength of the patient's age and vitality;
however, a decrease must be made after carefully considering age and vitality,
having observed both aspects as well as the relative strength and weakness of the disease.
If there is an excess in a particular constituent, one should reduce it with that same constituent;
one should prepare substances that are cold, hot, unctuous, or dry.
One should not excessively increase the intensity of sweet, sour, salty, or hot qualities.

In the case of Vātavyādhi (diseases caused by Vāta), the physician should administer oleation therapy; however, for those who are dry (rūkṣa) or whose conditions are of cold potency, he should skillfully effect their reduction. When Pitta is predominant in the disease, the physician should employ substances that are sweet, bitter, and astringent.
One should increase or decrease [the treatment] according to what is appropriate for sharp and hot qualities;
specifically, one should increase sharp, hot, and dry substances when *kapha* is predominant (verse 52),
and apply the opposite when the qualities are reversed.
When the doshas are combined, one should employ drugs with combined qualities.
A non-retentive enema (āsthāpana) improperly administered is like a venomous serpent; yet that very same enema, when properly administered, is like nectar for living beings.
Wherever an abundance of qualities is clearly perceived through proper application, there the wise person should practice the procedure of enema (bastikarma) with vigilance;
for no other such therapeutic action is found to be comparable to it. 55.

For the swift destruction of diseases and for the prevention of their recurrence, one must consider the strength of the disease, the patient, the digestive fire, and the medicine, as well as the constitution,
age, body, suitability, delicacy, and fortitude. (56–57)
Having determined through his intellect the specific application of each action for every particular stage, the wise man should perform it correctly and without sloth.
(58) It should be neither too cold, nor too hot, nor too sharp, nor its opposite.
One should prepare a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) that is neither too dry nor too unctuous, neither too thick nor too thin, neither excessive in quantity nor too small;
for if it is excessively cold, it becomes congealed by extreme coldness and is obstructed by the strength of the vāta.
It causes the limbs to become extremely rigid and is expelled with great difficulty;
being excessively hot, it produces a burning sensation, induces fainting, and passes out quickly.
Likewise, when it is overly sharp, it may even take away one's life.
The mild [oil] does not remove defects; it merely vitiates them.
(62) That which is excessively dry emaciates the body and provokes the wind (*vāta*).
That which is excessively unctuous produces extreme lethargy and destroys the digestive fire (*agni*). (63)
If it is too thick, it is exhausted [before reaching its destination] or does not emerge from the eye;
if it is too thin, due to its lack of potency, it results in non-union (ayoga). If it is of small measure, it does not reach [the target], or it returns with great difficulty.
Excessive quantity leads to over-application; therefore, these are censured.
When consumed in the proper measure, it is soft, hot, and salty;
yet if used improperly, it causes a burning sensation in the vagina and irritation of the genitals, lips, and tongue. 65–66.
Residing in the hips, bladder, waist, sides, navel, and the root of the abdomen, it assumes its full height throughout the entire body by means of its potency;
driven upward by the bodily forces, it is like fire fanned by the winds. (67)

Having passed beyond the seat of pitta, it draws up only a small amount of kapha (verse 68). A sharp [emetic] is administered after a hundred measures; one that is not too sharp does not remain [in the body]. A mild one remains, or even for an excessive duration, as does a sustaining (yāpana) emetic (verse 69).
Because it follows the downward movement of the *apāna* wind and strongly presses upon the rectum,
that second or third enema likewise [expels] the humors (*doṣas*), whether they be gross or subtle, even those that have entered deep within, in a shorter period of time. (70)
It liquefies the obstructed [feces] and draws out the stool;
it does not cause any complications and is easily administered. When applied by a skilled physician, this enema is highly praised. (71–72)

It stabilizes youth, acts as an aphrodisiac, improves the voice, complexion, strength, and digestive fire, and removes the imbalances of wind, bile, phlegm, and the bodily wastes; it is the supreme restorer of vigor for children, the elderly, and those in middle age. (73)
It brings clarity to all the sense organs and produces softness of the limbs.
Thus have been fully described the merits and demerits of the non-unctuous enema (nirūha).
When feces, wind, bile, and phlegm [are present] in succession, [the treatment should be administered accordingly]. 74–75.
And froth resembling a conch shell or crystal issues forth;
this produces supreme softness in those whose limbs have healed properly.
(76) Indeed, there arises a desire for food, clarity, lightness, or else softness.
The passage of feces, urine, and flatus, as well as clarity of the sense organs, [occur when yoga is properly practiced].
In the absence of yoga (ayoga), these would be the opposite; in excessive yoga (atiyoga), there would be an overflow of phlegm, bile, and blood, or a discharge resembling the washing away of flesh.

Hiccups, trembling, thirst, malaise, aching of the limbs, darkness of vision, exhaustion, loss of sleep, and delirium— these are the symptoms that arise when [the enema] has been properly administered, the patient has recovered, and has been sprinkled with lukewarm water. (79)
Or one should feed him a small quantity [of food], or with the meat-broth of wild animals (jāṅgala).
After he has eaten, one should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) using one handful (prasṛta) of oil;
by that, the Vāyu, having been displaced by the decoction enema (nirūha), is pacified.
This is the *āsthāpana* enema for cooling the rectum;
after that, one day later, the person should receive the *anuvāsana* enema as previously described,
provided their digestive fire is kindled, their body is firm, and they suffer from *udāvarta* with obstructed downward wind.

When the vāta is located in the hips and groins, [oleation] is recommended day after day. When the powerful wind has reached the colon (pakvāśaya) and the digestive fire is strong, it will cleanse that [dosha] like water. 83–84.
There is no substance superior to oil for subduing the wind (vāta);
through its unctuousness it overcomes roughness, and through its heaviness it overcomes lightness of the wind.
Furthermore, due to its heat, oil quickly destroys coldness and promotes nourishment.
There shall be clarity of mind, affection, as well as strength and a healthy complexion.

Just as a tree whose trunk and branches have been moistened at the root with oil becomes glossy with tender sprouts and shoots, and yields flowers and fruit in due time; so too shall it be for him. (86–87)
Likewise, by means of oil enemas (snehabasti), a man becomes firm-bodied and possesses robust progeny;
he is not overcome by the previously mentioned disorders caused by Vāta and Ama.
In one āḍhaka of the five roots (pañcamūla), there should be one and a half āḍhakas of the fruits (madana).

One should take three *kuḍavas* each of barley, jujube, and horse-gram; after boiling them in eight times as much water until one-fourth remains, one should cook one *prastha* of oil with this decoction and one *āḍhaka* of whey. 89–90.
Of kuṣṭha, śatapuṣpā, vacā, and madhuka;
of the seeds of kuṭaja and the seeds of madana;
of yavānī, pippalī, hareṇu, and devadāru. 91.
One should take one akṣa each of bilva, devapuṣpa, rāsnā, mustaka,
sūkṣmailā, and priyaṅgu; having prepared them with good salt, strained, and purified, one should place them in a clean vessel.

This oil, known as *phalataila*, is highly esteemed for those suffering from mandala-type skin diseases and for complications arising from enema administration; it cures upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*).
Likewise, it is proven effective for those with abdominal enlargements (*udara*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and intestinal worms.

In cases where the wind (vāta) in the back, hips, thighs, and calves is not functioning properly, whatever disorders have been described as curable by Nirūha enemas should be conquered by this [specific] enema, and it shall also destroy urinary obstructions (mūtrāghāta). 95–96.
Castor root, the three myrobalans (triphalā), balā, rāsnā, punarnavā, guḍūcī,
āragvadha, devadāru, palāśa, the fruit of madana, the root of turagagandhā, and the minor five roots (kanīyasa-pañcamūla). 97.

One should boil these, measuring one *pala* each, in a *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-eighth; having strained it thoroughly, one should collect that [decoction] and have these [drugs], measuring one *karṣa* each, ground into a fine paste. (98–99)
Śatāhvā, madhuka, mustā, priyaṅgu, hapuṣā, vacā, rasāñjana, tārkṣyaśaila, pippalī, and the fruit of kuṭaja (100)— these,
churned with a churning stick, made lukewarm, and mixed with oil, honey, and rock salt, [should be applied].
A Nirūha enema properly prepared with a decoction of meat and urine is purifying, digestive-stimulant, strengthening, and a cure for disorders of the duodenum and hemorrhoids;
it alleviates pain in the flanks, back, and waist, as well as pains arising in the sides, calves, and thighs. (101–102)
An enema prepared with castor oil pacifies Vāta obstructed by Kapha;
an oil enema (snehabasti) is prescribed when combined with appropriate measures of heat and salt.
In brief, it is of two types, and its dosage is now described.
A *prakuñca* is the smallest dose; the medium dose is one and a half times that;
and the highest dose is two *palas*. O Bhārgava, in the *mātrā-basti*, however, half a *pala* of water should be subtracted from the breast-milk [dose], as it is free from harm. 104–105.

Three *karṣas* are prescribed for a three-year-old, and one *pala* for a four-year-old; however, for a six-year-old child, it is recorded as being exactly one *prasṛta*. For those of twelve years, there are two *prasṛtas* each, and likewise four *prasṛtas* [for the next stage].
The sixteen-year-old and other groups [of patients] should be treated in the forenoon or during the intermediate periods;
however, for those in middle age or old age, one should gradually reduce the dosage according to the sequence,
having carefully considered the bodily humors, the digestive fire, strength, and the individual's constitution.
The measure for oil enemas (snehabasti) is such that a decoction enema (nirūha) is three times that amount.
This applies to those who indulge excessively in sexual intercourse, physical exercise, riding, or walking on foot;
to those in the prime of youth; to those accustomed to oleation (snehasātmya); and to those whose digestive fire and strength are firm. (109)
The wise physician should administer the highest dose of oil to those in whom wind is aggravated in the lower part of the body and to those who are of a predominantly windy constitution;
to those among these who are in a middle state, he should administer a middle dose.
"Considering age, disease, and strength, [one should apply] one or the other among the others";
thus the triad of enemas beginning with the *karma-basti* has been fully described—its definition, its variations, and its classifications in their entirety. 112.
Whatever is to be administered, in whatever [condition], in what measure, and in which [patients] it is appropriate—this is the method for Nirūha, as well as Sneha and the Nirūha itself;
thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa. (113–114)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Specific Enemas," in the *Khila* (Supplements).
Now begins the ninth chapter, the Determination of Blood-born Gulma (*raktagulmaviniścaya*).
Hereafter, we shall explain the chapter on the determination of blood-born gulma. 1.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
The wise Bhārgava questioned the Blessed Kaśyapa, the best of sages, the foremost among those who know all scriptures, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati).
How does this blood-tumor (raktagulma), which is difficult to treat, arise in women?
Furthermore, why does it not arise in boys and girls? And how is it that this condition is known as "blood-tumor"?
Why does the movement of the fetus stir even though it is insentient?
There is no great difference between these two— the conscious and the unconscious— even though there is such a vast distance between this fetus and the mass of blood.
Some do not accept a distinction [between the two], while others accept it on the basis of gender.
If there is indeed a distinction between them, for what reason is it being ignored?
It is logical that the emergence of pregnancy-longings (*dohada*) and milk occurs in the womb.

"The appearance of symptoms such as paleness of the cheeks and so forth—I do not see their arising in that [condition] as being appropriate; yet these very symptoms are seen in a blood-tumor (raktagulma). How is that so? (8–9)
Why is it that from the tenth month onwards it undergoes full maturation, yet during the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth,
and so on months, it generally does not suffer injury while remaining within the womb?
It is my opinion that this is a hardship for delicate women. How is this [treatment] to be undertaken, and what is remembered as its procedure?
In which specific conditions and in what manner is its application prescribed?
"At what time is one impervious to division, and what is it that should be divided? Once it has been divided, what should be done? Tell me this, O Lord.
Thus questioned by his disciple, he, the best among speakers, replied:
I shall explain in detail the cause by which menstrual disorders (raktagulma) arise in women, and the reason why they do not arise in boys and girls; learn all of this from me.
In the abdominal cavity of embodied beings, there are seven distinct receptacles for feces, urine, worms, digested food, undigested food, phlegm, and wind; in women, the uterus is the eighth.
It is from this [uterus] that the blood-carrying vessels discharge the menstrual flow (rajas). 16.
For that which has become like a flower proceeds month after month by the power of fate;
however, through its reversal, that very same thing is accumulated right there within the body itself.
For this reason, a blood-tumor (raktagulma) indeed arises in women.
Due to the absence of that intention, it does not arise in men.
However, the blood enters the body and the womb of a young woman of inferior birth; but if she is of full nature, it enters both her body and her womb. 18–19.
Within the womb, it transforms a portion of the [nutrients] into breast milk;
however, the remainder, such as blood and so forth, serves for digestion and sustains the body.
In the same way, immediately after birth, the fetus becomes fit for the mother's breast milk.
But the remainder becomes blood and creeps toward the womb;
when the bodily constituents (dhātus) are fully developed and established in the body, the womb releases the accumulated blood again in due time. 21–22.

When the blood-carrying channels do not carry the blood properly due to vitiation, it follows an abnormal path into the womb; by that means, a disorder arises. In the same way, a blood-tumor (raktagulma) is also produced by this very cause.
When a woman who is in her fertile period suppresses the urges that have arisen—
whether due to shame, fear, or sexual intercourse, or because they are occurring while she is in a downward position—
and when [the wind] is provoked by such other factors as these, it becomes upward-moving. (24–25)
The wind (vāyu), having taken up the blood, moves against the current and returns to the uterus; thus turned upward, it carries the woman's blood.
When the wind in a woman who has miscarried is treated improperly, [it causes these effects].
That wind, having risen up and being repelled by it, becomes mixed with blood;
having reached the womb and being obstructed, it attains stability.
There, the blood having become congealed, the wind moves in an irregular manner.
Carrying the royal [wind], it returns and causes obstruction like a fetus;
impelled by the vital air (māruta), that Gulma throbs repeatedly. I shall describe in their entirety all the symptoms it displays.
She coughs, suffers from piercing pain, has fever, and likewise suffers from diarrhea;
30 her entire limbs feel as if crushed, heavy, and she faints;
darkness frequently arises before her eyes and she indeed falls into emaciation. 31
She vomits frequently, and the food she has eaten does not agree with her;
boils arise on her abdomen, and a bluish discoloration appears upon her.
Furthermore, the space between her breasts, her navel, and the line of hair are congested.
The lips become dark, as do the nipples of the breasts; the two breasts overflow with milk and she experiences pregnancy-longings (dohada).
She craves various flavors and spits repeatedly.
She recoils from pleasant odors, and her complexion becomes pale;
having observed these symptoms of a pregnant woman as they truly are, she thinks, "This fetus is taking away my life," and suffers in grief. (35)
Then, at some time, if it undergoes discharge, she speaks among her kinsmen like one released from a tumor:
"Having been pregnant for a long time, now that the blood of the embryo has fallen away. (36–37)
"I do not see the form of the embryo; I have a great doubt regarding this.
To her, who was curious about the entire village, they replied:
"The divine embryo has passed away; it has been taken by Naigameṣa."
Thus the ignorant call this "all taken away" (sarvahṛtam), which is inauspicious;
those wise men who are skilled call it "overflowing" (paripluta).
What is called a "gulma" or "cay" is said to be blood, that is, *rudhira*. 39–40.

Because there is an accumulation of blood, it is known as *raktagulma* (blood-tumor). This does not move like a fetus; rather, it is so called because of its resemblance [to one]. Thinking "this is a fetus," she mentally imagines it as such.

The woman exhibits various and diverse movements characteristic of pregnancy; hear now the reason why she experiences these longings (dohada), for those very tastes are generally the causes for the increase of the bodily constituents (dhātus). 42–43.
From the very nature of the similarity of their origins, there arises a longing for those [objects] themselves;
the blood, combined with wind and bile, being accumulated, becomes disordered and brings about a craving for bitter, sour, salty, and other such tastes. (44)
Thinking "I am pregnant," she becomes filled with longing, affection, and resolve; from this, milk flows forth for the woman, and by that means it is produced.
All the nutrient-carrying channels are connected on all sides to the navel.
As the fetus grows, it causes pain to those women;
likewise, a blood-tumor (raktagulma) also increases while causing pain.
And because they are afflicted by these [symptoms], the nutritional essence (rasa) does not function properly.
From this, signs such as paleness of the cheeks and so forth arise.
Listen now to me regarding how one extends the time [of gestation] even in that case: here, because of its resemblance to full growth, it is determined that "this is an embryo. 48–49.
A woman guards [the embryo] against injuries like a hen protects its egg;
she never indulges in causes that lead to its destruction, such as physical exertion, fasting, pungent, hot, or alkaline substances, in any way whatsoever. (50)
Thus being treated, it may indeed progress for some time;
however, upon encountering a cause of destruction, it will soon break apart at the bottom, like a water-jar that has been damaged.
Some maintain that the maturation of the *gulma* occurs after ten months, like the ripening of a fruit through its own seasonal transformation;
and at that time, the disease would not be excessively difficult to treat. (53)
Therefore, the wise desire to apply therapeutic measures against it;
however, when the time is not yet ripe, those skilled in reasoning should treat it palliatively, like a fetus, thinking that an immature disease will not burst forth, according to its nature. (54–55)
Learn from me the distinction between a blood-tumor (raktagulma) and a fetus:
a fetus possesses limbs and minor parts, and it moves by means of those very limbs;
whereas a blood-tumor is round and moves like a clod of earth.
Moving from place to place, the embryo turns about in a twisted manner;
this tumor-like mass (gulma) below the navel turns about without being twisted,
and the embryo increases day by day in regular succession.
For the *gulma* increases very slowly in the opposite manner;
moreover, the fetus undergoes various stages month by month.
Furthermore, a pregnant woman does not suffer from fever or a burning sensation without a cause. (59)
For a woman with *gulma* may suffer from fever or burning sensations even without an apparent cause (60).
Even when such specific symptoms are present, a great doubt arises in the physician's mind due to the overlap of various disorders of pregnancy (61).
Having come together and consulted with physicians who are experts in the scriptures, one should administer treatment at the proper time; I shall explain this further below.
These two—the blood-born fetus and the blood-born gulma—are very similar to one another.
Having understood the case exactly as it is, the best of physicians should first perform the treatment.
For he who treats a gulma thinking it is a pregnancy, or a pregnancy thinking it is a gulma, becomes joined with infamy and sin. (63–64)
Therefore, when doubt has arisen, one should perform general therapeutic measures;
a physician should not undertake treatment for any disease that is unknown.
Now, if the time [of onset] is incomplete and the diagnosis is also uncertain—
If blood flows due to some cause, one should quickly stop it;
however, when the time for delivery has arrived, one should not stop the blood.
In that case, one should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) and provide liquid, unctuous food.
By this procedure, if there is a fetus, she will deliver it easily;
or if there is a uterine tumor (raktagulma), even that will be resolved by this incomplete [method].
For this reason, the flow of blood that has begun is not stopped.

In the case of Raktagulma (uterine hemorrhage), the initial administration of oleation (sneha) with due consideration is recommended; likewise, the venesection of the bāhu-sirā (the brachial vein) is advised to prevent suppuration,
as well as palliative measures and the extraction of any remaining morbid humors (doṣas).
A physician who understands the humors and is skilled in his craft should cause a woman suffering from disease to drink auspicious *pañcagavya* mixed with six *pala* of bitter herbs;
he should administer an enema (*āsthāpana*) with sharp substances and perform an oil enema (*anuvāsana*) according to the proper method.
One should have her eat wholesome foods along with milk, vegetable broth, meat broth, and so forth.
A woman suffering from gulma should avoid dry foods, those that cause burning sensations, heavy foods, physical exercise, sexual intercourse, and anxiety. (72–73)
Fever, anorexia, dyspnea, cough, emaciation, weakness, pain, and swelling are the complications of *gulma*; one should treat them with their respective remedies.
(74) [One should also use] meat juices of wild animals prepared in a decoction of *bilva* and *śyonāka*.

To induce relaxation, one should feed the patient with a blood-tumor (raktagulma) either a soup of horse gram (kulattha) seasoned with common quail (lāva), or for the purpose of mobilizing the humors,
one should drink a purgative consisting of trivṛt and triphalā.

For the purpose of pacifying the wind (vāyu), one should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) prepared with fruit oils, or a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana), once or twice, to alleviate pain and flatulence; [the mixture] consists of equal parts honey and oil, with an equal amount of warm water added to them.

Two karṣas of śatapuṣpā and half a karṣa of rock salt—78—with this, or with the decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) and other such ingredients, one should administer an enema to the woman; furthermore, her strength should be nourished with well-prepared meat broths and milk. 79
Thereafter, one should proceed with these powders for purification and expulsion [of the poison]:
Harītakī, Vacā, Hiṅgu, Saindhava salt, and Amlavetasa (80).
One should drink a powder of Yavānī and Yāvaśūka with warm water.
One should skillfully drink a combination of these three— harītakī, yavakṣāra, and sauvarcala— together with ghee, as it breaks up blood-gulma;
or one may take the powder of patra, elā, pippalī, and śuṇṭhī combined with viḍa salt.
One should drink either powdered rock salt (nāgara) or oyster-shell powder (śukti-cūrṇa) saturated with cow's urine;

or one should drink the paste of small cardamom (sūkṣmailā), cumin (kuñcikā), chaba pepper (cavya), long pepper (pippalī), and leadwort (citraka), along with the soup of balvaja grass or with rice-scum water (maṇḍodaka).
One should also cause the blood to break [and stop] with medicines indicated for arresting downward discharge.
If excessive bleeding causes exhaustion, the physician [should act] even when the disorder of the gulma has been removed or when some portion of it still remains. 84–85.
Furthermore, the physician should apply the treatment prescribed for *āsthāpana* (non-unctuous enema) there; out of fear of complications, he should gradually cleanse the patient thereafter.
Having burnt the lotus and other plants along with their roots, one should collect that ash.
Having thoroughly boiled that decoction, one should cook it with these powders:
ginger, long pepper, kuṣṭha, cavya, citraka, and devadāru.
Once prepared, one should apply it as a paste with a ladle; by practicing this, one is purified. 87–88.
By practicing the regimen of *śilājatu*, *abhayā*, and *ariṣṭa* according to the prescribed method, one is liberated [from disease]; furthermore,

that which has been described as the treatment in the chapter on the five types of *gulma* (5.89) should also be employed here, after carefully considering the relative strength of the patient's constitution.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
90. Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Rakta-gulma," in the Khilas;
now begins the tenth chapter, "The Treatment of the Pregnant Woman."
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the medical treatment of pregnant women.
1 As the venerable Kaśyapa has spoken:
2 I shall describe the subtle medical treatment for pregnant women according to their specific divisions.
In this way, both the fetus and the woman grow and are protected.
O King, among all diseases, fever is most difficult for pregnant women;
indeed, when scorched by the heat of fever, the fetus undergoes transformation.
Therefore, first learn from me the treatment for fever,

[which arises] from hunger, fatigue, anointing, dryness, heat, and the retention of undigested matter (āma), as well as from the improper application of oleation, sudation, and medicinal drugs, and from the derangement of the bodily fire (tejas).
From the heat of the mind, as well as from that of mountains,
and likewise from the fragrance of grasses and flowers, a fever arises in a pregnant woman.
A pregnant woman who has developed a fever should be kept on a fast for one day.
Thereafter, one should give her salt-free gruel devoid of fats; however,
a woman suffering from fever should avoid sharp foods and drinks, as well as sudation and physical exertion, and should drink only thin gruel (yavāgū).
When the doshas have been diminished by gruel (yavāgū), one should administer solid foods with soups (yūṣa).

When the doshas have been diminished by soups, a wise and intelligent person should administer meat broth or even milk; however, the administration of medicinal decoctions is not beneficial at that stage.
When the complication has arisen, the physician should administer medicine starting from the fourth month onwards,
having considered the duration of the pregnancy and recognizing the physical fever as being composed of vāta, pitta, and kapha.

One should employ moderate therapeutic measures after carefully considering the relative severity of the condition; having ascertained the strength of the complications and observed the patient's constitution,
and having determined the stage of gestation, one should administer purgatives.
When thirst has arisen, one should not drink water that is excessively hot;
for in a fever arising from wind (vāta) and phlegm (śleṣman), water acts like poison.
Furthermore, in a fever caused by bile (pitta), water that has been boiled and then cooled is recommended.

A preparation made from base metals or stones that has been cooled removes thirst. This procedure is specifically observed to be effective in acute fever; however, once the force of the fever has broken, a decoction prepared with thirst-alleviating drugs should be administered.

Having encountered fever—whether it be cold-fever or its opposite—the therapeutic sequence for head diseases should be applied according to the rules. When the force of the entire fever has been broken, heavy treatment is certainly not recommended. 17
An oil massage is not recommended for a woman during the early stage of fever;
if administered while the fetus is still young, it may lead to miscarriage.
Furthermore, one should not administer nasal drops to pregnant women.
By the administration of nasal medication (nasya), the life-force of a pregnant woman may be diminished;
she may give birth to a child who is crippled, blind, or has impaired sense organs.
By the inhalation of smoke (dhūmapāna), the pregnant woman is severely afflicted by the heat of the smoke, [and her offspring suffers likewise].
O Lord of the People, the fetus becomes discolored or may even fall due to the agitation or fear caused by head-purgation (śirovireka) in a pregnant woman; furthermore,
the wind (māruta) provoked in the body leads to the destruction of the fetus.
Or else, O King, the fetus becomes afflicted by wind-disease;
when the fetus is young, the pitta becomes violently aggravated by sweating and quickly causes the fetus to fall. Therefore, one should avoid sweating [during pregnancy]. 23
Sudation is prescribed for a stable [fetus], yet it causes discoloration of the fetus;
emesis during the early stage of pregnancy destroys the fetus by its own properties. [This occurs] especially due to pressure on the umbilical region and from agitation caused by the hands.
For a pregnant woman whose fetus is young, emetic therapy (sraṃsana) is not recommended;
due to its heaviness, heat, and sharpness, it may cause the destruction of the fetus.
Furthermore, non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) is not recommended for a woman whose fetus is young. (25–26)
The wise one should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana), for such is the determination of the scriptures; he performs the non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) along with the oil enema by his own power.
This is the certainty regarding a fetus that is deficient in limbs or leaking. 27.
Therefore, a wise man should not administer these to a pregnant woman.
However, one who understands the specific conditions of diseases should, after careful consideration, give the following:
vidārigandhā, kalaśī, and likewise gandharvahastaka.

A decoction of madhuka and bhadradāru, combined with sugar and saturated with the juice of mātuluṅga, should be administered to alleviate fever caused by vāta. The group of drugs beginning with vidārigandha, when boiled until it is not excessively cold, [should be used].
Combined with *bhadradāru*, it is considered a remover of wind-fever (vātajvara).
(31) Likewise, a decoction of castor plant (*eraṇḍa*), *varuṇa*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, and *madhuka*, combined with a paste of *rāsnā*, removes wind-fever. (32)
A lukewarm or cold decoction of the two groups of five roots (dvipañcamūla),
combined with a paste of rāsnā, is considered beneficial for fever caused by vāta.
Once the food has been digested, a thin gruel (peyā) prepared without salt should be consumed.
Kuṣṭha, yaṣṭīmadhuka, rāsnā, girikadambaka,
śatāhvā, padmaka, sārivā, uśīra, utpala, mustā, śṛgālavinnā, karavindī, and likewise vacā. (34–35)
One should grind payasyā, haṃsapādī, and punnāga— each in the measure of one karṣa— with the whey of curd (dadhimanda). Then,
the physician should boil a decoction of these parts.

The physician should prepare ten roots (daśamūla) in portions measuring two palas each; likewise, he should take half a pala each of balā and atibalā. As for those three—koraṇḍa, madhuśigru, and madayantī—they [should also be taken in the same measure]. 37–38.
One should take portions of barley, jujube, and horse-gram, each measuring one *prastha*;
having boiled these in a *droṇa* of water until reduced to the measure of one *āḍhaka*, one should add to it the previously prepared ingredients as a secondary addition (*pratīvāpa*). 39.

Likewise, milk, cow urine, vāruṇī liquor, and excellent curd—each measuring one kuḍava according to the physician—should be combined with sesame oil. Having processed this over a fire until it is properly cooked and slightly thickened, [it should be used]. 40–41.
One should rub all the limbs with this warm oil;
this very massage destroys vāta-fever after just three applications.
This massage is highly recommended when the fetus is stable, provided it is performed correctly.

Milk, milk-gruel, or the meat-juice of wild animals is beneficial for chronic fever (jīrṇajvara). For a woman, it should always be prepared with Vata-alleviating drugs; furthermore, if Pitta is involved, a decoction of the Sārivādi group [of drugs] should be used. 43–44.
One should cause the patient to drink, upon rising at dawn, a beverage combined with sugar and honey,
consisting of payasyā, kṣīrakākolī, mṛdvīkā, and madhuka; this drink, mixed with sugar and honey, is for fever caused by pitta (paittika jvara).

One should drink blue lotus, payasyā, sārivā, madhuka, and honey; 46 along with long pepper, black pepper, uśīra, lodhra, parched grain, and sugar—this mixture, combined with milk, should be stirred with a churning stick and drunk. 47
A pregnant woman who has developed a fever will be quickly relieved by that [treatment] for the Pitta;
one should therefore fetch the roots of *nalada*, *vañjula*, and *gundrā* (48),
as well as *sahā*, *sahadevā*, *mārkava*, and *pāṭalī*.
The tender sprouts of milk-bearing trees, as well as those of the *jambu* and *āmra*,
along with blue lotus, *sārivā*, *uśīra*, sandalwood, and lotus petals—
these, ground finely, shall constitute a cooling medicinal paste.

One *kuḍava* of barley flour and half a *pala* of *mañjiṣṭhā*, combined with ghee, are a nourishing remedy for women that removes fever caused by *pitta*. One should cook one *prastha* of oil with one hundred *prasthas* of sour liquid (*amla*). (51)
This oil, which removes burning fever, is praised as a destroyer of fever.
Now, regarding phlegm-fever (śleṣmajvara), Kaśyapa says that one should give a woman a very cold decoction of rāsnā mixed with honey to drink.
A decoction of *bhadradāru* combined with *rāsnā* and honey,
or alternatively a decoction of *candana* combined with *pippalī* and honey,
should be drunk to alleviate fever caused by *śleṣman*. A decoction of *rāsnā*, *vāsā*, and *amṛtā* should also be consumed for the same purpose.

A decoction of *śrīparṇikā* and *amṛtā*, combined with honey and *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, should be drunk in fever characterized by *kapha* and *pitta*. A decoction of the great *pañcamūla* [the five roots] should be used in fever characterized by *kapha* and *vāta*.
It is the established rule that a decoction of the vidārigandhādi group, combined with sugar and honey, should be drunk at dawn along with a paste of rāsnā;
Kaśyapa has stated that this should be drunk for fever caused by vāta and pitta.
In fever caused by pitta, cold gruel, pathyā (chebulic myrobalan), or even milk is wholesome.
Once the fever has subsided, a soup cooked with chickpeas and other pitta-alleviating ingredients is likewise beneficial.
In fever caused by kapha, lukewarm gruel prepared by a woman is recommended.
Likewise, mung bean soup, as well as mūlaka juice and that which is highly wholesome, should be administered, especially in this disease; however,
when the humors are combined, a wise physician should administer them according to the patient's strength.
In cases arising from the combination of all three humors (*sannipāta*), the pacification of the three *doṣas* is beneficial.
Now listen, O Lord of the People, to the treatment for that woman who drinks liquor, whether her condition be due to *vāta*, *pitta*, or *kapha*.
In cases of fever, one should give wine mixed with half as much water to a woman;
having infused it with wine, one should then administer the medicinal preparation (kalpa) made from the juices of *hareṇu*, *mudga*, *cuccū*, and *karkaṭī*.
One should feed light foods with a small amount of sour taste, devoid of salt and fats, soft, and fragrant;
this is when the disease has been broken by diet and the consumption of wine has been ceased. 64–65.
Kaśyapa states that the aforementioned treatment is wholesome when administered according to the specific condition;
furthermore, the medical therapy for diarrhea occurring in a pregnant woman will now be declared for those cases caused by Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha.

From eating incompatible foods, from indigestion, as well as from overeating; or from fear, agitation, or suppression of natural urges; from compression, distension, or depletion; and from consuming raw bulbs, roots, and fruits, as well as from partaking of contaminated water. (67–68)
Due to dryness, hunger, grief, the consumption of heavy and obstructive foods,
and the constant agitation of the water element, diarrhea sets in. (69) When diarrhea caused by undigested matter (*āma*) has arisen, one should administer digestive remedies.
The seeds of *kuṭaja*, *mustā*, and likewise *pāṭhā*,
as well as *ajamodā*, *sarala*, and the auspicious *ativiṣā*—
this [mixture] ground with lukewarm water should be drunk when there is undigested matter (*āma*) associated with phlegm (*śleṣman*). (70–71)

One part each of pāṭhā and candana, along with the fruits of kuṭaja and the preeminent ativiṣā—this should be ground with beneficial water and drunk when there is undigested matter (āma) associated with pitta; so indeed said Kaśyapa. (72)
O King, asafoetida, rock salt, nagakeshara, the two types of brihati, kootaja fruit, long pepper root, and ativisha— these are the principal ingredients;
this should be ground with lukewarm water and drunk when diarrhea arises from undigested matter (ama) caused by vata.

Bṛhatī and the other [herbs] should be drunk when a fever arises from a combination of humors (sannipāta) and when there is a need to consolidate digested matter; this is beneficial for all [types of patients], such is the certainty.
In cases of phlegm (ślaiṣmika), it should be combined with honey and mixed with rice-water.
The Ambaṣṭhādi group [of drugs] should be drunk to break up constipation and hard stools (76).
Alternatively, having ground the fruit of *koṭaja* (kuṭaja) and combined it with honey, one may take *dhātakī*, black pepper, *lodhra*, *kaṭvaṅga*, and *devadāru*. (77)
The filaments of the lotus ground with rice-water and mixed with honey,
when drunk by a woman, destroy phlegmatic diarrhea (śleṣmātīsāra). (78)
A decoction of *nyagrodha* and other such trees, sweetened with honey, is proclaimed by the experts as a remedy for the pacification of *pitta*-type diarrhea;
[it contains] *kaṇā*, *dhātakī* flowers, *madhuka*, and the pulp of *bilva*. (79–80)
A lotus combined with sugar and honey destroys the increase of pitta;
likewise, samaṅgā, the stone of the mango, madhuka, and the filaments of the lotus (81),
along with lodhra and mocarasa, combined with sugar and honey [are effective].
This formulation is prescribed as a remedy for the pacification of pitta-type diarrhea (82).
The minor pentad of roots (*pañcamūla*), excluding castor root, when boiled and combined with *kālā* and *kaṭvaṅga*, is beneficial and destroys vāta-type diarrhea (83).
One should drink lotus, *samaṅgā*, mango stone, *bṛhatī*, and the pulp of *bilva*, finely ground with curd; this destroys vāta-type diarrhea.
Pippalī, *dhātakī*, lotus, *samaṅgā*, and the juice of *moca* [plantain]— [these should be used].
O best of kings, this ground mixture of sugar-candy and indradhānya, combined with rice-water, is beneficial for vātika disorders accompanied by colic;
likewise, mustā, bilva-shoots, anantā, and madhuka [are beneficial]. 85–86.
One should drink finely ground [powder] with curd, combined with ghee and jaggery (*guḍa*), for the purpose of pacifying diarrhea caused by Vāta; thus says Kaśyapa.
(87) Pippalī, dhātakī, lodhra, samaṅgā, and the filaments of the lotus—

One should grind these into fine powders: *padmā*, *mocarasa*, the bark of the *dīrghavṛnta* tree, and *kesara*. Once they have formed a paste, one should administer them as a linctus with ghee, sugar, and honey.

This *kalyāṇaka* linctus is indeed a destroyer of all types of diarrhea. One should drink gruel prepared with the paste of the bark of the *kāśmarya* root and likewise the root of the *śyāmā* plant, along with whey and a small amount of ghee.
Thus, one who suffers from chronic dysentery becomes happy once again.
91. Kirātatiktaka, lodhra, and yaṣṭīmadhuka, combined with treacle, sesame paste, sugar, and honey—92.
Rice-water cures dysentery; likewise, one akṣa each of the pastes of wood-apple, bilva, and black gram, taken separately,
as well as tender plantain, long pepper, and ginger [cure it].
Half a *prastha* of *gauḍa* liquor made from molasses, prepared as a *khaṭa*,
when drunk together with clarified butter and honey, destroys chronic *vāhikā* (diarrhea) occurring after digestion and increases the strength of one's life-force.
A decoction of bāṇamūla combined with trapuṣī seeds,
mixed with sugar and honey, destroys bloody diarrhea (96). [Likewise,] padma, samaṅgā, madhuka, candana, and padmakeśara [are effective].
Milk combined with honey destroys bloody diarrhea (97).
One should drink black sesame seeds, samaṅgā, yaṣṭīmadhuka, and utpala with raw milk; this destroys bloody diarrhea (98).
One should drink the juice of *mauca* along with sesame, *lodhra*, blue lotus (*utpala*), and white lotus (*kamala*) combined with milk; this destroys bloody diarrhea.
[Verse 99] Likewise, *payasyā*, sandalwood (*candana*), *lodhra*, and the filaments of the lotus [are used for the same purpose].

A woman suffering from blood-dysentery (raktātisāra) who passes blood with difficulty and accompanied by pain in the anus should drink milk mixed with honey. Then, she should be fed with milk heated over a vessel made of copper or stone. 100–101.

One should then administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) to her with madhuka mixed with the scum of clarified butter (ghṛtamaṇḍa). For a pregnant woman who suffers from parikartikā caused by vāta, one should feed her a soup prepared with bṛhatī, bilva, and mānaka.
For a pregnant woman suffering from pitta-related complications, this is beneficial:
one should administer licorice (*madhuka*), *haṃsapādī*, and *vitunnaka*, well-ground and mixed with honey, along with rice-water. (103–104)
Now listen as I explain correctly what should be done for the phlegmatic type (ślaiṣmikā):
take kaṇṭakārī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and aśvattha in equal parts; having prepared this with salt, one should have it eaten or even drunk. 105.
Having prepared a well-prepared broth from śālaparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārikā, bilva, agnimantha, śyonāka, kāśmarya, and pāṭali, one should feed it or even have the patient drink it. 107.
Now, if a woman who is pregnant should develop stomatitis (mukhapāka) here, one should then have her take a gargle (kavala) consisting of a decoction of *haridrā* and *dāru*.
Following that, having prepared it with an unctuous substance (*sneha*), there should then be sugar-water (*śarkarodaka*). 108–109.
Having prepared a paste with Lodhra-water, one should perform that rubbing;
then, by consuming Ananta, Samaṅgā, Ghṛṣṭi,
and Mocarasa together with honey, one becomes comfortable.
When Ākṣepaka or likewise Apatānaka has arisen,
one should drink the juice of Mātuluṅga combined with Biḍa and Saindhava salt, or a decoction of Agnimantha or Varuṇa that has been boiled. 111–112.
The meat-juice of the common quail (*lāva*) or the grey partridge (*taittira*), as well as unctuous *vādūla* meat-juice which pacifies *vāta*, is highly recommended for drinking.
This procedure, when applied without mixing [other therapies], brings about comfort.
When afflicted by pitta, the sweet meat-juice of wild animals is beneficial;
it should be boiled with all the sweet [herbs] and combined with the sourness of pomegranate.
However, when arising from vāta and kapha, the taste should be sour and pungent.
Meat from wild animals (jāṅgala) combined with barley-alkali (yavakṣāra) is always beneficial;
likewise, soft applications warmed by the palms are beneficial, except in cases involving pitta.
Alternatively, an effusion of ghee (ghṛtaseka) should be performed, especially once the fetus has matured.
Whether it be hot or cold, having truly encountered such a disease, now learn of the treatment for vomiting as it is being proclaimed:
the juice of *mātuluṅga*, parched grain (*lāja*), the marrow of jujube (*kola*), and likewise collyrium (*añjana*). 117–118.
Likewise, a linctus consisting of pomegranate essence, sugar,
and honey specifically destroys vomiting caused by vāta.
This juice of pomegranate, cooked until it is savory and free from salt, is pleasing to the heart.
O King, buffalo meat that has been well-prepared removes disorders caused by wind;

or [one may take] parched rice flour mixed with sugar and honey, combined with a paste of the four aromatics (cāturjātaka) and beautifully scented with flowers, which is pleasing to the heart. 120–121.
A gruel made from parched grain (lāja-peyā), combined with sugar and honey, is beneficial for pacifying vomiting caused by pitta;
alternatively, the meat-broth of wild animals (jāṅgala-rasa), sweetened with sugar, is wholesome.
The tender sprouts of the mango and jambu trees, when white and well-boiled,
should be drunk mixed with honey, especially in cases of phlegmatic vomiting.
For the purpose of food, a soup prepared with mung beans and seasoned with pomegranate is beneficial.

One should administer mixed remedies for vomiting arising from the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta), provided they are free from oil and salt, heart-pleasing, and capable of destroying vomiting; however,
in the case of vomiting caused by worms (krimija), that which will be explained hereafter should be performed.
One should prepare a decoction of the roots of *varṣābhū* combined with *bhadradāru*;
a woman should drink that, mixed with honey, along with the aforementioned [remedy] for swelling.
Likewise, one may take the roots of *pippalī* and *aṅkoṭha*, together with the juice of horse dung.
Buffalo curd is the treatment for jaundice (kāmalā);
the juice of *mātuluṅga* mixed well with rock salt should be drunk. It is certain that this is the primary remedy for heart pain caused by *vāta*.
One suffering from heart disease caused by *pitta* should drink *priyaṅgu*, *pippalī*, *bhadramustā*, *hareṇu*, honey, and powdered *badara*. Furthermore,
one should take the paste of *pippalī* powder along with its leaves, bark, and *priyaṅgu*.
A linctus made from the juice of *mātuluṅga* is for a heart afflicted by phlegm (*śleṣman*).
A linctus consisting of *kulīraśṛṅgī*, *śaraṭa*, *bhārgī*, and *pippalī*, saturated with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, removes cough caused by wind (*vāta*). (131)

Madhūlikā, gokṣīrī, pippalī, and sugar, combined with grapes and honey, form a linctus that indeed cures pitta-type cough. Pippalī, triphalā, rāsnā, and bhadradāru, taken together with honey [also serve this purpose]. (132–133)
This linctus, which cures coughs caused by phlegm, has been proclaimed by the skillful:
madhuka, conch-shell powder, jīvalākṣā, and honey (134).
This linctus, combined with sugar, is a destroyer of cough due to chest injury.

The feathers of a peacock, as well as those of a porcupine and a hedgehog (135), along with long pepper seeds, long pepper fruits, and an equal amount of jujube root—all these powdered together—should be licked with honey and ghee; this removes asthma and phlegm. (136)

One should have these powders—jaggery, rāsnā, long pepper, grapes, black pepper, turmeric, and samaṅgā—to be licked with oil; this is highly esteemed for treating asthma, cough, and even tamaka-pāṇḍu. (137)
Alternatively, one should have the patient lick inside the house a preparation of *abhayā* and *āmalaka* combined with the bark of *śalyaka*, along with camel bone, curd, and oil;
likewise, *pippalī*, *āmalakī*, *mustā*, treacle, and sugar. 138–139.
One should cause the patient to lick powders of *harītakī* with honey and oil; this is praised as a palliative for all types of coughs and dyspnea.
[140] *Bhadradāru*, *harītakī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *kuṣṭha*—these too [should be used].
Clarified butter and treacle form a linctus that removes upward-moving wind (ūrdhvānila). 141.
Equal parts of long pepper (pippalī), red ochre (gairika), bhārgī, asafoetida (hiṅgu), and karkaṭakī constitute a linctus that pacifies hiccups in women. 142.
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, mustā, and tagara—this group is digestive-stimulating (dīpanīya) when taken with milk and honey.
Śatāvarī, darbhamūla, madhuka, kṣīra, and moraṭa [are likewise used]. 143.
The physician should administer the decoction, the paste, or the milk of *pāṣāṇabheda*, *uśīra*, and the fruits of *kataka* in all types of urinary retention; thus said Kaśyapa. (144–145)

The treatment for abdominal tumors caused by Vāta and those of the female reproductive tract has thus been duly described in brief; specifically, the therapy for those of Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha origins. 146.
In the fourth month, one should administer this medical treatment for women:
with clarified butter, or with food and drink, or with milk or sugarcane juice mixed with emetic fruits; one should induce vomiting properly, so says Kaśyapa. (147–148)
The wise man who desires his own well-being should administer a purgative using the juice of the *caturaṅgula* plant prepared with milk,
or else with fried leaves of *pūtīka* or flowers of *vāṭyālaka*. 149.
One should drink sour barley gruel so that it does not cause excessive urgency [of evacuation]. 150.
One afflicted with wind diseases (vāta) should drink castor leaves with milk, or when there is obstruction of flatus and urine, or when pain has arisen. 151.
In the fifth month, for a pregnant woman who has clearly abandoned sour and salty foods,
an asthāpana enema is beneficial, as is a sweet anuvāsana enema, O Lord of the People, in cases of glandular swellings, pustules, and edema.
In the case of a carbuncle occurring under the asterism Rohiṇī, or specifically during the sixth month, a physician who has mastered the scriptures should apply the appropriate remedies;
these include the application of alkali, surgery, and thermal cautery to pacify the swelling of the flesh. 153.
The setting of broken bones and surgical procedures as well—
O King, all of this one should employ for women in their seventh month who have been bitten by a snake or have consumed poison while pregnant. 154–155.
The treatment for poison should consist of emetics and other measures combined with anti-toxins.
Pāṭhā, amṛtā, the bark of soma, the two types of sāhvā, and likewise kuṭaja—
this [mixture], boiled in milk, should be drunk by a woman to remove poison.
Having decocted śirīṣa, the root of pāṭalī, taṇḍulīyaka,
the root of sinduvārita, and the root of sahacara, one should prepare a thin gruel (peyā) that destroys poison. 157–158.
Meat broth and other such foods, when eaten in moderation and with propriety, are beneficial;
one should also follow whatever is prescribed in the second section [of this treatise].
A pregnant woman who becomes weak in body and remains seated [should take these measures]. 159.
Fever assails her and her fetus perishes.
Furthermore, she who eats excessively, too much, or too frequently, and becomes greatly fainting, will undoubtedly lose her fetus. 160–161.
The fetus of a woman whose eyes have the appearance of being swollen with tears, whose ears and feet are cold, and whose hair is matted, perishes.
Furthermore, he who dwells above the navel and on both sides [perishes].

If a woman stands in the middle [of her bed], that fetus also perishes. (163) The fetus of a woman who experiences pain in the joints, has a distaste for well-prepared food, and desires motionless sleep, perishes. (164)
If there is swelling of the joints, inflammation of the limbs, and heaviness of gait for her [the pregnant woman], the son born of her will die; of this there is no doubt.
This is likewise true for one who is grieving, lamenting, or lost in deep thought.

The son born of a woman who has the habit of cracking her fingers does not live. (166) Furthermore, the son born of one whose milk is foul-smelling and whose hair is matted and soiled does not live. (167)
She whose mouth emits a foul odor, in whom pain arises,
or who is overcome by excessive sleep, does not survive with a dead fetus (mūḍhagarbha).
She who sees the sacrificial fire resembling the neck of a peacock [does not survive].
She whose feet and face are swollen, and who has a retained fetus, does not live (169).
She for whom there is pain in the sides, thirst, loss of consciousness, as well as labored breathing and obstruction of the eyes, she too does not live (170).

If a pregnant woman suffers from abdominal cramps, pain in the womb, a foul odor from the mouth, loss of consciousness, or delirium, she does not survive. Furthermore, she whose nose becomes like that of a crow and whose eyes have sunk is also lost. (171)
Likewise, O King, the fetus of a woman who desires the scent of birds is extracted by means of a blade;
and the fetus of a woman who desires white goat-meat or peacock-flesh is likewise brought forth by a blade. (172–173)
Clad in red garments, adorned with red garlands and unguents,
she smiles as she lies down or ascends to the cremation ground;
whether her fetus is immature or fully formed, that pregnant woman perishes.
She who in her dream mounts a donkey, a boar, a buffalo, a dog, or likewise a camel, becomes pregnant and perishes. She who bathes daily, remains clean, wears white garments, and is pure— 175–176.
One who is devoted to the gods and Brahmins shall always be gentle, pregnant, possessed of many sons, infinite, a sovereign lady, joyful,
as well as endowed with the qualities of Brāhmī, Sahadevā, and Indravāruṇī. 177.
O King, [one should take] jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, bhārgī, and likewise samaṅgā; rohipādā, the sprouts of the vaṭa tree, and likewise ātmaguptā; as well as ariṣṭa, pūtanā, keśī, and śatavīryā. 178–179.
One should collect these thousand-fold potent substances with the *prājāpatya* asterism and join them together;
then, under the *puṣya* asterism, one should wear them, as well as during the *uttara* asterisms.
Having fashioned a three-layered amulet from this, a pregnant woman should always wear it upon her hip.
O King, one who has given birth should carry [the protective amulet] on her head, or likewise cause it to be worn;
for a woman in childbirth, specifically, those [rites] that destroy Rākṣasas are beneficial.
Wherever there are symptoms here of disorders such as fever and the like, [these remedies should be applied]. 181–182.
"I shall now declare the dietary rules for those who eat food, and it should be known that these apply even to pregnant women," so said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Pregnant Women," within the Khilas. 10.183.
The eleventh chapter, on the management of the puerperal state.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter named "On the Management of the Puerperal State.
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.

Hereafter, I shall fully explain the specific medical treatments for women who have given birth; understand that according to the proper sequence. From the moment of conception, the physician must remain attentive toward the woman who has borne a child.
"How indeed might she give birth when the time is fully complete?"— thus he thinks again and again.
And when the time for delivery has arrived, fear arises because one foot of him remains here, while the other is in the abode of Yama.
Furthermore, in that case, if another woman has not emerged [after the birth], even though she has given birth, she is not a *sūtā*;
such being the case, there are sixty-four types of women with difficult births; this is the established rule.
The vagina may be prolapsed, injured, torn, or obstructed by urine; it may be swollen, discharging, numb, or painful;
there may be pain in the sides, back, and hips, as well as pain in the heart and choleric colic (visūcikā).

Spleen disease, enlargement of the abdomen, wind in the limbs, body ache, upward rolling of the eyes, lockjaw, stiffness of the neck, facial paralysis, abdominal pain, abscesses, swelling, delirium, insanity, and jaundice. 9.
Weakness, vertigo, emaciation, aversion to food, indigestion, fever, diarrhea, erysipelas, vomiting, thirst,
dysentery, hiccup, dyspnea, cough, and anemia caused by blood-born *gulma*.
Both flatulence and distension, as well as the retention of feces and urine;
diseases of the mouth, diseases of the eyes, catarrh, and throat-obstruction; consumption, facial paralysis, tremors, ear-discharge, and insomnia. 11–12.
Uṣṇavāta, graha, ādhaḥstana-roga, atha-rohaṇī,
vātāṣṭhīlā, vātagulma, raktapitta, and vicarcikā—
these sixty-four diseases of the puerperium have been described.
"How indeed is she to be protected from all of these?"—even physicians who know the science fall into such confusion; how much more so those of small intellect who have been trained by others? 14–15.
Therefore, one who knows that [treatment], who perceives its meaning with certainty,
and who is vigilant, should apply himself to the management of women in labor. One should understand both the general principles of that management as well as the specific deviations from it.
I shall describe in detail [the management] according to the suitability of the region, the country, and the family.
Having comforted the newborn immediately after birth,
the skilled midwife should place the infant face-down on her own lap, cradle it, and press its abdomen against her own abdomen.

One should press the abdomen with a ghaṭṭa to induce the expulsion of fetal defects, and one should wrap the sides of the belly with a large, non-defective cloth. By this means, the abdomen returns to its natural position and the wind (vāyu) is pacified.
The Sūti should always sit upon a bench covered with leather and filled with oil of Balā heated by fire; likewise, her womb becomes pacified.
Then, having well-anointed her with preparations of Priyaṅgu and Kṛsara, she should undergo fomentation.
Once she has been fomented, bathed with warm water, rested, and is free from fatigue,
one should fumigate her with kuṣṭha, guggulu, and aguru mixed with clarified butter. Then, having observed the strength of her digestive fire, [this should be done] for three days or five days.
One who eats wholesome food should drink unctuous substances (sneha) immediately after taking a dose of *maṇḍa*.
Upon the cessation of the unctuous effect, one should consume for three days a thin gruel (*yavāgū*) containing a small amount of fat and rock salt, seasoned with *pippalī* and *nāgara*. 23–24.
After the cessation [of the previous diet], there may be a soup of *kulattha* beans with oil and salt;
thereafter, a soup of *kulattha* with oil, salt, and sour [ingredients];
likewise, meat broth from wild animals (*jāṅgala*), and then these various leafy vegetables.
One should consume eggplants, radishes, and cucumbers fried in ghee;
for one month, she should diligently employ oleation and sudation, followed by the regimen of wholesome living with warm water thereafter. (26–27)
Relying upon three types of locations, I shall describe a threefold procedure:
In marshy regions (*ānūpa-deśa*), diseases characterized by wind and phlegm (*vāta-śleṣmātman*) are most prevalent;
because of the abundance of secretions (*abhiṣyanda*) there, oleation (*sneha*) is initially forbidden.

In this case, a preparation such as a *maṇḍa* (gruel) should be administered; it promotes digestion and enhances the strength of the digestive fire (agni). Sweating, sleeping in a windless place, and everything warm are recommended.
Indeed, diseases characterized by wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*) invariably prevail in a *jāṅgala* region.

Therefore, in this case, because of her natural affinity for oleation, the treatment consisting of unctuous substances and the like should be administered; furthermore, a specific distinction is recognized here regarding the newborn. Upon the birth of a boy, oil [is used], and upon the birth of a girl, ghee.

Once it has been digested, one should drink gruel prepared with digestive stimulants (dīpanīya) for five days or seven nights; thereafter, the regimen beginning with thin gruel (maṇḍa) should be followed.
In a temperate climate, this moderate therapeutic procedure is beneficial for him.
Foreigners and various Mleccha tribes also provide blood,
meat broth, and bulbs, roots, and fruits;
one should understand the dietary preferences of each family according to their specific requirements.
Due to propriety and the habitual nature of the family, that [treatment] follows exactly in that manner.
Therefore, because the commencement of treatment for puerperal fever is not absolute,
one should administer it after carefully considering the region and the habitual nature of the patient's caste.

The medical treatment for those diseases has been stated; now, hereafter, I shall describe the treatment for certain other diseases arising from difficult childbirth. Among all diseases whatsoever, fever is considered the most difficult to endure.
Therefore, I shall first describe its procedure according to its etiology, symptoms, and therapeutics (38).
A sixfold fever arises in women who have recently given birth; listen to me regarding its etiology according to the division into endogenous and exogenous types (39).
From the suppression of natural urges, from dryness, from physical exertion,

from excessive loss of blood, from grief, from the intense heat of a hyperactive digestive fire, from the excessive consumption of pungent, sour, and hot foods, from sleeping during the day, from eastern winds, and from the eating of heavy and obstructive foods; 40.

Fever arises in a woman from six different causes: from the flow of breast milk, from affliction by malevolent planets, from indigestion, and from difficult childbirth; that same fever, when its premonitory symptoms are subverted by opposing factors, [is known as *viṣamajvara*]. 41–42.
Through the combination of unctuous substances, cold water, bathing, drinking, eating, and so forth,
a terrible *sannipāta* fever arises that is difficult to treat. It is characterized by intense, continuous shivering and the exhaustion from riding.
When the body has become flaccid, when the vital winds (anila) and other humors are agitated,
when the pathways of the senses are exhausted, and when the bodily constituents (dhātus) are devoid of essence—
even a single provoked humor flows with great difficulty and causes great suffering.
Just as a worn-out garment, stained with filth on all sides,
is cleansed by those who know its nature after examining each of its parts,
so too is the body of the woman who has given birth afflicted and drained.
That which is heavily smeared with the power of the defilements is purified through suffering.
Just as an old house whose structural bonds have loosened on all sides would be unable to withstand the shaking caused by rain and wind, so too is that [mind] of such a kind. 47–48.

Likewise, the body of a woman who has given birth becomes emaciated from the exhaustion of labor and perspiration, and it becomes incapable of withstanding diseases arising from wind, bile, and phlegm.
Indeed, the bodies of all embodied beings are sustained by the very same humors (doṣas). 49.

When those [humors] have been exhausted, the fever characterized by burning heat in the woman gives rise to a condition where it quickly consumes the body, like fire consuming dry fuel; this occurs according to the increase of the humors that have grown solely due to those causes. 50–51.
The wise man should bring about the pacification [of the womb] and the restoration of the bodily constituents;
within six months, the constituents—blood and the rest—return to their respective positions in a woman who has given birth and is free from disease. (52)
Having reflected upon this and other factors, one should apply medical treatment.
Hereafter, the symptoms of fevers will be fully described:
irregular body heat, aching of the limbs, yawning, sneezing, and horripilation.

A bitter taste in the mouth, aversion to cold and a desire for heat, chattering of the teeth, delirium, dry eructations, insomnia, flatulence, and contraction of the limbs are the indications of Vāta fever. (55)
Thirst, burning sensations, delirium, vomiting, and a bitter taste in the mouth; 56.
A yellow discoloration of the face, nails, teeth, eyes, feces, and urine is observed, as well as dryness of the throat, and everything is perceived as if on fire. 57.

Dizziness, a desire for cold, fever, longing for heat, cough, headache, heaviness of the limbs, mildness of body heat, catarrh, and whiteness of urine and feces— these are the indications of pitta-fever. 58.
Drowsiness, lethargy, aversion to cold, spitting, a sweet taste in the mouth, weakness of the limbs, and a dislike for food are the indicators of a fever born of phlegm (kaphaja).
There is frequent shivering, frequent burning heat, and a temperature that is sometimes uniform and sometimes irregular. (59–60)
From *kapha*, there is difficulty in passing feces, urine, and flatus; from *vāta*, there is the displacement of the limbs and intestines;
from *pitta*, there is burning sensation, thirst, delirium, and a distracted state of mind;
and from *kapha* as well, there is heaviness, obstruction of the throat, and a cold sensation.
These symptoms have been described as the characteristics of sannipāta fever.
On the third or fourth day, the breast milk of a woman begins to flow; this occurs because the milk-carrying channels, which had been obstructed, are now stimulated.
