It causes stiffness of the breasts, thirst, a melting sensation in the heart, pain in the abdomen, flanks, and waist, body aches, and headache;
this is said to be the specific symptom of fever arising from the flow of breast milk. (64)
For he remains in the purification of the nectar merely by means of the sequence.

(65) If a woman who has recently given birth suffers from fever due to the agitation caused by the fear of being gazed upon by the planets or by the blows of the wind, I shall describe her symptoms. (66)
Trembling, groaning, wandering of the eyes, exhaustion,
shaking of the hands and eyes, yellowness of the face and eyes, (67) and in an instant a dark discoloration of the limbs, followed by an instant return to their natural color.
A thorough awakening, staying together with others, and the plucking out of hair (68);
it produces many symptoms resembling wind-fever (pavana-jvara),
and the ritual for destroying planetary afflictions (graha-ghna) and the regimen prescribed for wind-fever are beneficial for this [disease] (69).

One should treat with fasting a patient who has excessive secretions of phlegm, who is obese, whose body is not moistened by perspiration, whose discharges are scanty, who has indigestion, and who is unctuous;
whereas one who is dry, has lost blood, is emaciated, or is afflicted by Vata-fever and similar conditions [should be treated differently]. 70.
One should restore a woman who is exhausted and afflicted by hunger and thirst with soothing treatment.

For her, on that very day, a regimen beginning with gruel (*peyā*) is prescribed; for one who has undergone fasting (*laṅghitā*), a regimen beginning with rice-scum (*maṇḍa*) is intended—this is the two-fold regimen. 71–72.
For *peyā* kindles the digestive fire and pacifies the bodily constituents (*dhātus*),

while *maṇḍa* destroys the remnants of defects in the fetus and digests the morbid humors (*doṣas*). Therefore, *peyā* and *maṇḍa* are prescribed as beneficial at the beginning of the treatment sequence.

Both unprocessed and processed meat broth, as well as vegetable soup, should be taken two or three times; likewise, sudation, lightening therapy (apatarpaṇa), the judicious use of digestive medicines, decoctions, and oil massage—ghee is the supreme regimen for the destruction of fever. (74–75)
Cold exposure, fasting, physical exertion, fatigue, unwholesome diet,
and indulgence in those causes quickly bring about the strength of fever. When the fetus has been expelled from the womb, the doshas follow after it in women.

Therefore, emesis, nasal therapy, enema, and purgation fall away [are ineffective] when the humors are situated only slightly within the body; rather, those very same treatments should be applied with skill, having observed the relative strength and weakness of the humors. (77–78)
Neither emesis nor purgation administered with potent medicinal drugs is recommended for a feverish patient whose morbid humors (doṣas) have not been excessively discharged;
for when the body is heated by the internal fire, the bodily constituents (dhātus) become fully digested.
Having received a stronger medicine, they may attain the ultimate goal (immortality).
When the heart is agitated and phlegm is situated in the chest,
one should administer mild emesis in a case of phlegm-fever where the body is capable of it.

In cases of loss of appetite, constriction of the throat, or phlegm located in the head, when gargling is not possible, one should administer nasal medication (nasya). This should be done when the humors have been ripened by their combination and the fever has become mild.
One should administer a decoction after five days or seven nights;
a digestive (pācanīya) decoction after five days, and a carminative (ānulomika) one after seven days.
In cases of fever caused by *kapha* and *pitta*, one should give palliative medicine (*śamana-auṣadha*) after five days.
Due to its natural sharpness, it ripens in a short time;
furthermore, because of the weakness of the bodily elements (*dhātu*) and the nature of the disease itself, [it subsides quickly].
In a fever caused by *vāta*, once it is conquered, one should employ massages as well as meat-based diets (*rasabhojana*).
When the pure *vimala* [bile] is located in the colon (*pakvāśaya*), one should administer downward-moving (*ānulomika*) therapy;
one should also feed light food along with thin meat-broths of wild animals.
Furthermore, that fever characterized by *vāta* and *pitta* which does not subside in this manner [should be treated as follows]. 86–87.
Clarified butter quickly pacifies that [fever], just as a rain-cloud extinguishes a forest fire;
indeed, when the digestive fire is clear and mild, clarified butter alone is the supreme remedy.
For most diseases arising from improper digestion are primarily to be subdued by oleation.
In cases of *sannipāta* fever, in women, and when *vāta* is predominant, aged ghee processed with meat broth and vegetable soup is recommended;
among these, I shall first describe the treatment for *vāta* fever. 89–90.
One should collect the flesh of carnivorous animals, grains, mung beans, sesame seeds, barley, the ten roots (daśamūla), apāmārga, bhaṇṭī, eraṇḍa,
āṭarūṣaka, aśvagandhā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and bamboo leaves.

This mixture of fermented gruel (saṃkara-sveda), combined with dried cow dung and sour substances, should be applied in cases of Vāta-fever; it brings comfort in conditions involving the combination of humors (saṃsarga) and the like.
[One should also use] the two Pañcamūlis, Vṛścīva, Ekeṣīkā, and Punarnavā. 92–93.
Sahasravīryā, Nādeyī, Śatavīryā, Śatāvarī, Viśvadevā, Śukanasā, Sahadevā,
Sanākulī, Rāsnā, Ajagandhā, Pūtīka, Devāhvā, and Devatāḍaka. 94.
One should take two palas each of the two types of *haṃsapādī* for the purpose of decoction;
and *kṛṣṇāgaru*, *vyāghranakha*, *śatapuṣpā*, *palaṅkaṣā*, *kāyasthā*, *vayasthā*, *coraka*, *jaṭilā*, and *jaṭāmāṃsī*. (95–96)
Apetarākṣasī, yakṣaguhā, mahoṣṭralomikā, hareṇukā, haimavatī, kairava, suvahā,
vacā (97), vṛścikālī, bhārgī, śyāmā, and śigru— one should take these as a paste.
Having collected the oil, one should cook it to destroy Vāta-fever.
One should drink a decoction of the great Pañcamūla with Saindhava salt, or a decoction of Vidārigandhā with Saindhava salt should be drunk. 98–99.
One should collect rāsnā combined with sarala, devadāru, and yaṣṭīmadhuka;
likewise, bṛhatī, sarala, dāru, bhārgī, and varuṇaka;
as well as eraṇḍa root, rāsnā, and vṛścikālī.
One should drink this decoction while it is lukewarm to alleviate vāta-fever (101).
One should also drink water boiled with the root of *bilva* as an intermediate drink,
combined with the broth of the "five handfuls" (*pañcamuṣṭika*) along with sour and salty seasonings (102).
One should eat a meal at the proper time with the meat-broth of wild animals,
or with a decoction of barley, jujube, horse-gram, and the two types of *pañcamūla*, along with curd, barley-alkali, *cavya*, *citraka*, and ginger. (103)
One should drink that ghee prepared with long peppers (pippalī), which removes fever,
destroys the obstruction caused by Vāta and Kapha, and is an excellent stimulant for the digestive tract (grahaṇī).
Furthermore, one should administer a purgative using ghee prepared with Śyāmā and Tilvaka.
If, however, the tremors do not subside due to the predominance of wind (vāta),
one should fumigate her after she has been well-anointed with warm oil using *suradāru*.
She should also be smeared with all the fragrant substances (*sarvagandha*) ground with sour liquids and applied lukewarm.
One should cause the patient to bathe in a decoction of *syonāka*, *vāsā*, bamboo, *tarkārī*, castor plant,
*apāmārga*, and *kāśmarya*, using warm sour liquids. Once she has bathed comfortably and is rested, she should be covered with blankets made of meat, skin, or wool.
One should fumigate with the incense of *kuṣṭha* and *guggulu* mixed with clarified butter;
food and drink should be warm,
yet warm wind must be avoided, for warmth is contrary to *pitta*.
Therefore, one should treat a fever born of pitta that is not accompanied by severe complications with applications and ointments of medicinal herbs that are astringent, bitter, and sweet;
specifically, *śārṅgeṣṭhā*, *maruvā*, *pāṭhā*, *naktamāla*, and *vatsaka*. (110–111)
One should drink nimba, māragvadha, and uśīra with honey; likewise,
one should prepare sthirādi-pañcamūla, keśara along with kaśeruka, gopī, parpaṭaka, uśīra, and dhānyaka.
One should drink that decoction when it is cooled and reduced to one-quarter, mixed with honey and sugar.
Alternatively, one may take half an āḍhaka of water infused with the eight ingredients—musta, dvi-sārivā, uśīra, yaṣṭikā, lodhra, padmaka, and saptaparṇa. (113–114)
Having been kept overnight, that purified [mixture] should be drunk combined with sugar and one *karṣa* of finely ground *kaṭurohiṇī*.
This is the king of all medicinal infusions (*abhiṣava*), a remover of all fevers.
Grapes, *nāgapuṣpa*, black pepper, sugar, cinnamon leaf, cardamom, and *cavya*—this is the drink for fever caused by *pitta*.
*Bhadraśrī*, *tinduka*, *mustā*, *payasyā*, licorice, and *vacā* [are also used]. 116–117.
Their decoction should be drunk to destroy fever and diarrhea;
or one should drink the juice of mūrdhaka mixed with pṛśniparṇī and sthirā (118),
or that prepared with sārivā, candana, uśīra, drākṣā, and padmaka.
One should drink lājapeyā (barley gruel with parched grain flour), which removes vomiting, fainting, burning sensations, and fever;
or one should eat it with mung bean soup or with a sweet meat broth.
[The ingredients are: madhuka, kesaraka, gopī, nimba leaves, and kaśeruka. 119–120.
A linctus combined with sugar and honey cleanses the mouth;
when the force of the fever has subsided, one should administer a mild purgative to the patient.
A wise physician [should prepare this] with the paste of *caturaṅgula*, *mṛdvīkā*, and *trivṛt*.
One should apply a plaster made of tālīsa, uśīra, and candana combined with wood;
oil prepared with the paste (kalka) of madhuka and the paste of tagara, when used as an ointment or drunk, dispels fever.
Ghee prepared with the paste of *paṭola*, *guḍūcī*, *rohiṇī*, *āragvadha*, and *candana* removes fever.
Alternatively, ghee may be prepared with the *candanādya* group or the *paṭolādya* group of drugs. 124.
One should administer bitter ghee, or even the meat broth of the partridge and similar birds;
furthermore, sour foods and drinks, as well as hot and pungent ones,
must be avoided in pitta-type fever, and one should employ treatments that are antagonistic to pitta.

One should conquer Kapha-fever whose force has been broken by means of proper association [with wholesome people] through the drinking of medicinal decoctions, as well as with ghee for internal use and for massage. [The following drugs are used:
the two types of Bṛhatī, Puṣkara, Dāru, Pippalī, Nāgara, and Śaṭī.
One should first drink their warm decoction to ripen the morbid humors (doṣas).
Alternatively, one may drink a decoction of the two pañcamūlas, bhārgī, karkaṭaśṛṅgī, durālabhā, ginger, long pepper, and devadāru, combined with rock salt.
A decoction of these six ingredients— paṭola, dhānyaka, mustā, mūrvā, pāṭhā, and nidigdhikā— should be drunk mixed with honey.
One should drink warm water boiled with ginger (nāgara) and amaradāru.
One should feed [the patient] with a soup of young radish or the broth of wild animals, prepared with pungent and hot substances and made mild and unctuous;
one should also drink the purgative of *trivṛt* paste combined with cow's urine.
Or, at the proper time, one should drink auspicious ghee prepared with the ten roots (*daśamūla*),

along with equal parts of lac (*lākṣā*), nut-grass (*mustā*), the two types of turmeric (*haridrā*), dill (*śatāhvā*), *bhadrarohiṇī*, *devapuṣpā*, sweet flag (*vacā*), deodar (*dāru*), and pine resin (*sarala*).
The physician should cook oil with this [decoction] and use it as an ointment. [The ingredients are:
kuṣṭha, agaru, vyāghranakha, māṃsī, dhānyaka, sāmana, vakra, hareṇu, hrībera, sthauṇeya, kesara, and tvac. (134–135)
One should carefully cook oil with equal parts of these: *sarala* wood, *mūrvā*, *kālānusārivā*, *barhiṣṭha*, *śatapuṣpā*, *pṛthvīkā*, and *devapuṣpaka*. (136)
By this very massage, one dispels fever born of phlegm (kapha-jvara).
The remaining treatment here should be performed as for vata-fever, excluding [the specific measures for] vata;
[this includes] sweet foods and drinks that are unctuous and heavy.
In fever caused by *kapha*, one should avoid [aggravating factors] and employ counter-measures;
hereafter, I shall describe the treatment for *sannipāta* fever. That which exhibits all symptoms is incurable, while that with few symptoms is difficult to cure.

For one who is weak and whose digestive fire is extinguished, [the treatment] does not succeed at all (140). How much more so for women in childbirth, whose bodily constituents, strength, and vitality are depleted?
Nevertheless, the best of physicians should apply effort out of compassion (141).
Among the humors combined in a *sannipāta*, one should first pacify whichever humor is most powerful, and thereafter treat the remaining humors.
When these humors are of slightly differing strengths, the wise physician [should proceed accordingly].

One should first pacify phlegm (śleṣman), for it acts as the underlying associate of these [other humors]. Because of its heaviness, its slow digestion, and its location in the upper body, fever caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha is difficult to diagnose. 143–144.
In each respective state, that specific treatment should be administered; however, I shall now describe the general principles of medical therapy and their specific applications.
(145) [One should use] *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *arka*, *sudarśana*, *eraṇḍa*, and *parūṣaka*.
Having spread a hide soaked in *droṇa* of oil upon it according to the proper method, one should cause the woman who has recently given birth to sweat there while covered with heavy garments;
[using] ginger, the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *kaṭvaṅga*, and the two types of *dāru*. (146–147)
This decoction of pippalī, triphalā, bhārgī, karkaṭaśṛṅgī, and durālabhā,

combined with rock salt, honey, and asafoetida, should be administered for fever occurring in the forenoon and afternoon; however, it should be given in the evening for fever occurring in the late afternoon.
Paṭola, mustā, madhuka, and rohiṇī—
these should be drunk with ghee in cases of sannipāta where vāta is predominant; this same formulation, combined with triphalā and devadāru, [is likewise effective].
In cases of *sannipāta* where *kapha* is predominant, one should administer [the medicine] mixed with honey;
[using] *elā*, *madhūka*, *madhuka*, *śītapākī*, and *parūṣaka*;
or [using] *triphalā*, *sārivā*, *pāṭhā*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and *caturaṅgula*. 151.
In the case of *abhinyāsa* (a fainting fit) dominated by *pitta*, one should drink [the decoction] with honey and sugar;
it is prepared from *bhārgī*, *śṛṅgī*, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, *daśamūla*, *durālabhā*, *kaṭvaṅga*, *triphalā*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *pippalī*. (152–153)
One should cause [the patient] to drink a decoction containing rock salt (saindhava) and alkali (kṣāra) that promotes downward movement of the doshas;
or one should drink trivṛt combined with cow's urine, or vacā alone. When the doshas have moved downward and the strength of the grahaṇī has been restored, [the treatment is successful].

Then, one should drink well-prepared ghee at the proper time, or ghee processed with licorice (*madhuka*), ativiṣā, *rohiṇī*, and *bhadradāru*, which removes fever caused by the combination of all three humors (*sannipāta-jvara*). 155–156.
One should administer an anointing (abhyañjana) prepared with auspicious substances, or with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
or with oils processed with all medicinal herbs, both cold and hot,
as well as any other [remedies] that remove the three impurities. 157

One should perform the rinsing of the mouth with harītakī, priyaṅgu, mālatī, and āmalaka; or with vāsā or khadira. Likewise, the stone of the mango fruit, finely ground and combined with rasāñjana, [should be used]. 158–159.
For the teeth, gums, lips, and tongue, the primary treatment is rubbing [with medicinal pastes].
When the head is afflicted with heat, one should apply a plaster to the forehead consisting of curd, resin of *sarja*, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and *aśvagandhā*, mixed with honey. 160.
When a fever has persisted for more than eight days following a diet of light food,

or when there is a complication (saṃsarga) or a simultaneous derangement of all three humors (sannipāta), especially if accompanied by delirium with a predominance of Vāyu, or if there is colic, constipation, retention of urine, and particularly dyspnea; 161–162.
One should prepare processed old ghee and the meat-broth of wild animals,
along with the decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*), horse gram (*kulattha*), barley, *kuvala* fruit,
*kulīraśṛṅgī*, *rāsnā*, *śaṭī*, and the root of *puṣkara*. (163)

A decoction well-prepared from *durālabhā* and *bhārgī* (164) effectively pacifies his deranged *vāyu* and his fever once the fever's force has been broken by the administration of digestive (*pācanīya*) remedies (165).
When the impurity has been partially digested and the strength has become diminished, one should drink this pair of pacifying formulations well-cooled with honey:
either long pepper with durālabhā and grapes, or grapes with long pepper. (166)

Ghee prepared with the fresh juice of *guḍūcī* and *āmalaka*, along with a paste of *sārivā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *lodhra*, pomegranate, and *candana*, is indeed known as "Maṅgalyaka"; it destroys chronic fevers (*viṣamajvara*). 167–168.
"Indeed, for all fevers as well, this alone is like nectar," so said the venerable Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Commencement of the Puerperal State," among the Supplements (Khila).
Now begins the twelfth chapter, on the post-natal rites (*jātakarmottara*).
Now, therefore, we shall explain the chapter on the post-natal rites.
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.

Then, indeed, when the birth-rites for the newborn infant have been performed, in the very first month—after the protective fire-offerings, auspicious rites, and ceremonies for well-being have been completed—there is the ceremony of beholding the rising sun at dawn and the moon at nightfall.

In the fourth month, having bathed, adorned, and clothed the child in new garments, and having had him touched by a nurse with white mustard seeds, honey, clarified butter, and yellow pigment (*rocanā*), he is led out from the inner house and brought into the temple of the deities.

There, having worshipped the blazing fire with offerings of clarified butter and unbroken grains (akṣata), and having fully honored Brahmā, Īśvara, Viṣṇu, Skanda, the Mothers, and other family deities with perfumes, flowers, incense, garlands, food offerings, and many various kinds of edibles; then, having performed the recitation by the Brāhmaṇas, received their blessings, and saluted his elders, he should enter his own chamber again. Once he has entered, the physician should sprinkle him with water while reciting this mantra:
"Live for a hundred autumns, O child, protected by the gods."
"Purified by the blessings of the twice-born and greeted with joy by his elders.

(5) In the sixth month, on an auspicious day, having worshipped the deities and the twice-born, and having gratified them with food and honored them with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and having had the benediction (*svasti*) pronounced, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring four cubits in a clean place either in the middle of the house or in the center of the site, smeared with cow-dung and water. There, one should draw a circular or square mandala and place upon it gold, fine gold, silver, copper, bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), lead, iron, gems such as pearls and corals, all types of grains such as rice (*vrīhi*), and all kinds of bricks.

Milk, curd, ghee, honey, cow dung, cow urine, cotton, and other such items used as children's toys made of flour—namely, [figures] in the shape of a cow, elephant, camel, horse, donkey, buffalo, ram, goat, deer, boar, monkey, ruru-deer, śarabha, lion, tiger, ape, jackal, wolf, tortoise, fish, parrot, sarika-bird, cuckoo, sparrow, cakravāka-duck, swan, krauñca-bird, crane, peacock, krakara-bird, cakora-partridge, kapiñjala-partridge, and quail.

The physician, having prepared a mandala for him and offered an *arghya* oblation to the Earth with this mantra: "Thou art the first-born, thou art the source, and thou art imperishable," [proceeds] with the *śailaka*, *gṛhaka*, *rathaka*, *yānaka*, *syandanaka*, *śallikā*, *jijjhirikā*, *khairika*, *īśīkā*, *tumbīkā*, *duṣpravāhaka*, *bhadraka*, *saṃcollaka*, *pīṭha-pa---ndikā*, *duhitṛkā*, *kumāra-ka*, *golaganduka*, and other such female amusements.
O Mother of the world with its moving and unmoving beings, you are worshipped here, and you yourself perform sacrifice; as a mother, protect this boy of ours like a son.

May Brahmā approve this; *svāhā*. Then, having seated that boy—who has been bathed, adorned, and dressed in new garments—in the center of the mandala facing east, one should observe the omen in one's heart for a moment: "Whatever he first grasps or touches with his hands, or pulls toward himself, that he shall partake in. Having raised him up, the boy, accompanied by a careful nurse, shall play with these very toys, whether made of metal or otherwise.

"Being entertained by small, non-jarring, non-sharp, straight-moving, well-equipped, capable of drawing and carrying, resonant, and beautiful [instruments], he should sit down once every day for the sake of practice upon a ground provided with a bolster and a rug.
(8) Regarding this, there are these verses:
"On a clean, smeared spot, free from weapons, water, and fire..."
A wise person should not cause one who has been seated to remain so for long;
from sitting too long, there arise numbness, weakness of the hips, curvature of the back, fatigue, fever, and the suppression of feces, urine, and wind, as well as flatulence.
For the very young child sitting constantly upon the ground, sufferings arise immediately: the crushing impact that breaks the limbs;
from that crushing impact comes the state of having shattered limbs, as well as pain and the onset of fever.
Consequently, there is no growth for the fool, nor does his body ever reach maturity;
he is constantly preyed upon by flies, worms, and insects, by storms and gales, and by snakes, rats, mongooses, and the like.

Therefore, a child who is not too old, nor alone, nor a fool, nor afflicted by disease, and who has not yet performed the *apuṇyāha* rite and other such ceremonies, should be made to sit down. (14) Thus it is said.

In that very month, the physician should administer various kinds of fruits as food. For that is the "first feeding" (*annaprāśana*) for one whose teeth have emerged; or else, in the tenth month, on an auspicious day under a lunar mansion presided over by Prajāpati, having worshipped the deities and the Brahmins with meat and food accompanied by ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*), having had a blessing pronounced (*svasti-vācana*), and having spread *darbha* grass upon a leveled ground smeared with cow-dung and scattered with flowers, he should place full jars adorned with perfumes and garlands and *svastika* symbols in four locations.

Having prepared all the playthings and accessories as previously described, and having placed in the center food and drink consisting of the meat of any one of the common quail, grey partridge, francolin, or cock, along with various other well-prepared and desirable side dishes, the physician—facing east—should seat the boy, who is adorned, dressed in fine garments, and protected by the performance of rites for safety, facing west. Then, having kindled a fire and taken the food together with all the side dishes, he should offer oblations with this mantra. 15.

Just as ambrosia is to the gods and nectar is to the lords of the serpents, so food is the life-breath of living beings; indeed, they say that food is Prajāpati himself. From it arise the three aims of life and these very worlds.

"Therefore, O Agni, I offer food to you that leads to the bliss of immortality—Svāhā! May Prajāpati grant his approval. Having made a portion of the remnant of the offering the size of a thumb and well-softened, he should touch it and then place it in the child's mouth; after having eaten it three or five times, he should sprinkle water on the child. Then, having raised him up, he should give him small amounts of food as he desires it when he is twelve months old.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
Liquids prepared from the husked, roasted, and washed grains of old *śāli* or especially *ṣaṣṭika* rice—
seasoned with fat and salt and taken as a linctus— promote the nourishment of children. (19)
Likewise, a powder of wheat or barley, according to suitability,
cooked with viḍaṅga, salt, and fats, is beneficial as a linctus when warm;
for one whose stool is excessively broken, one should administer preparations of kodrava.
One should always give grapes, honey, and ghee to one whose constitution is dominated by pitta;
for one with a vāta constitution, food with salt and the juice of *mātuluṅga* should be given.
One who understands the place, digestive fire, strength, and time should administer these either every other day or every two days.
Or when he sees him hungry, then he should feed him what is suitable to his constitution.
Thus spoke the venerable Kaśyapa.
This concludes the twelfth chapter, titled "The Subsequent Rites for the Birth-Ceremony," among the Khilas.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter, on the treatment of *kukkuṇaka*.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of *kukkuṇaka*.
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
When the mother consumes sweet things for the sake of the prince— fish, meat, milk, vegetables, fresh butter, as well as curd, wine, liquor, flour-based foods, sesame paste, and sour gruel—
One who constantly consumes all kinds of moistening foods at every opportunity,
sleeps during the day after eating again and again, and wakes up unconscious—
the provoked humors (doṣas) of such a person move far away and remain there.
Then, because her channels are obstructed by the *doṣas*, the breast milk becomes vitiated;
when the child drinks that which is known as vitiated *doṣa*,
both mother and son here [suffer] due to their indulgence in salty and sour tastes.
Due to defects in the mother's diet,

from the entry or displacement [of the fetus], and even from exposure to heat or unwholesome substances, an eye disease arising from phlegm and blood occurs in that infant who has not yet begun to eat solid food.
He constantly sheds tears and does not become intoxicated;
being dejected, he rubs his nose and yearns for his ear. He rubs his forehead, the bridge of his nose, and his nose itself.
When one constantly rubs the eyes excessively with the hand,
cannot bear bright light, and tears flow from them,
and there is swelling in the eyelids— one should recognize that as *kukkuṇaka*.
I shall explain its excellent treatment exactly as it is:
one should cause the wet-nurse to vomit and properly administer purgatives;
once she has vomited and been purged, both her breasts should be drained.
One should cause all foods to be served according to what is appropriate.
One should eat what is wholesome and chew what is fit for consumption, while avoiding the opposite.
Furthermore, one should be self-restrained, wearing clean garments, and likewise remain untired and unstained by impurity.
Then, having straightened the child's wound on the path and wiped it clean, the wise physician, having removed the foul blood, should perform an irrigation with *eraṇḍa*,
*rohiṣa*, *tvakkṣīrī*, and *varuṇa*.
Having prepared this decoction, one should sprinkle the boy with it.
One should also press the leaves of *phaṇijjhaka* and *surasā*, along with *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, using the scum of *jāti* wine. 16–17.
One who knows the ritual procedure should apply this as an eye-drop with autumnal water for three days, or even for two days;
[using] the leaves of the *nekarāja*, the *bilva*, and likewise the *accha* tree.

The best eye-drop is considered to be that which is ground with the pulp of the finest *surāgrāma* fruit (19). Kaśyapa praises the application of a paste made from *kola* fruits boiled down, combined with *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, as a facial mask for eye diseases (20).
One should prepare a paste from equal parts of nekarājī, nīlī, surasa, white mustard seeds, and haridrā;
this ointment should be applied to destroy disease in the eyes.
It quickly removes the eye disease known as vedanā.
Having taken turmeric bark and long pepper in equal parts, one should prepare a paste with excellent prasannā wine to form an ointment stick (añjana-varti). 22–23.

A pillikā and an upalepa of these [substances] pacify diseases of the eyes; furthermore, one should administer as an eye-drop (cyotana) excellent sauvīraka, prapauṇḍarīka, lodhra, haridrā, sugar, and honey. 24.
Sprinkling with warm water would be excellent; this application is praised for all eye diseases. This superior method, approved by the Teacher, should be employed at night.
The leaves of *āṭarūṣaka*, *madhūka*, and *saindhava* salt,
as well as the leaves of *puṇḍarīka* and blue lotuses (*nīlotpala*),
combined with lukewarm water, will be beneficial as a medicinal wash (*pariṣeka*). (26–27)
O King, for an abhiṣyanda of kapha-nature, this proven remedy should be prepared:
having added kuṣṭha and jaggery to a decoction of amṛtā, one should grind them with water; this liquid wash is for those suffering from eye diseases.
Those balā-irrigations which were described by me for the emergence of teeth should be applied to those suffering from eye diseases caused by parasites,
having ground together cow’s milk, honey, conch-shell, and rock salt.

Having applied that plaster for seven nights, one should perform the ritual smearing according to the Vedic rites; having ground that [substance] and made it into pills, one should dry them completely in the shade.
Under the Puṣya asterism, all those leaf-like pills are perfected.
There should be two parts of *pṛśniparṇī* and likewise two parts of *aṃśumatī*;
three parts of *urupūga*, one part of *bṛhatī*, and then [one part] each of *rajas*, iron, and copper-iron.
Having ground [the ingredients] with goat’s milk, one should dry them and form them into pills;
these should be fumigated with goat dung and *śamī* leaves.
Likewise, both fresh and dried [pills] are used for eye diseases in children.

One should prepare an eye-salve (añjana) with the primary rasāñjana and the bark of haridrā; this añjana should be made into a medicinal wick (varti). One should grind equal parts of pippalī and śṛṅgavera together.
Then, one should prepare a small collyrium stick with the tip of a blade of *surā* grass;
otherwise, if the child experiences excessive eye pain,
observes fixed eyes, or appears with stiffened eyes, one should employ this procedure.
Having ground together long pepper, ginger, the leaves of the *surasā* plant,
the leaves of *kālamālaka*, and likewise *kuṭheraka*,
one should prepare a medicinal collyrium stick with wine.

One should grind *kapittha*, *bilva*, and *khadira* together with *pillikā* and *upadeha*; this will destroy [the disease] before long. Then, one should add a vessel of goat’s milk; this is the excellent *ścyotana*.
The physician should grind the leaves of the kapittha, aṭarūṣaka, and surasa with goat’s milk and use them as an eye-drop (āścyotana).
He should likewise grind equal parts of madhuka, parvatīya, and haridrā.
One should prepare that unsurpassed eye-drops (āścyotana) with goat’s milk; having ground together the scum of clarified butter (sarpirmaṇḍa), the best of liquor (surāgra), aindrī,
and sandalwood with water, one should make an ointment-stick (añjanavartikā).
One should grind together padmaka, utpala, and madhuka (44),
and apply it as a facial paste for eye diseases along with sugar and goat’s milk;
likewise, śṛṅgavera, mañjiṣṭhā, and the fibers of cotton (45).
One should grind together with water Triphalā, collyrium, and likewise Rasāñjana— these being equal parts— to quickly prepare an excellent facial paste (rasakriyā). 46.
Long pepper, ginger, black pepper, and collyrium; 47.
Triphalā, conch-shell navel, rock salt, and copper powder—these equal parts, ground together, are made into pills in the shade. 48.

Having dried it, one should administer it in cases of various disorders; in cases of *timira* associated with fluid, it should be given with *mārkaava*, and in *kothaka*, it should be ground with the juice of grapes and sour gruel (*kṣudrodaka*). 49.

The pill known as Kokilā is highly regarded for eye diseases; it should be administered by the best of physicians to children who eat wholesome food. The resin of *Naktamāla*, prepared with the scum of clarified butter (*ghṛtamaṇḍa*), [is used for this]. 50–51.
In cases of *timira* (blindness) and itching, this [ointment] is beneficial when prepared with breast milk.

One should prepare pills (*guṭikā*) consisting of golden ochre (*suvarṇagairika*), lac (*lākṣā*), rock salt (*saindhava*), black pepper (*marica*), sugar (*śarkarā*), and the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*). 52.
This pill is known by the wise as Lohitika (the Red One). It should be applied in cases of eye inflammation by one desiring swift relief.
Pippali, Triphala, Vacā, and Kaṭukarohiṇī [are its ingredients]. 53–54.
These six should be in equal parts; the seventh dust is that produced from copper.
These should be ground with water and heated repeatedly by the sun. One should then form them into pills and dry them thoroughly in the shade. 55–56.

One should administer the coarse powder, ground with ghee and goat’s milk, in a decoction for [treatment of] *timira*; it should be given with liquorice (*madhuka*) in cases of streaks (*rāji*). However, in cases arising from the vital spots (*marma*), all [the aforementioned drugs] should be used together in a decoction, as well as in all types of conjunctivitis (*abhiṣyanda*).

Combined with rock salt and mixed with water, it destroys itching (kaṇḍū). One should administer a decoction of the leaves of the leopard’s enemy (the neem tree); with this, slightly warm, one should sprinkle over eye diseases (akṣiroga). 58–59.
One should grind together *sarala*, *madhuka*, and *devadāru*; with this paste, one should apply a plaster to the face during painful conditions.
[60] *Rasāñjana* and *tārkṣyaśilā*, combined with honey, [should be used].
One should employ eye-drops (āścyotana) for the destruction of eye diseases.
The physician should prepare eye-drops consisting of sugar, ginger, breast milk, cow’s bile, and rasāñjana mixed with madhuka. 61–62.
One should grind turmeric and conch-shell navel with water;
this beneficial eye-drop should be prepared with a measured amount of milk.
One should cook turmeric from the mountains in the heat of the sun.
One should grind that [medicine] upon copper plates and sprinkle it with the juice of the *sārasa* plant;
once cooled and thoroughly strained, one should apply it as eye-drops mixed with breast milk to destroy eye diseases.
There should be a portion of ghee and twice as much honey;
at that time, one should apply this to the eye, and the child is liberated from eye disease.
(66) [One should also use] turmeric, conch-shell navel, and *bhadramusta* grass.
Having ground equal portions of vyāghranakha and madhuka,
one should first add śirīṣa seeds to them and form small cakes (pūpikā). These, along with oil, should be cooked in a copper vessel under the heat of the sun.
On the twelfth day, in a windless place and with great care, one should place that very *pūpikā* and oil into a stone vessel free from dust; then,
one should fill the eyes of the patients with this oil.
If administered properly, it quickly destroys the diseases of men; this formulation is highly praised.
(70) One should grind together equal parts of harītakī, āmalakī, haridrā, girijā, and madhuka with water. (71)
This is the primary eye-drop, beneficial for the pacification of diseases; this eye-drop is wholesome for both the elderly and children. (72) One should add one karṣa of fresh pieces of turmeric.
One should give a measured portion of it in a copper vessel, along with one āḍhaka of its essence;
when cooked over a gentle fire until ten parts remain, and then cooled and thoroughly strained, this excellent eye-drop is beneficial. 73–74.
One should wear the unexhausted scales of the *śakalīka* plant for eye diseases;
likewise, by wearing it on the neck or the head, one is freed from disease. [75] Or else, the roots of *ālaṅkatika*, *vāstuka*, and barley [should be used].
Having crushed nine of these, one should apply the thorns to the head;
by this, eye disease and headache—all such ailments—are pacified.
[One should also take] balā, atibalā, and trivṛt, along with the *garbhiṇī* [plant]. (76–77)
Having placed it in the hollow of her left hand, one should press it in an unprecedented manner;
then, one should smear that juice, mixed with honey, along her throat, together with long pepper,
ginger, yellow orpiment, and realgar.
Rasāñjana, tārkṣyaśilā, and the buds of sumanā— these,
ground together with honey and one-seventh part of jaggery,
constitute this preparation known as Kalyāṇikā, an elixir for all diseases.
One should take equal parts of black pepper and ginger,
grind them with sour curd, and smear the mixture onto a copper plate.
Having applied it for seven nights, one should then grind it again with curd.
Then, thin wicks should be prepared, and the physician should apply the collyrium known as *kautuka*. The medicine should be administered gently, without causing harm, and in the proper dosage.
Furthermore, the physician should perform the treatment for the child using a nurse who is from the same region and of the same lineage. 82, 47.
"For some may be bitter, while others may be sweet;
therefore, when treating him gently, one should administer even a sharp remedy in small doses.
Having thus instructed the protector of the earth, the great Ṛṣi [concluded his discourse on] the science of governance.
Then he described the entire medicinal treatment for children:
lodhra and yaṣṭīmadhuka ground together and fried in ghee, bound in a cloth.
A decoction of *guḍūcī*, when applied while warm, destroys all disorders located in the eyes;
thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa. (86–87)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, on the treatment of *kukkuṇaka*, in the *Vṛddhakāśyapīya-saṃhitā*. Now begins the fourteenth chapter, on the treatment of *visarpa*.
Hereafter, we shall explain the treatment of *visarpa*.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Vṛddhajīvaka questioned Kaśyapa, the best of physicians, who possessed splendor equal to the sun and was seated after having offered the Agnihotra sacrifice.
O Blessed One, this disease, resembling the venom of a poisonous serpent, is seen burning the skin, blood, and flesh as they become circular;
it is unbearable, especially for delicate youths. 4.

O Great Sage, out of a desire for the welfare of children, you ought to explain in truth the origin, the form, and the treatment of that being of terrible appearance, whose splendor is equal to a blazing fire.
Thus questioned by his disciple, the great sage spoke as follows:
"From the wrath of the blessed Rudra of immeasurable splendor,
as he bit his lips together, blood fell from them onto the earth."
From that, Lohitāṅka arose, as well as Vaisarpa, which resembles fire.
Therefore, these two are highly burning and cause intense suffering for human beings.
Because it spreads (sarpaṇa) in various ways through the body, it is called Vaisarpa.
From wounds, fractures, or bruises; from the crushing, cutting, or tearing of raw flesh; from the consumption of curd, sour substances, buttermilk, wine, vinegar, and *sauvīraka*;
and from sesame, black gram, horse gram, onion, and garlic. (10)
From the excessive consumption of the meat of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals; from eating incompatible foods, heavy foods, those that cause secretions, putrid, or stale food;
from sleeping during the day and from indigestion; and from the consumption of leafy vegetables and flour-based foods. (11–12)
Due to the consumption of wind, water, clothing, drinks, or food contaminated by poison,
or through other such causes, the vitiated *vāta* and other *doṣas* quickly produce *vaisarpa* (erysipelas) in an infant by thoroughly corrupting the blood and other bodily constituents.
In the same way, when one consumes milk that has been vitiated by aggravated *doṣas*, erysipelas (*vaisarpa*) arises from those *doṣas*;
there are three types: the *vātika*, the *paittika*, and the *ślaiṣmika*, as well as those born from two [doṣas] combined.
These seven types of vesarpa are declared to arise from the combination [of the humors];
vesarpa is never produced without blood and pitta.
It has its seat in the blood, originates from the blood, and pitta is situated within the blood.
Therefore, bloodletting is declared here to be the supreme remedy.
Having considered the strength, season, age, dosha, location, and body,
I shall hereafter describe its indications in due order.

When the wind (vāyu), provoked by the previously mentioned causes, quickly vitiates the blood and other constituents, it produces Vātarakta fever and eruptions (sphoṭas). 19. This [fever] does not [endanger] life.
For those whose bodies are purified from above and below, whose impurities reside in the external channels,
and who have only slight defects from the outset, the physician should first administer this treatment; thereafter, at the appropriate time, he should proceed with decoctions.

One should treat vātavaisarpika first with plasters, affusions, oleation, and massages, as well as bloodletting, wholesome regimens, and the consumption of appropriate drinks, foods, and medicines, according to the specific nature of the underlying complications.
One should cause him to drink old or very old ghee, or ghee from a jar;
or oil mixed with salt is beneficial for his quick massage,
prepared with sour gruel, wine, or *balā*.
One should cook oil with the paste of madhuka and the fresh juice of guḍūcī, along with an equal amount of milk; this is beneficial for its massage.
[One should also use] balā, rāsnā, the two types of bṛhatī, vacā, and punarnavā.
Having ground together pāṭalā, suṣavī, madhuka, and devadāru, one should cook oil with curd; this is beneficial for massage.
[Likewise, oil may be prepared] with bilva, agnimantha, kāśmarya, śyonāka, eraṇḍa, and pāṭala.
One should sprinkle the area with milk or boiled water;
or, for one suffering from vātavīsarpa, one should apply a plaster made of linseed, sesame, and mustard seeds fried in milk and ground with milk, kept in a windless place.

One should grind together *suṣavī*, *surabhī*, *rāsnā*, *varcīvat*, *punarnavā*, *ekāṣṭhīlā*, *palāśa*, and *devadāru* with water or sour liquid; then, one should apply this as an ointment that is unctuous and warm.
One should cause [the patient] to drink ghee processed separately with *tilvaka*, *trivṛt*, or *nīlinī*, or with all of them together, as a purgative; however,
when the *vāyu* (wind) does not subside through these treatments, [further measures must be taken].
Having well-anointed [the patient], one should cause them to sweat using cloths, or again with *veśavāra*,
or with these aforementioned unctuous substances, or with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), or with *kṛsara*,
or with the pastes of dried radish, or with the pastes of *śobhāñjana*.
One should apply a lukewarm poultice to this patient, or follow a regimen that is not excessively hot;
for when the Vāyu has been pacified by sudation, the Pitta may become aggravated like fire.
Therefore, one must act so that the Pitta does not become provoked and the Vāyu is pacified.

Likewise, the physician should employ treatments that alleviate vāta and pitta; in the case of paittika fever, the physician should administer the bitter ghee mentioned in the treatment of fever once the patient is free from āma, and having ascertained that the patient is oleated, he should administer a purgative.
One should drink this decoction of candana, padmaka, uśīra, as well as candana-sārivā,
mṛdvīkā, vidārī, kāśmarya, and parūṣaka,
boiled with vāsā; it destroys erysipelas and fever.
Uśīra, madhuka, grapes, kāśmarya fruits, blue lotuses,
kaśeruka, sugarcane joints, and parūṣaka fruits should be drunk according to the previously described method for the pacification of fever and erysipelas (visarpa).
Having decocted kairāta, madhuka, lodhra, sandalwood, bibhītaka,
padma, utpala, nāgapuṣpa, nāgara, and durālabhā,
one should drink it cold with honey for the pacification of visarpa (erysipelas). 16
One should cook paṭola, candana, mūrvā, guḍūcī, kaṭurohiṇī, mustā, pāṭhā, and yaṣṭīkā according to the previous method;
likewise, vyāghrataka, the two types of haridrā, kuṭaja, and kaṭurohiṇī.
One should drink that [decoction] consisting of guḍūcī, madhuka, and candana;
and one should drink that [decoction] consisting of picumanda, paṭola, dārvī, kaṭukarohiṇī, guḍūcī, and madhuka, as well as candana.
One should drink picumanda, paṭola, dārvī, kaṭukarohiṇī, trāyamāṇā, and yaṣṭīkā for the pacification of visarpa;
likewise, [one may drink] paṭola, nimba, mustā, candana, and uśīra.
One should administer a decoction of musta, āmalaka, uśīra, and sārivā as a drink for the pacification of pitta-type visarpa;
or one should drink a preparation of paṭola, musta, and āmalaka boiled with ghee.
A medicinal paste made from the bark of the udumbara, madhuka, priyaṅgu, and nāgakeśara, along with the filaments (kiñjalka) of the padma and utpala lotuses mixed with ghee, is beneficial;
as are [leaves] derived from the aśvattha, udumbara, plakṣa, vaṭa, vetasa, and jāmbava trees.

One should grind together equal parts of the well-powdered barks of śakṛt, udumbara, aśvattha, vaṭa, and lodhra, along with vetasa bark and śālūka, and soak them in ghee washed a hundred times; this should then be applied as a paste.
This plaster, mixed with rice-water, removes burning sensations and redness;
it should consist of uśīra, candana, śāḍvala grass, conch-shell, utpala,
and the roots of vetasa.
Hrīvera, sandalwood, uśīra, mañjiṣṭhā, kumuda, utpala, śārivā, and the filaments of the lotus constitute an unsurpassed ointment;
likewise, vidārī, sandalwood, uśīra, and candana-śārivā [are used].
The physician should apply a plaster of madhuka and kṣīraśuklā; likewise, a paste of tālīśa, padmaka, uśīra, mañjiṣṭhā, the two types of candana,
prapauṇḍarīka, and madhuka destroys burning sensations.

One should apply a plaster composed of pearl, conch-shell, pearl-oyster shell, rock-crystal, and red ochre, combined with ghee— either using all of these together or as many as are available— or likewise a plaster made from plantain, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, reed, and bamboo.
The roots of sandalwood, uśīra, padmaka, ṛṣabha, and jīvaka;
the leaves of the white water-lily and the blue lotus; mūrvā, saugandhika, lotus stalks, vīśa, śālūka, tṛṇaśūla, and ikṣuvālikā.
One should collect prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, tālīśa, kaśeruka, the roots of ikṣu and vetasa, along with anantā and the bark of milk-exuding trees, as well as śatāvarī, mañjiṣṭhā, and kumbhīkā.
Having thoroughly agitated these ingredients, the wise physician should let them soak in water overnight;
then, having drained that decoction, he should administer it as a wash,
or he should cook ghee with these same ingredients along with milk for use as an ointment.
With this very decoction, the physician should cook an equal amount of milk until it is reduced to one-fourth; he should then churn it with a churning-stick,
and from that, the ghee that rises should be further processed with eight times the amount of milk.
One should administer ghee cooked with the pastes of *payasyā*, *madhuka*, and *candana* for massage, food, and drink; it destroys *vaisarpa*. [The remainder of the verse follows:
"smeared with ghee..."
One should sprinkle [the area] with a cold decoction of yaṣṭīmadhuka, milk, sugarcane juice, or the bark-water of the vaṭa and other trees;
or one should apply an ointment made from the paste of vaṭa and other trees mixed with ghee.

Likewise, one should repeatedly apply clarified butter that has been washed a thousand times or a hundred times, or that which has been raised from milk, to this condition when there is burning; however, if the swelling spreads while accompanied by pain and lack of suppuration, [one should act accordingly].
For those whose internal bodies are purified, one should remove blood by means of leeches;
having drained the vitiated blood,
one should effect the purification of the blood with cool pastes made from the milky trees mixed with ghee, as previously described.
In cases of Kaphaja visarpa from the very beginning, one should administer emesis; or, for those with mild doshas, one should first perform fasting (langhana) and then apply this treatment:
Musta, Patha, the two types of Haridra, Kushtha, Tejovati, and Vaca.

One should cause this patient to drink a decoction of śārṅgeṣṭhā, triphalā, mūrvā, agni, haimavatī, vatsaka, ativiṣā, and kaṭukarohiṇī, and should also apply an ointment made from these same ingredients ground into a paste.
The physician should boil *āragvadha*, *somavalka*, *kuṭaja*, *ativiṣā*, *ghana*, *pāṭhā*, *mūrvā* along with *śārṅgeṣṭhā*, and *kuṣṭha*;
one should drink that decoction at the proper time and apply an ointment made from these same ingredients well-ground as a paste.
By this, his itching, urticarial patches, and swelling are quickly pacified;
or one afflicted by erysipelas and fever should drink a decoction of *amṛtā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *parpaṭa*, and *durālabhā*, mixed with honey.
Having decocted triphalā, uśīra, mustā, eraṇḍa, and devadāru, one should sprinkle [the area], or else with water from nimba leaves, or with the bark of śigru,
surasā, sphoṭa, kālamāla, and phaṇijjhaka.
One should administer water boiled with *sāṭarūṣa* as a sprinkling;
alternatively, a sprinkling with *khadira* water or cow’s urine is beneficial.
[Also beneficial are] house-soot, the two types of *haridrā*, and the sprouts of *mālatī*.
One should grind together viḍaṅga, the two types of haridrā, pippalī, talalaṇḍikā, mustā, amṛtā, the two types of haridrā, the tender leaves of paṭola and ariṣṭa,
kuṭaja, ativiṣā, mustā, and kuṣṭha.
House-soot, turmeric, and rock salt—
these formulations prescribed as half-verses should be applied as a paste mixed with a small amount of ghee; they eliminate swelling, itching, and pain.
Saptaparṇa, khadira, musta, the bark of āragvadha,
kuraṇṭaka, and devadāru constitute an unsurpassed medicinal paste;
likewise, a single application of palāśa ash mixed with cow’s urine is an excellent ointment.
For the purpose of massage, mustard oil mixed with alkali or rock salt should be used, or alternatively,
karanja oil; or one may apply a powder of kuṣṭha and rock salt by rubbing it over the body after it has been anointed with oil.

One should cook oil with svarjikā, ativiṣā, musta, tvak, elā, ilvālaka, arthavatsaka, śatāhvā, aguru, and kuṣṭha— all ground together. This should be applied as an ointment to destroy itching, urticaria, and eruptions.
Having ground the root of *śigru* and *ahiṃsrā*, one should cook ghee;
with that, one should anoint the patient's body, or alternatively with *kuṣṭha*-oil. If the disease is not pacified by this procedure, [then another treatment should be applied].
One should cauterize with circular burns those areas that are itchy and burning;
thereafter, one should administer purgation and bleed the patient.
Once the vitiated blood has been removed, one should perform treatments to purify the blood.
"With the pastes of triphalā mixed with ghee and combined with madhuka and udumbara"—
thus has the treatment for those erysipelas (vaisarpa) born from vāta and the other [doshas] been proclaimed, both in summary and in detail, and separately as well.
And this very same combination should be employed for mixed dishes:
old barley, śāli rice, mung beans, lentils,
and reṇuka beans should be used for food, as well as meat from wild animals and birds.
"One should treat masūrikā with its eruptions, as well as kakṣyā and pāmā,
which arise from the combination of pitta and blood, in the same manner as one treats visarpa;
so said the Blessed Kaśyapa."
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, on the treatment of erysipelas (*vaisarpa*), in the *Bhārgavīyā Saṃhitā*, within the section on miscellaneous topics (*khilasthāna*).
Now begins the fifteenth chapter, on the treatment of skin diseases (*carmadala*).
Hereafter, we shall explain the chapter titled "The Treatment of Skin Diseases. 1.

Thus indeed spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa. Then, having saluted the Blessed Kaśyapa—the best of sages, surrounded by a host of seers and blazing with Brahmanic splendor—the descendant of Bhṛgu (Bhārgava) asked: "O Blessed One, what is this disease called Carmadala? It spreads like a fire-burn and produces extreme affliction in the limbs of children. How does it arise? What is the cause for its occurrence in infants who drink milk, in boys who consume both milk and solid food, and in those of new age who eat fresh grains? What is its nature, how many types are there, and what are its [symptoms]?"

"You should explain what the symptoms and complications are. Then the Blessed One said: "O child, listen! Indeed, in this world, due to defects in breast milk, infants who are nursing suffer; and due to defects in breast milk as well as defects in food, children who subsist on milk and solid food—being delicate, having unstable bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and possessing bodies as tender as those accustomed to the womb-bed—suffer from contact with clothing, cradles, heat, wind, sun, sweat, poultices, their own impurities, urine, and feces; from lack of cleanliness, hand-pressing, excessive rubbing, and the like practices of their families. [These affect] the mouth, throat, hands, feet, scrotum, perineum, waist, and limbs..."

And it arises in the joints, but not in those who are well-nourished or in those who have reached middle age. What is the reason? Because for those whose skin, bones, and tissues are firm, hard, and compact, and whose bodies are strengthened by constant exercise, this disease does not occur as they are able to endure suffering.

Because it consists predominantly of wind, they declare it to be of the nature of air (*vāyvātmaka*). It is called "skin-splitter" (*carmadala*) because it tears the skin. It is of four types: *vātika*, *ślaiṣmika*, and *sānnipātika*. 6.

In this regard, if the mother or nurse of an infant is habituated to harsh conduct, irregular eating, fasting, and so forth, or if she excessively indulges in excessive walking, physical exercise, and fatigue, her wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated and vitiates the breast milk. Its characteristics are as follows: when placed in water, it floats, breaks apart, forms a film like a parasol, appears dark-brown, and is bitter, astringent, or tasteless in its flavor.

For a person drinking that [poison], these symptoms arise: circular patches on the body that are itchy, cracked, rough, and dark-complexioned; small, discolored moles; diarrhea; accompanied by trembling, dryness of the mouth, and horripilation; and suffering from *vāta-carmadala* (a skin disease caused by wind).

When, however, the wet-nurse, being under the sway of anger, distress, or by consuming hot, sour, salty, pungent, or burnt foods and eating excessively, her *pitta* becomes aggravated; being dispersed by the *vāyu*, it follows the milk-carrying channels and vitiates the breast milk. Its symptoms are as follows: when cast into water, it appears greenish, reddish, or blackish; furthermore, it is pungent, sour, salty, or bitter in taste, and hot to the touch.

In a person drinking that [liquor], these symptoms arise: circular patches appear that have a reddish-blue luster, a dark-yellow appearance, dry skin, and are hot; they are filled with putrid humors, spreading, tearing the skin and flesh, and when they burst, they resemble lotus petals or look like burns from fire. Consequently, the person suffers from diarrhea characterized by green or yellow stools and inflammation of the anus, and is frequently afflicted with burning sensations, dryness of the mouth, vomiting, and a peeling of the skin due to the excess of *pitta*.

Now, if a wet-nurse excessively indulges in heavy, sour, salty, sweet, and obstructive foods, as well as daytime sleep, laziness, and unwholesome habits, her *śleṣman* (phlegm) becomes aggravated; being stirred up by the *vāyu* (wind), it vitiates the breast milk. Its characteristics are as follows: it sinks to the bottom in water, is thick in appearance, abundant in oiliness, cold and slimy to the touch, and sweet in taste.

In a person drinking that [liquor], these symptoms arise: he is afflicted by numerous white, cold, motionless, glossy, and thick circular patches that cause only slight pain; he is covered with eruptions the size of mustard seeds that take a long time to suppurate and are accompanied by itching. Then, catarrh, anorexia, heaviness of the limbs, cough, and suppuration occur in him; he frequently passes slimy stools, groans, vomits phlegm, is overcome by drowsiness, and his palate and lips become white—this is *śleṣmacarmadala*. 9

When, however, she drinks milk that is affected by the combination of all three doṣas, then circular patches appear on her body—appearing blackish-red or like burnt jaggery, endowed with the qualities of all three doṣas, quick to suppurate, foul-smelling, cracked, and discharging a putrid, corpse-like secretion. With his entire body covered by these, he groans incessantly, cries with great distress, takes no pleasure in the breast, and suffers from diarrhea that is blackish or reddish in appearance. This condition, being of the nature of *sannipāta*, is incurable.
Furthermore, one who is afflicted with complications such as vomiting, thirst, fever, flatulence, swelling, hiccups, dyspnea, and hoarseness of voice should be rejected for treatment.
Regarding this, there are verses:
"One should not undertake the treatment of that which is incurable, but one should strive to cure that which is curable."
Whatever form one may perceive arising from dualities, or a maturation that exceeds its outward appearance—
having understood each of these, one should properly apply the remedy so that,
even when treated, it does not recur again and again without reaching pacification.
Therefore, this disease arising from birth is not to be trusted in any way;

consequently, it must be properly treated according to the therapy I shall describe. First of all, one should have the wet-nurse, who has been prepared with oleation, massage, and sudation, drink ghee mixed with the powder of *nīlikā*, or ghee mixed with the powder of *trivṛt*. Thereafter, she should eat soft boiled rice along with light and unctuous soups prepared with various ingredients and seasoned with pomegranate and rock salt; she should remain devoted to a bed and seat in a windless place. She must avoid physical exercise, eating when the previous meal is undigested, and sexual intercourse.

One should have her drink a decoction of vidārigandhā, eraṇḍa, bṛhatī, gokṣuraka, punarnavā, and pṛśniparṇī for the purpose of purifying the breast milk, or else a decoction of the two groups of five roots (pañcamūla). A paste of rāsnā, sugandhā, and nākulī is an ointment for the breasts; likewise, an external application (pradeha) combined with ajagandhā, avalguja, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā; or a paste of śatāhvā, madhuka, ajagandhā, kāśmarya, bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārikā, balā, pīlu, and guḍūcī; or a paste of bhadramusta, tvak, and aguru; or old ghee mixed with a paste of sesame.

Now, a decoction of *ūrūpūga*, *palāśa*, *pāṭali*, and *rāsnā* is for sprinkling (*pariṣeka*), or it may be done with lukewarm milk. Oil cooked with *devadāru*, *rāsnā*, *barhiṇa*, and *majjā* is for massage (*abhyañjana*); or oil cooked with *bilva*, *devadāru*, *cūta*, and *muktiphala*; or oil cooked with the two types of *balā*, *bilva* root, *suradāru*, and *āmrapeśikā*. Thus, the treatment for wind-afflicted skin diseases (*vātacarmadala*) has been declared. 15

Now we shall describe the treatment for the Pitta-type [fever]. It is as follows: one should treat the wet-nurse with oleation and massage, followed by emesis and purgation. One should induce emesis with a paste of *pippalī* mixed with *nimba* water, or with *pippalī* and salt for the purpose of eliminating the morbid humors (*doṣas*). One should induce purgation with *mṛdvīkā*, sugarcane juice, *abhayā*, and so forth; or with a combination of *mṛdvīkā* and *āmalaka*; or with milk combined with a decoction of the pulp of *āragvadha* fruit—having observed the patient's strength accordingly. One should then provide nourishment with gruel (*yavāgū*) or with soups prepared according to the rules for both processed and unprocessed foods.

Having prepared a decoction of *kāśmarya*, *madhuka*, *parūṣaka*, and *śītapākya*, one should administer it well-cooled and mixed with sugar and honey for the purpose of purifying the breast milk; likewise, one may administer a decoction of *payasyā*, *sārivā*, *amṛtā*, *madhūka*, and *mṛdvīkā* combined with sugar.

A paste of *prapauṇḍarīka*, *sārivā*, *uśīra*, and *candana* is an ointment for the breasts; or a poultice (*pradeha*) consisting of *madhuka*, milk, *śuklā*, *candana*, *rasāñjana*, and *tuṅgī*; or a paste of *yaṣṭīmadhuka* and *candana*; or a paste of *madhuka*, *candana*, *bhadramustā*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *rasāñjana*, and *añjana*; or a paste of *rasāñjana*, *sārivā*, *madhuka*, *candana*, *uśīra*, and *kalka*; or a paste of *kakubha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, *nala*, roots, *śālūka*, and *vañjula* mixed with clarified butter; or a paste of *viśa*, *mṛṇāla*, *padmaka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *padma*, and *rasāñjana*.

Having boiled Madhuka, Madhuparṇī, Veḍa, Vetasa, Śatāvarī, Nalamūla, Kadalī, Kuśa, Kāśa, Padma, Utpala, Ikṣu, Vidārī, the bark of Vaṭa and Udumbara, Jambū, Kumbhīkā, and Madhurā in one Āḍhaka of water until reduced to a quarter part, one should cook one Prastha of ghee with that decoction and twice as much milk. To this "pregnant" (sagarbha) preparation, one should add well-ground Mañjiṣṭhā, Vitūrṇaka, Payasyā, Dhātakī, Uśīra, Candana, Kṣīrakākolī, Prapauṇḍarīka, Kṣīraśuklā, Tālīsa, and Mṛdvīkā; having prepared it thus, one should apply it as an unguent.

Then, one should dust [the area] with this powder made from lodhra, madhuka, dāruharidrā, āmalakī bark, and leaf-powder; by this means, fever, burning sensations, redness, suppuration, ulcers, and so forth are pacified—this is the excellent treatment for pitta-type skin diseases (carmadalā). 16.

Hereafter, we shall describe the treatment for the phlegmatic (ślaiṣmika) type: first, having attended to the wet-nurse according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should have her drink gruel (yavāgū) prepared with nimba decoction and madanaphala, seasoned with distinct salt; or else, gruel prepared with the paste of madanaphala, sesame, and rice. For the purpose of removing phlegm from her body—which has been made comfortably salty and unctuous—one should induce vomiting by drinking long pepper (pippalī) with warm water according to the rules for emesis. Once she has undergone emesis, head-purgation (śirovirecana) should be administered.

One should eat soft rice with a soup prepared from any one of the following: mudga, satīna, the tips of vetra, paṭola, nimba, or mustaka. One should drink a decoction of kuṭaja fruit, mustā, priyaṅgu, śārṅgeṣṭhā, pāṭhā, lodhra, guḍūcī, and mūrvā—each in a dose of one akṣa—with lukewarm water as it becomes available; or one may lick a paste of pāṭhā and fresh ginger, or a paste of kuṭaja fruit and pāṭhā, or the powder of kirātatiktaka and mustā, with honey.

One should administer a decoction made from *bhadramustā*, *ariṣṭa*, *paṭola*, *mūrvā*, *dāruharidrā*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and the bark of *saptaparṇa*, prepared with honey under the pretext of a medicinal preparation. Furthermore, one should apply an ointment of the paste of *mustaka* and *mālatī* leaves to the breasts. Then, for purgation, one should employ *trivṛt* combined with *triphalā*, hot water, and salt; thereafter, a soup (*yūṣa*) is the prescribed regimen for food.

A medicinal paste (pradeha) composed of *kuṭaja*, *ariṣṭa*, *āragvadha*, *madana*, *svādukaṇṭaka*, *mustaka*, and *naktamāla*; or one combined with *kuṣṭha*, *śukanāsā*, *rohiṇī*, *mustaka*, *kirātatikta*, and *ativiṣā*; or one consisting of *surasā*, *śigru*, *mustaka*, *kālamālaka*, *viḍaṅga*, *hiṅgu*, and *parṇī*; or a paste of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and *dāruharidrā*; or a paste of *haridrā* and *rasāñjana*—these are to be applied. Furthermore, oil prepared with *bhadramusta*, *uśīra*, *āphoṭā*, *āṭarūṣaka*, *haridrā*, *karañja*, *sumanā*, and *ariṣṭa* should be used for massage.
On this subject, there is a verse: "Thus has the origin of *carmadala* been explained according to its color and form."
"It should be treated according to the sequence of curable and incurable conditions," so said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, on the treatment of skin diseases (*carmadala*), within the *Khila* section. 15.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter, the Treatment of Amlapitta.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of amlapitta;
thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.
From eating incompatible foods, from overeating, from indigestion, and from filling the stomach with undigested matter;
from uncooked flour-based foods, from fermented liquors, and from cow's milk products; and from consuming heavy or non-purgative foods, as well as from the suppression of natural urges.
From the excessive consumption of things that are very hot, unctuous, dry, sour, or liquid;
from the habitual use of molasses, products of sugarcane, and horse gram (kulattha); and likewise from roasted grains, parched grain-powder, and flattened rice (pṛthuka).
By eating repeatedly, by sleeping during the day, by excessive bathing and immersion in water,
by drinking water while still inside [the house], and by consuming food that has been kept overnight,
the *vāta* and other humors become aggravated; when any one of these occurs—
When the digestive fire has become weak, it diminishes the bodily heat;
furthermore, for that evil-minded person who continues to indulge in these very things,
whatever he eats or drinks is indeed consumed by that fire.
That which is over-digested (vidagdha) turns into sourness (śukta); when it remains in the stomach (āmāśaya), it is called *amlapitta* because it excessively vitiates the *pitta*.
This occurs in a person of restless mind who, out of greed, indulges in improper food.
Just as milk poured into a vessel of curd does not become sour so long as it is not dry, but quickly turns sour and becomes a mass of curds;
so too, food that is eaten and released into the acidic essence (rasadhātu) undergoes burning digestion.
While the locus remains unimpaired, whether one is awake or even sleeping,
the digestive fire (pācaka), impelled by the samāna wind through its connection with exhalation and inhalation,
and fanned by the udāna wind, thoroughly performs the act of digestion.
Thus the etiology has been stated; hereafter I shall describe the symptoms:
diarrhea, heaviness of the abdomen, sour eructation, headache, pain in the heart, distension of the belly, lassitude of the limbs, and rumbling in the intestines. (13–14)
The throat and chest burn, and horripilation occurs;
this is the general symptom, while the specific characteristics will now be taught.
From [an excess of] Vāta, there is pain, weakness of the limbs, yawning, and relief through lying on oily substances.
From pitta arise vertigo and a burning sensation, and relief is found in sweet and cold things.
(16) From kapha there is heaviness and vomiting, and relief is found in dry and hot things.
(17) This disease arises from the stomach (āmāśaya), where kapha and pitta are its substrates.
Therefore, from the very beginning, for the sake of cutting off its root while his strength and flesh are not yet diminished, a wise physician should prescribe emesis; indeed,
there is no other honored method for his pacification than emesis.
Just as a tree suffers from the reversal of its trunk and branches when its roots are severed,
so too does one suffer from the remnants of a fault that persists after it has been vomited up;
one should effect the pacification of such a condition through fasting and light meals.
When there is provocation of the *doṣas*, one should not suddenly administer liquid medicine using formulations that are wholesome and timely, yet merely palliative or digestive;
for, except in the case of those intended for emesis, such medicine will not be properly digested. (21–22)
When it has been slightly digested by means of specific activities and diet, that which was drunk then produces pacification, digestion, and breaking [of morbid humors].
(23) Nāgara, ativiṣā, and mustā; nāgara, ativiṣā, and abhayā.
Trāyamāṇā, the leaf of paṭola, and kaṭukarohiṇī— these three,
each weighing three karṣas, should be drunk according to the observation of the specific doṣa; or else a decoction of kirātatikta, or even that of rohiṇī alone.
For the ascetic whose defects have been removed through association and whose internal organ (āśaya) is purified, the wise man should strive to establish the digestive fire (agni).
Just as a fire that has been extinguished is rekindled by means of fine cow-dung powder and other such materials, [so too should the fire be maintained]. 26.
Just as fire, its strength gradually augmented, consumes even moist fuel,
so too the bodily fire, when fully aroused in those of purified bodies,
digests the food and drink of embodied beings, including even that which is substantial. 27–28.
When these [nutrients] have been properly transformed, diseases resulting from undigested matter (*āma*) do not occur;

instead, enthusiasm, contentment, nourishment, and bodily strength arise. Then, for the embodied being whose vital breath (*prāṇa*) has been generated through this specific sequence, [the following occurs].
One should expel the morbid humors located in the colon by means of purgation;
or one should administer emesis with lukewarm salt water, milk, sugarcane juice, honey-water, or bitter decoctions.
Triphalā, trāyamāṇā, kaṭukā, rohiṇī,
and trivṛt— of these five, half a pala each [should be taken], while the trivṛt itself is half that portion.
Having drunk this purgative, one is indeed liberated from amlapitta.
One should boil together half a pala each of patola leaves and the bark of the three myrobalans (triphalā),
one karṣa each of trāyantī, rohiṇī, nimba, and yaṣṭikā, and two palas of masūra lentils. 33–34.
One should boil it again until one-eighth of an āḍhaka of water remains as a clear residue;
then, adding one kuḍava of ghee, one should reduce it until half a prastha remains.
Having drunk that when it is neither too cold nor too hot, one is easily and quickly purged.
This quickly dispels even long-standing acid dyspepsia (amlapitta),

and it swiftly destroys vāta-pitta disorders, fever, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), erysipelas (vaisarpa), gout (vātaśoṇita), abscesses (vidradhi), blood-born abdominal tumors (raktagulma), and eruptive boils (visphoṭa). 36–37.
Ancient varieties of rice, mung beans, lentils, and kidney beans;
cow’s ghee or milk; and the meat of wild animals and birds; 38 as well as peas, pot-herbs, pūtīka, vāsā flowers, and vāstūka.
Furthermore, other vegetables that are bitter and light (39) are highly commended as food, as are whatever else is non-burning; likewise,
the practice of those habits mentioned above and the application of things suited to one's constitution (40).
Garlic, chebulic myrobalan, long pepper, ghee,
and aged wine increase the strength of the digestive fire; furthermore,
one should avoid the causes of this disease as well as the factors mentioned as its etiological origins.
For one who is moderate in food and conduct, who practices disciplined exercise,
who is free from restlessness, and who possesses self-control, this ulcer subsides;
and whatever humor (doṣa) may be the underlying cause for a particular person, it is for the pacification of that humor [that treatment is prescribed].
The physician should constantly strive for its pacification; thus it is quelled.
This [disease] generally occurs in embodied beings in marshy regions.
Therefore, one should treat it with medicines derived from arid lands.
If this [suffering] does not subside, one should go to another land;
that very place is home where there is health and those kinsmen who, whether they come or do not come, act for his benefit.
For the embodied being who is perpetually restless, miserable, and deeply afflicted,
all activities fail and his own kin become strangers.
Therefore, a wise person should always strive for health.
One who is free from disease attains the fruit of life and happiness.
(48) One who is afflicted by these complications—fever, diarrhea, anemia, colic, swelling, loss of appetite, and vertigo—and whose bodily constituents are depleted, does not achieve recovery. (49)
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, on the treatment of Amlapitta, in the Khilas;
now begins the seventeenth chapter, on the treatment of swelling (Śotha).
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Treatment of Swelling" (Śothacikitsita).
Thus spoke the venerable Kaśyapa:
For one who has vomited, purged, or been emaciated by fevers and other ailments...
For one who has been afflicted by a major fast, who eats incompatible or indigestible food, and who immediately consumes excessively salty, alkaline, hot, sour, and pungent flavors,
as well as the meat of pigs, sheep, and the like, or eats curd and clay; (3–4)

For one who excessively indulges in cold things, exposure to wind, physical exercise, or sexual intercourse, as well as for a woman who has given birth with difficulty, or whose fetus has been expelled, or who feels aversion toward her own medical treatment; 5. [In these cases, the blood does not flow properly.]
For those two who practice this very same cause,
a severe swelling of four types quickly arises:
that caused by wind (vātika), that caused by bile (paittika), that caused by phlegm (ślaiṣmika), and that caused by the combination of all three (sānnipātika).
Exogenous [poisoning] arises from wounds, crushing injuries, contact with fire and the like,
being bitten, urination upon, smelling, touch, or the application of artificial poisons (garayoga).
This is generally proclaimed as the cause for the provocation of all [the humors].

Previously, in the section on the etiology of fever, I have described each of these individually; hereafter, I shall correctly explain their specific symptoms. In the afternoon, there is a certain increase in swelling caused by the nature of Vāyu.
In the forenoon, [the fever] of one with a predominance of phlegm (ślaiṣmika) occurs; in the midday, that of one with a predominance of bile (paittika);
and in the first, middle, and latter watches of the night, there is a gradual decrease of these [fevers] respectively.
It is dark-colored or of the same color as the skin, and it rises and subsides quickly.
As if swarming with ants, it feels distressed and pricked;
in one afflicted by irregular fever, it eventually burns, the hair on it stands on end, it becomes unstable when touched by a finger, and it sinks when pressed.

The swelling born of Vāta increases in the lower body along with the vessels, ligaments, skin, and muscles; it is relieved by unctuous and warm treatments, is dry, and appears blue, red, or yellow, being frequently afflicted with a burning sensation. (14)

It ripens quickly, is accompanied by diarrhea, thirst, burning sensations, and fever; it is especially prominent at the navel and the base of the bladder. There is a constant craving for cold things, and swelling arises from the Pitta. (15–16)
It is stable, cold, very thick, smooth, pale, and slightly painful;
it is accompanied by nausea, anorexia, sleepiness, itching, hardness, and heaviness.
It attains growth only after a long time and subsides only after a long time. (17)
There is a specific enlargement of his chest, cheeks, and eye-sockets;
this swelling, caused by phlegm, induces cold fever and a loathing for cold, appearing blue, yellow, or reddish in hue, and is covered with a network of veins. 18–19.
A swelling (śvayathu) arising from the combination of all three humors (sānnipātika) is characterized by many complications and discharges,

possesses all symptoms, is accompanied by extremely intense pain, and is incurable. A swelling that is reddish, dark-brown, or livid, excessively hot, and associated with pricking, piercing, and aching pains [is caused by blood].
An exogenous swelling is accompanied by poison; it is copper-colored or black, and spreads rapidly.
It intensely causes nausea, anorexia, thirst, fainting, fever, and vomiting.
Thus, the sixfold characteristics of swelling have been described by me.
In men, [the semen] originates from the feet; in women, it originates from the mouth;
that which resides in the private parts of both is omnipresent, yet it does not achieve success.
Wind is declared to be the root cause of all swellings.

Just as bile [is the cause] of burning and phlegm of coldness, so too swelling increases by taking hold of the skin, blood, flesh, and fat; one should therefore quickly perform treatment for this dreadful condition according to its progressive stages.

In a patient with a body emaciated by swelling where kapha and pitta predominate, one should administer treatments such as emesis; the same applies when vāyu predominates. A patient suffering from swelling should eat śāli rice in moderation with the broth of mung beans.
Or, at the beginning, for one whose stomach and internal organs are light, [one should administer] ghee prepared with *sabālamūlaka-vyoṣa-pippalīka*, or with *pañcagavya*,
or with *kalyāṇaka*, *tikta*, or *daśamūlādika* [ghees]. 27–28.
Once the patient has been lubricated and sweated, one should administer emesis and then purgation.
Thereafter, for ten days, he should eat with milk or even abstain from food.
Following that, he should gradually habituate himself to barley-based food with buttermilk according to his strength.

One should consume soup made from five handfuls of herbs, or the broth of wild animals; one should also partake of curd, wine, fermented liquors, fats, vegetables, flour-based foods, and sour substances.
One must avoid unwholesome things, the primary causes [of disease], and instead practice what is beneficial.
Having risen in the morning, one should eat ginger with jaggery;
or one should constantly practice taking three *harītakī* fruits with jaggery;
or one may follow the regimen of increasing the dose of *pippalī* (the *pippalī-vardhamāna*), or take *pippalī* with licorice (*madhuka*). 32.
One should drink the powder or paste of devadāru,
bhārṅgī, and śuṇṭhī, or else the decoction of these three along with punarnavā;
or likewise, mahauṣadha, citraka, pippalī, or devadāru.
By consuming [the medicine] with buttermilk or milk, one will become comfortable;
