or milk boiled with the roots of *citrā*, *agnika*, *śyāmā*, and *trivyoṣa* [may be used].
One may also drink *mahauṣadha* or the paste of *devadāru* with milk.

One whose swelling is great should drink this—gandharvahasta, the three pungents (trivyoṣa), and the root of śyāmā as the fifth—boiled in milk; furthermore, one should drink cow urine, buffalo urine, or camel urine. 36–37.
One should apply these mixed with their respective milks for the pacification of swelling;
furthermore, one should cook ghee in a decoction of *punarnavā* with the pastes (*kalka*) of these [drugs]—*vyoṣa*, *mustā*, and so forth—day after day. (38)
This application is prescribed for all types of swellings (39).
Having drunk this powder— iron filings, the three pungents (trikaṭu), trivṛtā, and kaṭurohiṇī— with the juice of triphalā, one shall become comfortable (40).
One should powder triphalā, trivṛtā, dantī, viḍaṅga, gajapippalī, the three pungents (trivyoṣa), rohiṇī, devadāru, and citraka (41).
Having practiced this with twice as much iron powder along with milk, one is liberated [from disease].
Equal parts of the three pungents (trivyoṣa), the three fruits (triphalā), mustā, viḍaṅga, and citraka— these nine ingredients— and likewise nine parts of iron powder;
having licked this powder with honey, one should eat barley and ṣaṣṭika rice.
One may take *bhallātaka* with a soup of dried radish, or with milk mixed with *mustā*;
likewise, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, the three pungents (*trivyoṣa*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *agnika*, sesame seeds, jaggery, *viḍaṅga*, honey, ghee, and iron powder [may be used]. 44.
Indeed, the electuary known by the name Kaṭukabindu is a crusher of swelling;
this has been explained in general. Now learn from me its specific [applications]; therein, first of all, I shall declare the medical treatment for the Vātika type. 45–46.

Oil prepared in a decoction of *kulattha*, barley, *kola*, and both the five roots (*pañcamūla*), with these paste ingredients in equal parts— *śatāvarī*, *kṛṣṇagandhā*, *yaṣṭī*, *madhuka*, and the vitalizers (*jīvana*)— [is used for massage]. 47.
One should drink that [mixture] with milk at the proper time, and one should also apply it as an ointment.
Having ground together śatāhvā, madhuka, dāru, śvetā, gavādanī, and vatsādanī, one should apply it lukewarm to the swelling.
Having decocted varcīva, bilva, eraṇḍa, tarkārī, and punarnavā,
one should sprinkle the swelling with the resulting liquid while it is warm.
[50] Of sesame, mustard, wheat, and barley...
One should apply a poultice (upanāha) made of powders mixed with oil;
likewise, a poultice may be made of roasted castor seeds (eraṇḍa-bīja).
[The ingredients for this are] castor, root of the wood-apple (bilva), bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā. 51–52.

Karañja, ciribilva, and śvadaṃṣṭrā, taken in equal parts and applied as a paste mixed with ghee, destroy swelling caused by Vāta. This same formulation, used as a sprinkling (pariṣeka) according to availability, brings comfort.
Śārivā, dried radish root, śukanāsā, and mahauṣadha;
54 kuṣṭha, mustā, water, and lambā—this application is a destroyer of swelling.
Also, śvadaṃṣṭrā, castor root, bilva root, and mahauṣadha. 55

One should boil milk with the decoction of these [herbs] whose roots are from the Purāṇas; having taken the milk when only the milk remains, one should administer it at the proper time with ghee and sugar according to the patient's digestive fire. This destroys swelling caused by Vāta.
One should drink castor oil with cow's milk or with cow's urine. By this, his remaining morbid humors and the swelling are eliminated;
he should eat light foods that are combined with unctuous and warm substances.
Now I shall describe the treatment for that arising from pitta:
with equal parts of *abhayā*, *āmalakī*, *dantī*, the three purificatory actions (*trikarma*), honey, sandalwood, *saṃjīvanīya* drugs, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and the flowers of *madhūka*. (59)
Ghee cooked with milk is the best ointment for swelling;
this should also be administered as a drink to alleviate the disease of swelling.
[The herbs used are] Jīvaka, Ṛṣabhaka, Aindrī, Madhuparṇī, and Śatāvarī.
A plaster consisting of *mudita*, *vetasa*, and *sarasāñjana*;
or *tālīśa*, *uśīra*, *mudita*, *candana*, and *sarasāñjana*;
and *madhuka* and *padmaka*—this plaster destroys swelling.
One should administer a paste of śatāvarī, haṃsapadī, madhuparṇī, citraka, bandā,
and tālīsapatra for swelling and other such conditions;
furthermore, a decoction of the bark and roots of milk-exuding trees (kṣīradruma) should be used for sprinkling.
Milk boiled with Trivṛt, Madhuka, Mṛdvīkā, and Kāśmarya, along with sugar and milk, is beneficial for digestion and the pacification of rāga-pāka;
or one should administer another purgative according to the specific condition.
One should consume milk and liquid foods that are not too clear, smooth, or cold, but rather sweet and light, in the prescribed quantities;
now listen further to the treatment for swelling caused by *kapha*.

One should drink a decoction of *hrīvera*, *agaru*, *dāru*, *cavya*, *citraka*, *nāgara*, *abhayā*, *pippalīmūla*, the two types of *rajanī*, and *hiṅgu* in appropriate proportions, or one may drink these ground with cow’s urine; this destroys swelling (*śopha*). 68.
One should drink a decoction of citraka, āragvadha, mūrvā, viḍaṅga, āmalaka, abhayā, pippalī, śārivā, and pāṭhā with honey. Likewise,
one should take equal parts of devadāru, pāṭhā, and śṛṅgavera [in a similar preparation].
Likewise, one should drink puṣkaramūla boiled in cow’s urine;
as well as pāṭhā, mustā, abhayā, dāru, citraka, viśvabheṣaja (ginger),
pippalī, ativiṣā, mūrvā, and tāḍakapatrikā.

In cases of afflictions, one should drink that [milk] purified [by straining], which destroys phlegm and swelling. (72) A plaster consisting of tagara, agaru, mustā, sarala, devadāru, kuṣṭha, and tvac prevents swelling caused by phlegm. (73)

One should grind *kālā*, *godhāpadī*, *hiṃsrā*, *suṣavī*, *tālapatrikā*, and *śītakamūla*, and apply it as an ointment to his swelling. Likewise, one may use the bark of *kuṣṭha* and *chatrāka*, the root of *yātu*, and *trikaṇṭaka*.
Having ground *bhadradāru* and *sugandhā*, one should apply it as a paste with warm water to treat swelling (75).
Likewise, dried radishes, *bhadramusta*, and *sārivā*,
ground with cow's urine, form a plaster that wards off edema (76).
An ointment of Palāśa ash mixed with cow’s urine, applied to a single part of the body, or its use as a wash, is prescribed for swelling caused by Kapha; likewise,
water boiled with the five roots (pañcamūla) or cow’s urine alone may be used.
A decoction of the leaves of nimba, aṅkoṭha, uru, pūga, tarkārī, kuṭaja, naktamāla, and bamboo is used for immersion baths.
[Also used are] triphalā, citraka, the two types of vakra, the two types of haridrā, and kuṭheraka.
Śyāmā, ākhuparṇī, kaṭukā, kākamācī, suvarcalā, vārtākī, nicula, nimba, viḍaṅga, viśvabheṣaja (ginger), rāsnā, punarnavā, mūrvā, kuṣṭha, vyāghranakha, and vṛṣa. (80)

A paste made from the roots of *śigru* and *arka*, gathered as they are available and ground with cow’s urine, should be applied as an ointment; a decoction of these same ingredients should be used for sprinkling.
An oil cooked with these very same liquids serves as an unguent that destroys swelling.

The roots of *paṭola*, *triphalā*, *viḍaṅga*, and *rajanī*—these six should each be one *karṣa*; likewise, the fruit of *rocanī* should be double that amount (two *karṣas*). *Nīlikā* should be given in a threefold quantity, and *trivṛt* in a fourfold quantity.
One should drink this powder mixed with cow’s urine in the proper dose. Having been purged at the appropriate time, one should eat meat broth from wild animals.
[The ingredients are: Triphalā, Sarala, Devadāru, the two types of Rajanī, Rohiṇī, and Vacā. (84–85)
One should cook the powders of pippalī, pippalīmūla, nāgara, ativiṣā, musta, the two types of kṣāra, viḍaṅga, pāṭhā, agaru, citraka,
and iron filings with cow’s urine.
Having taken a cluster of grapes and made pills the size of jujube fruits, one should then drink one or two of them with warm water;
thus, one afflicted by swelling is freed from edema born of phlegm. 87–88.

For this [decoction] brings about the pacification of disorders of the *grahaṇī*, anemia caused by *kapha*, hemorrhoids characterized by *kapha*, abdominal enlargement, and urinary disorders (*prameha*).
(81) [The decoction of] the five roots (*pañcamūla*), *varuṇaka*, *sarala*, and *devadāru*...
Hastikarṇapalāśa and the fruits of Nicula;
Palāśa, Kākalā, Kālā, Guḍūcī, Devapuṣpaka, Ahiṃsrā, Śreyasī, Hiṃsrā, Kṛṣṇagandhā, and Punarnavā. (90–91)
Kāyasthā, vayaḥsthā, coraka, jaṭilā, jaṭā, alambuṣa, sorupūga, prapunnāḍa, along with nāgara; śigru, godhāpadī, bhārgī, tarkārī, and dried radish (śuṣkamūlaka). 92.

Oil prepared with these [ingredients] according to their availability, when used for three types of massage (abhyañjana), destroys severe swelling in a person characterized by a predominance of vāta and kapha. [The ingredients are:
both types of haridrā, mañjiṣṭhā, yaṣṭīmadhuka, and candana. 93–94.
Long pepper, bālaka, pītadru, and likewise padmaka;
māṃsī, uśīra, tagara, melā, agaru, and kuṭannaṭa (95); śrīveṣṭaka, sarjarasa, mūrvā, kuṣṭha, and priyaṅgu.

Oil should be cooked with these [ingredients]; its application as an unguent destroys swellings (śotha). This treatment has been described for [skin diseases] born of the humors (doṣaja); for those of exogenous origin (āgantuja), the treatment is like that for erysipelas (visarpa). Loss of digestive fire, fever, thirst, emaciation, anorexia, drowsiness, and vertigo [are the symptoms]. 96–97.
Dyspnea, ulcers, and diarrhea are the complications to be treated with their respective remedies. 98.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa. This concludes the seventeenth chapter, on the treatment of swelling, within the Khilas. 17.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter on the treatment of colic (śūla).
Hereafter, we shall explain the medical treatment for colic.
Thus said the venerable Kaśyapa.
Due to agitation, fear, excessive study,
or the fault of drinking too much water at the time of hunger;
due to the suppression of natural urges, riding in vehicles, undigested food, or the consumption of fallen, wet, or dry grains.
The provoked Vāyu, entering the region of the abdomen with piercing pains, pricking sensations, tremors, and distension,
causes colic (śūla) when accompanied by Pitta or Kapha.
Or, being impelled by both [wind and bile], one experiences pain;

when a hungry person suffers from wind, it takes a fierce form with terrible onsets that cause labored breathing. One should recognize this as *pitta-śūla* (bilious colic), which occurs while food is being digested in one afflicted by sweat, burning sensations, and thirst. 4–5.

One should recognize the fourth type of colic as arising from the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta), characterized by mild pain, a sense of fullness immediately after eating due to an excess of phlegm (kapha), and causing stiffness and nausea.
Unbearable by all its symptoms and curable only with great difficulty,
this wind is said to be powerful and of fierce velocity; when enraged, it destroys the body in an instant.
Therefore, at the very beginning, the physician should quickly cause the patient afflicted by vāta-śūla to undergo sudation after anointing the limbs with oil;
this may be done using vāta-alleviating hot immersions, poultices, warm bolus-sudations, or warm milk-porridges.

One suffering from Vata-type colic should habitually consume the juices of wild animals such as the ena deer, as well as those of domestic birds such as the common quail, seasoned with rock salt, and characterized by being unctuous, hot, and sour.
Or one suffering from colic should drink warm milk prepared with wind-alleviating herbs,
or oil, fermented gruel (śukta), whey, or sauvīraka, along with sauvarcala salt.
Having finely ground black long pepper, ginger, rock salt, *tumburu*, asafoetida, alkali, barley-alkali, *viḍa* salt, and *śaṭī*, one should add [the powder of] *pravarā*.
In cases of Vata-type colic, one should drink lukewarm Peya with water;
a patient suffering from Pitta-type colic should drink cold milk and then vomit it, or drink as desired water mixed with sugar.
Or one should touch the person afflicted by colic with pearl necklaces as white as conch shells, kunda flowers, or the moon, or with lotuses;
or with vessels made of silver, bell-metal, crystal, or gold, cooled by the moon and sprinkled with water. 12
The spot where the pain touches should be repeatedly fanned with plantain leaves;
or one should prepare a soft bed strewn with lotus petals and sprinkled with sandalwood water.
In the cold season, one should enjoy an unblemished bed provided with pillows within a warm chamber;
these beds should have lotus petals shimmering inside,
and the foods consumed should be heart-pleasing, cooling, sweet, and laxative.
Properly prepared gruels or cooling decoctions,

mixed with honey, pleasant to the taste, and combined with powdered sugar, should be administered for the eradication of pitta-type colic; this applies when there is undigested matter (āma), excessive morbid humors (utkleśa), or when food has been improperly digested (vidagdha).

For the sake of complete purification, one should induce vomiting at will with warm rock salt water in cases of phlegm-induced colic; once vomited, the patient should be lightened by fasting until well-exhausted.
One should have him drink a digestive decoction of the *pippalyādi* group mixed with alkali and asafoetida, warmed;
or one should feed him gruel prepared with those same ingredients.
One should gradually consume mixed food, or employ powders, ghee, boluses, alkali enemas, pastes, and decoctions, each according to its specific part and its prescribed method. 17
This proven remedy, which destroys colic, flatulence, abdominal distension, tumors, and diseases, was proclaimed by the seers through the power of meditation and yoga.
[It consists of] asafoetida, pāṭhā, the three pungents (tri-kaṭu), alkali, rock salt, and citraka.
One should have *hapuṣā*, *abhayā*, *cavya*, *ajājī*, *dhānya*, and *puṣkara*;
as well as *amlavetasa*, *vṛkṣāmla*, *yavānī*, *dāḍima*, *śaṭī*, and *sauvarcala* made into a fine powder. (19–20)
Indeed, this powder, when drunk with warm water, curd-whey, buttermilk, or *tutāsavas*, destroys the pain of flatulence, cardiac distress, bladder colic, and abdominal tumors (gulma);
it also overcomes splenic enlargement, hemorrhoids, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, cough, asthma, and urinary retention. 21.
Combined with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, it likewise destroys urinary retention (22).
[One should take] *amlavetasa*, *vṛkṣāmla*, *yavānī*, alkali, and *citraka*;
as well as asafoetida, *cavya*, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), *kaśaṭī*, *jīvantī*, and the three aromatics (*trikaṭu*) (23).
The wise person should prepare fine powders of equal parts of pippalī, pippalīmūla, badara, śirivārikā, nāgadantī, bilva, and the five salts (lavaṇapañcaka). 24.
Then, one should prepare *vaṭaka* boluses with the juice of *mātuluṅga*.

These highly efficacious boluses should be drunk with lukewarm water, wine, or sour liquids for the treatment of abdominal tumors (*gulma*), upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), and colic (*śūla*), as well as for dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*). 25–26.
In cases of heart diseases, prolapse of the rectum, and pain in the penis and bladder,
one should drink a mixture of salted earth (viḍa), pomegranate, asafoetida, rock salt, and black pepper,
combined with the juice of citron (mātuluṅga); this removes colic and flatulence.
These, combined with trikaṭu, pṛthvīkā, cavya, citraka, and rock salt (saindhava),
or with cumin and long pepper root, constitute an excellent remedy; likewise, sochal salt, vacā, asafoetida, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), and harītakī [are beneficial].
Combined with *sureśaya* (mustard) and barley, it destroys the power of the *śūla* (piercing pain) in an instant;
likewise, one *palika* measures of parched grain (*saktu*), rock salt (*saindhava*), and *citraka*, mixed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), [achieve the same].
Having placed *vacā* together with these in a single vessel, the physician should roast them in a frying pan (*kaṭāha*).
Then, having removed that ignited [substance], one should drink that alkaline liquid (kṣāra) in the proper dose,
combined with rice-water, to alleviate the pain of colic and abdominal tumors;
or one should drink castor oil combined with a decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla) and barley.
Oil mixed with a decoction of grapes is likewise used for colic caused by vāyu;
it is also used with sugar for pitta-type colic, pitta-type gulma, and splenic disorders (plīha).
[This oil is prepared] with pomegranate, vyoṣa, hapuṣā, pṛthvīkā, kṣāra, and citraka.
One should cook ghee with equal parts of ajājī, pippalīmūla, cavya, dīpyaka, and saindhava salt, along with milk, over a gentle fire;
when combined with a soup of kola and mūlaka, it destroys vātagulma.

This ghee, which is like nectar, destroys colic, constipation, dyspnea, cough, irregular fever, cardiac oppression, as well as anorexia, disorders of the grahaṇī, abdominal pain, anemia, and defects of the female reproductive tract. (36)
With bilva, kuṣṭha, yavakṣāra, vacā, citraka, and saindhava (37);
with enīyaka, viḍa, vyoṣa, tintiḍīka, and amlavetasa;
and likewise with hiṅgu, sauvarcala, ajājī, dāḍima, and indrayava (38).
Ghee prepared with punarnavā, kāravī, and haṃsapadī, along with four times as much curd, combined with vinegar and kāñjika, and with the decoction of the two pañcamūlas, kola, and kulattha; 39.
This ghee cures colic, abdominal tumors, trembling from wind (vāta), knots, heart-pain, and obstructions caused by Vāta; it also removes the twisting and whirling of Vātakuṇḍalikā,
prepared with sauvarcala salt, yavakṣāra, vacā, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), and citraka.
Ghee prepared with *harītakī* and *viḍaṅga*, milk, and combined with *bhadrarohiṇī*— this ten-ingredient (*daśāṅga*) ghee cures colic and destroys splenic disorders,
abdominal tumors, worms, dyspnea, cough, and hiccups. (42)
One should administer *phalavatī* combined with *śatapuṣpā*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *pippalī*, the fruit of *pippalī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and two types of mustard seeds;
this quickly dispels flatulence, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), and colic pain.
Having combined warm water with oil, along with urine, honey, sour gruel, and fermented rice-water, the wise physician should add these powders into that mixture:
*śatāhvā*, *pippalī*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, and *devadāru*. (45)

One should administer this enema, which destroys colic, distension, and constipation, using the prescribed measure for an *āsthāpana* enema, to a person who has been lubricated and fomented with *pūtīka*, *hareṇu*, *bilva*, and *madana*. (46–47)
When urine is obstructed by wind (vāyu), when it is suppressed, or when there is abdominal distension and the feces have moved into a wrong channel, this powder enema (cūrṇabasti) is beneficial.
One should boil eight palas of *gandhapalāśaka* in one droṇa of water.
Then, one should administer a decoction enema (nirūha) combined with kaṣāya, vacā, pippalī, phala, and saindhava,
along with honey, oil, and one kuḍava of śatāhvā, for those suffering from flatulence, pain in the flanks, the heart, or the bladder.

One should boil kulattha, yava, kola, and the two types of pañcamūla in one droṇa of water; this decoction, which generates strength, complexion, and digestive fire, and removes pain in the hips and abdominal tumors, should then be combined with oil. 51.
A decoction (kaṣāya) prepared with pippalī, kuṣṭha, vacā, indrayava, sarṣapa, hareṇukā,
saindhava, and tagara, along with ghee, should be used as a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) for the pacification of udāvarta, kuṣṭha, and gulma. (52–53)
And the wise man should immediately administer this food cooked in oil with medicinal pastes, which increases strength, complexion, and digestive fire:
pippalī, bilva, madhuka, śatāhvā, phala, and citraka. (54)

Combined with equal parts of devadāru, vacā, kuṣṭha, and the one called puṣkara, along with twice as much milk, this is beneficial for those suffering from upward-moving wind (udāvarta), as well as colic, abdominal distension, prolapse of the rectum,
and the suppression of feces, urine, and flatus.
It destroys pain in the hips, thighs, and back, as well as hemorrhoids, suppressed flatus, anal pain, frequent straining, and dysentery.
[The formulation consists of] kuṣṭha, viḍaṅga, ativiṣā, dāru, dārvī, and hareṇukā.
Cardamom, ajamodā, hrībera, ginger, puṣkaramūla, śaṭī, 58 sthirā, kaṭphala, rāsnā, long pepper, cavya, citraka,
śyāmā, śatāhvā, yaṣṭimadhu, rock salt, madana, and vacā. 59
One should cook *gandharvataila* or [other] oil with half an *akṣa* each of *nicula*, *nīlinī*, *dantī*, and *bilva*; this is an *anuvāsana* enema that destroys abdominal tumors,
*āḍhyavāta*, colic, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), and scrotal enlargement.
It removes dysuria accompanied by earache and abdominal distension (ānāha).
A wise person [should take] fifty palas of the ten roots (daśamūla), one āḍhaka each of madana fruits, and [the same quantity] of pūtīka, dantī, surabhī, and śvadaṃṣṭrā. 61–62.
One should take twenty palas of each of these—
barley (*yava*), jujube (*kola*), and horse gram (*kulattha*)— and boil them in one *prastha* of water until reduced to one-fourth; into that decoction, one should cook one *āḍhaka* of oil.
Half an āḍhaka of cow urine, along with barley, long pepper, rock salt, and the triad [of drugs], as well as barley,
śatāhvā, and valīnakas— this formulation, when combined with kuṣṭha and vacā, should be used as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) for the face.

One should administer *phalataila* (oil from the fruits of *Embelia ribes*) in cases of stiffness of the thighs, and pain in the waist, back, anus, and groins, as well as in cases of splenic enlargement (*plīha*), upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), and abdominal tumors (*gulma*). Thus, the treatment for colic (*śūla*) has been proclaimed by you in detail.
"By means of various proven applications, out of a desire for the welfare of living beings.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
This concludes the eighteenth chapter, on the treatment of colic (*śūla*), within the *Khila* sections.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter, the Subsequent Chapter on the Treatment of the Eight Fevers.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the subsequent chapter on the treatment of the eight fevers.
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa.

The etiology of those arising from one, two, or three [factors] has been previously explained; I shall now fully describe the treatment of *sannipāta* according to its causes. [The causes are: unwholesome... [text truncated]
One should boil the roots of bilva combined with jaggery, agnimantha, śyonāka, kāśmarya, and likewise pāṭalī,
and drink the decoction together with alkali and rock salt.
Samaṅgā, madhuka, musta, and bhadradāru, along with sugar and guḍūcī,
should be administered as a drink for vāta-fever;
likewise, vidārigandhā, eraṇḍa, the two types of bṛhatī, and pṛśniparṇikā [should be used].
Combined with *bhadradāru*, it is considered a remedy for fever caused by wind (*vāta-jvara*).
A decoction of *vidārigandhā*, *kalaśī*, *gandharvahastaka*,
*madhuka*, and *bhadradāru*, when mixed with sugar, [is likewise effective].
A decoction of castor oil plant (eraṇḍa),
varuṇa, the two types of bṛhatī, and madhuka,
combined with a paste of rāsnā and saturated with the juice of mātuluṅga, should be administered to alleviate fever caused by vāta.
A lukewarm or cold decoction of the two groups of five roots (dvipañcamūla),
combined with a paste of rāsnā, is considered beneficial for fever caused by vāta;
it may also be prepared with rāsnā, sarala, devadāru, and yaṣṭīmadhu.
One should drink a decoction of the vidārigandhādi group with rock salt (saindhava),
or at mealtime, one should eat food accompanied by the broth of the *pañcamuṣṭika* group, seasoned with sour and salty ingredients, as well as with the meat-broth of wild animals (*jāṅgala*).
For internal drinking, one should drink water boiled with the roots of *bilva*,
the two *pañcamūlas*, *varcī*, *vama*, *eṣīkā*, *punarnavā*, *sahasravīryā*, *nādeyī*, *śatavīryā*, and *śatāvarī*.
Viśvadevā, Śukanasā, Sahadevā, Sanākulī, Rāsnā, Jagandhā, Pūtīka, Devāhva, Devatāḍaka,
the two types of Bālā, Haṃsapādī, Kāthotthī, and Upalaṅkaśā.
Black aloe-wood, tiger-claw, centifolia jasmine,
bdellium, kāyasthā, vayasthā, coraka, jaṭilā, jaṭā, apetarākṣasī, yakṣā, guhāhvā, and uṣṭralomikā.
Having collected hareṇukā, haimavatī, kaiṭarya, suvahā, vacā,
vṛścikālī, bhārgī, and śigru in the form of a paste,
one should cook oil that destroys vāta-fever.
One should prepare a meat broth of wild animals processed with aged ghee,
along with one *kuḍava* each of the ten roots (*daśamūla*), horse gram (*kulattha*),
barley, *kulīraśṛṅgī*, *rāsnā*, *śaṭī*, and the root of *puṣkara*.
A well-prepared decoction of *durālabhā* and *bhārgī* quickly pacifies his vitiated *vāyu* and fever;
I shall now explain the treatment for that which arises from *vāta* and *śleṣman*.
One should first drink the warm decoction of *bṛhatī*, *puṣkara*, *dāru*, *pippalī*, *nāgara*, and *śaṭī* to bring about the digestion of the morbid humors (*doṣa*).
[Then one should take] the two *pañcamūlas*, *bhārgī*, *karkaṭaśṛṅgī*, and *durālabhā*.
One should drink nagara, pippalī, and dāru combined with saindhava salt;
or, a decoction of these six ingredients— paṭola, dhānyaka, mustā, mūrvā, pāṭhā, and nidigdhikā— mixed with honey, should be drunk.
Triphalā, the Jīvanīya drugs, Pippalīmūla, and sugar, prepared together with Grahaghna, destroy fever caused by Vāta and Kapha;
likewise, Nāgara, Daśamūla, Kaṭvaṅga, and the two types of Dāruka [are effective].
Pippalī, triphalā, bhārgī, karkaṭaśṛṅgī, and durālabhā—
this should be drunk lukewarm with rock salt for fever caused by vāta and śleṣman.
The physician [should administer] one akṣa of the paste of kaṭurohiṇī, which is bitter.
One should quickly drink asafoetida mixed with rock salt along with lukewarm water;
this, when drunk, brings relief in fevers caused by kapha and vāta.
A decoction of the great five roots (mahat-pañcamūla) is likewise beneficial in fever arising from kapha and vāta.
One should drink warm water boiled with nagara, amaradāru,
and bāla; or one should feed the patient with the soup of mūlaka or the broth of wild animals (jāṅgala), prepared with pungent and hot substances and mixed with a small amount of unctuous material.
With lac, priyaṅgu, mañjiṣṭhā, yaṣṭīmadhu, uśīra, and bālaka; with sandalwood, agaru, bāhlīka, śrīveṣṭaka, and kuṭannaṭa; and with mūrvā, śatāhvā, sarala, sāla-resin, and roca.

A physician should cook one āḍhaka of oil with half-pala measures of each [drug] in one droṇa of milk; once it has been properly prepared, he should remove it from the fire and store it in a well-protected place.
This is the Lākṣādi-taila (the oil beginning with lac).
Long pepper, ativiṣā, mustā, śālaparṇī, dūrvā, candana, yava, uśīra, sārivā, nidigdhikā,
rohiṇī, āmalaka, and bilva— these are well-prepared with trāyamāṇā.
Ghee cures headache, cough, chronic fever, and wasting;
it acts as an emetic for diseases of phlegm and a purgative for those of bile.
It should be employed as a cleansing agent (śodhana) and a pacifier (śamana); however, in one who is emaciated, only pacification (śamana) should be performed.

A gruel made with *maṇḍa* and other ingredients is prescribed for fever caused by *sāma* (undigested matter), as well as for that born of *vāta*. One should perform Pitta-alleviating treatments for fevers arising from poisonous herbs.
Hereafter, I shall explain the medical treatment for *sannipāta* fever.

That which possesses all symptoms is incurable; that with few symptoms may be cured with great difficulty. It does not succeed at all in one who is weak and whose digestive fire is extinguished—how much less so in children, whose tissues, strength, and vitality are depleted?
Nevertheless, the best of physicians should apply effort out of compassion;
among the combined humors (doṣas), he should first pacify whichever humor is most powerful, and thereafter address the remaining humor.
When these doshas are of nearly equal strength,
the wise physician should first pacify phlegm (kapha), for it acts as their underlying associate due to its heaviness, its tendency toward difficult digestion, and its localization in the upper body.
Therefore, whatever has been prescribed for fever caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha,
that specific treatment should be applied in that particular state;
[this consists of] pippalyādi, vacā, dāru, vayasthā, and sarala.

When there is an excess of phlegm (kapha) with undigested matter (āmadoṣa), a drink prepared with asafoetida (hiṅgu), alkali (kṣāra), and rock salt (saindhava) should be given; by this, the morbid humors (doṣas) are quickly digested and constipation (vibandha) is relieved.
[Likewise, a decoction of] ginger (nāgara), kaṭphala, coriander (dhānya), musta, parpaṭaka, and vacā [is effective].
Devadāru, abhayā, bhārgī, and bhūtīka as the tenth—
this decoction, boiled with rock salt (saindhava) and asafoetida (hiṅgu), should be drunk when vāta and kapha are predominant;
it is highly recommended for those suffering from diseases of the regions above the clavicle and for those afflicted by fever.
Śaṭī, pauṣkara, pippalī, bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārikā,
śuṇṭhī, karkaṭakī, bhārgī, durālambhā, and yavānikā— this formulation beginning with śaṭī destroys colic, abdominal distension, and constipation, and subdues kapha and vāta.
One should drink viḍaṅga, ativiṣā, bhārgī, pauṣkara, citraka, śaṭī,
śārṅgeṣṭā, pippalī, and śuṇṭhī when vāta and kapha are predominant; or one may drink durālabhā, vacā, dāru, pippalīmūla, and nāgara.
One should drink a decoction of *puṣkara* (costus) and *śaṭī*, combined with salt, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), and alkali (*kṣāra*),
in cases of *sannipāta* fever, constipation, and fevers where *vāta* and *śleṣman* predominate.
Jīvaka, Ṛṣabhaka, Śṛṅgī, Puṣkaramūla,
and Śaṭī are recommended in cases of Sannipāta, as well as for coughs caused by Vāta and Kapha; likewise, the two types of Bṛhatī, Puṣkara, Dāru, Pippalī, Nāgara, and Śaṭī are beneficial.
One should drink their warm decoction at the outset to digest the morbid humors (doṣas):
durālabhā, vacā, dāru, pippalī, bhadrarohiṇī, mahauṣadha, karkaṭakī, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā.
A decoction containing salt should be drunk to alleviate fever caused by the simultaneous derangement of the three humors (sannipātajvara).
A decoction of devadāru, vacā, musta, kairāta, kaṭurohiṇī, guḍūcī, and nāgara also alleviates sannipātajvara.
Triphalā, rohiṇī, nimba, paṭola, the three pungents (kaṭukatraya),
pāṭhā, guḍūcī, vetāgra, saptaparṇa, and vatsaka are recommended for chest congestion, throat diseases, and mouth diseases.
Kirātatiktaka, mustā, and vacā boiled together in one [mixture] destroy excess kapha when drunk and kindle the digestive fire; likewise,
water boiled with paṭola, mustā, madhuka, and rohiṇī [is beneficial].
One should administer this formulation, combined with the three fruits (triphalā) and deodar (suradāru), stirred with honey, in cases of sannipāta where kapha is predominant;
[and also] with āragvadha, vacā, nimba, paṭola, uśīra, and vatsaka.
This decoction of śārṅgeṣṭā, ativiṣā, mūrvā, triphalā along with durālabhā,
bhadramustā, balā, pāṭhā, madhuka,
and bhadrarohiṇī quickly pacifies fever born of the three doṣas.
Nāgara, daśamūla, kaṭvaṅga, and dārvī remove stiffness, swelling, flatulence, and heaviness;
one should have the child consume [this] somehow or other.
That [honey] brings about the healing of fresh, recently inflicted wounds;
for poison, having encountered honey, displays its own strength,
whereas honey quickly pacifies that [poison] and heals the wound.
Therefore, by its very nature, honey consumed by men along with something hot leads to the end of life due to the conflict with the three *doṣas*,
because of their equality [in potency] and the combination with heat, just as in the case of honey and clarified butter.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Specific Qualities of Honey," among the Khilas.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter, "On the Specific Qualities of Milk."
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the specific qualities of milk.
Thus said the venerable Kaśyapa:
[the milk] of the cow, the buffalo, the goat, the woman, the camel, the ewe, and the female elephant.
The waters have already been described as "the swift-moving" (turaṅgya);
furthermore, understand from me these eight types of milk which, due to their specific qualities,
sustain the life of living beings by the will of Prajāpati in his city.
O Jīvaka, the birth of trees, of forest plants, of trees, and of the class of vanaspati, as well as of creepers, herbs, and shrubs, is said to possess the qualities of the five elements.
Of various kinds of grasses and grains, as well as of embodied beings— this and other such categories are declared to be the essence of the earth;
while that of Soma consists of wind, fire, water, and intellect, [which are] the essence of Prajāpati.
Beyond this, the milk and other products of cows and such animals arise from the quality of their food;
just as in ancient times, when the Ocean of Milk was churned, the divine nectar (amṛta) emerged— the essence of all medicinal herbs— by which the immortal gods became deities.

Likewise, the essence of all medicinal herbs arises as milk within the wombs of cows and other such creatures; for that reason, it is like nectar and is especially the means of sustenance for womb-born beings.
Milk is indeed wholesome for children; milk is said to be life-giving.
Milk promotes nourishment, causes growth, and increases strength.
Milk bestows *ojas* (vital essence) upon men; milk brings about the qualities of vitality.
This milk causes conception even for barren women; it is beneficial for those who are emaciated, wasted, suffering from edema, afflicted with pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman),
constantly engaged in physical exercise and fatigue, and for those whose bodies are perpetually devoted to women.

Milk is declared to be supreme for those whose semen is depleted, as well as in cases of severe miscarriage, diseases of blood and bile (raktapitta), hemorrhoids, intoxication-induced wasting, fever, and the emaciation of the fetus due to wind disorders (vāta).
The general qualities of milk have already been described here;
now I shall speak of the specific characteristics of cows and other animals,
as well as grasses, shrubs, and medicinal herbs, for their very essence is indeed milk.
They eat food that is mostly sweet and especially salty;
because of the excellence of those essential qualities, the milk of cows is praised,
for the sweet taste is proclaimed to be the best among all tastes.

The milk of cows is considered to be always sweet and nourishing; because it contains the foremost of medicinal substances, that milk causes purgation. For this reason, the milk of cows is said to be a rejuvenative elixir (*rasāyana*).
This is indeed proclaimed as the specific quality of cow's milk: even female buffalo, along with worms, insects, moths, snakes, and those dwelling in grass,
do not consume grass that is deficient in it.
They plunge into water, especially into the depths;
for this reason, their milk is astringent and cooling.
Because it is cold, it is difficult to digest, yet it is unctuous, heavy, and a destroyer of burning sensations.

The milk of buffaloes is considered to have fewer qualities than that of cows; the milk of goats, however, is light, removes the bodily humors (doṣas), and possesses strength, because of the smallness of their bodies, because it overcomes pungent and bitter tastes, and because of its own small quantity and potency.
Because it is produced in small quantity, that milk is thick; due to its thickness, it is nourishing, cooling, constipating, sweet, strengthening, and wind-harmonizing,
owing to its being kept in a large vessel and its consumption consisting mostly of dark and sweet grains.
Due to its abundance and density, camel milk is strengthening and nourishing;
it is specifically described as heavy, aphrodisiac, and sweet,
being especially favored by camels because they consume little food and prefer it to be unsalted.
In the first month of the past rainy season, upon the arrival of the month of Proṣṭhapada,
auspicious and pure celestial water named Haṃsodaka fell from the sky;
it was purified by the splendor of the sun and rendered free of poison by Agastya.
Thus, it is unctuous, aphrodisiac, and strengthening; it is heavy during the late autumn (hemanta),
and when water falls during the winter (śiśira), it provokes phlegm and wind.
In spring, when it rains water that is astringent, sweet, and parching,
that which falls there upon the earth—
When that vessel is neglected due to a defect in the vessel itself,
the water truly assumes various tastes upon reaching the ground;
all water that falls immediately [there] becomes unwholesome and out of season.
It is slightly alkaline, increases phlegm and wind, is beneficial for pitta, and produces excessive coldness.
Dew-water is light, dry, and removes blood and bile;
thus, water born of the atmosphere is said to be of four kinds in its true nature.
[It is] beneficial to the heart...
Rivers that flow eastward from alkaline sources aggravate phlegm;
those flowing westward have light waters that increase bile and destroy phlegm, though they are windy.
Of these two, sea salt is alkaline; water that ripens as salt is sweet, heavy, and causes obstruction (ābhiṣyandi).
Water from saline soil (audbhida) is cold, pacifies pitta, and has a sweet post-digestive effect (svādupāki).
Water from a pond is considered heavy, foul, and turbid due to the impurities of decaying vegetation;
water from a lake is sweet, astringent, pleasant-tasting, pure, and clear;
and water from a well is likewise [pure].

Thus, water derived from the earth is said to be of eight kinds; it is light, highly palatable, unctuous, cool, and endowed with all tastes. It quenches thirst, gladdens the mind, subdues phlegm, and destroys worms.
It destroys demons, promotes longevity, is aphrodisiac, and cures fainting;
it is teeming with minute creatures,
thick, turbid, slimy, and impure.
One should avoid [water] that is tainted by the flavors of villages or fields, corrupted by poisonous roots, infested with birds, worms, or moss, excessively hot, or slimy;
and one should also avoid it when women are pregnant.
Water is especially recommended for wet-nurses, whether healthy or ill, because it possesses a great abundance of the qualities previously mentioned;
it is said to be sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka) and, due to its coldness, it subdues pitta.
Whether it be cold or even hot,
if [the medicine] is drunk before a meal, it causes emaciation in the child;
if drunk during a meal, it brings about a moderate state.
When drunk over food, it bestows corpulence;
a decoction with warm water is digestive and is used in cases of fatigue, types of diarrhea, thirsts, fainting, and excessive parching of the throat.
Water that has been boiled and then cooled by adding cold water should be prescribed for children as it destroys all the *doṣas*; however,
hot water should be avoided for an infant.

Having abandoned blood-bile (raktapitta) disorders, one should generally drink hot [liquids] in diseases consisting of wind (vāta) and phlegm (kapha); whether it be a child, a wet-nurse, or a pregnant woman,
in certain specific diseases, warm-cooled [water] is highly beneficial.
Then, in autumn, when the atmosphere is praised [for its clarity] yet scorched by the rays of the sun,
one may drink from a lake, a river, or a pond.

In the winter and the cool season, water from wells, springs, or natural flows is indeed recommended; in the summer and at the onset of spring, it is likewise praised. During the rains, well-water is recommended for the sake of health, as is water that has been heated and then cooled.
Thus spoke the Blessed Kaśyapa.
This concludes the twenty-third chapter, concerning the specific qualities of water, within the Khilas.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter, concerning the specific qualities of meat.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the specific qualities of meat.
Thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa:
Meat is aphrodisiac, strengthening, and increases vitality.
Meat provides nourishment for the elderly and the emaciated, increasing their flesh;
for those suffering from consumption and those with wasted bodies, meat alone is the ultimate recourse.
There is nothing else equal to meat for increasing health and virility.
The meat of men whose semen has been depleted increases the reproductive fluid;
likewise, it causes conception even for barren women and young boys,
and ultimately provides nourishment.
It is the supreme pacifier of wind for pregnant women;
at the time of delivery, it is meat [soup] for women; and during the period of gestation, it is the most excellent, flavorful medicine for infants.
Meat broth is beneficial for men who are fond of women, as well as those who constantly engage in physical exercise,
those who are emaciated, those suffering from consumption (yakṣman), those wasted by fever,
and those whose vital strength has been struck down by wind (vāta).
Well-prepared meat broth, seasoned with asafoetida, cumin, and asafoetida (hing),
and cooked in fat with milk, is especially recommended for those with a predominance of Vāta;
when Vāta and Pitta are predominant, it should be sweetened with sugar by men.
A fatty meat broth should be drunk by those afflicted with blood-related diseases; likewise,
a meat broth prepared from emaciated animals, whether sweet or even salty,
is recommended for children, those with wasted bodies, and during pregnancy.
This meat, prepared with the essence of its own juices, is beneficial for those who desire nourishment for the body;
it is well-cooked, seasoned with salt, pungent and appetizing, stimulates the digestive fire, and is a source of vital rasa. 12–13.
Vesavāra seasoned with sugar or salt is appetizing; likewise, meat that is ground, powdered, cooked, or roasted on a spit and heated over coals is beneficial in diseases of phlegm (kapha).
Therefore, Jīvaka, meat that is slightly sour and salty is beneficial;
it may be prepared by being ground into a paste or cut into pieces and cooked in a sealed earthen pot (puṭapāka).
One should serve meat prepared with asafoetida, rock salt, biḍa salt, black pepper, sour substances, cumin, sprouts, coriander, ginger, and fresh ginger, along with palāśa and bhūstṛṇa grass. 16–17.
Now, meat broth prepared with ghee and milk is desired;
through the specific process of cooking the broth, it becomes strengthening.
That was the elixir (rasāyana).
Hereafter, O Vṛddhajīvaka, I shall describe the specific methods for preparing the juices of meats and their particular qualities; listen to that.

The meat of cows increases phlegm and bile, is heavy, causes a burning sensation, and is nourishing; the meat of the rhinoceros is similar to that. The meat of the nyanku is prescribed for vata disorders, subdues phlegm and bile, and is light.
One should know that the meat of the elephant is salty, nourishing, pungent and bitter;
it is hot in potency and increases phlegm and bile.
The meat of the *gokarṇa* is similar to that, as is the meat of the *gavaya* and the *ruru*.
The meat of goats and sheep is sweet in taste and digestion, heavy, hot, and likewise subdues wind and bile.
The meat of the boar is aphrodisiac, sweet, and digests slowly. (23)

Know that the meat of the buffalo possesses those same qualities; the meat of the pig is heavier than that. Likewise, the meat of the donkey, the horse, and the spotted deer destroys phlegm, increases wind, is dry, pungent and bitter in taste, and light.
The Śvadaṃṣṭra, Vṛṣadaṃṣṭra, Ṛṣya, and Śarabha are wind-dispelling, hot in potency, and pungent in taste. The Golāṅgūla and Vānara are similar to them, though they are predominantly sweet.
Wolves, bears, crows, jackals, lions, tigers, and hyenas—
these eaters of raw flesh increase virility, are hot in potency, and aggravate pitta;
they are astringent and bitter in taste, destroy vāta, and are pungent in their post-digestive transformation (vipāka).
The nakula, mouse, porcupine, babhru, and śalyaka, as well as the iguana (godhā) and its kind, are astringent-sweet, cooling, aphrodisiac, and belong to that same group.
So too are those such as the hare and the kuraṅga deer, as well as the sṛmara and the camara.
They are light, hot, increase bile (pitta), and are not very nourishing.
(30) The meat of the peacock (*bārhiṇa*) is sweet, hot, an antidote to poison, heavy, and nourishing;
that of the wild cock (*kaukkuṭaja*) is similar, and that of the domestic cock (*grāmyakaukkuṭa*) is equal to it. (31)
Scattered-feeders (viṣkira) such as the krauñca and the vartīka are considered equal to the peacock;
therefore, the vartīra is light, while the vartīka is lighter, and the latter is the lightest of all.
The partridge (tittiri), however, is pungent in its post-digestive effect, hot in potency, and conquers phlegm and wind.
The kapiñjala, cakora, and upacakra are similar to those [partridges].
The lohapṛṣṭha, raktapṛṣṭha, raktākṣa, and jīvajīvaka,
as well as others born in the Himalayas, are sweet, aphrodisiac, and nourishing.
The *guravaḥ* (heavy birds) are cooling in their post-digestive effect (*pāka*) and likewise astringent in taste. They are:
the *khañjarīṭa*, the *vapukkāra*, the *krakara*, the *dīrghapuṃsaka*, the *koyaṣṭika*, the *kapota*, the *raktapāda*, and the *vasantaka*. (35)
The bhṛṅgarāja, hārīta, kokila, śuka, and sārikā— these and other such birds are covered by downy feathers, provoke cold winds,
are sweet and astringent in taste, destroy phlegm (kapha), and have a pungent post-digestive effect (kaṭupākin).
The vulture, crow, hawk, blue jay, falcon, owl, sparrow, hare-eater, mouse, boar, and other such meat-eaters— these are known as *prasaha* birds;
they are sweet, subdue the wind (*vāta*), and have a pungent post-digestive effect (*kaṭu-pākin*).
Those that are nourishing and possess a hot potency are always beneficial for those suffering from consumption (śoṣa).
The plavas, bakas, balākās, tīṭṭibhas, kuraras, as well as the raktākṣas, mallikākṣas, and vāraṭas— [these are beneficial]. 39–40.
The Nandīmukhas, Megharāvas, those called Śaras, Jalakukkuṭas, Samudrakākas, Kuharas, Goṭubhas, Gaṇḍamālakas,
Kāraṇḍavas, Sajomūtas, and other such aquatic creatures [were there]. 41.
They are sweet in digestion, aphrodisiac, and heavy. (42) The *haṃsa* (swan), however, is exceedingly heavy, aphrodisiac, and increases phlegm and bile;
so too are the *śarāri*, the *pākahaṃsa*, and the *cakravāka*. (44)
Likewise, others are known as web-footed birds, equal to swans in their qualities;
such as the *krauñca*, the *kuliṅga*, the *draviḍa*, the *padmapuṣkarasādaka*,
the *vārdhīṇasa*, the *sārasa*, the *sāraṅga*, the *dhāma*, and the *ṛṇyalika*.
These and other such land-dwelling birds are considered heavy (guru).
They are sweet in taste and post-digestive effect (pāka), hot in potency, and possess a salty quality; they are aphrodisiac, pacify vāta, and increase kapha and pitta.
The *nalamīna*, the *jhaṣa*, the *pāṭhīna*, the *carmapīvara*,
the *celīma*, the *śakulārbha*, the *śilīndhra*, the *gargara*, the *puṣkara*, the *gokara*, the *mūca*, the *vāraḍa*, and the *śūlapāṭala*. 48.
The black fish, the white fish, the cow-fish, and likewise the rohita; the śakalī, the mahāśakalī, the campa, the kunda, and then the madgura;
the ilya, the śaṅku, the cicaraṇa, the rājīva, and likewise the śapharī. 49–50.
These and many other various species of fish are sweet in taste and digestion, they subdue Vata, and are aphrodisiac and nourishing;
they should be known as having a hot potency, being heavy, and increasing Kapha and Pitta. 51.
Others, however, have light digestive capacities and possess a slight bitter aftertaste (52).
The Rohita and Nalamīna fishes are considered light.
Likewise, the tortoise, the Duṣṭi, the crocodile, the Makara, and the Avakuśa (53).
The *timi*, the *timidghala* with ten thousand teeth,
the *iñcaka*, the *śuktika*, the *śaṅkha*, the *avalūka*, the *jalasūkara*,
the *śambūka*, the *candrika*, the *śṛṅgī*, the *karkaṭa*, and the *śakuṭīpaya*. 54.
These and other aquatic creatures are sweet in taste and post-digestive effect (pāka), heavy, hot in potency (vīrya), and increase phlegm and bile; among those from marshy lands,
the goat is the best, and among fish, the Rohita is the most excellent.
Among aquatic creatures, the pearl-oyster and the tortoise are excellent; among birds, the vāraṭa is so;
among deer, the eṇa is preeminent; among peckers, the parrot is the best. Among wild animals, the [rhinoceros] is supreme; among birds, however, the quail is the best.
Among birds that scratch for food (*viṣkira*), the partridge is the foremost; among those that seize their prey (*prasaha*), the crow is the foremost.
Blood is said to be light compared to meat, while fat and skin are heavier than meat; marrow and bone-marrow are heavier than those, and the head is traditionally held to be the heaviest of all.
For the shoulder is lighter than the head; therefore, the side is considered lighter than that.
The thigh is said to be lighter than the side, while the flesh of the foot is considered heavy.
Fat, marrow, and bone-marrow are known to be beneficial for vāta and pitta.
They are sweet in taste and digestion, and due to their unctuousness, they aggravate phlegm (śleṣman). Blood [is] a pacifier of blood; flesh increases flesh.
Young and middle-aged animals are heavy, aphrodisiac, and nourishing.
Elders are characterized by an excess of wind (vāta) and are dry; women are lighter than men.

A bird is lighter than a wild animal, while an aquatic creature is heavier than a bird. Furthermore, O Jīvaka, those with large bodies are considered heavy, whereas those with small bodies are considered light.
It should be understood that even those who eat little may be heavy [in flight] if they consume much food;
those that travel over small areas are light, while those that go to distant places are heavier than the sluggish;
those that frequent small regions are small, and those that eat little are light. (64–65)
Meat that comes from a large animal living in a mountainous region, meat from a heavy-bodied animal, meat from an animal that has eaten heavily,

meat from an animal bound by a snare, meat that is dried out, meat from an animal killed by hunger or disease, meat from an animal killed by dogs, and meat that is bloody— such meat is said not to be very nourishing. (66)
Meat killed by carnivorous beasts is unfit for consumption; dried meat does not provide great benefit. Meat killed immediately after being distressed increases the bodily tissues (*dhātus*);
however, putrid meat is heavy, lacks essence, and is neither aphrodisiac nor nourishing.

Thus, a physician who understands the specific properties of meats should always prescribe them for food in the case of children, pregnant women, those with young children, women who have had difficult births, or those who are emaciated. 69.69.105–107ab. One who knows the truth, by applying this, attains success—thus said the Blessed Kaśyapa, the elder Jīvaka. Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Specific Qualities of Meat," among the Supplements (Khilāni). Chapter 24.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter, on the suitability of regions.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the suitability of regions.
Thus said the venerable Kaśyapa.
He questioned the best of sages named Kaśyapa:
"How should those who do not know the suitability of regions for health perform medical treatment?
In the midst of which region, however, is Kurukṣetra established?"
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, the great sage Kāśirāja,
began to explain this unblemished reply:
"Kurukṣetra is at most one hundred yojanas from the Middle Country."

Those born in the Middle Country generally consume all six tastes; being heroes among those who eat and drink, they eat in that manner repeatedly. The Eastern Country, however, should be known as sweet, cool, and heavy.
First, Kumāravartanī, and likewise Kaṭīvarṣa;
then Mahārāṣṭra in Magadha, Ṛṣabhadvīpa, Pauṇḍravardhanaka, and Mṛttikāvardhamānaka.
Karvaṭa with Samātaṅga, Tāmalipta with Cīraka, Priyaṅgu, Kauśalya, and Kaliṅgapṛṣṭhapūraka—
among these, mortals suffer from splenitis as well as goiters.
Men who mostly eat rice with jaggery, those who consume fish as food,
and those whose diet is generally sweet, are characterized by an excess of wind (vāta) and phlegm (śleṣman).
For them, pungent, bitter, dry, and hot food is [beneficial].
Whatever else is phlegm-subduing, that should be employed for them;
likewise, *kañcīpadā*, *navadhvānā*, *kāśmīrā*, and *tulyā* [are used], as well as *vānasī*, *kumudārājya*, and *ciripāli*. 12.
Cīrarājya among the thieves, Pulinda among the Draviḍas, Karaghāṭa among the Śabaras, Viveha among the Maṇḍapas, Kāntāra, Varāha, and Ghaṭā among the Ābhīras; (13–14)
Relying on the southern direction, this much portion of the region situated in the borderlands has been obtained: namely,
the Kāśyapasaṃhitā and the Vṛddhajīvakīyatantra.
It rests only upon this much of the perceived portion.
